NHS trust to review 4,500 more breast cancer cases after failings

BBC News Thu, 24 Sep 2026 13:07:40 GMT

Hospital chiefs in County Durham have agreed to review up to a further 4,500 breast cancer cases after failings including delayed diagnoses and unnecessary surgeries were found.

Hundreds of patients suffered harm under County Durham and Darlington NHS Foundation Trust, according to a review of cases dating back to 2023.

The BBC previously investigated the failings and has spoken to multiple women affected, including one who said she felt "mutilated" and the trust's mistakes were "absolutely unforgivable".

Ahead of agreeing to expand the review to cases dating back to 2015, members of the trust's board offered "sincere" apologies for the failings and harm caused.

At an extraordinary meeting of the board held in Durham, board chair Alison Marshall said: "I would like to offer a sincere apology to all the women and their families who have been affected by the failings in our breast services.

"I can't imagine the impact that has had."

She said they could "not turn back the clock" but would be "open, honest and transparent" about the failings.

Chief nurse Gill Hunt told the board concerns were first raised in 2015 after a "service reconfiguration" and loss of breast surgical trainee posts.

Over the following years patients and bodies such as the Northern Cancer Alliance, Care Quality Commission and NHS England raised multiple issues, she said.

The key "themes" included treatment "not aligned to best practice", excessive surgery and delayed diagnosis, she said.

The trust's breast surgery lookback review began in April 2025 by examining cases between January 2023 and February 2025.

Hunt said 538 cases had been reviewed so far with 321 having experienced some form of harm, including one death.

About 640 patients had also contacted a special helpline asking for their cases to be reviewed, the board heard.

The review cost about £523,000 in its first year and involved nine reviewers looking at about 80 cases a month, the report said.

The board agreed to extend the review by one year at a time back to 2015, which would encompass up to 4,500 further cases and take an estimated five years to complete.

Hunt said the expanded review would "provide a proportionate and evidence-led clinical approach" in response to "emerging findings", while decisions would be "supported by clear clinical rationale and formal governance review".

Other "important learning" to come out of the review so far was about how bosses should respond to concerns raised by patients or other agencies, Hunt said.

"We are committed to doing the right thing," she said.

Chief executive Steve Russell said the trust was "incredibly conscious women and their families" had experienced "distress, uncertainty and harm".

He said no apology could undo that but the trust would "support women who have been impacted" in any way possible.

For example, some women who had undergone unnecessary mastectomies could be offered breast reconstruction surgery as they previously should have been, Russell said.

He also said the trust was currently exceeding national standards for breast cancer treatment, including for the number of women having breast conservation surgeries and being offered immediate reconstruction.

"None of that changes what has happened to women in the past but hopefully gives confidence the changes made in the service have had an impact on the outcomes," Russell said.

He said patients today could be "confident" they would be "treated appropriately" and get "good clinical outcomes".

The helpline, which is available by phone or email, would remain open with any concerned patients encouraged to contact it "irrespective" of when they were treated, he said.

Denise Howarth attended the board meeting along with other patients.

The 51-year-old from Consett, County Durham, who had an unnecessary mastectomy, said she was "pleased" the review would be extended as there could be many more cases still to be revealed.

But past patients needed to be contacted with "dignity" and "compassion", she added, to try and reduce the "shock" and "pain" of being told their cases were being reviewed because of possible failings.

She also said a public inquiry needed to be held and, as her case dated back to 2012, the trust's review should also look back further than 2015.

Rachel Gray, 41 and from Sunderland, said she contacted the helpline after hearing of women "being harmed", with the review finding she could have avoided having a mastectomy at the age of 37.

She said discovering that made her "want to crawl out of my skin".

The board's decision to review more cases would mean there would be "more answers" and women finding out what had happened to them, she said.

She also said she thought the review would find more women harmed "than what they are predicting".

Medical negligence solicitor Chloe Gibson, who is representing women affected by the breast cancer scandal, said she welcomed the board's decision but warned the process would be "very long" and last until the 2030s.

Waiting for their cases to be reviewed would cause "further anxiety and trauma" for many, she said, adding: "Justice delayed is justice denied."

She also said the review should look further back than 2015 while a full public inquiry was the "only way proper scrutiny and full accountability can be achieved".

Crashed RAF jet steered to 'avoid built-up areas' before pilots ejected

BBC News Thu, 24 Sep 2026 12:29:39 GMT

An RAF jet was steered to "avoid built-up areas" before two pilots ejected out of the aircraft, an air force commander has said.

Gp Capt Gez Currie, Station Commander, said: "The aircraft would have been aimed in a direction that the pilot believed was open field, in order to avoid built-up areas and anybody on the ground."

The Hawk T2 aircraft had been flying out of the RAF Valley station on Anglesey on Wednesday when it plummeted to the ground in nearby Pencarnisiog, narrowly avoiding homes.

The trainee and an experienced professional, who parachuted out of their plane moments before it crashed, are expected to make a full recovery after they were treated for minor injuries.

Hawk operations have been paused by the RAF as a "precautionary measure" while investigations into the crash are ongoing - the Red Arrows are included in the pause as the aerobatics display team use the T1.

The Ministry of Defence (MoD) confirmed that the squadron of Hawk jets at RAF Leeming, in Yorkshire, has also "paused" flying.

Currie said the pilots were in hospital being cared for and were with their families.

He would not give personal details about them and said the investigation was in its early stages, adding "it's far too early to even suggest what has happened in this occasion".

He said: "It was a trainee, with a highly experienced instructor on a routine sortie, across the Anglesey area."

According to the MoD, a sortie is "one mission, one complete trip".

He added that in the two-and-a-half years as station commander, and in his 30-year career as an air traffic controller, "this is the first time I've experienced this".

Eyewitness Ollie Zalot said he was initially concerned that people on the ground could have been hurt as the crash happened near buildings, while Anglesey councillor Neville Evans said he thought it had been a "very lucky escape considering how close" the crash was to a village and caravan park.

A video of the crash shared on social media on Wednesday appeared to show the two pilots ejecting from the aircraft before it nosedives and crashes in flames.

Separate footage also showed a plume of smoke and flames rising from the rear of a jet as it rolled down the runway before the crash. As the jet climbed, the flames seemed to disappear.

Mikey Kay, a BBC security analyst who also served in the RAF for 20 years, told the BBC that while it was too early to say, it was possible that the cause of the crash was not an engine failure.

In a statement on social media, the RAF said: "Both pilots are doing well, they are in extremely good spirits and expected to make a full recovery.

"A formal investigation into the circumstances surrounding the incident is now under way and, as a precautionary measure, the RAF has temporarily paused Hawk T1 and Hawk T2 flying operations."

The Hawk T1, and newer T2 versions are transonic, two-seat training aircraft used to train fast jet pilots.

The Red Arrows, based at RAF Waddington in Lincolnshire, are included in the pause, however they were not due to fly again until Le Touquet Airshow in France this weekend in any event. It is not known when the restriction will be lifted.

FBI investigating claim hackers have stolen details of all its agents

BBC News Thu, 24 Sep 2026 12:23:52 GMT

The FBI is investigating a claim by a cyber-crime group that it has stolen sensitive information on all bureau staff - around 38,000 people.

The group, Shiny Hunters, says it has every agent's name, role, badge number and personal details including home address, phone numbers and spouse information.

Professor Ciaran Martin, the former head of the UK's National Cyber Security Centre, said - if confirmed - it was "as serious as it gets when it comes to data breaches."

In a statement posted on X, the FBI said it was aware of the claim and the agency was "actively and aggressively investigating the matter".

The criminals claim to have breached the FBI's servers on Monday night and began contacting reporters on Tuesday sharing samples and screenshots of the stolen data.

The BBC has seen a small portion of the data, which appears to be genuine.

According to Reuters, some of the data contains details about officials' ​job assignments, including sensitive work against Chinese spies, Russian intelligence and drug cartels.

ShinyHunters is an international collective of hackers, believed to have originally started in France. It has been behind a number of high-profile breaches including on Rockstar Games in April and a highly disruptive hack on education platform Canvas in May.

The group claims to have found a vulnerability in the Oracle cloud storage system used by the FBI to breach multiple systems including FBIJOBS, FBI BEAST, which does background checks on employees and applicants, FBI MedLink, which holds agent's medical records and FBI BICS, which holds investigation information.

In its message on the dark web, the group said it did not hack the FBI system for money.

Instead, the cyber-criminals are asking the agency to retract an advisory that it issued in May about the gang, saying it was "offended" by its characterisation.

That FBI's public service announcement described ShinyHunters as "threat actors" who often "use their real or exaggerated claims of access to sensitive or personal information to prompt payment from victims".

"They target major companies across tech, finance, and retail, often stealing millions of customer records at once," the advisory said.

ShinyHunters said it would give the bureau one week to correct or remove what it says are false allegations or they would publish the full databases.

The FBI did not respond to multiple requests for comment from the BBC.

In its statement on X, the agency said it was trying to determine whether or not the hackers had breached its systems or a third party.

"We are actively and aggressively investigating this matter and working closely with those third-party providers that support FBIJobs. gov to mitigate any and all risk," the post said.

In a statement to the BBC, a cyber-security expert said it was a "retaliation attack", which demonstrated that "no organisation is safe from the group".

"The group clearly wants to control the narrative around their activities, ensuring nothing is said that could dent their reputation," said William Wright of Closed Door Security.

Meanwhile Andrew Brandt of cyber-security firm Huntress said it may provoke the FBI to track down and prosecute members of the hacking group.

"ShinyHunters must feel pretty confident they won't get caught to threaten a government agency like this," he said.

Carroll reveals he was sexually assaulted in 2021

BBC News Thu, 24 Sep 2026 12:18:04 GMT

Andy Carroll has also played for Reading, West Brom and French sides Amiens and Bordeaux

Former England striker Andy Carroll has revealed he was sexually assaulted by a man in 2021.

The 37-year-old, who was automatically granted anonymity as a victim of sexual assault, has made the details public in an autobiography titled 'Owning it'.

The incident took place at Carroll's home, during his second spell with his hometown club Newcastle and led to the perpetrator being jailed for three years.

Carroll, now a player/co-owner of non-league club Dagenham & Redbridge, says he decided to include the incident in his book "at the very last minute" after discussing it with his girlfriend Lou Teasdale.

A friend of his former partner, who was away at the time, was set to stay over after coming to his home to watch a boxing match.

Carroll says the incident occurred while he was sleeping and he then threw the man out of the house, before knocking him unconscious as he tried to return.

Carroll, who also played in the Premier League for Liverpool and West Ham, called the police and was "sobbing" in the arms of his children's nanny.

The unnamed attacker was found guilty of sexual offences and placed on the sex offender register. Carroll testified in court, a process he says was "humiliating and embarrassing and absolutely horrendous".

Carroll wrote: "I was sexually assaulted, there I said it. Scary to even think about and only a few people knew about it before now.

"Me and Lou spent a lot of time discussing whether to mention it in this book or not. I avoided my publisher for so long that they probably suspected I got cold feet.

"Scary to talk about but it's made [me] the person I am today as much as any of the good stuff. And if me talking about it helps just one person then good, it will have been worth it."

Carroll, who won nine England caps, added: "What happened to me affected every facet of my life. I'd think about it every day, making it difficult to focus on anything else, including football… The trauma of what happened to me hasn't gone away."

Carroll joined Dagenham in July 2025 and has made six appearances in the National League South this season.

If you have been affected by any of the issues in this article, you can find information and support at BBC Action Line

Are we back in big tech's 'move fast and break things' era?

BBC News Thu, 24 Sep 2026 11:29:20 GMT

"Move fast and break things."

It was a mantra coined by the tech giant Meta and used until 2012, which came to define the bad old days of social media running riot in a feeding frenzy of user data.

Yet now we have large companies scrambling to develop ever more powerful AI, in an intense global race to be first to build the world's most advanced models, egged on by US President Donald Trump.

Despite numerous pledges, commitments and open letters over the years from the industry, promising to prioritise safe, responsible AI aligned with human values, examples of bots behaving badly – to put it mildly - are now coming at us thick and fast.

OpenAI's agents seem to feature quite prominently in the current roll call of AI products taking their remits to extremes.

The Australian government is fuming at the firm's most recent disclosure, that its products accessed both public and non-public data from part of the country's online Medicare healthcare system.

It happened in June, but OpenAI didn't notice until August. It notified the authorities in September.

As Camilla Chan, founder of the cyber-security firm X-Phy, puts it: "The future of autonomous AI cannot rest on companies discovering their own failures and reporting it afterwards."

Worse still, the agents were reportedly able to plot the attack using a German web forum they secretly took over in June, according to ABC.

When the website's editors noticed and started deleting pages, the agents shared code designed to retrieve them.

And that happened before the Hugging Face incident, described at the time as the world's first AI-enabled cyber-attack.

It raises a question - if the Medicare incident had been carried out by a person rather than an AI agent, would they be in big trouble?

"If this was an individual hacking Australia's Medicare system, they'd be looking at jail time," said Dr Andrew Rogoyski from the Institute for People-Centred AI at the University of Surrey.

"The fact that it's an AI seems to allow the company to shrug their shoulders and get away with 'accidents happen'."

Australia says it is carrying out an urgent review into whether any laws have been broken, but part of that rests on being able to prove intent – which OpenAI denies.

And its government may have to ask itself some awkward questions about the strength of its cyber-security defences, including whether the healthcare data could have been better protected.

The industry has warned countries and institutions to prepare for a new world of supersized cyber-attacks powered by AI.

A popular solution to keeping the tech on the straight and narrow lies in two parts: slowing down the pace of its development and implementing international regulation to police it.

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham highlighted the need for new global AI standards in his first international speech at the UN General Assembly.

And last night both Sam Altman from OpenAI and Dario Amodei from Anthropic addressed the UN Security Council and pleaded for both – despite Trump not being at all enthusiastic about this approach.

"The only control or 'guardrails' that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the USA has that, in spades!" he posted on Truth Social earlier this month.

He has since said he intends to appoint an AI tsar, so perhaps somebody has had a quiet word.

Yesterday, I spoke to a senior executive at the top of one of the US's biggest AI firms and asked him what he expected international regulators to be able to do that he was seemingly unable to do inside his own lab.

I didn't get a straight answer, but my interpretation is that nobody wants to apply the brakes only to see their rivals race ahead - and they don't trust each other enough to go first.

Global regulation would force them all to toe the line - and also remove some of the weight of responsibility from the industry itself.

AI is increasingly becoming a toxic brand, but to remind people of the benefits of the technology - and why it isn't facing an outright ban - the industry urgently needs some quick wins.

The problem is the tech sector has always been very good at promising the future, without delivering so much in the present.

And that also applies to future problems. Alarm bells rang loudly when former Anthropic safety researcher Joseph Coxon said he believed the tech had a 10% chance of destroying humanity within the next 10 years.

Some experts warn that we should be wary of these claims.

"There are known risks which are serious enough to be getting on with," Sir Nick Clegg, former head of global affairs at Meta, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.

"Whether it's bioweapons, whether it's cyber-security hacks, whether it is the implications of how people are going to be affected by an increasingly intimate and perhaps in many cases emotionally dependent relationship with AI entities going forward.

"There's enough to be really, really worried about already, without thinking that homo sapiens [are] going to be eliminated by next Tuesday."

'I can't see it stopping' - Middlesbrough's young men discuss gangs after A66 crash

BBC News Thu, 24 Sep 2026 06:29:47 GMT

Inside Hemlington Boxing Club in Middlesbrough, music is drowned out by the sound of gloves hitting pads.

For young men here, nights in the ring are far better than the alternative.

Because outside, away from the bright lights of the gym, riders wearing balaclavas roar past on quad bikes in the darkness.

"You see it all the time," says Dylan, a 20-year-old who trains at the club.

"But I just can't see it stopping. The police can't really do much against it."

Attention has turned to organised crime in Middlesbrough since seven people, including two police officers, were killed last month in a crash.

A Volkswagen Passat that had been pursued by officers travelled the wrong way along the A66 and collided head-on with a police car.

For young men like Dylan, who knew one of the lads killed, there are worries about how easy it is to get sucked into a criminal way of life.

"You could walk around the corner and there's just a gang of lads stood there and they shout you over," he says.

Dylan and other boxers tell BBC Newsbeat they blame a lack of safe activities and opportunities for young people in the area.

He says getting into the sport has kept them away from gangs on the streets.

"It stops you going down these bad tracks of crime, drugs, and what most of the lads my age are doing," he says.

"It's just not something I want to be involved in, really," says Dylan.

"I don't think anyone would, but some people just get forced down these routes."

In a report published last month, the Centre for Social Justice found that north-east England has the highest rate of NEETs in the UK.

About one in five 16 to 24-year olds from the region is not in education, employment or training.

Dylan works as a joiner and says he's lucky to have found a job that "keeps you busy and keeps your brain active".

"I think that's where it's going wrong, because people haven't got anything to do," he says.

"So they go into [crime], and it just spirals from there.

"I wish it would all stop, but it's not going to because no-one's got the answer for it."

Michael Cahill, 23, Jakub Matusiak, 23, Makai Saddington, 18, Theo Rae and Cole Worthy, both 17, were killed in the crash, as were PC Matthew Blades, 37, and PC Tom Clough, 38, who were in the police car.

Of the men in the Passat, only Michael Cahill had no convictions. The other four had 30 between them for crimes including car theft, drug possession, assaulting police officers and driving offences.

After the crash, the prime minister called on social media companies to take down posts celebrating dangerous driving.

TikTok posts from an account thought to belong to Makai Saddington had appeared to share this type of content.

Louis, 16, who also trains at Hemlington, says similar clips pop up "everywhere" on his own feeds.

"I've seen quite a few videos on driving cars at high speeds," he says. "I just don't think it's cool."

He says he'd known Theo Rae since the two were at primary school, and was shocked by news of the fatal crash.

Louis says the boxing gym gives him somewhere safe to spend his time, instead of chasing an adrenaline rush from breaking the law.

He wants more people to have access to "sports, or something they enjoy which isn't doing dangerous stuff".

Alex, 21, has been training at Hemlington for just over two years.

"If I wasn't here I'd just be out with my mates, or I'd just be sat at home doing nothing," he says.

For Alex, it's not hard to see how others end up spending their time out in the streets.

"Realistically, what are you going to do on a night?" he says.

"There's nothing to do. Everyone's just out and about, especially the kids."

Alex says crime has become "normal" in the area.

"You can't hide from it," he says.

"People find it a game almost, recording things for TikTok. It's a 'catch me if you can'."

Since the A66 crash, Alex says, his family has been telling him to "get out" of the area.

"You hear nothing good from Middlesbrough any more," he says.

"It's just got a bad reputation.

"I wouldn't want to bring my kids up round here with all the stuff that's going on".

James, 24, who recently moved away to Peterlee, about an hour's bus ride north, says he used to see "quite a lot" of gang activity.

"It might be drugs or knife crime or little petty things," he says.

Cleveland Police has been criticised since the crash, and some residents previously told the BBC they'd "rather die" than dial 999 because their trust in the force was so low.

James and the other boxers who speak to Newsbeat take a more balanced view when it comes to the police, but agree more work is needed to improve relations.

The authorities need to "get to know the people more, understand the people more" to build trust, says James.

"I think the moment you relate to people, that's the moment you've opened the door to getting people's trust."

Cleveland Police Chief Constable Victoria Fuller tells Newsbeat the aftermath of the A66 crash has been hard for the force, with "an incredible amount of grief" for the two officers who died.

But, she says, the local area has been "portrayed in the national media in a way that we don't necessarily recognise".

"We appreciate there are issues here. We know that there are things that policing needs to do, others need to do to make this area feel safer and be safer," she says.

Fuller says a "minority" intent on causing harm "can have a real disproportionate impact on communities" and encouraged people to report problems.

She says the area should "be grateful" for lads like those at the boxing gym who'd chosen to "walk away" and not get involved in crime.

"We hope that people will look out for each other, spot signs of when people are getting drawn into crime and report it to us so that we can help people."

I couldn't live with the agony of migraines anymore but my GP called me dramatic

BBC News Thu, 24 Sep 2026 05:23:15 GMT

Warning: This article contains details of mental health struggles including references to suicide

When Lauren Evans told her doctor she was suicidal because of the "pure agony" of her chronic migraine, she was told she was being dramatic.

Lauren, 29, was seven when she got her first migraine and went on to have them regularly - by the time she was 24, they were happening every day.

"People need to understand that a migraine is a full body experience," she said.

Migraines are often misunderstood as "just a headache" despite being a neurological condition that can leave people unable to work, socialise or function in everyday life, according to a migraine expert.

The Welsh government said it was working to improve access to neurological services.

Lauren, from Swansea, said: "Although the 'headache' is in the head it can affect body temperature, digestive system, speech, light sensitivity, limb numbness, ability to walk and carry out a journey, brain fog, sleep, neck pain, mood swings, visual aura, sound sensitivity, cravings, vertigo.

"I would wake up daily either in pain or worried about when it would start."

She also spent a huge amount of time researching triggers and spent "hundreds on various things just to see if that would help" - from vitamins to chiropractors.

Lauren was training to become a biomedical scientist in the NHS but the lights and overstimulation of Singleton Hospital were so intense she had daily migraines.

She added that she often felt dismissed by colleagues who implied she was faking her condition but was lucky that her manager was supportive.

Some colleagues would accommodate her by turning off the lights, she said, but others said: "If you don't get your annual leave approved, you can just say you've got a migraine and you won't come in."

She continued: "That was so untrue. So you're battling, not just your physical health, you're battling all the mental side that comes with it as well.

"If I went home every day at the sight of a migraine, I would never be in work. There wasn't a day without pain and if there was, I'd be waiting for it."

To manage her symptoms, Lauren changed her working hours, starting at 08:00 BST and finishing at 16:00 so she could get home to take medication, but was still "in agony".

"I couldn't make plans because I knew I'd be suffering in the evening. My weekends would basically be spent recovering," she said.

Lauren said frequent attacks affected her relationship and left her feeling isolated: "It was a dark time. It got to the point where I was like, 'I can't do this for another year'."

Lauren said she went back to the doctor to try to find another option.

"I was like 'I've tried quite a lot of things. Is there any referrals I can have?'

"I actually disclosed that I'm starting to feel suicidal and I'll never forget the words out of her mouth because I burst into tears immediately - she said: 'That sounds very dramatic, doesn't it?'

"I told her I had written a note to my family to say I couldn't live with the pain anymore."

She was referred to a neurologist but, four years on, she still has not been able to speak to them.

Lauren saw a crisis team in December, was signed off work for a month and her migraine attacks began to ease.

She decided it was time to leave her biomedical scientist career and now has a job at an insurance firm, and feels like a different person.

"I have never done so many hobbies in my life," she said.

"Jewellery making, painting... and running 50k in September for a charity."

Her new medication is working well, but she added: "If it got bad again, I honestly wouldn't know where to turn to."

Swansea Bay health board said it was "very sorry to hear of the patient's concerns" but could not comment on individual cases without consent and "would welcome the patient getting in touch with us so we can discuss this further".

It said it had a "specialist headache clinic that covers conditions such as migraine, which GPs can refer people to when appropriate".

Experiences like Lauren's are all too common, said Katy Munro, senior GP headache specialist at the National Migraine Centre and host of the Heads Up podcast.

"There are various barriers to people getting good help for migraine," she said.

"What we're trying to get away from is that preconception that migraine is just a very bad headache."

Munro said headaches were a symptom of migraine attacks, but so were "visual disturbances, nausea and vomiting, sometimes numbness and tingling, sometimes abdominal pain, sometimes dizziness".

They are also a spectrum condition, she said, from episodic - meaning people have mild or rare attacks - to chronic, where they have more than 15 days a month affected by migraine symptoms.

"If you have a migraine attack and you put up with it and then you have another one and put up with it, your brain actually gets more irritable," she said.

That means the migraines become more regular and can become chronic if effective treatment is not applied.

The first barrier to treatment, Munro said, is that a lot of people believe they are "normal headaches".

She said people should always get repetitive headaches checked out by a GP.

The next barrier is that GPs often just note down the headaches as a symptom rather than diagnose migraine, while the third barrier is the medication that was offered in the past, though this has improved in the last five years, she said.

"We need better education throughout the whole of society about how significant migraine is to people who suffer from it."

The Migraine Trust speaks to about 5,000 people with the condition each year through its support services and Rob Music, chief executive of the charity said: "We have seen a concerning trend in enquiries relating to decline in mental health and wellbeing."

"When people are already struggling with the impact of migraine, being met with doubt that it really is 'that bad' by employers, healthcare professionals and even loved ones can be devastating," he said.

The Welsh government said it recognised the effect migraines could have on people's lives and guidance was available to help NHS staff diagnose and manage conditions.

The UK government said the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) had "clear guidance on the diagnosis and management of migraines, and we expect healthcare professionals to follow it and deliver high-quality care to all patients".

If you or someone you know has been affected by the issues raised in this story, information about available help and support can be found via BBC Action Line.

Future of Amazon rainforest may hinge on Brazil presidential election

New Scientist September 23, 2026

On 4 October, Brazilians will go to the polls to elect a president and government. Former president Jair Bolsonaro, under house arrest, cannot run. But his son Flávio is on the ballot. If elected, the 45-year-old senator is widely expected to govern as his father did, which is sparking fears for the future of the Amazon rainforest.

During Jair Bolsonaro’s presidency between 2019 and 2023, deforestation in the Amazon soared, reaching a 15-year-high in 2021.

“We have nothing to believe Flávio will do anything differently from his father. If anything, the signs are that it’s going to be far worse,” says Claudio Angelo, international policy coordinator at Brazil’s Climate Observatory. “This is a do-or-die moment for the Amazon, really.”

Advertisement

Super El Niño set to cause ‘terribly dangerous’ drought in the Amazon

Flávio Bolsonaro is looking to unseat President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, known as Lula. With the younger Bolsanaro currently embroiled in a corruption scandal, the environment has received relatively little attention during campaigning

“But for the rest of the world, the major question here is the Amazon,” says Philip Fearnside, an ecologist at Brazil’s National Institute for Amazonian Research (INPA).

The Brazilian Amazon’s 4.2 million square kilometres of rainforest regulate global climate patterns and hold huge stocks of carbon – roles that are increasingly important as climate change accelerates.

“The Amazon is a key element in whether climate change escapes human control, which is very close to happening,” says Fearnside. If the forest collapses, he says, the associated increase in emissions “would be the straw that breaks the camel’s back”.

Free newsletter

Annual Amazon deforestation surged from 7536 square kilometres in 2018, before Bolsonaro took office, to 11,594 square kilometres in 2022, shortly before he departed.

Experts say the former president encouraged a wave of land-grabbing and illegal mining with his pro-development rhetoric and gutted environmental agencies so they were powerless to stop invaders.

“It’s still hard to believe what happened,” says Izabella Teixeira, Brazil’s environment minister between 2010 and 2016, initially under the presidency of Lula and later under the presidency of Dilma Rousseff.

Since returning to office in 2023, Lula has restored the power of environmental agencies, halving Amazon deforestation to 5731 square kilometres between August 2024 and July 2025.

Deforestation could trigger Amazon tipping point in the 2030s

In a recent TV interview, Flávio Bolsonaro refused to say that climate change existed, instead referring to “extreme climate events” and “cyclical periods”. And during his time as a senator, he proposed legislation that critics said threatened Brazil’s native vegetation. Given this record, and his close ties to his father – and to Donald Trump – experts are concerned that his election would be followed by an increase in deforestation rates.

“We don’t know exactly what Flávio Bolsonaro’s policy will be,” says Teixeira. “But we do know he is a climate change denialist and believes environmental protections are irrelevant.”

Brazil’s largest Indigenous organisation, APIB, had said it fears Flávio Bolsonaro will open Indigenous lands to critical-mineral extraction, and that a Bolsonaro victory would mark “the return of a death project”.

Stark photos show quest for profit cutting swathes through the Amazon

Flávio Bolsonaro’s campaign also pledges zero illegal deforestation by 2029. “There are two ways to achieve that. One is to actually stop deforestation. The other, more likely way, is to just legalise the deforestation that’s going on,” says Fearnside.

A spokesperson for Lula’s campaign told New Scientist that the president’s current term was about rebuilding environmental institutions after Jair Bolsonaro’s presidency of “total neglect and denialism”. The next term would be about “implementing and gaining scale”, with a focus on tougher enforcement, climate adaptation and Brazil’s 2035 climate targets.

The Flávio Bolsonaro campaign did not respond to questions about its environmental policy.

Testing the Amazon’s ability to soak up increasing carbon emissions

Angelo says Brazil’s environmental organisations fear a Flávio Bolsonaro government would resemble Trump’s second term. He says the political know-how gained from the Jair Bolsonaro presidency could allow them to enact laws more quickly.

Flávio is also likely to face fewer political constraints than his father, not least because he has said he would appoint five new supreme court judges.

“Wildcat mining would explode, deforestation would go up and everything we already had during the first Bolsonaro administration would come back even stronger,” says Angelo.

Lula’s environmental policy has also been criticised.

His government has promoted major infrastructure projects such as improving the BR-319 Amazon highway and backed new oil exploration near the mouth of the river basin – projects that would drive deforestation and lock in fossil fuel production.

We used to think that deforestation in the Amazon would dry out the local climate, but the effects may be even more extreme and varied

Still, the choice remains stark, says Angelo. The election will shape not only the future of the rainforest but also global climate diplomacy.

In an era of failing climate leadership, Lula oversaw new initiatives including a self-sustaining fund to pay tropical countries for keeping forests standing and a global road map to transition away from fossil fuels.

Under Flávio Bolsonaro, Angelo predicts that Brazil would probably withdraw from climate diplomacy and ignore its own international climate commitments.

“I don’t think a fourth Lula term would be great for the environment – but it’s really our only hope of keeping the forest standing and keeping any climate policies in place,” says Angelo.

When will the AMOC collapse? We don’t know, but should still prepare

New Scientist September 23, 2026

Most climate impacts are like repeatedly shooting ourselves in the foot: we keep emitting greenhouse gases, the planet warms and more heatwaves happen, and wildfires, and flooding, and drought. Science tells us that this is mechanistic: pull the trigger and you will get hurt.

Europe faces incredibly harsh winters and unrelenting droughts if the vital AMOC ocean current fails – but when disaster will strike and how bad it will be remains uncertain. Now there is an ambitious plan to give us a warning

But in some cases, large uncertainty remains. One particular concern is the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC), the system of currents that transport a tremendous amount of heat from the Gulf of Mexico to Europe. As ever more icebergs and meltwater from Greenland rush into the north Atlantic, the AMOC is thought to be slowing down. Eventually it could even collapse, bringing “ice age” winters to Europe, raising sea levels in North America and disrupting vital monsoons in Africa and Asia.

Will that happen? We don’t know. Some research says the AMOC could cross a tipping point in centuries, some says decades and some says it has crossed it already. If we start reducing emissions, it may not happen at all. Scientists have long described it as low probability but high impact. You might think of it as climate Russian roulette.

Advertisement

Scientists have long described the AMOC’s collapse as low probability but high impact

To tackle this uncertainty, scientists are trying to build an early warning system to alert us that the AMOC is going to cross a tipping point. It is unclear whether that warning would give us enough time to avoid this, or merely to prepare for the impacts, but both are better than doing nothing, which is what we are doing now. We may not know the probability of the AMOC collapsing, but we know it is increasing.

So far, the uncertainty around it has been an excuse to ignore it, or treat it as a distant problem. In fact, the uncertainty makes it even more important for policy-makers to take action now, in the same way we fund militaries for wars we hope will never come. Whether we decide to invest in mitigation or adaptation, we won’t regret it, since all of it will help with our bigger climate problem. Stop emissions, take the gun away and no one needs to get hurt.

Copying others can help young orangutans build a broad diet

New Scientist September 24, 2026

Young orangutans who spend little time working out for themselves how to build a broad diet can partly compensate by watching how other orangutans choose what to eat.

The findings suggest that orangutans have different strategies for developing broad survival skills, says Revathe Thillaikumar at the Max Planck Institute of Animal Behavior in Germany.

Young orangutans acquire a substantial body of knowledge before they can survive independently, which they must do by the time they are 8.5 years old. This includes understanding what foods are safe to eat, where to find them and how to process them in a rainforest offering hundreds of food options of varying levels of accessibility – from easy-to-access leaves to the more inaccessible but also more nutritious seeds at the heart of a tough, spiny neesia fruit.

Advertisement

Orangutan mothers seem to plan playdates for their offspring

Scientists already know that orangutans can acquire this knowledge both by observing their mothers and other individuals in their social circle – a process known as social learning – and by exploring entirely on their own without any input from others, which is known as individual learning. But how these two forms of learning work together – and how they affect what orangutans learn to eat before becoming independent – hasn’t been clear.

To find out, Thillaikumar and her colleagues analysed nearly 7000 instances of learning recorded during more than 1700 hours of observations of wild Sumatran orangutans at Suaq Balimbing, a research station in Indonesia. The observations, collected over 12 years, tracked 21 youngsters as they closely watched other orangutans who were interacting with foods and other objects.

The young apes varied considerably in how much they relied on different kinds of learning, with some using more social learning, and others exploring independently much more often. This might, in part, reflect personality differences, and might also be influenced by early development – including differences in how mothers care for their young, says Thillaikumar.

See Chris Packham at New Scientist Live 2026

Youngsters who learned by watching others also tended to continue manipulating new objects or trying new foods for about 145 minutes after they had closely observed another orangutan. This activity is reminiscent of the way in which children will spend time imitating an activity they have just seen demonstrated by an adult, says Thillaikumar. “Yeah, it’s practice.”

Next, the researchers drew on about 4700 hours of feeding observations for 13 of the youngsters to estimate the range of foods they had learned to eat by the time they reached independence. Unsurprisingly, the team found that the individuals who had engaged in plenty of social learning and plenty of individual learning had acquired the broadest diets.

But they also found that young orangutans who engaged in very little truly individual learning could partially compensate and develop a reasonably broad diet if they were good social learners.

A male Sumatran orangutan chewed the leaves of a plant used in Indonesian traditional medicine and placed them on a wound on his face

Elizabeth Lonsdorf at Duke University in North Carolina says she’s impressed by the sheer scale of the work, following young orangutans through the rainforest across their entire, lengthy period of dependency on adults. She was particularly intrigued by how often social observation was followed by young orangutans practising the techniques they had observed. “In simpler terms, they show clearly what we see in human children and other apes – that they watch others perform a behaviour and then go try it out on their own.”

The variability in learning styles – even at an individual level – is especially interesting, says Michael Tomasello, also at Duke University. It suggests that no single form of learning can tell the whole story. “Predicting dietary breadth at maturity requires looking at all types of learning.”

Dogs pay more attention to consonants than vowels when we speak

New Scientist September 24, 2026

When dogs hear their owners speak, they are listening for consonants in words rather than vowels, a new study suggests, apparently mimicking a similar human bias that is found across many languages.

Although dogs don’t have language, they live in a speech-rich environment, says Attila Andics at Eötvös Loránd University in Hungary.

“We knew from our previous studies that dogs care about what we speak and how we speak, but until now there was no evidence that dogs’ experience with speech can actually shape how their brains function,” says Andics.

Advertisement

‘Singing’ dogs may show the evolutionary roots of musicality

To investigate how a life with humans and listening to constant talk has impacted dogs’ brains, Andics and his colleagues recruited 20 adult human Hungarian speakers and 20 companion dogs with Hungarian owners.

Andics says while many Eastern European languages are consonant heavy, Hungarian isn’t.

“There are some studies suggesting that consonant bias during speech segmentation is weaker, or not there, in people who mostly listen to Mandarin or Danish, in which languages consonants are not, or not that much, more informative about word boundaries than vowels,” he says.

During the experiment, the human and dog participants separately listened to continuous, unsegmented speech streams of nonsense words while connected to EEG monitors, measuring the electrical activity of the participants’ brains.

See Chris Packham at New Scientist Live 2026

Consonants and vowels alternated throughout these streams, with no pauses or other acoustic cues separating them, says Andics.

There were three types of nonsense streams. In the first, recurring consonant patterns formed consecutive three-syllable words – such as “mozite”. In the second, stronger vowel patterns formed the skeleton of the words – such as “zobefu”. And in the third, there were no recurring patterns at all, with syllables in a random order – such as “fumoza”.

He says the team made use of a phenomenon called “neural synchronisation”, in which brain activity can take on the rhythm that we detect in the sounds we hear.

“The more reliably we detect that rhythm, the more rhythmic the brain response becomes,” says Andics. “We expected that if a species’ brain has a preference for consonants, it should follow the rhythm of the words more easily when consonants form the structure of those words.”

Oldest known dog extends the genetic history of our canine companions

The difference was substantial, the scientists found. In dogs, the neural response to consonant-based regularities was 42 per cent stronger than the response to vowel-based regularities, and 55 per cent stronger than the response to the random stream.

“So, this is how much more dog brains tracked word rhythm when consonants defined the words,” says Andics.

In humans, the response to consonant-patterned words was nearly 25 per cent higher than to vowel-based regularities and 77 per cent higher than to the random condition. The team thinks that dogs who weren’t exposed to human speech wouldn’t have this bias, although they haven’t yet tested this idea.

“We argue that the only reason companion dogs have a consonant bias is that human speech, and specifically the characteristics of words, reshaped their brains,” says Andics.

Babies born too soon seem to have stronger connections in one of the major brain areas that supports language processing if they regularly heard their mother read them a story while in intensive care

Nick Enfield at the University of Sydney, Australia, says the team convincingly shows that these dogs display more sensitivity to statistical patterns in consonants, rather than in vowels.

But with some important caveats – especially that these are Hungarian dogs, living with Hungarian speakers.

“There’s 7000 different languages in the world and some of them rely a lot more on things like tonal distinctions,” says Enfield. But if you do want your dog to pay attention to you, there may be a practical take home, he says.

“The lesson here may be to give your dog a name with more consonants in it than one with more vowels.”

Science DOI: 10.1126/science. adw7709

Backpack massages muscles when it detects they’re fatigued

New Scientist September 24, 2026

A backpack can detect when muscles become fatigued and automatically massage the affected areas. This seems to help muscles recover better than heat therapy or pre-programmed massages, like those delivered by chairs and cushions.

About 1 in 6 adults in the UK have some form of back pain. This can occur when back muscles become fatigued through exertion or prolonged or repetitive activity. Persistent fatigue can impair local blood flow and tissue recovery, potentially contributing to chronic pain.

From back pain to cancer, how the interstitium could transform medicine

Tired back muscles can be relieved through heat therapy and automated massage, which often involves rollers moving across the back in pre-programmed patterns. But these tend to be standardised treatments that don’t take into account people’s individual muscular issues, says Chengsong Yu at the Wuhan Institute of Technology in China.

Advertisement

Looking for a more bespoke approach, Yu and his colleagues have developed a wearable system, like a backpack, that uses electrodes on the skin to monitor electrical activity in four groups of back muscles. The system then determines which muscles are fatigued, and how much. Cables move a soft massage head to the affected areas, where sensor feedback allows the system to continually adjust the force according to the fatigue levels, says Yu.

To test their device, the researchers asked 11 men and four women, aged 20 to 26, with no known health issues, to spend 2 minutes resting, followed by 2 minutes repeatedly lifting dumbbells while seated. This induces fatigue in the rhomboids, the muscles between the shoulder blades.

Free newsletter

All the participants wore the backpack during the dumbbell exercise so it could record their muscles’ electrical activity, but only some then received the backpack’s massage. The remaining participants divided into groups that received another type of pre-programmed massage, had heat therapy or rested.

During the exercise, the electrical activity in the participants’ rhomboids fell as the muscles became fatigued, indicating weaker muscle activation. But after the backpack treatment, this activity was about 2.6 times higher compared with after the pre-programmed massage, indicating greater recovery. It was also about 1.9 times higher than after heat treatment, and four times higher than after resting.

“We were encouraged by how clearly the adaptive system improved muscle recovery compared with preprogrammed mechanostimulation and thermal stimulation,” says Yu.

The same principles that help astronauts stay strong in microgravity can help us all resist the slow collapse of ageing – and it’s not all about hitting the gym more

Conor Walsh at Harvard University says the device is a move in a “creative direction” for combining soft robotics with mechanical therapy to address back pain and muscle fatigue. But it needs to be lighter and less bulky before it can become a practical solution, he says.

“There are definitely some very interesting engineering features in the system, and I see a lot of value in this as a proof of concept for this technology,” says Olivier Lambercy at ETH Zurich in Switzerland. “But if you want to use it in the context of people working on the assembly line as they claim, I think this is a bit far into the future.”

The team hopes to make the design smaller and more compact, and to test it in a larger group of people working in real-world conditions that may cause back pain, says Yu.

Taking HRT in perimenopause may ward off cardiovascular disease

New Scientist September 24, 2026

Taking hormone replacement therapy during the perimenopause or early menopause may reduce the risk of heart attacks and stroke. A study of nearly 2800 women over 20 years suggests that starting HRT around this time lowers the risk of serious cardiovascular events. However, much more research is required to understand how the treatment may have this effect and the optimal time to take it.

“I want to emphasise: our study does not support using menopausal [hormonal] therapy to prevent cardiovascular disease,” says Samar El Khoudary at Virginia Commonwealth University.

Everything is perimenopause now – but what if it’s not?

A recent study in Spain suggests that nearly 80 per cent of women experience vasomotor symptoms – hot flushes and night sweats – around the menopause. However, other research from this year suggests this varies substantially around the world. These symptoms can be treated via HRT, which is available in different formulations, such as tablets, patches, gels and sprays. These replace oestrogen and progesterone, hormones that fall as the menopause approaches.

Advertisement

The controversy around HRT started in 2002, when a large trial linked it to an increased risk of breast cancer, heart attacks and stroke. The method of this trial, and subsequent ones, has since been called into question. Newer research has also put the results into context by comparing them with other lifestyle choices, such as alcohol intake. In 2021, a study found that HRT doesn’t increase the risk of early death.

What’s more, earlier studies generally looked at women around the age of 60. This is despite menopause usually occurring between the ages of 45 and 55, and some people taking HRT during the perimenopause.

Free newsletter

Now, El Khoudary and her colleagues have looked at 2737 participants in the Study of Women’s Health Across the Nation, which was made up of women in the US aged 42 to 52 at enrollment. All these women experienced hot flushes and night sweats, but only 755 took some form of HRT over the 20-year study period.

During this time, 224 fatal and non-fatal cardiovascular events occurred. The researchers estimated that the women who started HRT 10 years or less after the onset of vasomotor symptoms were 27 per cent less likely to experience these events than those who didn’t take HRT. The effect was much less clear among women who initiated the treatment more than 10 years after their onset, says El Khoudary. The timing seems to be “very critical”, she says.

As to why HRT may have this effect, El Khoudary says the “underlying mechanisms are complex and multifactorial”.

Oestrogen is involved in regulating cholesterol and blood sugar levels, and contributes to blood vessel flexibility. Previous research suggests that HRT dose and formulation – which may vary depending on the person’s age – affect artery structure, which may impact heart health. The perimenopause is also increasingly being recognised as a period of distinct vascular changes.

The brain undergoes a full renovation during menopause. Although these changes are profound, we’re learning that the long-term impact needn’t be all bad

The researchers also found that HRT’s seemingly protective effect was most pronounced among the Black participants, who may be more likely to experience vasomotor symptoms. Further research is needed to uncover why the results vary among women of different races, says El Khoudary.

For now, people shouldn’t start HRT to prevent cardiovascular events. Another recent study suggests that oral HRT is linked to a 0.09 per cent higher risk of venous thromboembolism (the formation of blood clots in the veins), a 0.06 per cent higher risk for ischaemic stroke (when a blood clot or other blockage cuts off blood supply to the brain) and a 0.03 per cent higher risk of a heart attack per year.

“The most important thing to understand about observational studies is that they cannot establish causality,” says Tara Iyer at Brigham and Women’s Hospital in Boston. El Khoudary now wants to see randomised, placebo-controlled trials testing the cardiovascular effects of HRT during the perimenopause and early menopause.

JAMA Internal Medicine DOI: 10.1001/jamainternmed.2026.2922

Benedict Cumberbatch’s nature show is stunning, if a little cloying

New Scientist September 24, 2026

How to Live on Earth, a new nature documentary hosted by Benedict Cumberbatch, starts with bizarre footage of farmers in China tickling pear trees with giant feather dusters. Because pesticides have killed off the bees, farmers must now pollinate pear blossoms themselves. It shows how absurd and broken our relationship with nature is. We are destroying the ecosystems that we depend on.

Now published to YouTube as “the world’s greatest how-to video”, the documentary aims to explore not just this problem, but also possible win-win solutions, Cumberbatch told me in an interview at a London hotel.

“We’ve had people warn us of the perils of our direction of travel. This is reshaping that narrative,” says Cumberbatch. “If we start working with nature rather than against it… it’s for the betterment of ourselves.”

Advertisement

Producer Jonnie Hughes has worked on projects with David Attenborough including the documentary A Life on Our Planet. While the cinematography in the new documentary is stunning, it is not a masterpiece like that film was. Passing characters like an elephant guard in Chad are never developed, and lyrical descriptions of local communities living in harmony with nature felt cloying to this jaded journalist. The barrage of nature solutions in far-flung regions might confound viewers wondering how to take action.

But the film raises a pragmatic question that is often shunned by environmentalists: how can a capitalist society learn to value nature’s ecosystem services rather than just its resources? In the film, we watch companies profit off gold mining on a tributary of the Amazon river, while Indigenous communities bear the cost of mercury pollution.

As an alternative, the documentary discusses the idea of a natural asset company, which would allow investors to buy equity in an ecosystem. The sale of carbon or biodiversity credits, water supplies or sustainable crops could potentially generate revenue, while value would increase as the ecosystem is restored.

Hughes, who once created a short biodiversity film that then-prime-minister of the UK Boris Johnson showed to the G7, is screening the documentary for Wall Street investors as part of New York Climate Week this week. To make change, environmentalists must give politicians and businesspeople a new story to tell, he says.

“It’s a good story that sustainability is not about sacrifice; it’s about benefit,” says Hughes. “People start thinking, ‘Hang on, what’s this green rush going on?’”

When I asked Hughes if Cumberbatch was the next Attenborough, the actor jumped in to protest that “there’s no one like Sir David”. But if you want to think about how we might start halting the biodiversity crisis that Attenborough helped reveal, How to Live on Earth is a good place to begin.

Skin patch that collects sweat could predict ovulation

New Scientist September 24, 2026

A patch that measures oestrogen and progesterone in sweat could give wearers insight into their reproductive changes. This may be particularly helpful when predicting ovulation if they are trying to become pregnant.

The patch “has the potential to be less invasive than blood tests and sonograms [for gauging ovulation], and to provide more useful information than currently available wearables”, says Gillian Goddard at the NYU Grossman School of Medicine in New York, who wasn’t involved in the research.

Our fertility window could be extended by making ovaries softer

Reproductive hormones, such as oestrogen and progesterone, regulate the menstrual cycle. For instance, high levels of oestrogen cause a surge in another hormone, luteinising hormone, that leads to ovulation. Progesterone prepares the lining of the uterus for a fertilised egg to implant and grow.

Advertisement

Existing fertility trackers generally rely on signals such as body temperature, which rises after ovulation, or a series of blood or urine tests to assess hormone levels. More accurate tests include transvaginal ultrasound, which tracks the growth of ovarian follicles that will release an egg and helps determine whether ovulation has occurred. However, this is invasive, requires a clinic visit and only provides a snapshot of someone’s reproductive status.

In 2023, Wei Gao at the California Institute of Technology and his colleagues demonstrated that a wearable patch could detect levels of oestradiol, the primary type of oestrogen produced in ovaries, in sweat. Now, they have developed a patch that also measures progesterone. “Monitoring [oestradiol and progesterone] together could potentially provide a more complete picture of the hormonal trajectory before and after ovulation, rather than a single event,” says Gao.

The patch, which uses a mild electrical current to induce sweating, contains a sensor with two DNA molecules engineered to bind to either oestradiol or progesterone. Each molecule then generates a distinct electrical signal. This gives an estimated level of both hormones, which is transmitted to a smartphone app.

Free newsletter

Detecting hormones in sweat is difficult because the composition of the liquid varies. To get around this, the researchers added a dried buffer to the sensor that is rehydrated by sweat, bringing the sample’s pH and salt concentration into a consistent range. “You can think of it as standardising the sweat before we measure the hormones,” says Gao.

The researchers tested the patch – which requires about 9 microlitres of sweat and takes 90 minutes to produce a reading – on nine women. Some of these women were of reproductive age, while the others were postmenopausal.

The team found that the hormone levels measured by the patch closely tracked those from blood tests, with correlations of 0.83 for oestradiol and 0.93 for progesterone. A score of 1 would mean the two measurements matched perfectly.

How monitoring your sweat could reveal the state of your health

In another part of the experiment, the researchers tested the patch on three women – one of reproductive age, one who was perimenopausal and one who was postmenopausal – over 28 days, the average length of the menstrual cycle.

The changes in hormone levels detected by the patch broadly matched those seen in the women’s blood samples and what would be expected for their ages. For instance, the patch worn by the woman of reproductive age showed the expected oestradiol and progesterone fluctuations across the 28 days, while the patch worn by the postmenopausal participant showed consistently low levels of these hormones.

The next step is to test the patch on a larger group, and to see how reliably hormone levels in sweat track those in blood across different ages and reproductive stages, says Gao. The team also plans to compare the patch against established ovulation measures, such as urine tests, he says. We need to know whether the patch can predict ovulation early enough to be useful, given that hormonal changes vary between people and over time, says Goddard.

Device DOI: 10.1016/j. device.2026.101299

OpenAI agent hacked an Australian government healthcare website

New Scientist September 24, 2026

Australia’s national health website has been hacked by an OpenAI agent. It was able to access non-public files and is the first publicly revealed case of an AI agent breaching the defences of a government portal.

Full details of the hack haven’t yet been revealed. But the essence of the incident, as outlined by Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, who is in New York for the United Nations General Assembly, is that on 18 June, an artificial intelligence agent belonging to OpenAI infiltrated the public-facing Medicare statistics reporting service portal. This includes aggregated statistics collated from individual medical services, such as from GP surgeries.

“‘The AI agent accessed both public and non-public files,” said Albanese on 23 September.

Advertisement

Is AI really getting dangerously out of control?

OpenAI said in a statement that it learned about the security breach during a review of “misaligned model activity”. The firm says its agents had been trying to look up statistics about Australia and then “took actions we did not intend”. It says it hasn’t found evidence of any patient data being accessed.

Though the company learned of the breach in August, it didn’t notify Australian authorities until 10 September, which it did by emailing a public government mailbox. It then took more than five days to reach the cybersecurity department.

“It took the company way too long to inform the government what had occurred, and the nature of the way that that notification occurred as well was unacceptable,” Albanese told reporters.

Albanese also revealed that he and Sam Altman, the CEO of OpenAI, had a conversation in which he expressed Australia’s “extreme concern about this incident”.

Free newsletter

David Tuffley at Griffith University, Australia, says it isn’t the first time such a breach has occurred, even if it is the first government hack by an agent from a big AI firm to be made public, and it won’t be the last.

These agents don’t always stick to the rules, he says, as the Hugging Face incident earlier this year, where another OpenAI agent hacked into another AI company, demonstrates. “People throw up their hands in horror and say: ‘Oh no, it’s rogue AI.’ But it’s not, it’s really just AI doing what it was trained to do,” he says.

Failure to bring agents to heel should have criminal consequences, just as it would if it was a person who led the cyberattack, says Clément Canonne at the University of Sydney. “The issue with private data is once it’s leaked, it’s not going to come back.”

Tauranga mum questions funding cut for daughter with Rett syndrome

New Zealand Herald September 24, 2026

Four-year-old Remi Henderson requires round-the-clock care.

Remi Henderson’s needs are growing but her family’s disability funding has remained the same.

The Tauranga 4-year-old has Rett syndrome, and an early reassessment of her disability support put her family’s funding at about 40% less than their existing allocation.

Rett syndrome is a rare genetic neurological condition that causes children to lose skills they previously developed.

The family’s original annual funding allocation was reinstated after an appeal, but her mother feels it still doesn’t meet her daughter’s growing needs.

Disability Support Services said it has asked for the assessment to be reviewed and expects the family to be supported as a matter of urgency.

It said a new national approach introduced in February was designed to make assessments more consistent and to better account for the needs of family carers.

Remi’s mother Mandy Henderson cares for Remi around the clock and is questioning how the family could receive less support as her needs increased.

Remi began to regress at 1 and was diagnosed with Rett syndrome at 2 after extensive testing.

Now, at 4, Remi can’t walk, crawl, roll, sit or stand independently.

She can’t use her hands, feed herself or reliably signal pain or discomfort. She also has epilepsy and seizures in her sleep.

Henderson gave up her fulltime job to provide 24-hour care.

She manages three seizure medications, handles equipment and dressings, feeds Remi, gets her to appointments and therapy, and supervises her constantly.

When Remi was diagnosed, the family received $9805 a year in individualised funding from Disability Support Services, the service which helps eligible disabled people manage supports such as personal care, household help and respite.

That funding is reassessed every five years. But after Remi experienced a major regression, more seizures, and hospital stays, Henderson asked for an early reassessment.

Her first two requests were declined before an urgent reassessment was eventually granted.

The result blindsided her.

The indicative funding range under the new assessment model was just $5700 to $6100 a year, around 40% less than the family already got.

“I feel like I’m being gaslit,” she said.

“Like, telling me, ‘actually, she’s not that bad. You’re just making it up’. When she is that bad, her needs are very high.”

Henderson said she was shocked, as Remi’s needs had increased as she grew and lost more physical abilities.

The family submitted letters from Remi’s paediatrician and physiotherapist, but Henderson said no one explained how the new figure was reached.

Their assessor appealed, and the original $9805 was reinstated.

She said it was exhausting having to fight for basic support while the family was already stretched caring for Remi.

A lack of transparency was at the heart of her concerns.

She said the assessment relied on parents describing their child’s needs, filtered through how an assessor interprets and records those answers, rather than an objective, standardised measure of what a child can and can’t do.

Henderson said she knew of another child with Rett syndrome who was funded about $42,000 annually, and another child without Rett but with similar needs who received $90,000.

She did not believe either family was given too much, but questioned why allocations varied so widely if the system was intended to provide consistent assessments.

“If this is considered a fair and accurate assessment, is this the level of funding considered appropriate for a child who requires 24/7 care?”

As Remi’s needs increased, Henderson said the family was struggling to care for her alone. Some tasks, such as bathing Remi, required two people.

Henderson said the family had no nearby relatives to help.

More funding would allow the family to pay for help during the busiest parts of the day and eventually allow Henderson to return to work.

“I would love one sleep a week. Just to breathe.”

Remi’s older siblings, aged 7 and 9, were limited in what they could do outside the home as their parents needed to care for Remi.

Henderson said the older children were “amazing” with their sister, but she worried they were missing parts of their childhood.

“I just don’t feel like it’s sustainable for me to be her everything 24 hours a day, every day, for her whole life.”

The family also spends thousands on Remi’s therapy.

Money raised through a fundraiser helped cover some costs towards a recent $15,000, three-week programme in Rotorua, but Henderson said it was almost gone.

Disability Support Services general manager DSS transformation Alastair Hill said the service had asked Remi’s Needs Assessment and Service Co-ordination (NASC) organisation to review whether Remi’s needs had been correctly assessed.

An NASC assesses people’s disability support needs and works with them and their family to identify the support they may be eligible to receive.

“We expect the NASC will work with Remi’s family on the outcome of that assessment as a matter of urgency, to ensure that appropriate support is able to be put in place.”

Hill said the service would stay in contact with the NASC while the review was completed.

After an assessment, families received a funding plan outlining their funding, what it covered and what it was intended to support. It could be provided in writing if requested.

The service introduced a new national approach to assessing and allocating disability support in February, which aimed to make assessments more consistent and better account for the needs of family carers.

This followed an independent review in 2024 that found assessments and funding decisions had not always been consistent or fair.

When asked about differing levels of financial support being offered to families of children with similar levels of need, Hill said each family’s circumstances were different, so funding allocations could vary.

“We expect NASCs to work with families carefully to assess need,” he said.

Disability Issues Minister Louise Upston said she recognised the demands faced by families caring for children with complex needs.

She said families should be able to understand how their needs were assessed and how decisions about support were made.

Upston said the independent review found inconsistencies in needs assessments and funding allocations.

Families reported finding the assessment and allocation process difficult to navigate, and assessments did not always account for the realities of disabled people’s lives and family circumstances.

“Those concerns have been listened to and we have responded to the review.”

Upston said Disability Support Services was also beginning work on a new carer support package, including financial support, respite and practical assistance, shaped by consultation with community and carer groups.

Zoe Blake is a multimedia journalist at the Bay of Plenty Times and Rotorua Daily Post.

A showery and blustery weekend, with the potential for heavy snow, is forecast as families hit the road for the start of the school holidays.

MetService said a series of cold fronts was set to sweep over New Zealand, bringing frosty, wet and windy conditions from today.

“There will be some wetter weather heading our way for the weekend – especially on Sunday,” MetService said, urging travellers to keep an eye on the forecast.

Showers over the southern South Island are set to spread north and linger in the west today and Saturday, before the main band of rain arrives with a front on Sunday.

Heavy snow is also possible above 600m in parts of Central Otago, Southern Lakes and the Canterbury High Country south of the Rangitata River on Sunday morning.

MetService meteorologist Samkelo Magwala said the fronts would move through quickly, limiting rainfall totals despite brief heavy rain in some places.

Meanwhile, meteorologist John Law told the Herald it wasn’t all bad news, with warmer weather and sunshine possible in parts of the country too.

After a frosty start in parts of the North Island, Law said showers would push towards the western side of the country today.

“For the eastern side of the South Island, we are still going to find a few showers creeping across as we head through the day.”

Law said places such as Hawke’s Bay were set to be lucky with a “pretty decent” day and some spells of sunshine.

On Saturday, the wet weather was forecast to move up the country.

In the South Island, he said places from Fiordland to Buller would likely catch a few showers.

“On the North Island I think we’ll find it’s still a cloudier, showery story for places from say Northland all the way down that western coast through Waikato, Waitomo, Taranaki and even down towards Manawatū and the Kāpiti Coast,” Law said.

He said the further east you are, the drier and brighter it would likely be.

MetService said Sunday would be a more “active day” as a front shifted across the South Island.

Law said a change in wind direction would move up from the south, introducing wetter weather towards Southland and Otago and heavier rainfall for the West Coast.

Southwest gales are also possible in coastal Clutha, Christchurch and along the Kaikōura coast.

MetService said as the front moved up the country, northwesterly gales would blow through the Cook Strait and into Wairarapa and southern Hawke’s Bay.

Law also said the wet weather would move towards the North Island by the afternoon.

Auckland was expected to receive showers and spells of rain, with the heaviest on Sunday evening.

“The good news, the unsettled weather is short-lived due to a high-pressure system in the Tasman Sea, providing a settled start to the new working week,” MetService said.
