Rotorua NZNO conference: What nurses want from the next Government

New Zealand Herald September 24, 2026

Members of the New Zealand Nurses Organisation at the union's 2026 national conference in Rotorua on Thursday. Photo / Megan Wilson

More nursing staff, growing the Māori nursing workforce and reinstating pay equity agreements are among the top things nursing union members want from the next Government.

Five New Zealand Nurses Organisation (NZNO) members from different Health New Zealand districts told the Rotorua Daily Post their views at the union’s 2026 national conference at Novotel Rotorua Lakeside on Thursday.

Palmerston North specialist palliative care nurse and Te Rūnanga representative (the Māori arm of the NZNO) Diane Perenara said she would like to see more funding and support for training Māori nurses to grow the workforce.

Te Rūnanga representative Billie-Jean James, who works in Health NZ Taranaki’s mental health inpatient unit, said she wanted to see investment in aged care, pay equity for women and the housing crisis to be addressed, to help eliminate preventable hospital admissions.

NZNO delegate and Rotorua Hospital ED nurse Lyn Logan and Dargaville Hospital nurse Shayna Mariscal both wanted more nursing staff.

Waikato Hospital healthcare assistant Michael Deibert said he would like the next Government to reinstate pay equity agreements.

Former Green MP and political activist Dr Sue Bradford gave a speech about the Government’s controversial pay equity changes.

Announced by Workplace Relations Minister Brooke van Velden last year, the changes included tightening the thresholds for a pay equity claim to be advanced. This meant 33 current claims had to be restarted, as long as they complied with the new criteria.

The changes, designed to save billions of dollars, addressed escalating costs of pay equity claims and budget concerns.

Bradford said active claims by those in the nursing sector were “cancelled overnight”.

She said National, NZ First and Act were responsible for this “massive attack on workers”.

In the election lead-up, she encouraged people to ask their electoral candidates about their positions on pay equity, “particularly Labour and Opportunity’s candidates”, if they would commit to a full repeal of the amendments within the first 100 days if elected.

The Green Party strongly advocated for restoring and extending pay equity provisions, while Te Pāti Māori had been “highly critical” of last year’s changes, she said.

“We’ve had many decades of struggle for workers’ and women’s rights ripped away from us.

“The time to reverse it is now.”

University of Otago, Wellington, professor of public health Philippa Howden-Chapman spoke to the conference about how housing impacted people’s health.

She said houses needed to be warm and safe, as younger and older people spent “about 90% of their time inside”.

“The worse the houses, the harder it is for people to keep well.”

Howden-Chapman said crowding was the “key risk” in housing.

“If there’s not enough space for a sick child to be in the house in a separate room … infectious diseases in particular spread rapidly.”

She said nurses were “pivotal” to the Healthy Homes Initiative – a community led, government-funded intervention aimed at improving health outcomes for children at risk of housing-related illness in low-income families.

Howden-Chapman said nurses doing home visits asked residents what they needed to live in a warm, dry and healthy home.

She said more than 25,000 children were hospitalised annually with preventable housing-related conditions.

Between 2014 and 2021, yearly childhood hospitalisations reduced by almost one-third in families visited by nurses, she said.

Aged Care Association chief executive Tracey Martin spoke about the challenges facing aged residential care.

Martin said aged care residential facilities were caring for people with “increasingly complex clinical needs”.

She said hospital capacity, nursing shortages and the cost of healthcare were discussed without giving sufficient attention to the aged care residential sector.

“That separation has consequences.”

When an aged care residential facility could not recruit nurses, beds became unavailable, leaving older patients longer in the hospital.

“When the appropriate care is unavailable close to home, families and whānau may face difficult decisions about where their loved one can receive care.

“If aged care fails, the health system fails.”

She said the association was working to establish the cost of delivering aged residential care to inform discussions about the sector’s future funding.

“The funding of aged residential care must recognise the actual cost of delivering the clinical care that residents need, and that includes the cost of the workforce necessary to deliver that care.

“We need to recognise that the sustainability of aged residential care, the future of the nursing workforce and the ability of our hospitals to function efficiently are all connected.”

Megan Wilson is a health and general news reporter for the Bay of Plenty Times and the Rotorua Daily Post. She has been a journalist since 2021.

Hamilton Gardens’ medieval plants take off after seven-year construction

New Zealand Herald September 24, 2026

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

This is a modal window.

Beginning of dialog window. Escape will cancel and close the window.

End of dialog window.

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

Hamilton’s medieval-themed garden has sprung to life as plants ”let loose in the soil” welcome the public to a space seven years in the making.

Arches and passageways, medicinal herbs and 280 tonnes of concrete make up the Hamilton Gardens attraction – but one detail has eluded its creators.

A medieval bell has been hard to find, says Hamilton Gardens director Lucy Ryan.

“They’re not out there.”

For now, a recording will chime on the hour while the search continues for the real thing, Ryan said.

The Medieval Garden opened to the public at 10am on Thursday after seven years of planning, research and construction.

Work on the garden began in 2019, with the main construction phase starting in 2023.

Partly modelled on the ruins of the St John of the Hermits monastery (San Giovanni degli Eremiti) in Sicily, Italy, it has been designed to evoke a medieval European world.

It is part of Hamilton Gardens’ vision to create a “living museum” of 30 gardens representing periods and civilisations from Ancient Egypt to the present.

The challenge was to make the garden historically convincing while creating a place visitors wanted to linger, Hamilton Gardens horticultural and operations manager Gus Flower said.

Delicate herbs and plants grow among the concrete, revealing the garden’s story, he said.

The plants were kept in pots at the nursery during construction, before being planted in the garden, Flower said.

“Now they have been let loose in the soil.

“When the sun comes out, it moves, it grows.”

Flower said the final stages required a careful balancing act, with contractors finishing the concrete work around newly established plants.

“And we’re still friends,” he said.

For medieval people, however, the plants growing inside such gardens were much more than decoration.

Flower said many had practical uses for food and remedies, as people experimented with plants and passed down knowledge of their uses.

Gardening today might be more associated with “pretty flowers and a nice lawn”, but medieval gardens had a more immediate purpose, Flower said.

“These had a real purpose, making them really, really precious.”

Flower said the garden represented a period following centuries of conflict involving groups such as the Angles, Saxons and Vikings.

“There’s a lot of war going on; people just knocking lumps out of each other.”

By the 12th and 13th centuries, places where people could rest and receive care were developing, alongside growing knowledge of plants and their uses.

Researching that relationship between people and plants was one of the most fascinating parts of the project for Flower.

It also gave him a new appreciation for springtime.

He said it was difficult to comprehend what the end of a severe European winter would have meant for people contending with disease, conflict and food shortages.

“To reach [spring] was quite an achievement for some people.”

Flower said the concept gardens allowed Hamilton Gardens to reach beyond a traditional botanical garden audience.

Each garden uses landscaping to tell a story, immersing visitors in various cultures and historical periods, encouraging repeat visits, he said.

Seven years after work on Hamilton’s Medieval Garden began, Flower is now watching its first spring unfold.

The herbs are spreading, the trees will mature and, over time, the hard edges of construction will soften, creating the sense of enclosure the designers were aiming for, he said.

“To see all the [plants] coming out: magic.”

Election 2026: In supermarket break-up battle, voters unlikely to defend duopoly – Editorial

New Zealand Herald September 24, 2026

New Zealand's supermarket industry is in the political spotlight as parties pitch plans to break up the Foodstuffs and Woolworths duopoly. Photo composite / NZME

Busting New Zealand’s supermarket duopoly is shaping up as one of the busiest battlegrounds of this election.

After years of governments talking around the issue while the Commerce Commission did studies, and everyone hoped an Aldi-shaped caped crusader of competition would ride to the rescue before anyone actually had to do anything – we are now awash in policies.

Parties are hoping to sign voters up for their loyalty programmes with promises to bring the price of doing a shop down, by making the market more competitive.

The two Foodstuffs co-operatives and Australian-owned Woolworths together hold a massive 82% share of the local market.

National and NZ First want to split Foodstuffs’ three grocery retail brands into two chains – Pak’nSave and New World/Four Square – both competing with Woolworths.

Labour proposes to force the same companies to start cleaving off their wholesale businesses from their stores, aiming to give smaller grocers a leg-up with better access to wholesale products.

The Greens have gone the Mamdani-esque route of seeking to create a publicly owned supermarket chain.

We’ll have to wait and see whether one of these turns out to be a doorbuster deal for voters or more window shopping.

Either way, the flurry of action is a nice change from handwringing over the outrageous cost of staying alive, while the weekly shop just kept getting more expensive.

National’s proposal has created the biggest waves. Foodstuff denied it was running a co-ordinated campaign against the policy after its store owners across the motu publicly expressed their distress last week.

From emotive interviews in the news to plaintive social media posts from no doubt hard-working people in branded vests.

The desire to put a human face on their businesses and co-operative is understandable.

And these messages have garnered more support on social media than one might expect given the widespread concern about living costs. Locals backing locals.

But the cynics are also well represented.

Kiwis are hurting financially, and the weekly grocery shop is a regular reminder of that.

While fuel prices have come down, food prices just keep going up.

Since January 2020, there has been just one month where the annual percentage change in the Stats NZ food price index went down, and by a measly 0.3%. The steepest post-Covid rises are locked in.

Many factors impact this, including other rising costs for businesses, but supermarkets are the face of it.

In the eyes of some, the oversized top end of this industry is reaching villain status in the face of this new political onslaught.

But it has never really escaped the cloud cast by the 2022 study that found supermarkets collectively made $1 million in “excess profits” every day.

Voters won’t be bringing breadsticks at dawn to the ballot box to defend the duopoly from Government intervention.

The Sam Walker files: Why the NRL’s greatest minds love this one-man mystery

Sydney Morning Herald September 25, 2026

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

Johnathan Thurston lets loose that trademark machine-gun cackle. Then lets slip a dirty little secret.

Sam Walker isn’t quite the mercurial, playmaking version of a small dog chasing cars in the street.

“And I got that sense very early on from watching Sammy,” one of the greatest halfbacks of all time says.

“It’s not like he goes out there and plays everything off the cuff at all. It just looks like it.”

Daly Cherry-Evans has played 377 NRL games, and would have had as many teammates, too. None have read the game like his latest, and last, NRL halves partner.

Andrew Johns hasn’t seen a halfback from the same mould as Walker in 15 years.

In total, the champion playmakers the Herald canvassed boast more than 1500 games of NRL experience between them, along with 14 premierships, 109 Origins and 124 Test matches. And they all agree.

Sam Walker – who will make a remarkable 27-day recovery from a syndesmosis injury to take on the Dolphins in Friday night’s grand final qualifier – is a playmaker unlike any other.

Ben Walker is the old playmaker who knows Sam best. Though Ben’s own two grand final wins in those all-conquering Broncos outfits of the late 1990s and successful Queensland coaching career pale next to his efforts as a family man and father.

Especially when he welcomes you into his favourite father-son catch-up with one of the NRL’s best halfbacks.

“The beauty of being able to talk to him after a game is asking what he saw in a moment before executing a pass or a kick,” Ben explains.

“And I know the way he plays looks a bit chaotic and off the cuff, but those explanations of, ‘I know this defender has a habit of turning in on this play’, or, ‘The fullback can drift too far across field late in a half’ – that’s where you learn he’s far more considered and more calculating than people would think.

“He’s certainly more methodical than most halfbacks that I’ve come across or coached, and I played with some great ones. He’d do it as a kid, too. Friday night footy at home, we’d be forever pausing, rewinding, asking why a play had happened or analysing it.

“So those big highlight plays, most times I’d say he would have been thinking about that well before the game during the week, if not two weeks beforehand.”

For Thurston, one skinny, silky and supremely skilled halfback can see another working out how to thrive, not just survive, in a sport of car-crash collisions with a Steeden pinballing about in the middle.

“I got the sense he knew how to handle a rushing defensive line, mostly because he had to,” Thurston says of his early encounters with Walker in his junior representative days.

“Sam’s quite comfortable in that uncomfortable space – when you’re digging deep into the line with the ball, he can react to the defence, make a good decision, knowing he could get whacked.

“You learn how to adapt to that. Because when you’re the smallest player on the field, you just have to.”

Johns, meanwhile, adores the risk-taker in Walker. The last-bob gambler who will take those calculations and considerations – all those weeks, months and years of pre-game legwork – and still try something most players wouldn’t dare dream of.

Like the cross-field, 50-metre kick that landed smack bang on the chest of Daniel Tupou against the Warriors in 2024.

“No one has played the game anything like the way Sam does – he treats the NRL and Origin like his own backyard,” Johns says.

“The closest I have seen is Alfie Langer, and they’re so similar in so many ways: risk-taking, impulsive, attacking halves. He’s just a breath of fresh air.”

Especially so for Cherry-Evans, who will line up alongside Walker at Suncorp Stadium on Friday night, knowing he may have only 80 minutes left in the NRL after 16 years at the top level.

How two of the game’s great freewheeling halves would combine and conduct Trent Robinson’s small galaxy of attacking stars posed one of this season’s curliest questions. Cherry-Evans’ signing at Bondi brought scrutiny on both sides of the scrum base.

“I might be the senior half in the combination,” Cherry-Evans says, “but I really love listening to Sam talk about footy. And what he sees in the game, I’d say it’s a bit different to anyone else I’ve come across.

“I’ve definitely learned things from him this year and considered things I probably never would have because the way he approaches the game is so unique. It’s the little things he sees, and they’ll stay in-house, but I’ll take them with me as a playmaker, for sure.”

Those who encounter Walker, 24, around Roosters HQ, or his and Langer’s old Norths Tigers stomping ground, notice two things: the ready smile, and seemingly never too far behind, a ready Steeden. A perusal of photos from any pre-game scene shows the No.7 with football seemingly glued to his hands.

Johns notes: “Sam will carry and pass with his left hand, but kick long with his right foot, and kick short with his left and right. I haven’t seen too many players ever with that much skill.”

Ben Walker confirms the rare ambidexterity.

“His handwriting is atrocious, but he writes left-handed,” he says. “Then when he plays cricket, he bowls and throws right-handed, which helps with his grubber kicks, because it means he’s guiding the ball down with his left hand.”

Luke Keary, meanwhile, enjoyed the same vantage point as Cherry-Evans, and Cooper Cronk offered a guiding hand when Walker first arrived at the club as a schoolboy prodigy.

Keary speaks the same way as Cherry-Evans about Walker.

“Ninety-five per cent of kids that come into the NRL are shaped by their junior system and a lot of that looks very, very similar to first grade – the same overall shapes and principles anyway,” he says.

“So Sammy arrives with this different outlook and, yeah, it takes him time to adapt, but I think that’s why he succeeded straight away for Queensland in Origin. Origin is built on those big moments and the quicker and bigger the game gets, then the better he goes, because he’s a bit different to most halves.”

Cronk’s comments as Roosters halves consultant a day after Walker’s SCG debut ring true five years and 106 games later. Particularly given the No.7’s absence was so keenly felt in the Tricolours’ week one finals loss to Penrith, when they were held scoreless from the 24th minute, despite Nathan Cleary being sent to the sin bin.

After an 18-year-old Walker carved up the Warriors in 2021, Cronk told Fox Sports’ NRL360 he had “nothing to do” with the teen tyro’s rise.

“The only 5 per cent that I’m going to work with [him on] is some strategy around why he runs. If he can understand why he ran or threw that pass, then you’ve got a player,” Cronk said.

“To be a dominant halfback you’ve got to be creative for yourself first before creating for other people, so your eyes have got to go see what’s in front of you – is there something for me?

“The eyes will tell you what to do, and then your instincts take off on the back of that.”

League columnist

Five years on from Cronk’s prescient words, the Roosters need Walker’s instinctive brilliance more than ever. Even if, as the champion playmakers explain and enthuse, there’s so much to his game than just impulse and aptitude.

The backdrop of his month-long recovery from ankle surgery, paused $6 million contract talks, Cherry-Evans’ looming NRL swansong and the ubiquitous spotlight that come with a glamour club are all just fruit for the sideboard.

Because as Johns says: “Sometimes all you can do is just sit back and wonder. How on earth did Sam Walker just do that?”

‘I’d feel ill after interviews because I said too much’: How Julia Jacklin eased into her new gem

Sydney Morning Herald September 25, 2026

Out of contract and flush with time, Julia Jacklin – one of Australia’s most celebrated songwriters – decamped to a pub for her new album.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

It’s very possible Julia Jacklin has watched Looking For Alibrandi more than any other person in the world. While crammed in a small Collingwood studio making her fourth album The Gem, Jacklin and producer Robert Muinos would sit and fiddle with recordings while Pia Miranda’s Josephine Alibrandi flitted on a TV screen stuck near the mixing desk.

“I would be scared to know how many times we watched [that film],” Jacklin says with a smile, sipping tea in a hotel lobby bar in Sydney’s Surry Hills.

Serendipitously, the film played in cinemas as part of its 25th anniversary celebrations while the band was recording; Jacklin and Muinos went to a screening and snapped a photo with actor Kick Gurry, who played Alibrandi’s love interest Jacob Coote.

“I never ask people for photos,” Jacklin laughs. “He was in the bar area, and I was like ‘I have to get a photo’. I’ve seen that movie a thousand times, and it’s a perfect movie … We either watched that or The Muppet Christmas Carol.”

If recording for The Gem sounds low-key, that’s because it was. After three acclaimed records recorded in various studios around the world – Don’t Let the Kids Win (2016), Crushing (2019), and Pre Pleasure (2022) – Jacklin wanted to embed herself in her beloved Melbourne, which she’s called home since moving from Sydney in 2017.

Jacklin, one of Australia’s most celebrated contemporary songwriters, was also out of contract with her label for the first time in her career, allowing her precious time to look around and find a place to whittle away at a new record. She settled on a pub called The Gem.

Located in Collingwood, The Gem is a local institution filled with quirky decor and a devoted local crew who will pile in to push the furniture against the walls so bands can play in the corner. When Jacklin first moved to the city, she became a regular.

Handily, Muinos’ Rat Shack studio is right above The Gem, a small but mighty space with a piano packed in the old laundry and a constant drip coming from the ceiling. Jacklin completely loved it.

“We had to ask the kitchen staff if they wouldn’t mind turning down the radio when we were doing a vocal take,” Jacklin says. “We had to think about the neighbours if we were going to do a drum take. We had to just ask people not to walk down the hall [sometimes] ... It was really tight. Some of my most favourite memories of recording music are from that little room, just all playing together.”

The ramshackle room also afforded Jacklin the environment to make the album she truly wanted to make. Her last album, Pre Pleasure, was a rich mix of orchestral and electronic elements. For The Gem, she wanted to strip back those elements and pursue something lo-fi, like some of her favourite records by Gillian Welch and Emmylou Harris.

“Sometimes you can get into this headspace of like, ‘Oh, but I’m not allowed to make a record like that’,” she says. “That ‘I’m not good enough to do something that’s lo-fi.’ It’s hard to explain… I love Pre Pleasure, but I thought I had to elevate the production so it was a very different process. Whereas with this one, I allowed myself to make something that I actually enjoy listening to and gave myself the permission to not feel like I needed each record to go up in production standards.”

It was also the longest time Jacklin has spent recording an album, stretching over a year and a half. She would turn up to the studio – waving hello to the hairdresser and tattooist that also worked above the pub – and get to work. “It felt like I was in the world while making music instead of tucked away in a hidden studio, which is usually how it goes,” she says.

The Gem sounds alive and live, like you’re hanging in that cramped laundry while someone hammers on the piano right next to you. There are lovely intrusions of the outside world – some street noise and sirens waft through the mic on certain tracks – and each instrument feels physical and near; you hear the scratches of nails on guitar strings and fretboards, you hear the full reaches of Jacklin’s distinctive, warm voice.

Lyrically, Jacklin has dug deeper into her constant study of love and relationships, how they can support and clash with personal liberation. God, or the idea of an omnipotent being (another lifelong theme throughout her work), is also present on The Gem.

“My use of God is not in any way tied to a Christian God,” she says, slowly picking her way through her sentences. “On this record in particular, I think I’m using God as a metaphor for having the ability to have more knowledge and power than I can have as a human being with my two feet on earth … and feeling so frustrated by the limitations of that.

“In particular,” she continues, “If I Had the Hand of God is about how intense this job can be and how much it takes me away from my family, my life at home, for a majority of my adult life. Because it’s all-encompassing when you’re doing it … It’s truly just very relentless.

“An album cycle can last for two years. As you get older, you can come out of a two-year album cycle and be like, ‘Oh my God, this person had a baby. This person’s been really struggling with something, but they didn’t tell me about it because they didn’t want to stress me out because I’m doing this’.

“I’ve gotten better at it, but I have found it quite difficult to do this work that I do feel services people in many ways. I do believe that I’m doing something good with my life, and I am communicating with people and helping myself and therefore others feel. But it means that you also can’t be the best person at home, which I’ve always struggled with.”

We’re meeting in the middle of a busy promotion schedule for The Gem. Jacklin would be the first to admit she’s not necessarily comfortable with press and promotion – particularly during this album cycle when nearly every interview is filmed and clipped to become short-form content. The somewhat grim reality of having to sell a product – herself and her work – weighs on her mind.

But certain things have become easier over the years. “I think when I was younger, I was so desperate to be understood,” she says. “So then sometimes the press cycle would actually seem like this way to talk about myself. If I was being really honest, I think a lot of the time I was actually talking to people in my life through interviews. You’re just desperately trying to be understood constantly … I used to feel ill [after interviews] because I would’ve said too much, I would’ve given too much away, because it felt good in the moment.

“The thing is I love music journalism,” she continues a bit later on. “I’m genuinely so passionate about it and I’m not one of those people that talk shit about Pitchfork, for example … I love that people take what we do seriously enough to write about it and to interrogate it. That’s the biggest compliment and it’s such an important part of such a symbiotic relationship of art.”

Aside from a new album, 2026 also marks the 10-year anniversary of Jacklin’s debut album, Don’t Let The Kids Win. It’s been on her mind today, in fact, while driving past her old school and university.

“I played [the title track] recently and one of the verses choked me up that used to not choke me up,” she says, smiling. “Things have happened in my life since I wrote it that made one of the things I was talking about feel a lot more intense … I don’t think I even fully understood it, but I was able to articulate that you never get used to time passing. If you brace against time, your life is just so much harder. You just have to relax in whatever way you can.”

Julia Jacklin’s The Gem is out now. Jacklin performs at the album’s namesake, The Gem in Collingwood in Melbourne, on Saturday and Sunday.

After two days with Evonne Goolagong Cawley, I couldn’t help but text her one final question

Sydney Morning Herald September 25, 2026

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

One magical muggy night, many moons ago, under the thatched roof of a beachfront backpacker bar on a quiet island off the coast of Thailand, I came to understand the fulsome greatness of Evonne Goolagong Cawley.

I was playing Trivial Pursuit at the time – specifically, a sun-weathered 1980s edition – and between sips of Singha and tom yum goong, it became unmistakably clear that the Australian tennis legend was my key to victory. Time and again, whether going for an orange wedge (sport and leisure) or a yellow one (history), “Evonne Goolagong Cawley” was the correct answer. I can’t remember the exact questions but her name – that instantly recognisable and unforgettable name – just kept coming up.

Who was the first Indigenous woman to win Wimbledon, in a career featuring seven Grand Slam singles titles? Evonne Goolagong Cawley.

Who was the first mother to win a Wimbledon singles title in the open era, achieving the feat in 1980, 66 years after Dorothea Lambert Chambers? Evonne Goolagong Cawley.

Card after card came and there was no escaping her exploits, which is no surprise once you take an even cursory glance at the gravity of her career. Eighty-six titles. Eighteen Grand Slam singles finals. Female world No. 1 in 1976. Australian of the Year in 1971.

Not only that but she was a transcendent joy within the sport – a player of legendary lightness, more poetic than prosaic. She did not storm the court, they said, but danced across it, more ballerina than baseliner. Study her closely and Evonne Goolagong Cawley begins to feel like an inexorable sporting truth – an Australian athletic exemplar and source of immense Aboriginal pride.

Who is the only tennis player in history to defeat Margaret Court, Billie Jean King, Martina Navratilova and Chris Evert, all in Grand Slam finals? Evonne Goolagong Cawley.

Who played in the singles final of the Australian Open seven years in a row throughout the 1970s, winning four titles? Evonne Goolagong Cawley.

As that Trivial Pursuit game edged closer to the death and the stars above Koh Chang came to life, whenever a question started with “Who” and I didn’t know the answer, I found myself blurting out “Evonne Goolagong Cawley!” (Related note: for questions starting with “Which”, I recommend answering “Battle of the Bulge”, and for questions starting with “What”, always consider “Coca-Cola”.)

Scoff if you will, dear reader, but I am here to tell you that I won that game, and handsomely so. And now, many moons later, I am in another beautiful, humid setting, approaching a modest suburban house near Noosa, to interview this tennis icon, cultural heroine and national treasure (not to mention trivia hack) – to ask new questions and see if she is still the answer.

Who says hello at the front gate wearing a blue linen shirt and colourful sheer skirt, with wavy brown hair framing a face of ineffable vitality? Evonne Goolagong Cawley.

Who takes me into her home and laughs and laughs and laughs – joyously and uproariously – 47 times (by my count) over the course of three hours? Evonne Goolagong Cawley.

Who is somewhat hobbled by health issues these days, yet unwaveringly pragmatic and unrelentingly positive? Evonne Goolagong Cawley.

And who has something important to say – something to share about life, and love, and the universe – after 75 years on this planet, 51 of them married to the same lovely man?

Evonne Goolagong Cawley does.

It’s been raining, and so everything outside has that luscious and alive feeling, but it’s damp, too, so we sit at the dining table off her open-plan kitchen and lounge. Evonne faces away from the window, chunky sunglasses handy, just in case the light becomes too much. We’ll discuss why later, along with the reason the love of her life, Roger Cawley, 76, is in an electric wheelchair, with a pair of walking sticks for getting up and down.

For the moment I want to go back to her Mum and Dad, Melinda and Kenny, and what Evonne got from them. Her dad, she says, was a very hard worker, which is how he ended up in the Riverina wheat-belt town of Barellan. He was a crack shearer and car- tinkerer – the great warm sun watching over his family. Her mum, meanwhile, was their placid moon – the type of person who strummed the guitar and sang her eight children to sleep every night. Every morning, she taught little Evonne perhaps the most important lesson of her life.

“Mum would always say, ‘Bye, have a lovely day!’ And then when I came back she would say, ‘Did you have a lovely day?’, because that’s what concerned her,” says Evonne. “She never asked how I’d played, and that followed me throughout my career – making sure you have fun.”

What stands out in her mind from that place and time isn’t golden fields, but the rivers that snaked through the region, from the Murray to the Murrumbidgee, and the fun her family had swimming and fishing. “Isn’t it funny, the detail that sticks out in your brain?” says Evonne, smiling. “I see the gum leaves touching the water, and sending out ripples.”

She was two years old when she found an old tennis ball, tattered and dirty, somewhere underneath the back seat of a junker her dad was working on in the front yard, but that ball became a treasure and totem – a magical object she squeezed for comfort. “I wonder if squeezing it strengthened my hand at an early age?” she ponders. “Later on, Dad cut a handle out of a piece of wood from an apple crate, and I used it to hit that ball against the house walls and the water tank.”

Inspiration came next, after a trip to the Barellan General Store, where she picked up a copy of Princess magazine, featuring a fairytale about a young tennis player who wins fame and fortune at a prestigious tournament in England. The place sounded so magical that I thought it must be make-believe, she writes in her new book, Only Ever Evonne (out September 29). When I found out Wimbledon was a real place in London, I was blown away.

The article became a treasured keepsake but also a self-fulfilling prophecy, daring her to learn the formalities and intricacies of the game, then master them. Her resulting playing style was characterised by fluid strokes, ethereal touch and graceful movement. Not for nothing did she earn the nickname “Sunshine Supergirl”.

When the ball connected with my racquet, she writes, I felt connected to everything: the court below me, the sky above me and the world around me. It was an almost spiritual experience.

The best way to describe her play? Maybe with one of those five-dollar words that grizzled sports editors hate: insouciance. She had a legendary lightness, rarely seen since, but echoed in the proprioceptive balance of someone like Roger Federer. He was famous for that same poised, one-handed backhand (with heavy topspin). Evonne spotted the resemblance immediately. “Watching him turn his shoulder, and go over and up, I’d think, ‘Ooooh, that must have felt gooood,’ ” she says, laughing, “with that complete, fluid follow-through.”

She remembers little about specific points, games, matches or sets, but knows exactly what it felt like in that state of flow. “I just remember the ball looked this big,” she says, holding her hands around an imaginary sphere the size of a human head, “and the line seemed so fat and wide,” her hands apart like she’s lifting a toaster. “There was no noise, and a feeling of complete slow motion. I just had so much time, and then I would hear the noise of the point finishing, with a winner.”

More laughter follows, and then a smiling sigh.

“I never watched myself,” she points out. “That goes back to what my coach used to say, ‘Don’t believe in what you read, believe in yourself.’ I carried that with me, too.”

That coach, of course, was Victor Edwards. Anyone who has seen the three-part ABC miniseries Goolagong will recognise the pivotal part “Mr Edwards” played in her story. Her first impression of him, from when she was nine years old, was of a tall man wearing a white V-neck jumper and cream slacks, who looked and sounded “immaculate”.

“The good points about him?” she says. “He was a very good coach. I really understood his directions.”

But working with him meant leaving home and boarding with his family in Sydney, where Evonne was shy and homesick, yet could at least test herself in serious junior tennis tournaments. She started living there temporarily at 11, and cried every night in those first weeks.

“The one thing that kept me going was that I just loved playing tennis. I loved it enough never to tell Mum that I cried every night, or any other thing that happened with my coach,” she says, pausing. “Basically, he was a dirty old man. But he didn’t get away with it. I stopped it pretty well.”

It started when she was a teenager, with his words – “If you want to learn about sex, come to me” – before progressing to deeds, such as the day he cornered her in the office of the local tennis club. “He gave me a tongue kiss, and I surprised myself and said, ‘You do that again, I’ll bite it off!’ ” she says, laughing. “I just walked out, and didn’t tell anyone else.”

Occasionally, his dark words and deeds coalesced, too, such as the moment in a taxi in London, when she was in her 20s and he turned to her, put his hand on her leg above the knee, and declared his drunken feelings – part affection, part threat. “You know I love you so much,” he said, with scotch on his breath, “I could rape you.”

Evonne simply turned and looked out the window, and realised she needed a plan for when they got back to the hotel. That plan was to make so much noise that people would inquire. When he followed her into her bathroom and tried to pull her into the bath, she called out loudly, and it worked. “I got a call in the room from reception – a noise complaint – and was able to say, ‘I’m sorry about that, Mr Edwards is just leaving.’ ”

He’s a consistent figure throughout her story, scolding her both publicly and privately after losses, spreading rumours about her weaknesses as a player, while also exercising restrictive financial control. She wasn’t free of him until the late 1970s.

“I guess I’d been through enough then that I knew how to handle it, and it just ran off my back. But now I think back to everything I’ve done, and I realise I was quite tough,” she says, beaming, “in a quiet sort of way.”

Evonne Goolagong Cawley, perhaps more than anyone I’ve ever met, sees the good over the bad. This is a conscious choice – a kind of governing philosophy for living. She was given elocution lessons as a young woman in Sydney, for example, and where many might see a transplanted Indigenous girl being forced to walk in a white world, all she saw was preparation for her travels and the adventure of life.

The culture shock was real, but largely a source of fun, not fear. Like the time she was flummoxed on a trip to Newcastle, when it was her turn to make tea. A group of women called out and asked what was taking her so long: “I said, ‘It takes a long time to get the tea out of these stupid little bags!’ ”

Nothing seemed to weigh her down. At Willoughby Girls High School in Sydney’s lower North Shore, she had to write an essay in which she pretended to be an early settler, and described her day in the new colony. “What happened during my day was I tended my sheep, smoked my tobacky, and when the Aboriginal people came on my land, I shot ’em,” she says. “I got 10 out of 10!” If that strikes you as inherently racist – that an Aboriginal child be asked to write an imagined account of bloody dispossession and is rewarded for doing so – it was nothing compared to facing her first overtly racist comment, after playing doubles against two older ladies.

“When it was time to shake hands, one of them said, ‘This is the first time I’ve had the pleasure of playing against a n-----.’ And I did get really upset,” she says. “I didn’t tell Mum until later, and she said, ‘Don’t worry bub, they’re just ig-or-ant’. Mum never went to school – ig-or-ant – but she knew everything. And she knew that’s what racism is about: ig-or-ance.”

Evonne knew that she had a platform for presenting Indigenous Australians in a positive light, but she felt no pressure to do so. “Being a role model never entered my mind,” she says. “Mum always said, ‘Just be yourself,’ and I just loved playing so much, it was all I ever wanted to do. I loved travelling to different countries, meeting different people.”

That became harder when she toured South Africa. Many felt let down by the decision to go, given the Apartheid policy, but the decision was made by her coach. She does remember, however, the stark dichotomy in the grandstands. “It did scare me when I first went there, to see all the crowds – people sitting in the black section and the white section, all in suits and hats.” But she also remembers a black woman approaching her to share a thought. “I don’t know what the fuss is about,” Evonne, laughing now, recalls her saying. “You’re not even black!”

Tennis great Margaret Court looked after her well on that visit, she recalls, eating with her every night. Court also used to invite her to stay at her home in Perth whenever they were playing against one another in Western Australia. Court, of course, has more than courted controversy in recent years, with her conservative faith compelling her to oppose same-sex marriage and compare transgender acceptance to “the work of the devil”. Long before that, she resisted calls to better compensate female players, and for good measure asserted that “lesbianism has ruined women’s tennis”.

Evonne doesn’t agree with those sentiments. But equally, she finds it hard to hang someone who showed her such kindness. Her husband, Roger, explains: “Margaret was just someone who had a religious experience,” he says. “God spoke to her at a time when she was feeling really down. But that point of view she has is so unnecessary, for such a great person.”

Evonne feels sad not just for the hurt caused to the LGBTQI+ community, but to those within their shared tennis community, like her good friend Billie Jean King. “I don’t agree with many of the things Margaret has said, but my main thing is that love is the main thing,” she says. “I believe that God is love for everyone.”

On the second day that I interview Evonne Goolagong Cawley, she comes armed with a prop. It’s a deck of “angel cards” – one of many so-called oracle decks (like tarot cards) enjoyed by people who consider themselves searchers. She bought them in a local crystal store. “Every few days, I do them before I go to sleep,” she says. “And last night after we spoke, this card came up.”

The title says Learning Experience, and it has a picture of a hooded figure holding a lantern, meant to convey inner peace and security, derived from overcoming hardships. Without the challenges that life has presented to you, you wouldn’t be the person that you are today, it reads. This is a time for you to reflect upon the incredible strength you have.

“I agree with that,” she says. “I feel that all these hardships in my life have made me a strong person.”

She shuffles the deck, fans them out, and I pluck one from the middle. The card is Holy Love: You are blessed to receive this card today, for it shows that you are being surrounded by loving energy, and the cup of your heart will be filled, until it overflows with goodness.

How nice.

“Oooh, I’ve never had that one,” she says. “Well there you go!”

The holy love story of Roger and Evonne begins in 1970 at a wine and cheese party on the outskirts of London, when the young man with long hair and roguish charm spotted the self-conscious tennis star on the fringe of the soirée. “I remember you coming in,” says Roger, “and I remember you staring, and I remember me staring, and that was it.”

That night, after a short drive through town, they found themselves dancing on the seventh green of Guildford Golf Course, at one point looking up from their giggling moonlight waltz – an English boy and an Aboriginal girl – to find a cow gazing up at them in puzzlement.

“I had read all about her in magazines,” Roger says. “But when I saw her, something went click, and from that moment on I was besotted, and by the end of the year I was totally in love.”

“He seemed really nice, this man – and funny! That’s what got me. He definitely knew how to make me laugh,” Evonne says. “We’ve been married 50 years now. Actually, 51!”

I wonder what they’ve learnt about love – or if they have any advice for people hoping to last that long?

Roger: “You’ve got me!”

Evonne: “I’ve forgotten!”

They devolve momentarily into cackles and guffaws.

Evonne: “You’ve gotta have a sense of humour – about everything. That’s what keeps us going through the really bad times.”

Roger: “We laugh at the silliest things, and the same things, at the same time.”

Their daughter, Kelly Inala Cawley, was born in 1977 – Inala meaning “peace” or “peaceful place”. Then son, Morgan Kyeema Cawley, was born in 1981 – Kyeema being “the dawn” or “new beginning”. And that was a beginning, in a way, of a whole new chapter in their mother’s life.

Evonne retired in 1983 and, as with almost any top-tier athlete, she went through a period of mourning – re-evaluating her reason for being. “It was so depressing,” she says. “It was like going into a dark space.” She was given medication but unfortunately has allergic or adverse reactions to many drugs, including antibiotics, anti-inflammatories and yes, anti-depressants. “I think I just sulked. I was miserable.”

Emerging slowly, she found a new way to enjoy life, and spent a lot of time fishing where they lived in South Carolina. “It’s so relaxing and beautiful. It’s calming. And being Aboriginal, you’re connecting to the land, the water, the trees – the beauty of the place – and you’re very much a part of it.”

Evonne’s father had passed away in 1974 at the absolute peak of her career, but when her mother finally died in 1991, it became the catalyst for a move home from the United States. She had seen and done so much. Had her hair styled by Vidal Sassoon and her photo taken in the Oval Office with [former US president] Ronald Reagan. She counted Kenny Rogers among her close friends, even travelling to the Bahamas to go scuba diving with the country star. “One time when Kenny came to stay with us in South Carolina, I called up Mum – who was a big fan – and I said ‘Mum, I’ve got someone here to talk to you.’ It made her so happy.”

Evonne wanted to be back on her mother’s country, too. Very early in her career, Edwards had disparagingly attributed any lack of focus on court as Evonne going “walkabout” – now she wanted to do so properly. She went to mission shacks and rock-art sites, always meeting with elders and gaining their permission to visit sacred places. She camped by rivers and slept under the stars and drove down a dirt track in South Australia, headed for the Anangu Pitjantjatjara Yankunytjatjara (APY) Lands, where she was allowed to do sacred women’s business.

“It was amazing. I can’t talk about it, but they were all laughing at the expressions on my face,” she says, laughing yet again. “That answered a lot of questions that I had. Very powerful. Good for the soul. I felt stronger and more connected to everything – to the universe.”

The tale of Roger and Evonne doesn’t end here, in this living room in southern Queensland, but their story is – at least right now – confined to this place. Ordinarily an active couple, this is the first year in many that they haven’t been able to travel, due to an array of health concerns.

First, Roger. He had a heart attack in both his 50s and 60s, and a third one only recently, along with a diagnosis of distal dystrophy – a genetic disorder characterised by the slow weakening and eventual atrophy of his muscles. “I woke up one morning and couldn’t move,” he explains. “Every muscle in my body was throbbing. I was scared stiff.”

His doctor had no idea what it was, but specialists at the Mayo Clinic eventually identified the problem and suggested vague forms of mitigation and preparation. “The thing they were putting off saying is that I can’t get rid of it,” he says. “There’s no way it goes away. It just gets worse. That took some adjustment.”

And Evonne?

“Here’s my bag of health issues,” she says, plonking a big plastic folder on the table between us, filled with notes and prescriptions. Her most pressing condition is the fallout from a concussion last year, after catching the toe of her shoe on a step outside her front door. “I just fell flat on my face and body, really hard, and I remember seeing stars. But I got up straight away.”

Fooled into a false sense of security, it wasn’t until a trip to Darwin in support of her charity – the Evonne Goolagong Foundation – that she felt the brunt of the blow. She was thirsty, and so tired, too, with vertigo. She shows me a leaflet about concussion in which she’s underlined in biro all the symptoms she experiences.

Trouble focusing. Trouble remembering things. Slow and foggy. Sensitivity to light and noise. Having trouble sleeping. Feeling dizzy. Feeling tired. Feeling anxious or worried. Feeling more frustrated.

I find it hard to picture her frustrated.

“I keep it to myself,” she responds, laughing.

The other issue is giant cell arteritis – an inflammatory condition causing everything from stiffness to soreness to throbbing headaches. She doesn’t know if it’s progressive or temporary. She knows she’s supposed to take Prednisolone for the concussion and Tocilizumab for the giant cell arteritis, but she has bad reactions to both drugs, including a bloated face and raised cholesterol. Oh, and she’s recently had a nasty bout of respiratory syncytial virus, and hip surgery to boot.

“It’s just been one thing after another, and all of it confusing,” says Roger. “One thing affects another, and that affects another, but when you’ve got five or six things going on in the body and you can’t take all the medicines required, it’s complicated.”

Meanwhile, they still have responsibilities with the Evonne Goolagong Foundation, which uses tennis to help Indigenous children access education, providing scholarships and encouragement and guidance. It’s hard for them to attend foundation events, but that means more time at home with their grandchildren.

“I make the popcorn, and I buy those little two finger Kit-Kats,” says Evonne, grinning. “They go straight to the other room, to watch what they want.”

It doesn’t really matter what they choose either, or even if it’s something she’s seen before.

Evonne: “That’s one of the good things about memory loss …”

Roger: ” … You can watch something again on Netflix because you don’t remember it!”

Time and again, “Rog” and “Gong” finish one another’s thoughts, almost like they’re playing a game of tennis, each exchange between them a serve and return, drop shot to net volley, lob followed by smash.

Roger: “We can’t play any more, or run, but we go out to lunch and laugh together.”

Evonne: “We’ve both got an illness, so we look after each other!”

Roger: “I think that when something happens, you just …”

Evonne: “… live with it, and try to laugh.”

I take that as my cue to leave the happy couple to their life, but later, after they’ve enjoyed a day of more giggles and angel cards – after they’ve been to the local golf club for a counter meal with the grandkids, and sat down to watch something new or old on Netflix, I text Roger one final question.

Not a Trivial Pursuit question, but a question that might sound trivial to anyone but Evonne. I want to know the answer to the question that used to greet her when she walked in the front door every night as a child – the one her mother asked: Did you have a lovely day?

Roger replies immediately: “She did, and thanks for asking!”

Then three text message dots appear, and they pulse like the ripple of a gum leaf on the surface of the river. Evonne has a return shot for me – one of those graceful and gracious single backhand winners down the line: “And she hopes you had a lovely day, too.”

Only Ever Evonne by Evonne Goolagong Cawley (Allen & Unwin) is out September 29.

Why 2009 was the greatest year in travel history

Sydney Morning Herald September 25, 2026

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

I want you to cast your minds back to a time when Donald Trump was still the host of a bikini contest, Netflix was mailing you DVDs, the financial crisis had rendered you borderline unemployable and Instagram hadn’t been invented; a time when we were still poking each other on Facebook, a platform used for hooking up with people, not destabilising democracy.

It might not sound like it, but this was the backdrop to the beginning of the greatest period in travel history: the year 2009.

Of course, it’s a bold claim to say that something is the greatest of anything, unless that something is a beer in Japan. And, while I’m sure people glorify the Before Sunrise romance of travel in the ’90s, or smoking on planes in the ’70s, those planes also got hijacked way more often. And if I hooked up with the love of my life, agreeing to meet them at a train station in Vienna in six months’ time, I’d say that was a wildly impractical way to start a relationship.

This is what made 2009 such an incredible year in the history of travel. Not the lack of plane hijackings (although that certainly helped), but the fact that it had the benefits of technology, before technology got around to killing the benefits of analogue travel.

There was mystery and uncertainty, freedom and flexibility. Even with infinite access to information, it still felt like we were discovering something about the world, as opposed to walking through it in secondhand shoes.

Sign up for the Traveller newsletter

The latest travel news, tips and inspiration delivered to your inbox. Sign up now.

With that in mind, I want you to come with me on a journey back to the halcyon days when guidebooks and online booking platforms coexisted in perfect harmony. To a time when a photograph was a memory, a story was in a book, and travel was as good as it ever was, and better than it ever will be. It might be a vanished era, but with the magic it left behind, you can still relive the joy of travelling like it’s 2009.

When reaching for this tree, it’s best to start with the lowest-hanging branch; 2009 was the year before Instagram started. I’m not going to say Instagram ruined travel, but it did dramatically expand the audience to our trips.

It became all too easy to share our journeys and reap the delicious dopamine of likes and followers. No longer were we lugging around Kodachrome slides in our rucksacks, nor did we have to waste hours at internet cafes uploading photos on dodgy connections. Phones made it instantaneous, filters made it polished, and what was supposed to be a memory became a piece of content.

Instagram was the grease on a slippery slope, and we’ve been sliding down it ever since. It destroyed our ability to be present in the moment when we travel – we’ve become so concerned with capturing and sharing it, we’ve forgotten how to enjoy the moments themselves.

How to travel like it’s 2009 Ditch social media, even if it’s only for your trip. I did for years, until the Tripologist (aka Michael Gebicki) told me it was career suicide (far be it from me to argue with his wisdom). My time away from social media was blessed. I stopped caring about what other people did or thought and focused only on what was in front of me.

I only booked one hotel in 2009, and it took me a solid hour of stumbling around Shinjuku Station to try to find it. At one point, I was so spun out, I pulled up at a konbini, grabbed a beer and a fluffy egg sando, and entertained the thought of camping there for the night.

To compare, when I was travelling around South-East Asia that same year, I didn’t book a single thing and spent many joyful afternoons walking up and down beaches in search of the cheapest guesthouse I could find.

It was a golden age for the romance of spontaneity and the convenience of technology, when you could comfortably book hotels online in Japan (and be fairly certain of how to find them), but didn’t have to book a single thing in places such as Thailand. There were still hundreds of family-run guesthouses that didn’t even have Wi-Fi, let alone a profile on booking. com or Airbnb.

How to travel like it’s 2009 There are still places in Thailand you can turn up to with no plans, and nothing booked. My favourite is Koh Phayam where, despite a growing presence on online booking platforms, a number of bungalows are the kind you find with your feet, not your fingers.

Applying for jobs in 2009 was wild. Employers would straight-up tell you they were going to pay you next to nothing, treat you like dirt and, if you didn’t want the job, that would be fine, because 10 other people would jump at the opportunity.

In the face of this, travel seemed like a pretty good alternative. And the best bit? Those one-off cash payments, the ones that were meant to stimulate the Australian economy during the Global Financial Crisis. Well, I used mine to stimulate an economy, alright, but it wasn’t the Australian one; I took that money to South-East Asia and stretched it as far as it could go.

But it wasn’t just the free money that made this such a good time to travel. The downturn was global, flights were reduced and it was the worst year for travel numbers this side of the century (COVID excluded). If you were lucky enough – or willing to go into debt – you could experience what it feels like to travel when tourist economies are cheering your arrival, not lamenting your presence.

How to travel like it’s 2009 I’m not in a financial position to cut you a cheque for 900 dollarydoos, but I can suggest avoiding destinations such as Bali and Barcelona, and travelling to places such as Fukushima, where tourists are considered a blessing, not a burden.

To save a few bucks, I’ve recently gone back to staying in hostels. Something I’ve noticed when staying in these places is that people have largely stopped talking to each other, and it’s not uncommon to walk into the common room and see a dozen kids glued to their phones.

It’s absolute madness, as I’ve long believed that conversation is a traveller’s greatest commodity. To travel and not talk to strangers is like eating an egg without salt. You can do it, but it lacks the zest that makes it special.

Where this left us in 2009 was with the perfect combination of physical and digital connection. Through the general ether of the internet, all of us were connected, but conversation was still the true currency of the traveller. I learnt about all my favourite places through word of mouth, but I could also meet a fellow traveller in Cambodia, add them on Facebook, and then end up crashing on their couch in London nine months down the track (thanks, Mike).

How to travel like it’s 2009 Talk to strangers and stop using your phone as a crutch. It’s easy to trawl through restaurant reviews or reels, but learning about the world through that tiny screen will never compare to talking to someone and uncovering the real thing.

Anywhere digital nomads sniff out a cheap room and decent Wi-Fi, you’ll find oat milk lattes. These people will fly halfway around the world just to have all the comforts of home, all the while celebrating the fact that they’re only paying half as much to enjoy them.

I call out oat milk lattes here, but this isn’t fair to oats or their milk; it could have easily been the acai bowl, or avocado toast, or any menu item with “Buddha” in the name. What we see is, essentially, homogenisation – places that were once hubs for new experiences have become soft landings for anyone with the purchasing power of their country of origin.

Of course, some might say that destinations such as Koh Phangan and Canggu were already ruined in 2009, and that if you really wanted to experience them, you would have had to Eat, Pray, Love your way there 10 years earlier. But at least there was still a semblance of originality, and not the Ctrl-V versions of the destinations we have today.

How to travel like it’s 2009 Drink coffee where the locals do. It might be as black as my heart, or as sweet as condensed milk, but it’s still better than supporting businesses that are made exclusively to cater to travellers who want away to be much the same as home.

As a celebrated stingy traveller, I love a budget airline. I’d rather save a few bucks on a flight than watch the latest season of The White Lotus, and no depressing meal wrapped in foil could ever taste better than arriving in a country with an appetite.

But that doesn’t mean I’m not a massive hypocrite.

And while I love what budget airlines have done for my own wallet, it’s hard to deny their correlation with the rise of overtourism. They’ve made flying cheaper and more accessible, but in doing so, they’re also bending destinations under the weight of their own success, and not all those destinations are happy about it.

It’s not like budget airlines weren’t around in 2009 (my flight to Japan back then was a Jetstar sale for a glorious $500), it was that their market share was still small enough that cheaper access didn’t come at the expense of locals the way it does now.

And while overtourism already existed in places such as Venice, you could still discover a place such as Kyoto without the crush of tourists that compounded over the next decade.

How to travel like it’s 2009 I can’t, in all good conscience, tell you not to fly on a budget airline, because I do it all the time. But I can say that once you land somewhere and plan to travel around a bit, take a train or a bus because it’s way more rewarding than flying, as some of the best parts of a destination are the ones we all too often fly over.

These days, all you have to do is whack a question into Google, and our AI overlords will skim the internet, like I skimmed SparkNotes, to spit out the answer. And, based on the travel planning I’ve done using these tools, they do just about as well as I did in my exams (spoiler: not great).

What made 2009 awesome for this was that between blogs, forums and Wikitravel, you could find just about any answer you were searching for, but without having those answers rammed down your throat.

How does one cross the border from northern Thailand to Laos? Well, the good news is some random on the internet has taken the time to write a play-by-play of the experience, making an obscure border crossing slightly more accessible to the wayward traveller.

You had The Man in Seat 61, the guides on Travelfish, and even TripAdvisor, back when it was more of a user-generated forum, and not another excuse to sell tours. It meant that you had enough information to make the unknowable achievable, and still enough mystery to call it an adventure.

How to travel like it’s 2009 Don’t use AI to plan your trips. You can’t trust everything it tells you, and it changes the way our brains retain information. Instead of finding the answers, we’re being given them, and it makes travel planning way less mentally rewarding.

I loved my digital camera. It was a wonderful, waterproof thing that tragically ended up at the bottom of the Mekong, and no matter how many rocks I stuffed in my pockets, I could never quite get deep enough to reach it.

This camera (RIP) represented something that I loved about travel in 2009; not everything was being recorded. Some things could never (and should never) be captured, and taking a camera with you was a conscious choice.

Sometimes, it just wasn’t worth the hassle.

But these digital cameras also saved us from the horrors of camera film and waiting to see your images. After losing my camera, I decided to go full analogue, buying a film camera and using it for the rest of my trip. I lugged around a dozen rolls of film for a whole month. When I finally got home and had them developed, there were photos of elbows, blurry streets and people so overexposed, it looks as though they were being abducted by aliens.

How to travel like it’s 2009 A digital camera is an incredible travel accessory, simply for the separation it puts between you and your phone. Any step that keeps your phone in your pocket (or better yet, in your bag) is another step towards immersion in a trip.

Back in 2006, I taught English in Hanoi. I stayed in a guesthouse with a bathroom that flooded whenever I showered, a television that required antenna ballet and a door that didn’t close, no matter how much I tried to jam it into the warped frame. Couple this with the fact that my backpack was full of cash and traveller’s cheques, and you can understand what being one robbery away from total ruin did to my opinion of accessible ATMs.

Fast-forward only a few years to 2009, and it felt like the world was still big enough to discover something new, but the infrastructure was robust enough that you could easily access cash, cold beer and the occasional burst of air-conditioning.

And it’s not just about the cold beer (although that can’t be undersold), but more important things such as adequate medical attention. Even when I dislocated my shoulder in Laos, I could get an X-ray, a poorly translated consultation and some wicked painkillers, as opposed to trying to pop my shoulder back in with nothing but rice whiskey and a solid yank from a mate.

How to travel like it’s 2009 Infrastructure continues to improve, and while the world is getting smaller every day, we should never deny locals access to things for our sense of nostalgia; if they want flat-screen televisions and high-speed internet, then far be it from us to stand in their way.

Ride-sharing appsAs someone who has been robbed in taxis twice, the advent of ride-sharing has been a blessing. No more getting dropped off in the completely wrong part of Phnom Penh (and having to pay to go back to where I asked). I mean, who can be arsed with haggling?

Google FlightsSome people scroll TikTok, some people play Candy Crush, and some people (me) spend their time strategising and hypothesising on Google Flights. It’s a silly little habit, one that recently nabbed me $1400 flights from Auckland to Buenos Aires, an absolute steal in this economy.

Travel writer

Aviation safetyDespite what a bunch of recent stuff-ups at Sydney Airport might suggest, we really are living in the golden age of aviation safety. And if the entertainment is meh, and the food is garbage, the only thing I really care about is whether my plane sticks the landing on the other side.

MapsThere was nothing quite like scribbling down the directions to your hostel in a notebook and then trying to decipher your hieroglyphics at two o’clock in the morning. While I bemoan maps for how they’ve transformed life into something reviewed and rated out of five stars, my terrible sense of direction means I am unable to go back to a life without them.

Text translatorsWhen I was in China, I ordered by pointing at items on the menu and hoping for the best. Now, thanks to text translators such as Google Lens, I’ll never end up with a trough of chillies in front of me again. My brother ate the whole thing. He swore they didn’t burn on the way in, but the whiteness of his face the next morning said they sure as hell burned on the way out.

For Olivia Berry, the 21-year-old photographer whose images are on these pages, travelling like it’s 2009 means resisting the urge to have every experience pre-approved by an algorithm.

Her camera of choice is a Fujifilm X-T30 II, a digital camera with film-inspired settings that she carries everywhere, rather than relying on her phone.

“You can pull out your phone at any time and take photos of anything without thinking twice,” she says. With the Fujifilm, she adjusts the ISO, shutter speed and aperture herself. “There is way more thought behind capturing a photo this way and it’s more enjoyable.”

Her travel bag also contains watercolour paints, a notebook and pen, and whatever flyers or leaflets strangers hand her along the way. She uses the notebook for directions, phone numbers and the occasional diary entry, and sometimes paints a view rather than photographing it.

The same instinct shapes where she goes. Berry asks locals where they eat with their families, wanders rather than searches and has deliberately skipped places because they were everywhere on Instagram.

“When I was in Florence, all my friends and I had been hearing about was the ‘wine window’, a hole from which you order and receive your drink. We ended up walking past it accidentally. It was surrounded by people standing with their phones waiting to record the moment their drink came through the wall.

“There’s nothing wrong with this, it’s just not for me. If I’m visiting a country or place I’m visiting it because I want to feel what it’s like to live there,” she says. “That’s the true experience.”

‘Cracking auction, Gromit!’ Original Aardman puppets go under the hammer

The Guardian Thu, 24 Sep 2026 21:41:31 GMT

Wallace and Gromit stop-motion models and other beloved creations raise money to train new generations of animators

Wallace’s reaction as the auction got into full swing might have been a trademark “good grief!” – and the enthusiasm of some of the bidding could have caused even the phlegmatic Gromit to show surprise.

Fans of Wallace and Gromit and other beloved creations of Aardman Animations seized the chance to grab souvenirs when more than 200 pieces – including Wallace, Gromit, Shaun the Sheep and Chicken Run puppets from Aardman productions – went under the hammer on Thursday.

Sought-after items included Wallace and Gromit stop-motion models from the Bristol studio’s hugely popular 2024 film Vengeance Most Fowl.

Lot 216, for example, was Wallace in his traditional outfit of a knitted green tank top, red tie and brown trousers. The catalogue said he was in “smashing condition”, and gave details of his construction: “Wallace’s head is moulded from clay; while his body is made of silicone to facilitate smooth repositioning by the animators.

“He has a skeleton, just like every salt-of-the-earth lad, it’s just that his happens to be made of metal. His teeth, shirt collar, tie, pen, and pencil are fast-cast resin and his eyes are plastic.” It sold for an eye-popping £50,400.

A puppet of Gromit on all fours from the same film was “crafted over a fully jointed internal metal armature, allowing him to be held in his most natural pose”. It fetched £31,500.

The catalogue made it clear these were not toys but pieces of art needing special packaging, shipping and careful handling. “Please also be aware that exposure to extreme temperatures may cause damage,” it said.

Another eye-catching lot was number 219 – Wallace and Gromit’s nemesis, Feathers McGraw, disguised as a nun. The catalogue reminded bidders of one of the best Wallace and Gromit lines: “Feathers McGraw? Don’t be ridiculous. That’s just an innocent nun, out for a pleasure cruise.”

It went for more than £30,000 while a second Feathers puppet – with the villain wearing his red rubber glove disguise to make out he was a chicken rather than a sinister penguin – did even better, selling for almost £57,000. Crime, it appears, does pay.

It was not only Wallace, Gromit and Feathers that proved popular. Aardman aficionados snapped up pieces related to the studio’s early days, including clay puppets of Morph and his pal Chas.

Every lot started at £100 but as bidding got under way at teatime in London, it was clear they were not going to stay low for long.

The Morph and Chas puppets, made from plasticine by Aardman co-founder Peter Lord and accompanied by handwritten care instructions, one of the first lots to be auctioned, sold for £3,780.

Mischievous Morph first appeared in 1977 as part of Take Hart, before starring in his own series of adventures. Another lot – lunch for six with Lord in Bristol – was bought by someone for more than £11,000. A stop-motion masterclass with an Aardman animator sold for just over £20,000.

Storyboards from Wallace & Gromit: the Wrong Trousers signed by another Aardman grandee, Nick Park, went for almost £4,000. A 9cm-tall clay rabbit that appeared in The Curse of the Were-Rabbit cost almost £10,000.

Bidders whose budget could not stretch to a Wallace or Gromit puppet could buy more modest souvenirs such as lot 89 – dry stone walls and gate from the Shaun the Sheep TV series. That came with “adhesive remnants from where the pieces were secured to the set”. It sold for a more affordable £567.

The sale, run by the memorabilia auction house Propstore, marked the 50th anniversary of the studio, with the profits to be used to train new generations of animators.

Ngaio Harding-Hill, the director of attractions and live experiences and archive at Aardman, described it as an “unprecedented opportunity” to own a part of the studio’s 50-year history.

Harding-Hill said the collection had been carefully curated by the Aardman team to make sure the studio’s five decades were reflected in the auction.

She said: “Proceeds from the auction will be invested in talent development initiatives across Aardman, including bursaries at our world-class training facility, the Aardman Academy, meaning every sale is contributing to nurturing the next generation of animation talent.”

I was arrested protesting Netanyahu’s New York visit. Here’s why we took a stand

The Guardian Thu, 24 Sep 2026 21:20:55 GMT

I refuse to play host to a man who has overseen the slaughter or injury of more than 64,000 children in Gaza with American taxpayer dollars. I refuse to be complicit in genocide

Benjamin Netanyahu belongs at The Hague; not in the streets of New York City, and certainly not before the United Nations general assembly. The international criminal court has a warrant out for his arrest for war crimes and crimes against humanity. The UN’s own commission of inquiry has found that Israel is committing genocide in Gaza and named Netanyahu as its chief architect.

As the Democratic nominee for New York’s 13th congressional district, I refuse to allow a war criminal to roam the streets of our city unchallenged. I refuse to play host to a man who has overseen the slaughter or injury of more than 64,000 children in Gaza with American taxpayer dollars. I refuse to be complicit in genocide.

That is why I was arrested today outside of the United Nations alongside hundreds of my fellow New Yorkers.

Israel has killed more than 73,000 people in Gaza. It has bombed hospitals, schools, places of worship, fishing boats, and refugee tents. It has collectively starved an entire population as a tool in its genocide.

It has subjected men, women and children to systematic sexual torture and imprisonment. It has threatened to kill people for flying kites, killed more than 1,000 people since its so-called ceasefire, and fired 335 bullets into a car carrying five-year-old Hind Rajab.

And when it comes to consequences, world leaders offer carefully worded statements that don’t even amount to a slap on the wrist.

Here in the US, establishment Democrats and Republicans alike have shielded Netanyahu from prosecution for his crimes and sent over $21bn of our tax dollars in just two years to fund Israeli bombs.

The Biden and Trump administrations both obscured evidence, lied about what Israel was doing in Gaza, funded the carnage, and isolated and arrested people that spoke out against it. Just last week, the Trump administration proposed a $2.8bn weapons sale to Israel including 2,000lb bombs.

New Yorkers refuse to be silent. That’s why today’s civil disobedience, led by Jewish Voice for Peace, NYC-DSA, Sunrise Movement, CAAAV, Palestinian Youth Movement, Adalah Justice Project, the US Campaign for Palestinian Rights and more had 400 participants including more than 100 people arrested to demand an end to this injustice.

And NY-13, and New York City, is with us. This summer, Harlem, Washington Heights, Inwood and the West Bronx unseated a five-term, Aipac-backed incumbent. Their message was clear: invest in their babies here at home, not in bombs dropped abroad.

They made me their Democratic nominee with a mandate to pass legislation like the Block the Bombs Act and fight back against our country’s insatiable war machine. Across this city, New Yorkers elected candidates to Congress and the state assembly who’ll fight to stop the bombs, divest from death, and invest in a politics of life.

Families in Palestine, Lebanon and Iran are not our enemies.

Our enemy is a system where billionaires get rich from stoking hatred and war while our own communities go without. Tonight, shelters across uptown and the Bronx will be full. This past year, more than 100,000 children in New York City’s public schools have experienced homelessness. And right now, families are feeling the physical toll of cuts to Snap and Medicaid, and New York City Housing Authority residents are once again forced to sleep in inadequate housing.

I ran for Congress because I am done being told that there is never enough money for our communities while watching our government write blank checks to enact atrocities. Every dollar spent on slaughtering communities abroad is a dollar stolen from our communities here at home.

In 1967, Dr Martin Luther King Jr stood at the pulpit of Riverside church in my district and warned that a country that spends more on war than “on programs of social uplift is approaching spiritual death”.

Members of Congress have a responsibility to act with courage in the face of grave injustice, not to continue funding it. Unfortunately, nearly 60 years later, not much has changed.

Palestinians are facing unthinkable conditions every single day under an Israeli apartheid regime that that disappears men, women and children into military prisons known for their physical, sexual and psychological torture.

And here at home, families in my district have to endure their schools, clinics and food assistance being cut to pay for war, and ICE kidnapping our neighbors for speaking up for Palestinians, while nearly 40% of the babies in my district are growing up in poverty.

From NY-13 to Palestine, all children, and all people, deserve the safety and the resources to live dignified lives. That’s why I take to the streets, and that’s why I’m headed to Congress: to stop sending our tax dollars to arm genocide, to end senseless wars, and to build a government accountable to the working people of this country.

Our communities deserve leaders with an unwavering moral compass, who understand that our shared humanity is sacred, and that fights to build a politics of life even when it is politically costly. If that requires my arrest, so be it.

Darializa Avila Chevalier is the Democratic nominee for New York’s 13th congressional district
