Far-right activist Daniel Thomas charged over alleged dinghy slashing in Channel

The Guardian Thu, 24 Sep 2026 21:20:36 GMT

Thirty-seven-year-old charged with one count of criminal damage and failing to disclose his phone pin to police

The far-right agitator and anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas has been charged with criminal damage and failing to disclose his phone pin to police following an incident in the Channel on Tuesday, where he allegedly slashed a dinghy while a French rescuer was on board.

Thomas, 37, of no fixed abode, has been charged with one count of criminal damage along with an offence under section 53 of the Regulation of Investigatory Powers Act 2000 (Ripa), for allegedly failing to comply with a notice to disclose a phone pin to police.

He has been remanded in custody to appear at Basingstoke magistrates court on Friday.

The charge came as the Home Office recorded 781 arrivals in 10 boats on Wednesday, the highest number for a single day so far this year. Responding to the figures, the government said it would “push further and harder” to crack down on the people organising the crossings.

Chris Derrick, of the Crown Prosecution Service, said: “The CPS has decided to prosecute Daniel Thomas following an investigation by Hampshire Constabulary into an incident on Tuesday 22 September.

“Our prosecutors have worked to establish that there is sufficient evidence to bring the case to court and that it is in the public interest to pursue criminal proceedings.

“We remind all concerned that proceedings against the defendant are active and he has the right to a fair trial.”

Hundreds of people gathered outside Basingstoke investigation centre, where Thomas was believed to be held, on Thursday evening.

They included scores of mainly men dressed all in black, though the vast majority were not covering their faces. One person said he had come from Manchester to take part in the protest.

Some chanted: “Free DT” and “Oh, Danny, Danny”. One person had brought a sign reading: “Get Danny out.”

Extra police were drafted in from forces as far away as Kent, and a police drone hovered above the protest.

Thomas’s footage appeared to show him approaching one of the dinghies, which was empty, shouting: “Let’s get rid of that boat.” After the rescue worker got onboard, Thomas shouted: “Get off the boat. You’ve got time to get off the boat.” His footage shows his boat speeding away before the rescue worker climbed back on to the larger boat.

Thomas, who goes by the name Danny Tommo, had spent the afternoon in a boat, filming himself as he tracked two dinghies carrying asylum seekers from France to the UK. The livestreamed footage was watched by more than 200,000 people.

A longtime associate of fellow far-right activist Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, AKA Tommy Robinson, Thomas this summer gathered dozens of nationalist protest groups under the umbrella anti-immigration movement Patriot Platform.

The organisation was behind marches this month in Dover and Portsmouth, when masked men in black gathered and protested over immigration and asylum policy. Thomas repeatedly told his followers they should march silently, without violence, and avoid doing anything that could lead to arrests.

Thomas apparently managed to film and upload footage of his own arrest before police were able to stop him. On Wednesday night a 56-second clip was uploaded to his YouTube platform showing a police officer telling him he was being arrested on suspicion of criminal damage and “recklessly endangering someone’s life”.

Thomas said: “I understand. I knew this was coming.”

The latest Home Office figures put renewed focus on the government’s handling of small boat arrivals in the UK. A government spokesperson said: “Our progress this year in tackling small boats is indisputable, with crossings down by 42% and the lowest recorded over the summer months since 2020. But this week’s events show that while the peaks we are seeing are far below those of previous years, we need to push further and harder in order to eradicate this vile trade.”

Wednesday’s arrivals take the provisional total for Channel crossings for the year so far to 18,565. Home Office data indicates this is down 42% on this time last year (32,188) and 26% below the figure at this stage in 2024 (25,165).

This week ministers have also been concerned by two uncontrolled landings from the Channel in two days. Most small boats carrying asylum seekers to the UK are escorted to shore by rescue services or Border Force vessels, and no unescorted small boats had been recorded since 6 September 2025.

The education secretary, Lucy Powell, said: “You can’t stop everything all of the time,” after 21 people were detained when a boat evaded Border Force to reach the beach of Samphire Hoe in Dover on Wednesday. Another dinghy made an uncontrolled landing in Folkestone on Monday morning.

The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, has ordered an urgent review by Border Security Command, describing the failure to intercept the two boats as “not acceptable”.

Speaking on BBC Radio 4’s Today programme, Powell said: “Of course, it’s a concern. That’s why the home secretary has demanded and ordered this urgent review, because this is not what we want to see. This is not acceptable.”

On Thursday a 42-year-old man was jailed after throwing a plastic bottle at a police line and swearing at officers during an anti-migrant protest in Portsmouth.

Del Somerville, of Paulsgrove, was sentenced at Portsmouth crown court to two years in prison having previously pleaded guilty to the charge of violent disorder. He is the first to be sentenced over violence that erupted after the arrival of a small boat in the Hampshire city on 6 September.

Judge Daniel Sawyer told him his sentence would act as a deterrent to others after subsequent protests in the area. Describing Somerville as a “thug”, he told the defendant: “Police officers dedicate their lives to the protection of the public regardless of their own views, the very least they can expect is that those who engage in protests treat them with respect and the courts punish those who assault them.”

NHS bodies in England impose two-year minimum wait for ADHD and autism assessments

The Guardian Thu, 24 Sep 2026 21:00:30 GMT

Patient groups decry ‘scandalous’ delays as four integrated care boards take step due to soaring demand for diagnoses

NHS bodies are forcing people with suspected attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and autism to wait at least two years before they can be assessed as they struggle to meet surging demand for diagnoses of neurodiversity.

Four NHS integrated care boards (ICBs) covering large regions of England have adopted the approach because they cannot afford the cost of the number of assessments that people are seeking.

Patient groups are warning that the “scandalous” delays such policies involve may damage children’s chances of succeeding at school, deny people the help they need to manage their lives, and increase the risk of suicide. The charity ADHD UK denounced minimum waits as “heartless and dangerous”.

In all, 15 ICBs, which between them cover 19 million people, have brought in various ways of rationing assessments for ADHD and autism to try to balance their books. These include limiting the number of assessments the ICBs will pay for in any given year and using “clinical prioritisation” criteria to restrict assessment to those with the most serious signs of neurodiversity.

Disclosure of the NHS’s widespread efforts to delay and deny access to assessments comes before the publication of a major government-commissioned review of the colossal increases in diagnoses of mental illness, as well as ADHD and autism, in recent years. It was ordered last year by Wes Streeting, the then health secretary, amid concern that the weight of requests for assessment, diagnosis and care was overwhelming the health service’s ability to meet demand.

The 700-page report of the review, led by Prof Peter Fonagy, was due to be published on Thursday but was unexpectedly postponed until early next month.

Sources familiar with the document told the Guardian that it painted a detailed picture of how the fast-rising demand for help with mental illness conditions, ADHD and autism has left those affected struggling to get rapid access to NHS care and increasingly reliant on private providers.

Fonagy’s report raises serious concerns about the sector, especially about the consistency and quality of the assessments it provides and the fact that there are “financial incentives associated with assessment activity”.

It also lays bare the scale of the challenge that the increasing number of diagnoses of mental illness, ADHD and autism pose for the NHS, as well as schools, employers and families, by highlighting up to 24-fold rises in the prevalence of neurodiversity in boys since 2000.

It reveals that the percentage of seven- to 18-year-old boys with autism rose from 0.2% in 2000 to 4.7% in 2025. Prevalence among boys aged six to 11 rose from 0.4% to 6.3% over the same period – a 16-fold jump.

Similarly, the percentage of seven to 18-year-old boys diagnosed with ADHD rose from 0.4% to 5.1% between 2000 and 2025 – an almost 13-fold leap – and from 0.7% to 3.8% – up five-fold – among boys aged six to 11, according to figures provided by the Clinical Practice Research Datalink.

“Minimum waits” after referral by a GP mean people in the areas affected cannot seek an assessment by a private sector provider. That is even though private clinics now undertake half of NHS-funded assessments of ADHD and a third of those for autism, because many patients exercise their legal right to choose non-NHS care, given the NHS’s own limited capacity to do the assessments.

Such curbs by the NHS are likely to force those who can afford it to pay a private provider for an assessment for themselves or their child, which can cost several thousand pounds. They are being implemented at a time when there are 960,000 people in England waiting for an ADHD assessment and another 295,000 awaiting one for autism.

West Yorkshire NHS integrated care board has introduced a minimum waiting time of two years from referral for anyone seeking an ADHD or autism assessment with an independent provider. That was in response to its bill for such assessments soaring from £7m in 2023-24 to £21m last year, it said.

The West Yorkshire ICB’s decision applies to the 2.4 million people for whom it commissions and pays for care in Leeds, Bradford, Kirklees, Calderdale and Wakefield. Its area includes the constituency of Pontefract, Castleford and Knottingley – the parliamentary seat of the health secretary Yvette Cooper.

Private providers that the North East and North Cumbria ICB funds to assess people “are working to an approximately 78-week minimum waiting time for an initial assessment”, it says.

Somerset ICB is operating a minimum wait of 52 weeks, while the equivalent in Devon is a lot lower, at 14 weeks. Kent and Medway ICB has also decided to impose a minimum wait.

This month, in Hampshire and the Isle of Wight, assessment for ADHD and autism has been restricted to those patients who meet the ICB’s priority criteria.

“It’s scandalous that any NHS body should impose a two-year minimum wait for ADHD and autism assessments,” said Henry Shelford, the chief executive of ADHD UK.

“This is the health service denying people care they need, and care that is available, and slamming the door shut on people who need an assessment of their symptoms to give them a diagnosis and unlock essential care that helps people hold down jobs, stay in education and stay out of crisis services.

“A minimum wait is heartless and dangerous. It is institutionalised cruelty.’

A spokesperson for Finally Seen, which tracks NHS restrictions on the right to choose, said: “A two-year minimum wait is not a waiting list. It is a locked door with a date on it.

“The right to choose still exists on paper. In practice it is being rationed by the calendar, which is a blunt and bleak way to treat a legal right.”

The British Medical Journal recently revealed that 17 of the 36 ICBs had introduced minimum waits of 12 to 16 weeks before patients could have a new hip or knee fitted or cataract removed, even though the NHS is meant to give 92% of patients planned hospital care within 18 weeks.

Mel Merritt, the head of policy and influencing at the National Autistic Society, said: “Restricting access to autism assessments denies people support because, while it shouldn’t be the case, a diagnosis is needed to get help. For children, this can mean years of wasted school while they wait for an assessment and further waits to get a plan for support and adjustments to be put into place.

“A diagnosis doesn’t only confirm if people are autistic or not, but also their needs and what adjustments could make a massive difference to being able to participate and enjoy life. The Independent Healthcare Providers Network, which represents many independent assessment services, urged the NHS to let private clinics offer as many appointments as were available.

Sean Phillips, its head of policy, said: “For someone struggling with suspected ADHD or autism, those extra months or years without diagnosis and support can have a profound impact on their mental health, education, work and family life.

“With more than a million people already waiting, we should be using all available capacity to get people the support and treatment they need as well as ensuring that their legal right to choose the best provider for them is being upheld.”

Rebecca Gray, the director of the NHS Alliance’s mental health network, said local NHS leaders were “keenly aware of the deep frustration caused by long delays and are doing all they can to address them.

“But the need to balance budgets and the pressures of soaring demand have – in some places – led to ‘minimum waits’ or even the closure of some waiting lists.

“The current situation is unsustainable and delivers a bad deal for patients and taxpayers.”

The Guardian Thu, 24 Sep 2026 20:55:15 GMT

There was a comic-strip feel to another eventful evening in the world of Cristiano Ronaldo. Where to start? It was the 67th minute when his No 7 went up on the fourth official’s board, prompting Ronaldo to remove the captain’s armband from his left bicep before departing to a universal ovation, but for the pocket of Wales supporters. The referee, Donatas Rumsas, hurried him off the pitch but Ronaldo, his hair glazed copper, was presumably ruminating on a series of missed chances, a sitter from a few yards at the start of the second half, and a disallowed goal. The grandiose “Siu” celebration went to waste, though try telling that to the locals who worship him.

In the end, Portugal earned a narrow Nations League victory courtesy of another Al-Nassr forward, João Félix’s first-half strike from the edge of the box beating Danny Ward in the Wales goal. Nuno Mendes, among the Portugal players who passed up chances, moved infield and located João Félix, who 20 yards from goal sent a shot in via a nick off the Wales captain, Ben Davies. The Wales squad is thin and many of those who started here have been lightly raced of late but they could have snatched an equaliser when Brennan Johnson hit the crossbar and Rúben Dias desperately denied Lewis Koumas.

All eyes were on Ronaldo, back playing in Lisbon for the first time since last October, at the José Alvalade Stadium where he made his name as a teenager. The 41-year-old started, as Jorge Jesus promised he would, and despite Ronaldo talking of a new era, different tactics and even a different language, alluding to Jesus’s predecessor, Roberto Martínez, this all felt rather run of the mill. Rúben Neves, another player stationed in Saudi, replacing João Neves in Portugal’s three-man midfield was the only change from their World Cup last-16 exit to Spain in Dallas.

Jesus, who twice managed Benfica and spent three years here in charge of Sporting, knows all about Ronaldo, having spent last season coaching him at Al-Nassr and passionately defended the striker on the eve of this game, describing him as a symbol of Portugal. It is hard to disagree on that front. Ronaldo-mania is omnipresent in Lisbon, chiefly inside the official Portugal stores in downtown Praça da Figueira, where you can buy CR7-branded briefs, face masks, action figures, lanyards, Lego, replica Ballon d’Ors and even a Ronaldo box set celebrating his time at Sporting.

Craig Bellamy acknowledged Wales would have to suffer against a team boasting five Champions League winners, but began confidently. Bellamy does not have the same quality in his squad, with Harry Wilson, Wales’s best performer in recent years, and Karl Darlow, these days the undisputed No 1, among those absent through injury. A harmless Ben Cabango header was Wales’s sole effort at goal in the first half and while they did not trouble the goalkeeper Diogo Costa, Bellamy stressed the best way to flummox the hosts was by retaining possession.

It was not always that simple. Ronaldo passed up four decent chances in the first half alone, the best of which was from about 12 yards out and left him scuffing his boots in frustration. There was a free-kick flighted into the Wales wall. He should have done better when Bruno Fernandes presented him his first sight of goal amid huge cheers from the locals, but his touch was rusty and the ball bobbled off his left foot. He later volleyed wide from an awkward angle at the back post.

The chances kept coming for Ronaldo. Four minutes into the second half, he knelt on the turf behind the Wales goal-line, puffing his cheeks after somehow passing up the opportunity to double Portugal’s advantage. Rúben Neves put in a delicious cross from the right flank but Ronaldo, unmarked and alone with his thoughts in the six-yard box, shanked the ball over off his left shin. If that was a near-miss, then he had the ball in the net approaching the hour, but a VAR review showed Ronaldo was offside when accelerating beyond Cabango to meet another Fernandes pass.

Jos Buttler injury and Kusal Mendis century derail England as Sri Lanka level ODI series

The Guardian Thu, 24 Sep 2026 20:19:41 GMT

Wicketkeeper sustains hamstring injury while taking run

Series goes to a decider at the Oval on Sunday

A beautiful batting surface and a greased lightning outfield made this second one-day international wildly different from the first 48 hours earlier. Unfortunately for England, on the wrong end of a thriller, the result was wildly different too.

Set 322 to win, and boosted by a rapid-fire 143-run opening stand between Ben Duckett and Tom Banton, England had appeared on course to wrap up the series with a match to spare. But Sri Lanka refused to give up, delivering a famous shutout and profiting from an injury to Jos Buttler to win by 16 runs.

It was agony for Buttler, who had earlier pulled up with a hamstring problem on 66 when the equation was 68 to win off 75 balls. Re-emerging when this became 27 needed off 14, the 36-year-old was unable to run singles, watched Will Jacks hole out for 52, and then eventually perished himself in the final over.

As it is, the series now heads to a decider at the Oval on Sunday that Buttler will miss and where Sri Lanka will be buoyant. Their captain, Kusal Mendis, had delivered a sparkling 121 from 100 balls, before Dunith Wellalage’s three-wicket haul and a fine display of death bowling brought a run of four defeats on tour to a juddering halt.

“It is always disappointing when you lose,” said Harry Brook, having seen England stumble to 305 for nine. “I thought Sri Lanka played exceptionally well, especially the last 10-15 overs. They were electric in the field. They nailed every ball.

“Jos being the player he is, getting injured at that moment isn’t ideal. You can’t dwell on that too much. I don’t think he ever had any doubt in his mind. It was a matter of when we were going to send him out really.

“Tight games are always good games to watch and good games to be a part of. Having the opportunity to play in a decider will only benefit us.”

Headingley may have been bathed in sunshine for much of the day but half-full stands perhaps said something about the appetite for September internationals in this part of the world. Although try telling that to the Sri Lankan supporters, who outnumbered those of Pakistan during the recent Tests and loved every minute.

Their afternoon was lit up by Kusal Mendis and was aided by a string of useful cameos from his teammates. Plenty was loaded in the favour of the batters but the right-hander’s innings was no less thrilling, with 14 fours and three sixes pinging sweetly off the bat to seal his first international century on English soil.

One crucial chance came and went for England, however, when a top-edge off Jamie Overton sent one high into the sky on 17, Gus Atkinson misjudged the ball’s trajectory in the deep and it spilled out of his hands. Had it stuck, England’s task with the bat would probably have been far more straightforward.

Atkinson was the pick of the England bowlers, at least, finishing with two for 55 from his 10 overs and his removal of Kamindu Mendis for 54 – Brook clinical under another high ball – broke a 137-run stand for the second wicket. Rehan Ahmed, who saw his first ball disappear for six, came back well to pick up two for 48 from eight overs.

It was tough going in the main, however, with hard length the order of the day for the quicks but the margin for error minimal. Overton saw two chances go down off his bowling and Kusal Mendis successfully review a phantom nick behind on 99. Jofra Archer and Josh Tongue likewise leaked runs, while Jacks was no doubt yearning for the assistance he had enjoyed 48 hours earlier.

Things were no less tricky when it was Sri Lanka’s turn in the field and Duckett and Banton tucked into some wayward new-ball bowling. But the introduction of Wellalage’s left-arm spin flipped the script, inducing a collapse of three for 14 in 23 balls that sent something of a pleasure cruise into far choppier waters.

Duckett was bowled through the gate for 67, Banton was stumped for 73 trying to launch a fourth six, and Brook was pinned lbw for one on review. When Joe Root chipped Sachindu Colombage to cover for 15 – the leg-spinner having otherwise endured a difficult second album following that eye-catching debut on Tuesday – England were suddenly 203 for four in the 29th over.

Buttler responded in incendiary fashion. But when his hamstring popped and was followed by Ahmed gloving behind for a five-ball duck, Sri Lanka believed once more. In the end an excellent display of yorkers from their quicks that starved England’s lower order of boundaries proved the difference.

Netanyahu calls Israel’s war in Gaza ‘opposite of genocide’ in UN speech

The Guardian Thu, 24 Sep 2026 19:28:08 GMT

Israeli PM attacks critics and calls New York mayor Zohran Mamdani ‘antisemitic’ in inflammatory address

Benjamin Netanyahu delivered an inflammatory address to the United Nations on Thursday, decrying what he said was a global anti-Jewish conspiracy and swatting aside criticism of Israel’s war in Gaza, as he faces down international isolation and a fight for political survival in upcoming elections in Israel.

As planned protests erupted on the streets of New York City, Netanyahu took aim at critics of the humanitarian crisis in Gaza, the international media, regional leaders such as Turkey’s Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, the leftwing commentator Hasan Piker and the New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani in an address that doubled as a stump speech to ignite his rightwing base for the elections.

Invoking his late brother Yonatan Netanyahu, a commando killed in a 1976 raid to free Israeli hostages from a hijacked airliner in Entebbe, Uganda, he repeated the lines: “We are going to win. We have no other choice.”

Dozens of delegates, inspired by a Palestinian call, walked out of the General Assembly Hall of the UN headquarters as Netanyahu took the stage, leading a speaker to pound his gavel and announce: “I’m calling for order in the hall.”

Palestinian representatives organising diplomatic missions to bring staff for a planned walkout of Netanyahu’s speech said they wanted to “send a clear message to Netanyahu and his government that no one is willing to aid, abet, or be complicit in its genocide and war crimes and illegal occupation, which all peace-loving states and peoples demand must come to an end”.

“If there are any other moral cowards in the audience, I urge them to walk out,” Netanyahu said before launching into his prepared remarks.

The speech revealed little new in terms of Israeli policy over the war in Gaza, militant settler violence in the West Bank, or Israel’s plans to end other regional conflicts including its joint war with the United States against Iran.

But he argued that the world faced an existential threat from Iran, suggesting that several missiles from Tehran could have destroyed the UN, and cited quiet support from world leaders for Israel’s actions that could not be aired in public.

“Devastating Iran’s nuclear facilities was … very hard to do,” he said of launching joint US-Israeli strikes in February. “But for me, it was one of the easiest decisions I’ve ever had to make as prime minister. Because if we hadn’t done it, we’d all be dead.”

He branded Turkey’s Erdoğan as a “tyrant” who “hosts Hamas terrorists”, decried Mamdani as the “antisemitic mayor of New York”, and declared that Israel’s war in Gaza is not genocide – “it’s the opposite of genocide”.

“So, to all those spreading these lies about my country and about our brave soldiers, whether they sit in this hall or in the office of the antisemitic mayor of New York, I say this: shame on you!” he said.

Netanyahu delivered the controversial address to the United Nations on Thursday just hours after Palestinian leader Mahmoud Abbas said his delegation was “unlawfully” denied visas by the Trump administration to attend the meeting of world leaders.

In a video address from Ramallah, broadcast in the General Assembly Hall, Abbas condemned Israel’s policies in Gaza, the West Bank and East Jerusalem as a “malicious colonial plan” to establish a “‘Greater Israel’ and erase the Palestinian presence”.

Citing the humanitarian crisis in Gaza and the violent expansion of settlements in the West Bank, Abbas said that the Israeli government “now threatens the very life and existence of the Palestinian people in their homeland”.

“Do not allow another Nakba and further massacres like those of 1948 to continue taking place,” he added, referring to the expulsion of Palestinians upon the founding of Israel.

For the second year in a row, the US state department denied visas to Abbas and the Palestinian Authority delegation, arguing that they had failed to live up to their commitments to seek peace with Israel.

“As a consequence of their failure to reform, contrary to their commitments to the United States, and their ongoing activities that undermine the prospects for peace, the United States will extend sanctions that deny visas to PLO members and PA officials,” the state department said last week in a statement.

In his speech, Abbas said his delegation “[rejects] these unlawful punitive measures, as well as the accusations and justifications on which they were based”.

He said: “Preventing the Palestinian delegation from reaching United Nations headquarters is inconsistent with the obligations of the United States as the host country.”

As he spoke, protests were forming on the streets of New York near the United Nations headquarters in advance of Netanyahu’s arrival.

Hundreds of demonstrators crowded into the street on Manhattan’s east side in midtown and held signs that said “End the Genocide” and wore shirts reading “Fund people not bombs”. By the end of Netanyahu’s speech, more than 100 demonstrators, including several local elected officials, had been arrested by New York City police.

Earlier this summer, the mayor, Zohran Mamdani, had said that Netanyahu was “not welcome” in New York, and said he was reviewing whether Netanyahu could be arrested by city police under an international criminal court warrant for his arrest.

He has since tempered that stance, saying this week that he wouldn’t attend the protests but promising to protect their “right to [protest] in this city”.

Netanyahu is not expected to meet Donald Trump, who is in Washington to host the Chinese leader, Xi Jinping, nor with other senior US officials, as he faces growing international condemnation over his hardline stance. Netanyahu has said that he needs to return to Israel quickly because of the election campaign and the holiday of Sukkot, which begins on Friday.

Issues such as whether tolls or navigational fees could be imposed by the littoral states Oman and Iran would be settled later in the process.

#NotAllLesbians – we can’t let the Massachusetts bar drama turn us all into a punchline

The Guardian Thu, 24 Sep 2026 18:48:31 GMT

The Last Ditch Bar saga is a case of ridiculous lefty infighting. But well-meaning people often have to tolerate nonsense

I have just wrapped up an emergency meeting with the International Office of Homosexual Affairs and would like to share a statement regarding the recent incident in Greenfield, Massachusetts.

Here we go: those shenanigans, reported in a viral story by the Boston Globe, don’t represent us all. #NotAllLesbians.

But, of course, I shouldn’t be centering myself here. Nor should I be assuming knowledge in a way which reinforces oppressive hegemonic structures. So let me hold space to share the details of everything that has transpired with all you folx reading who have not had the privilege of devouring every detail of the drama already.

The story begins at the Last Ditch Bar and Arts Venue, which opened up last year as a place for “dykes, transsexuals, gender freaks, workers, and their friends”. One of the bar’s key selling points was that it required KN-95 masks (“or better”) at all times, to accommodate the immunocompromised and the Covid-conscious. Well I say “selling points”, but a big issue with Last Ditch is it didn’t do much selling. In keeping with its values, it had an open-door policy, stating that nobody would be turned away if they couldn’t pay the cover charge, including “unhoused people”. This was very generous of them, but also a formula for losing money.

In order to try to stop hemorrhaging cash so they could continue to pay rent, the venue eventually decided to move to a mask-optional policy. This caused an uproar. A sample comment on Instagram: “I hope your venue gets firebombed for robbing my fellow immunocompromised people of their Saturday plans just to scrape extra revenue from ablists [sic].”

And from there the story wades deeper and deeper into “surely this isn’t real, surely this is a psyop by rightwingers who want to make the queer community look unhinged” territory. An emergency Zoom meeting was declared and lasted over three hours. A performer called Soe Noire accused Jackie Matellian, the last remaining operator of the venue (the other founders left; one so they could enrol in clown school), of shedding “WHITE THEY THEM TEARS”.

The bar was not “a safe environment nor interested in revolutionary praxis”, Noire added. Matellian, who is working four different jobs in a desperate attempt to pay off the $50,000 loan for the business, was contrite. “There’s conflict, but we just hope that there’s more repair than conflict,” she told the Globe.

Alas, it’s the conflict (and the lesbians) which has made this story go so viral. It fits squarely into a genre I will call “moderately ridiculous lefty infighting”, which is beloved by sensible centrist authors and the rightwing press. Stories of progressives leaning into all the most extreme stereotypes are guaranteed to be turned into parables of why leftists are self-absorbed drama queens who can’t get anything done. Fox News is already all over the Last Ditch drama, and Bari Weiss’s Free Press jumped on it with glee. Meanwhile, Newsweek is drawing parallels with a story about a white Jewish Philadelphia teacher who spent years presenting herself as Black and Palestinian. “The stories are different but their respective absurdity rhymes,” Newsweek writes. And by “rhymes” they mean: they are both good opportunities to attack progressives.

But while there is a lot of absurdity in the Last Ditch saga, I think it’s worth stressing that it is still ultimately a story about a woman who tried to create an inclusive space where some of the most vulnerable people in society could feel accepted. It’s easy to laugh at all the shenanigans, but the world would be a lot better if it had more people like Jackie Matellian in it: kind, well-meaning people who try to live their values. Of course, the problem with people like Matellian is that, because they are kind and well-meaning, they can sometimes tolerate too much nonsense. Narcissists who use a marginalized identity as cover for bad behaviour can find themselves drawn to places like Last Ditch because it’s the only space in which they will be indulged.

I don’t know whether going viral is going to be a boon for Last Ditch, but it’s certainly been good for the Boston Globe. The (masterfully written) piece is responsible for a surge in subscriptions this week. According to its editor, it’s the best performing story of the year and is “on pace to shatter all sorts of Globe records”.

And I think that takes us to the real moral of this story. If you want to save local news you can forget all about adopting AI or pivoting to video, the secret is pivoting to lesbians.

Why is the UK’s suppressed climate national security report significant?

The Guardian Thu, 24 Sep 2026 18:27:58 GMT

Warnings about the catastrophic effects of vital ecosystems collapsing were not published under previous PM

UK shares findings of damning climate crisis national security report suppressed under Starmer

UK spy chiefs warned government ministers of the catastrophic impacts on national security from the collapse of vital ecosystems around the world, driven by the climate crisis and the overexploitation of nature. But their report, which was supposed to be published almost a year ago, was suppressed under Keir Starmer. Now the government is briefing foreign ministers from other countries on the findings, with a view to gathering global support for more concerted action on the risks.

In the first report of its kind, the UK’s spy chiefs set out stark warnings of the catastrophic risks to the UK from the collapse of vital ecosystems around the world, driven by the climate crisis and our failures to protect nature. The Guardian has seen part of the report and has spoken to a large number of people familiar with its contents, which warn of food shortages, conflicts, mass migration and other threats to the UK’s national security, including going as far as the risk of nuclear war or the breakdown of society. These threats are not regarded as some far-off or remote contingency: disastrous impacts, for instance on the UK’s food supply, could be expected as soon as 2030, it warns.

The report, which was originally commissioned under the previous Tory government, looked at the potential consequences of a range of scenarios such as the collapse of the Amazon rainforest, which scientists have warned could be close to switching from a rainforest to a savannah-like system under the impact of heating and deforestation. The authors found these could result in food shortages in the UK, which imports about 40% of its food. The report also reviewed the development of new pandemics from areas deforested and overexploited, border disputes among countries affected by the climate crisis, increased Russian and Chinese influence over critical mineral supply chains, and civil tensions within the UK as these impacts play out.

Collapsing ecosystems overseas – the Congo basin was also a focus – could result in mass migration as people are forced to leave areas no longer habitable, triggering potential unrest and “more polarised and populist politics in the UK and its allies”, along with “more strain on national infrastructure”, and conflict could result from countries fighting over scarce food supplies. While the risk of nuclear war is still regarded as small, it is a potential impact.

One person who had seen the whole report described it to the Guardian as “apocalyptic”.

The report was supposed to be published in full last October, before the Cop30 climate summit in held in Belém, in the Brazilian Amazon. But Downing Street officials intervened at the last moment to prevent its publication. The Guardian revealed the report’s key findings at the time through leaks, as subsequently did other media, but nothing was officially forthcoming until January, when, after several refused attempts under the Freedom of Information Act, a partial summary of parts of the report was released to the Green Alliance thinktank.

Scientists have issued numerous stark warnings of a future of droughts, floods, storms and severe heatwaves, if global heating exceeds 1.5C above preindustrial levels.

This report is different, however, because it comes from the UK’s joint intelligence committee, the cross-government ministerial advisory body that oversees the work of the UK’s spy agencies and is tasked with monitoring national security. It examined the climate and nature crises for their potential to damage the UK’s security and defence, and found the UK underprepared for the impacts.

The government has not issued a formal response. The fact that the report has not been published means ministers can hide from its implications, according to Adrian Ramsay, the Green party MP for Waveney Valley, who has called repeatedly for its publication and led a parliamentary debate on it earlier this year. A parliamentary committee has also tried to persuade ministers to disclose the findings, and their response to them.

Moreover, while the report warns of what will happen if ecosystems break down, the UK has slashed its overseas development aid, hurting the vulnerable countries where many of these ecosystems are located. International climate finance has been reduced from £11.6bn in total over the five years 2021 to 2026, to about £2bn a year for the next two years, and the previous ringfencing of spending on nature and forests within that budget has been dropped. Many nature conservation projects in vulnerable countries were among those cut, the Guardian previously revealed.

However, this week the government has taken the first steps towards acting on the report’s findings, under the guidance of the foreign secretary, and former energy and climate secretary, Ed Miliband, with the backing of the prime minister, Andy Burnham.

On Wednesday, Miliband led a briefing about the report’s findings to foreign ministries from around the world, including those of the EU, Kenya and Australia, which is in charge of the negotiations at the next UN climate summit, Cop31 in November. Ministers were not given full copies of the report at the closed-door meeting at the UN general assembly in New York, but were given verbal summaries of its findings.

Miliband, who told the Guardian he would put the climate at the heart of foreign policy, also announced £330m for the Global Environment Fund (GEF), one of the principal vehicles for funding nature protection in the developing world. The UK will also provide £400m for Brazil’s Tropical Forests Forever Facility (TFFF).

Jonathan Hall, managing director of Conservation International UK, told the Guardian: “The Starmer administration’s decision to drop the longstanding precedent to spend a significant proportion of our international climate aid on nature and forests was totally unjustified. This [spending] is both scientifically essential and very popular with the UK public, according to polling, so Miliband now needs to build on the contributions to the TFFF and GEF and reintroduce a clear target for at least a third of UK climate aid to be dedicated to natural ecosystems and tropical forests.”

Asked about the risks of pushing the EU’s like-minded trading partners away, Haddad said: “At the end of the day, if you are not part of the internal market and if you are not contributing to the financial capacity of the internal market, you don’t get the same kind of protection.”

The Guardian view on a supersized El Niño: a natural phenomenon and human folly are a lethal combination

The Guardian Thu, 24 Sep 2026 17:37:39 GMT

Hundreds of thousands are expected to die, millions to go hungry. This is not just about weather patterns, but about injustice

Some warnings are so grave that it is almost impossible to fully comprehend them. The descriptions of a super-sized, “Godzilla-level” El Niño already heating our planet would sound hyperbolic were they not issuing from eminent scientists. They say that the weather pattern, which occurs roughly every two to seven years, may be the strongest in at least a millennium. With its peak yet to come, the temperature rise in the Pacific Ocean has already surpassed the previous high.

The consequence will be huge amounts of heat in an atmosphere already experiencing frighteningly higher temperatures due to the human-caused climate crisis. Next year is almost certain to be the hottest on record globally, breaking this year’s record. The World Food Programme has warned that 50 million people are likely to be pushed into acute hunger. Others estimate that the extra heat from El Niño alone will cause the deaths of 450,000 people by February, from Nigeria and Indonesia to the US. That extraordinary toll is in addition to those killed by the wildfires, droughts and floods it is likely to bring – and also to deaths caused by global heating.

While the weather system develops in the Pacific Ocean, its knock-on effects will be felt far away. It increases drought risk in a large swathe of the world, while increasing rainfall elsewhere. India has already experienced a 50% shortfall in essential monsoon rains this month, affecting crops. In Sri Lanka, reservoirs for drinking water are running dry. European countries may be indirectly affected, with a stormier autumn, but the primary impact for them is likely to be on food supplies.

While there is ongoing debate about the impact of global heating on the pattern itself, a major study published last month found that strong El Niños in recent decades have been supercharged by the overheating of the planet due to fossil fuels. It is beyond doubt that the effects of this natural phenomenon are compounded by human-made folly and injustice. Domestically and internationally, the poorest will be worst hit, due to factors such as living conditions and underlying health, while being the least able to pay their way out of trouble. At the same time, the wealthy few will continue to enrich themselves from an economic system built on pumping out more emissions. Defenders of the status quo will continue to insist that we cannot afford to clean up our act. It is more than ever evident that we cannot afford not to do so.

The UK foreign secretary’s warning to other countries at the UN on Wednesday that El Niño and the climate and nature crises threaten their national security and defence was welcome. Andy Burnham, as well as Ed Miliband, should be seizing the opportunity to make the political case for tough action on emissions, and accelerating efforts to prepare the UK for increasingly extreme weather. The Climate Change Committee, which advises the government, warned in a landmark report in May that the country is “built for a climate that no longer exists”.

Globally, boosting the loss and damage fund to ensure support for developing countries, which have contributed the least to the climate crisis but are likely to suffer most, should be a priority. This unprecedented El Niño poses an immense threat. It could also be a spur to action against global heating and its associated injustices, which otherwise will only deepen.

The Guardian view on vocational GCSEs: why now?

The Guardian Thu, 24 Sep 2026 17:35:58 GMT

Ministers’ commitment to cutting youth unemployment is admirable, but how new qualifications will help is unclear

The first question that should be asked about plans to launch a batch of vocational GCSEs is: how will these differ from the roughly 50 similar courses that already exist? Is this primarily a rebadging exercise, aimed at boosting the qualifications’ status and name recognition, while signalling how seriously non-academic education is taken by Andy Burnham and his education secretary, Lucy Powell? Or is there something the matter with the existing courses that they want to put right?

The independent curriculum review completed last year recommended a moratorium on new technical awards, except where there is an “exceptionally compelling” case for change. It also proposed that the Department for Education analyse existing ones, including how well they prepare pupils for 16-19 education; no such research has appeared.

Last year, around 170,000 16-year-olds in England and Wales took a level 2 BTec qualification alongside GCSEs – the two most popular being health and sport and leisure. They are also studied by post-16 students at further education colleges. While the number of entries is dwarfed by the overall annual total of 5.7m GCSEs, it is not the case that all individual GCSEs have higher take-up. In 2024, for example, just 6,723 pupils took a GCSE in dance.

The fact that technical awards are not on the radar of many pupils and parents does not mean that they lack value. The low awareness of vocational options is widely recognised as a problem and was cited by Pepe Di’Iasio, the general secretary of the Association of School and College Leaders, in response to this week’s announcement. Clearer signposting is expected to be among the recommendations of a review chaired by Charles Clarke, a former education secretary, when it is published later this autumn.

The second question about vocational GCSEs is how they will relate to the plans for new V-levels (level 3 qualifications like A-levels), to which the government is already committed. V-levels are due to replace all existing vocational level 3s apart from T-levels, after ministers rejected a campaign aimed at saving some older courses. Will vocational GCSEs be viewed as stepping stones to the new V-level courses? If not, how will duplication and repetition be avoided?

For schools, the key issues will be practical. Construction is one of the new GCSEs promised. But there are already many vacancies for construction‑related college teaching positions and it is not clear where a workforce for teaching 14- to 16-year-olds building skills would come from – or whether training teachers for new subjects should take priority over existing shortages.

The government’s commitment to getting more young people into jobs is admirable, and ministers are right to push for more work‑experience opportunities. But given the difficulties in this area encountered by T-level students – which led to a watering down of the initial requirement for a placement – it is doubtful whether the aim of getting large numbers of 14- to 16-year-olds into workplaces is realistic.

There is nothing wrong with rebranding level 2 technical awards and reshaping them if they are shown to be deficient. But given their ambitious reboot of post-16 options, as well as hugely challenging reforms of the special educational needs system, ministers should beware of new GCSEs becoming a distraction. If they are serious about boosting vocational learning, it is the overlooked further education sector that needs attention.

Alcaraz tops the bill as the Laver Cup returns to London still aiming to prove its worth

The Guardian Thu, 24 Sep 2026 17:16:42 GMT

The Ryder Cup-style event has struggled financially since its legendary founder, Roger Federer, retired but still offers a spectacle unlike any other in tennis

The sight of a tennis player marching to the bathroom between sets has become increasingly common in modern tennis but Alexander Zverev’s journey back to the locker room in Prague nine years ago remains particularly remarkable. On this occasion, Zverev happened to be sandwiched between two of the greatest male players of all time. Neither legend was happy.

To his right, an incensed Roger Federer spent their walk back to the locker room brutally laying down the law: “I want a fist pump or a ‘Let’s go!’ every fucking point you win,” he said. “And every point you lose, you fucking take it like a man. Because the problem is, when you don’t have the [result] you want, it’s like: ‘Ah, I knew it. Fuck, shit.’ I don’t want … honestly!”

As Federer mercilessly told Zverev off, cursing, shaking his head and even mocking the then-20-year-old’s negative body language until they disappeared into the locker room, his message was amusingly ad-libbed to Zverev’s left by Rafael Nadal, the good cop: “Not one negative face,” he ordered.

Prague 2017 marked the first year of the Laver Cup, an event masterminded by Federer and his longtime manager Tony Godsick. If ever there was an image that validated and underlined the value of the competition, a Ryder Cup-style event that pits Team World and Team Europe against each other, it was this one.

Catching such an unfiltered glimpse into Federer’s demeanour away from the cameras was rare enough, but this was even more remarkable considering the recipient of Federer’s passion and ire happened to be the fast rising world No 4, one of the players hoping to end his reign at the top of the sport.

Nine years on, the Laver Cup returns to London at an interesting point in its development. After initially being viewed as an adversary to the Davis Cup and ATP events, it is now an official part of the calendar and has firmed up its place in the tennis ecosystem. The event has allowed the likes of Federer, Nadal, Novak Djokovic and Andy Murray to compete alongside each other as well as a score of other top players. Although there is naturally far less star power on the tour today, its current iteration is clearly led by its one global star: Carlos Alcaraz.

The tournament’s organisers have long held visions of this event attaining a similar status within tennis as the Ryder Cup; one of the most important events on the calendar. It is difficult to imagine that happening for various reasons, starting with the decision to return to London. While it has always presented a good spectacle, a glance over the Laver Cup’s company accounts suggests a more complicated story.

The tournament made operating losses of £1.8m in Vancouver in 2023, and on the face of it a much healthier £2,000 in 2024, when the event was held in Berlin. However, this includes “non-tournament revenue”, in other words an injection of cash. Without that additional money, Berlin 2024 would have lost £1.5m.

By far its best performing events were Boston in 2021, which made an operating profit of £4.9m, and London, which delivered £4.1m in 2022. This is surely a significant reason why the organisers were willing to return four years later. The accounts of San Francisco 2025 have not yet been published. At the moment, it appears that there are a limited number of markets where this event can truly be profitable.

Every year since 2017, arguments have raged about whether the Laver Cup should be described as an exhibition, a word that many view as a filthy phrase that describes an unserious hit-and-giggle affair. These arguments seem quite irrelevant. This is obviously, at the very least, a special event considering some of the invitations are arbitrary, its rules are convoluted and there are no ranking points on offer.

However, one of the common characteristics of a top tennis player is their intense competitiveness. This event has produced plenty of high-quality tennis and tightly contested matches between players trying their hardest to win.

But there are limits to the competitive nature of these events. It is hard to imagine the Laver Cup generating the emotions, negative and positive, that some of the biggest events will do. Alcaraz is never going to sit down with his team at the end of the season and anguish over how he let the Laver Cup get away, nor will he put his body on the line and prioritise this event over more important tournaments.

That’s fine. The Laver Cup doesn’t have to be enormous or massively meaningful to add great value to the sport. Since its inception, it has been a slick, well-run event that has been willing to innovate and present the sport in a different light. The sight of longtime rivals suddenly working together is incomparable to anything else in the sport and it has been fascinating to see the players’ competitiveness come alive under different circumstances.

In the final stretch of a gruelling season, when most players are tired and diehard fans have spent the past nine months watching tennis in the exact same format every week, the Laver Cup also represents a nice interlude before the final run-in to the ATP and Davis Cup Finals. Perhaps most of all, it has repeatedly delivered on what should be the most important aspect of all sporting events: entertainment. It will do so this weekend as tennis returns to the O2 Arena once more.

How Labour could solve the youth jobs crisis

The Guardian Thu, 24 Sep 2026 17:03:03 GMT

Readers respond to an editorial on creating opportunities for today’s young people to build future careers

Your youth unemployment editorial (18 September) sees the crisis clearly, but reaches for the wrong tools. Placements, apprenticeships and work coaches cannot conjure jobs that do not exist. We need macro solutions to macro problems. Youth unemployment is not a crisis of skills or geography. It is insufficient government deficit spending. There is not enough money circulating to employ everyone who wants to work and that is a policy choice, not an accident.

Macroeconomists divide the economy into three sectors: government, households and businesses, and the rest of the world. One sector’s spending is another sector’s income. Put simply, government spending is income for the non-government sectors.

All transactions across these three sectors add to zero. With the UK running a persistent current account deficit, money flows continuously abroad. Unless the government runs a deficit large enough to offset that outflow, households and businesses cannot accumulate financial assets. So jobs vanish, wages stagnate, and young people bear the brunt.

Indeed, unemployment has long been used deliberately as an inflation management tool. As the US economist Stephanie Kelton notes, orthodox economic policy assumes that a certain amount of unemployment is necessary. When the Bank of England raises rates, it intends to slow activity, and the inexperienced young are always first out of the door.

So what should Labour do? Not pay employers £3,000 to hire someone that the market won’t touch (an admission that demand is absent), but become the employer directly. A job guarantee, publicly funded and locally administered, would offer anyone a job at a living wage doing socially useful work. It expands in downturns and shrinks in booms, stabilising wages precisely when the economy needs it. It is not welfare. It is work.

As a currency issuer, the UK is not constrained like a household. The question is never “can we afford it?”, but “do we have the real resources?” On youth unemployment, we plainly do. Simon Ripton Co-founder, Resilient Economy CIC

It doesn’t take a graduate qualification in economics to see that Rachel Reeves’s increase in employers’ national insurance contributions has reduced their ability to take on new people. She has also created a timebomb – as, by reducing the number of new people getting jobs, she has also reduced the number of people able to start paying into pensions.

What will happen if young people not in education, employment or training (Neet) never get jobs and so those not on benefits don’t get pensions? I believe the government pays the pension contributions of those on benefits, so surely they could reduce costs by putting money into creating more jobs?

How does one stop being a Neet at 24 when jobs don’t magically appear just by getting older? My son is 27 and did what he was supposed to do and got a first-class degree in a Stem subject, but now I support him on my pension. He was unable to do a placement for his degree because of Covid, and 6% compound interest means that his student loan is now a third more than when he graduated.

He has applied for almost 500 jobs, temporary and part-time roles, graduate training schemes and apprenticeships. He has even done a government-funded data technician digital skills boot camp, and is now close to giving up. Susan WestQuorn, Leicestershire

What politicians and civil servants fail to understand about the low take-up of apprenticeships is how bad the situation became under the Conservatives.

Youth services were decimated, young people’s work opportunities and expectations were squeezed, and the voluntary sector was allowed to wither.

What is needed is something like the Future Jobs Fund, which created real jobs in community organisations, provided positive work experience and developed relevant skills.

I was with great sadness that I read that Phil Gates’s country diary piece was to be his last (Country diary: A lesson from my final diary after nearly 40 years – keep looking closely, 19 September). It has become my habit to check the column as soon as I get my hands on the paper to see if it was a “Phil Gates diary day”, then to savour it.

This is partly, perhaps, because his diaries are from my own county, but mainly because I have never failed to learn something new and interesting about some overlooked or unspectacular species in the natural world, despite this being my subject.

The information in his column would usually find its way into my teaching. I well remember my class of 10-year-olds calculating and measuring their jumps after learning from Phil’s piece that a springtail can use its furcula to jump many times its own body length. Jim McMannersTrimdon Grange, County Durham

I do not know anything about Phil Gates, but I must have read and enjoyed countless country diaries by him over the years. These became especially important during a long period of being unable to get outside independently or walk at all. Country diary became my news from the world outside – not news about the never-ending machinations of humankind but of the world I really missed: the sights, sounds and backstories of the wild flower and the calling bird.

Now that I am taking my first slow steps into local woods, I intend to follow the Phil Gates method and marvel at what I can find at my feet. There is indeed much marvelling there to carry me on into my 70s as I get back on my feet. Thank you, Phil Gates, whoever you are. Ann MacAskillSheffield

Briton quickest in practice for Azerbaijan Grand Prix

George Russell has insisted he will keep fighting for the Formula One world championship until it is mathematically gone but while he made an encouraging start to his efforts by going quickest in practice for this weekend’s Azerbaijan Grand Prix the makeup of said numbers remains somewhat in limbo.

Russell is 81 points behind his Mercedes teammate Kimi Antonelli going into the race in Baku which is taking place on Saturday to avoid clashing with Azerbaijan’s national remembrance day. The Italian has eight victories this season including the past two in a row, coming through to win from 19th on the grid in Monza and then taking the flag in Madrid.

Despite having a mountain to climb Russell has maintained the stoical and determined attitude he has demonstrated all season.

“I’m going to keep fighting at every single race until it’s mathematically impossible,” he said in Baku. “I want to try and win every single race and put it on pole at every single race. That’s my goal and that’s what I’m working towards every single weekend.

“There’s obviously a huge [points] deficit but it’s not even really a consideration right now. I’m in this position because the performance hasn’t been strong enough.”

As things stand nine meetings remain with a potential 233 points still on the table. However with the races that close the season in Qatar and Abu Dhabi still under threat of cancellation because of the war in the Middle East, that number may come down. If both races are cancelled it is understood they will be replaced by one round at Imola, reducing the total by 25 points.

F1’s current position is that the races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi will go ahead with a final decision now expected in mid October, after the current triple header of races in Baku, Malaysia and Singapore.

Mattia Binotto, the Audi team principal confirmed that this was the latest the sport could leave it for logistical reasons. “As we discussed during the F1 Commission last Monday, mid-October is the last call for such a decision,” he said. “The main challenges are more organisation and logistics.”

After the decision the mathematics will at least be clear. If all nine remaining races take place Antonelli would still take the title if he is 100 points ahead in Mexico or 75 clear in Brazil.

On track Russell opened well in Azerbaijan, quickest in first practice in a session where Antonelli lost half his run time with a hydraulic problem. In the afternoon Mercedes were once more on top, looking ominously quick on the street circuit which is energy-starved and plays to their car’s strengths in energy harvesting and deployment. Russell was quickest again, a full half a second up on Antonelli with their nearest competitor, Red Bull’s Max Verstappen, eight-tenths back in third.

Raphinha: ‘In my head I was leaving Barça, but a few small words can change you’

The Guardian Thu, 24 Sep 2026 17:00:25 GMT

Two years ago the Brazilian thought his time at Barcelona was ending but, two La Liga titles later, he is now captain and the most potent No 9 in Europe

For once, Raphael Dias Belloli puts the brakes on. The man who seems to be in perpetual motion, a footballer forever on fast forward, pauses, goes quiet for a moment and then, softly, utters something that says so much: “I think maybe people saw in me something I didn’t realise was there.” He did not know he was a leader, but he likes it. He did not know he was a captain, but according to his manager he is the “perfect captain”. And he did not know he was a No 9 either, but right now he is the best No 9 there is. In Barcelona or anywhere.

There was a time when Raphinha did not know whether he would be in Barcelona, when, feeling unwanted, he had accepted it was over, but this week he extended his contract to 2030. He will be 33 then: he would like to retire here and they would like him to retire here, too, a legend built on empathy and affection. “This is the best decision the club has made,” said Hansi Flick, the head coach Raphinha says changed his life. Sometimes you cannot get what you want so you have to settle for the best.

The first word Raphinha uses when training has finished and the tape starts rolling at Sant Joan Despí, when he is addressed as the world’s top No 9, is “false”. It comes with a smile; turns out there is nothing false about this 9. Seven games into the league season, the man filling in at centre-forward has scored 12 goals, plus two in the Champions League. The scorers leading the way in Europe’s other top leagues are five behind. No one in Barcelona’s history has started a season like this. And, no, Raphinha says, he has never played there before: “Even as a kid I wasn’t a 9.”

As if it is even about the goals. There may be no one as enjoyable to watch as Raphinha; no one as admirable or important either. The touch at speed is astonishing and there is a wild intensity about everything he does, only it is not wild, he says; it is worked upon, the entire system depending on him. The press defines Barcelona’s identity and it is, Raphinha says, “mechanised”. No, he is not going to reveal how but it begins with him. “As captain, he goes and everyone follows,” Flick says. “We always start with the No 9 and he has that incredible hunger and intensity, the mentality and attitude we need.”

Yet this is not what Raphinha or anyone expected. This summer Robert Lewandowski, Ferran Torres and Marcus Rashford departed, having contributed 38 league goals between them last season. They were supposed to be replaced by Julián Álvarez but Atlético Madrid refused to sell, leaving Barcelona with no striker. “There was a moment of need,” Raphinha says. “There was no No 9 for the [friendly] against Basel, so I played there.”

It was not supposed to be permanent, although Flick suspected it might be and was warming to the idea: Barcelona had not given up on Álvarez yet and the coach considered other solutions, including Anthony Gordon. This was better. Raphinha did not score but Barça got five.

“In pre-season we did a few tests: the manager liked what he saw and after Basel he told me a bit about his idea,” Raphinha says. “The adaptation came over the last two years, getting used to coming inside, closer to goal. But we tested [me as] an actual No 9 and it went well. There’s the occasional detail that has to be explained, but I’m OK. Before Elche [on the opening day], he asked if I was comfortable there or wanted to go back to my position. I said it was fine, see how it goes, we can always change back.”

Raphinha scored two against Elche, one against Athletic, two against Rayo and another at Valencia. Against Racing there was a hat-trick and another against Sevilla: right foot, left foot, header. Raphinha showed his old qualities and new, less expected ones: the movement, timing and clinical finishing of a classic No 9, efficiency to go with the intensity. Only one La Liga player has a better shot conversion rate. Against Feyenoord came two more.

Nor is it just about him. The point of Raphinha is that it is not even about him. Only once this season has he not scored, and against Levante he created the first two, then handed over the penalty for Lamine Yamal to add the third. Barcelona have scored five, two, five, five, five, four, seven and three, respectively in winning their first eight games.

Flick had done it again. “I always have and always will say that he changed my mentality, changed me as a person,” Raphinha says.

By 2024, Raphinha was convinced he had no future at Barcelona. His numbers were good: 10 goals and 12 assists in his first season, 10 goals and 13 assists in his second. But Lamine Yamal was emerging and, more importantly, Raphinha did not feel backed, completing 90 minutes seven times in 60 games under Xavi Hernández. It had not escaped his attention that Barcelona thought about selling him; it had not escaped anyone’s attention that they wanted to buy Nico Williams, publicly keen to reunite the pair that tore up the Euros.

Barcelona failed twice, and were all the better for it. A Photoshopped image of Williams in his No 11 shirt on social media hurt, Raphinha admitted. But Flick had arrived and if there is something even more powerful than the desire to prove people wrong, it is the desire to prove people right.

“In my head, I knew I was leaving,” Raphinha says. “That was [mentally] done, that’s the truth. I was in Brazil and Flick called. He said come talk to him before taking a final decision. I met him and he said he trusted in me, that I was going to be important, that the team[’s play] would be good for me. In a moment like that, a few small words can change you. I felt a lot of faith in me. He gave me the confidence to play my football. I got an idea into my head: give everything, your life, regardless of the personal moment you’re in.”

Love won out, even if Raphinha is swift to add: “If you get results people are going to love you; if not, they’re not.” Feeling supported and valued changed everything. His success is a human story, his qualities human ones. He led Barcelona to the league. Flying in from the left, Raphinha scored 34 goals and provided 26 assists in 57 games. Another title followed in 2025-26 and although injuries reduced his contribution, there were 21 goals and eight assists in 33, Flick’s faith gratefully repaid.

His teammates’ faith, too. The dressing room had voted Raphinha as a club captain, third in line. He had not expected it and was genuinely touched. There was something in that moment, in the realisation of how they felt about him, how much they believed in him, that was transformative. Now Flick has named him his first choice.

That moment brings pause, thought. “When I saw people had voted for me, it was like a switch had been flipped, a shift in mindset,” he says. “People could see something in me I didn’t realise was there, and that’s changed me. Before being captain, I didn’t know how much I would like it. Having that responsibility has also changed my mentality, helped me. I never thought I’d like being Barcelona captain so much. You feel you matter. It’s an honour. It’s not just wearing the armband.”

He is a natural, as pure a captain as there has been since Carles Puyol – even if he did need to be told. It is there in the relentless example he sets: Raphinha has sprinted the second-furthest distance in La Liga and Gradient Sports has measured only three players with more final-third pressures per 30 minutes out of possession. Raphinha says: “I talk less than most captains but I know people are watching. They think: ‘If this guy’s running like an animal, I have to follow.’. If you talk too much and then don’t do what you have to, people aren’t going to listen.”

Yet what teammates saw in him went deeper, to his very being. Leadership is there in the empathy, kindness and understanding too, in Raphinha returning the support that was good for him, an approach at once collective and individual. He says he can see when Lamine Yamal is drifting from games and how to reconnect him, every celebration shared with the teenager. A clip went round recently in which he quietly tells Gordon not to be afraid. And no clip was more powerful, more eloquent, than the moment when Flick sat on the bench, alone, lost in his thoughts and Raphinha consoled him, drawing him out of his dark place, roles reversed.

“The coach-player relationship is the most important in football,” Raphinha says. “From the moment [Flick] arrived, we could talk to him about anything – and anything is anything. That time, I saw him, head down. At first, I didn’t really understand why. I asked what was wrong. He said he felt the team wasn’t playing well. From what I remember, I told him it was OK, we’d won and we would play well again. I prefer a thousand times to win playing badly than lose playing well. Win games, confidence and the football comes.

“What kind of leader [I am] depends on the moment. If I have to be slightly tougher, I can. But I prefer nicer moments, jokes. The last two years have been spectacular so I haven’t had to be the pesado [pain in the arse] often. I know that annoys people but someone has to do it sometimes.”

With a squad like this, especially? Four of Barcelona’s first team were born in 2007. “Buah!” Raphinha says, laughing. “That hurts: it shows I’m closer to the end than starting out at 18, 19, like them. But I’m in spectacular physical shape so [retirement] is some way off. It’s very easy with them. There are young players but they’re very responsible about their career, their lives. Once in a while, you have to [be paternal] because they’re kids. But they understand. If they get told off, they know it’s for their own good. I’ll tell them.”

Is there something of the father figure in him with Lamine Yamal in particular? “No, no,” Raphinha jumps in. “Big brother, that’s better.” And Lamine Yamal is the star who should win the Ballon d’Or, he says: for his “individual numbers, collective titles, and the magic on the pitch, charisma. There’s no doubt. For me, he has to take the prize, no matter what. Even if I wasn’t Lamine’s teammate, for what he does, the numbers, the titles – and I think titles are important – he’s the candidate. One of one. Of three trophies, he won two with Barcelona. He won the World Cup with Spain.”

Only the Champions League escaped them; for two years Barcelona have come close, and it is their obsession now. “The semi-final against Inter [in 2025] hurt the most,” Raphinha says. “Against Atlético [in the quarter-final in 2026] we could have gone through, we could talk about things that could have gone differently, decisions. The BBC has been warned it risks entering a “doom spiral” of endless cuts and weaker public support for its services, as insiders anticipate the imminent closure of some TV and radio services.

Morale at the corporation is said to be extremely low as a series of cuts are slowly revealed to staff. In the latest announcement, the BBC said it would be reducing the number of local specialist correspondent roles.

It immediately triggered concerns about the loss of expert, local knowledge. The cuts are part of a plan to save £500m and shed up to 2,000 jobs.

Staff are now expecting announcements over the closure of programmes to follow next week. Matt Brittin, the BBC’s director general, has been open with staff for several months that popular shows would have to go, to ease the broadcaster’s mounting financial pressures.

There has been speculation that the BBC Three channel could be closed for the second time in its short history. BBC Three, which launched shows including Fleabag and This Country, was moved online in 2016 before the decision to take it off television was reversed in 2022.

BBC radio output is also likely to be affected. Between 350 and 400 hours of audio content will be cut by the end of the next financial year.

BBC Local staff have now been told the corporation would be reducing the number of specialist correspondent roles. Instead, there will be “two dedicated, multi-platform correspondents in every BBC region”.

Earlier this week, staff at BBC Sport were told that 36 more jobs were going, including some senior production journalists.

Staff morale had already been hit by a series of cuts announcements this year. In June, it said there would be 550 job cuts in news, nations and TV and radio content. It included the end of Radio 4’s The World Tonight after more than 50 years.

Brittin is making the cuts at the same time as battling staff over pay – and holding weekly meetings with the government over the BBC’s future funding model.

In a comprehensive statement on the cuts, the National Union of Journalists said they risked locking the BBC into producing worse content and lower public support for the licence fee that funds it.

“The BBC’s ongoing campaign of cuts is devastating and demoralising for our members and severely undermines the broadcaster’s ability to serve audiences across the UK,” said Laura Davison, general secretary of the National Union of Journalists. “The latest wave of cuts piles on the misery already being felt.

“The more cuts the BBC makes, the more its services suffer. This makes it more difficult for the broadcaster to justify public spending, which in turn leads to further cuts. The BBC is at risk of entering an inescapable doom spiral if it continues in this direction.

“This is where the UK government must step in. The BBC has been undermined by years of underinvestment and interference.”

At the TUC conferencelast week, delegates passed a motion instructing the body to press the government to intervene over cuts to public service broadcasters.

Senior management roles are also being reduced, with 10% of “senior leaders” going. About 700 roles are expected to go across the BBC’s corporate divisions.

Vistry is the laggard in a housebuilding sector full of cracks

The Guardian Thu, 24 Sep 2026 16:19:38 GMT

Group shrinks ambitions from 20,000 to just 12,000 homes a year in an attempt to balance the books

The entire housebuilding sector is in a funk, grumbling about energy prices, the cost of labour, regulation, planning delays, taxes and more, but few have messed up a bad hand quite like Vistry. Three years ago this mashup of the Bovis, Linden and Countryside brands aspired to build 20,000 houses a year, and made itself the darling of the incoming Labour government by betting big on “affordable mixed-tenure housing” in partnership with councils, housing associations and institutional landlords.

The City, too, fell for former executive chair Greg Fitzgerald’s promise that a “capital light” approach of pre-selling homes via a partnership model would yield oodles of cash. The share price doubled to almost £14 between October 2023 and August 2024.

Fitzgerald departed in May after too many profit warnings and now, with the shares down to the bare foundations of 262p, it’s time for new chief executive Adam Daniels’ review of what happened. Short version: the logic of the partnership stuff wasn’t so silly, but the execution was horrible, especially in the south of England.

“The pace of change meant that the operating model, controls and culture did not scale consistently with the group’s volumes [of construction],” he said, a polite summary of a growth strategy gone awry. For good measure, a proportion of the land bank would not be acquired “under the investment approval criteria that will be applied in the future”, which read as a confession that Vistry simply overpaid for plots.

The good news, of a sort, for shareholders is that the damage to the balance is not deemed so severe that fresh equity is required. Daniels’ prescription for recovery, however, is a long exercise in getting smaller and living with shrunken ambitions.

The aim is to build 12,000 houses a year, rather than the 20,000-plus imagined by Fitzgerald. A greater proportion of those homes will be in the north of England. As for return on capital employed – a critical metric for housebuilders – the old idea was 40%. That’s been cut to 30%, and only by 2031.

It all sounds perfectly reasonable: keep things simple, fix the balance sheet by eating into the land bank, and concentrate on the parts of the country where market prices (which still matter for a mixed-tenure model) are holding up better.

In Vistry’s favour is the fact that, for all its financial troubles, it’s still in the government’s good books. Last month, the company received a £350m direct grant to construct 3,000 affordable homes under the £39bn social and affordable homes programme. If you take the long view, there is a possibility of a turnaround if Daniels can live up to the promise of better execution. At the age of 35, he has time on his side – and may need it.
