Macklemore has announced a “Free Palestine” tour, a series of live shows that will feature the US rapper performing alongside musicians and friends to raise funds for humanitarian causes in Palestine.

The news comes after Macklemore (AKA Benjamin Haggerty) was removed from Ed Sheeran’s US stadium tour after he called for a “free Palestine” onstage and said he wanted the people of Gaza and “the occupied West Bank” to know “we have not forgotten about them”.

The speech, made on 4 September, prompted venue owners to refuse to allow any concerts featuring Macklemore to take place on their property.

Sheeran responded to the backlash over Macklemore’s removal with a written statement in which he declined responsibility for the decision and said: “I am not complicit.”

All Sheeran’s remaining support acts subsequently dropped out of the tour – Irish songwriter Aaron Rowe, Billie Eilish’s older brother Finneas and Danish band Lukas Graham – alongside the Irish trad group Beoga, who were to accompany Sheeran for portions of the show.

Macklemore posted on Instagram alongside his tour announcement: “If these last couple of weeks have shown us anything, it’s that something has shifted over the last three years. There has been a collective awakening around Palestinian liberation, the power of billionaires that try to censor that call, and what we expect from artists right now. “It’s 2026. Being apolitical during a genocide doesn’t work anymore. People are asking artists to show up, educate themselves and be in community. To use the stage for more than entertainment. To push back when the call for a Free Palestine is met with attempts to silence it. “What happened to me is bigger than one artist or one stage. When the billionaire class can decide which voices are allowed on stage and which ones are too dangerous to hear, everyone should be paying attention.”

On his solo return to the stage in Philadelphia on 19 September, Sheeran read an apology about “making mistakes” from a teleprompter. “I don’t want to disappoint fans, and I’ve never wanted to be an activist musician, but this has put me in the middle of an important and passionate argument about freedom of speech and the most complex political issue on the planet,” he said.

Small groups of fans protested outside the venue, with some of them having sold their tickets in protest. Other concertgoers said they were sticking by the musician. A tearful Sheeran told the crowd: “Everyone is telling me to cancel, and I’m feeling all of my friends and family and people I know abandon me and I look at the end of the week and I see 50,000 people who haven’t abandoned.”

In the days since the controversy kicked off, Sheeran is estimated to have lost almost half a million followers across social media, according to data from Social Blade reported by the Independent.

Macklemore’s statement continued: “So, as you all know, my schedule freed up a bit.” He said he had been using his time to contacts “artists who have shown up and used their stages to stand in solidarity with the Palestinian people, regardless of the consequences. Artists who understand that our platforms mean very little if we’re only willing to use them when it’s safe.”

No further lineup details have yet been released for Macklemore’s tour. “Because of how quickly all of this has come together, a lot of the conversations, schedules and details are still being worked out,” he wrote. “But this is a moment of momentum, and there is work to be done.”

Macklemore’s tour will begin in Dublin on 26 October. Two of Sheeran’s former support acts are Irish and many Irish musicians have been outspoken in their support for the Palestinian people, citing their own country’s history of occupation and oppression, as Rowe did in his statement explaining his departure from Sheeran’s tour:

“As Irish people, we know all too well about genocide, forced famine and violent occupation,” Rowe wrote. “I need to be true to myself and my ancestors who resisted colonisation, and fought for a freedom that I enjoy today in Ireland.”

The list of organisations to benefit from the concerts has been shared: Anera, Glia, Gaza Soup Kitchen, Taawon, Heal Palestine, Palestinian Youth Movement, Middle East Children’s Alliance, Jewish Voice for Peace, Medical Aid for Palestinians. Institute for Middle East Understanding, Palestine Children’s Relief Fund and UNRWA USA.

A press release said that these organisations “represent the array of work in support of Palestinian people. That includes medical care, humanitarian assistance, education, community support, advocacy, organising and media work connected to Palestinians.”

Further dates in Paris (29 October) and London (30 October) have been announced, with North American dates to follow. Fans hoping to get tickets are encouraged to sign up for presale access at macklemore. com.

Irish rock legends’ 16th studio album, described by the Edge as ‘a messy, provocative, sacred collection of songs’, to arrive in November

U2 have officially announced their first album of new material in nearly a decade, entitled Carnaval de Luz, to be released on 13 November.

Closing out the album’s 12 tracks is Torn, the final recorded performance by Dolly Parton, who duets with Bono on a song described in press materials as “a tender country song detailing broken family ties, that holds wider resonances”. Parton died aged 80 on 25 August.

Guitarist the Edge described Carnaval de Luz, U2’s 16th studio album, as “a messy, provocative, sacred collection of songs”, while Bono promised “loud guitars, deep bass, some ecstatic rhythms … the same imagination that brings us our creativity can also bring us monsters. So we make the drums louder. We build a bigger fire. We make our stories wilder and funnier. We make the melodies sweeter and the songs, they better shine, because if the world is in darkness we better not be.”

The album caps an industrious spell for the Irish rock legends, who have already released two EPs this year: Days of Ash and Easter Lily.

Speaking as Days of Ash was released in February, Bono trailed the release of the new album, saying it would have “a carnival vibe … a more defiantly joyful feel” than the vexed political songwriting of that EP, which reflected on ICE, Iran, Ukraine and the Israel-Palestine conflict.

Days of Ash was praised by the Guardian’s Alexis Petridis, who said the “zeal, purpose and belief” of the band’s peak years “has been recaptured here”.

The new album announcement comes 50 years, to the week, after drummer Larry Mullen Jr, then aged 14, pinned a message to the noticeboard of Dublin’s Mount Temple Comprehensive School which read “drummer seeks musicians to form band”.

The quartet, rounded out with bassist Adam Clayton, were all there from the very first meeting, and went on to become arguably the defining rock band of the late 20th century thanks to critically acclaimed and commercially successful albums such as The Joshua Tree and Achtung Baby.

They extended their success into the new millennium, with a trio of back to back UK No 1 albums: All That You Can’t Leave Behind, How to Dismantle an Atomic Bomb and No Line on the Horizon. Their most recent albums are a loosely connected trilogy between 2014 and 2023: Songs of Innocence, Songs of Experience and Songs of Surrender, the latter a collection of reworked versions of material from their back catalogue.

Carnaval de Luz reunites the band with Brian Eno and Daniel Lanois, the duo who produced The Unforgettable Fire, The Joshua Tree and Achtung Baby. Eno co-writes and plays synths on three tracks, while Lanois plays pedal steel on the Parton duet. More contemporary names also feature in the form of EDM megastar Martin Garrix, co-writer of Glorify, and pop star and producer Ryan Tedder, co-producer of Silencio.

The latter track, a raucous rock’n’roll song, has been released alongside the album announcement. The first track from the album, Street of Dreams, was released in July.

At Trump meeting, Xi Jinping lays out terms to avoid US-China military conflict

The Guardian Thu, 24 Sep 2026 15:52:13 GMT

Chinese president’s proposals for lessening tensions come amid period of intense competition between the two countries over AI and trade

Trump-Xi summit – latest updates

Xi Jinping has called for extensive cooperation with Washington to avoid the “Thucydides trap” that could put the US and China on a military collision course amid rising tensions over artificial intelligence, trade and Taiwan.

At the start of his summit meeting with Donald Trump in the White House, the Chinese president laid out terms for a mutual understanding that he said could steer the two competing superpowers away from future military conflict and on to a road of mutual gain.

Rather than confrontation, conditions for “achieving the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and making America great again go hand in hand” and should be the goal, Xi said, citing Trump’s political catchphrase.

“We should strengthen communication. China and the United States are different in national conditions, but through candid, in-depth and continued dialogue, our two countries can understand each other better, seek common ground while shelving differences, and build up mutual trust,” said Xi, with Trump looking on.

“We should coexist in peace. China and the United States, as two major countries, stand to gain from cooperation and will both lose in confrontation. Our two militaries should maintain regular dialog and improve mechanisms for crisis communication and prevention.”

With such conditions in place, Xi said, “the Thucydides trap can be overcome”, refering to the phenomenon, defined by the Greek historian, of tensions that arise when an emerging power challenges the dominance of an established power.

Xi invoked the phrase in his meeting with Trump in Beijing in May, asking the US president how he planned to avoid it.

His proposals for lessening tensions – which also included the invitation of 100,000 young Americans to visit China on student exchanges – come amid a period of intense competition between the two powers over artificial intelligence and trade, with each side imposing tariffs on the other.

Trump had earlier welcomed Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, to the White House, noting that he was the first Chinese leader to make a second state visit to the US. The previous visit occurred in 2015, when Barack Obama was president.

“President Xi and Madame Peng arrive at an important moment for America, the 250th anniversary of our founding,” he said.

Trump said he had forged “a truly great friendship” with Xi. “President Xi and I have made tremendous strides on the issues facing our two countries,” he said. “Our teams have been working to encourage a more balances trading relationship, including the new market access for American farmers and ranchers.”

He said the current visit would include discussion overs security, technology and AI – which he called “super intelligence”, a term he introduced in his speech to the United Nations general assembly on Tuesday.

Xi also extolled his personal relationship with his American counterpart, saying: “President Trump and I have respect for each other. We have built personal rapport and stayed in touch.”

Addressing Trump directly, he said: “During your visit to China this year, we agreed to build a constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability. I am ready to work with you to steer the giant ship of the China-US relationship on a steady course towards the future.”

The White House welcome ceremony came after Trump had taken the unusual step of going to Andrews air force base in Maryland the evening before to greet the Chinese leader and his wife on the tarmac.

Much of the same pageantry was repeated in Thursday’s ceremony, with both countries’ national anthems being played. Trump was flanked by his wife, Melania, while members of his cabinet and senior aides – including Natalie Harp, Trump’s dedicated assistant nicknamed “the human printer” by fellow staffers – looked on.

Trump and Xi were scheduled to hold bilateral talks after the ceremony and the welcoming speeches.

Despite the harmonious tone adopted by both leaders, analysts have voiced scepticism about the possibility of longstanding stable arrangements being arrived at over a host of issues.

In the race for AI, the US has placed strict export controls on microchips, semiconductors, software and chip-making equipment in a bid to slow China’s development.

A truce agreed between Trump and Xi in South Korea last year aimed at keeping tariffs lower had been due to expire in November but has now been extended until February, the US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent said.

Analysts believe the extension suggests Trump continues to be dissatisfied with Xi’s concession offers on trade and wants to keep the pressure on in the hope of getting a better deal if the two meet again at the G20 summit scheduled to be held in Miami in December.

Despite the trade war between the two countries, Chinese imports have continue to surge into the US. China is on course to run a $1tn trade deficit for the second year running.

Rick Wakeman performs piano concert to 150 rescued moon bears in Vietnam

The Guardian Thu, 24 Sep 2026 15:40:28 GMT

Former Yes musician plays at sanctuary to raise awareness of animals that remain stuck in cages at ‘bile farms’

Rick Wakeman has played to all kinds of people around the globe, but he has now performed to an audience he had never encountered before – an enclosure of 150 bears.

The former Yes musician, who has gone on to have a prolific solo career, played the piano at a Vietnamese bear sanctuary.

“Before you ask, I won’t be playing the teddy bear’s picnic,” he joked ahead of the performance. Wakeman, who is a supporter of animal welfare causes and has rescue dogs and cats of his own, is conducting the concert to raise awareness of moon bears kept in cruel conditions for the extraction of their bile.

He said he was a bit worried about how hot it is going to be. “You know the heatwave we had in England? It’s double that,” he said. “They offered to rig up a fan for me, but I figured that will just blow more hot air around.”

His concert was performed live on a Yamaha grand piano positioned in Animals Asia’s bear sanctuary in the Tam Dao national park, and Wakeman had written some new compositions especially for rescued bears.

Asked whether the bears would enjoy the music, he said: “They’ve not got much choice, really. It’s a well-known fact that all animals react to music, especially gentle melodic music. So what I am going to do is piano music that is melodic, and I can only hope that they will come up to the perimeter of the sanctuary and have a listen.”

Wakeman has been sponsoring rescue bears since 2016 and recently adopted a new one: “He’s only 20 months old, a big fella, I went to see him today. He came out right to the edge and stood on his back legs and just stared at me, it was brilliant.”

Bile is extracted from bears for traditional Chinese medicine by putting a needle into their gall bladder and drawing it out. The bears are kept in poor conditions in countries including China and in Vietnam, where it has just been banned, but where some bears are still in captivity in cramped enclosures. It is the fourth-biggest market in the illegal wildlife trade in east Asia, resulting in a dramatic decline in the Asiatic black bear populations in Vietnam, with nearly a third of their numbers lost around the world in just 30 years.

Of the sanctuary, which he has been visiting this week, Wakeman said: “To see the bears be rehabilitated, having a life they never had before, some have never put their feet on grass before. They are so wonderful, that we can do such horrendous things to animals is beyond belief. Before this, they were chained in cages sometimes for 10 or 20 years in conditions where they couldn’t even turn around.”

He is playing to raise awareness for the bears still stuck in cages in Vietnam and to urge the government to get them released: “We have 150 bears at the sanctuary, but there are 125 bears left in cages in the old bear bile farms, and there are four dying a month. We have to get them out quick and into the sanctuary.”

He treats his rescue dogs and cats to music back at home in Suffolk. “I had one cat who used to jump on the grand piano, and if I stopped playing he would put his paw in the strings and rattle them until I played again. I know if my dogs don’t like it, they will get up and walk out, and my cats don’t like metal, grunge or rap. They want a melody.”

Wakeman spends hours watching the bears. “If you see these bears it is hard to put into words, they are almost human the way they look at you,” he said. “If you see them, you can’t help but be moved. They aren’t tame but they are very safe, very happy, they play, they romp. I witnessed two today jumping in a bubble bath and playing. They’ve got a life back.”

Dr Jill Robinson, the founder and CEO of Animals Asia, said: “We are beyond blessed to have Rick’s support for Animals Asia and the bears. His love for them is immeasurable and can be heard in the beautifully haunting music he has written for them. We’re all so excited to hear his performance in the open air at our sanctuary in the stunning setting of Tam Dao national park. I can’t wait to see how the bears respond.”

Wakeman added: “I hope they lay down and have a listen, that would make my day. I would have a big grin on my face.”

For the generations who grew up watching Humpty, Jemima and Big Ted, the mere mention of the BBC’s Play School evokes a pang of childhood nostalgia.

The show, which featured much-loved presenters such as Floella Benjamin and Johnny Ball, became synonymous with wholesome children’s television during its run of more than 20 years on air.

After a 38-year break, the BBC has announced plans to bring back the programme as it tries to win over parents desperately seeking quality children’s programming amid a torrent of online content.

The programme will be revamped for the digital age and will include content for the BBC’s new CBeebies Parenting YouTube channel. It is a sign that the corporation is doubling down on its drive to create more for the digital platform, where children’s content of varying quality has been booming for years.

The BBC said the companion YouTube content would provide “practical play ideas, expert guidance and resources for parents and carers”.

Its decision to revamp Play School comes amid continuing concerns over online children’s content, with complaints of low-quality and addictive slop. The issue is being examined by MPs on the culture, media and sport select committee.

However, Play School’s return also fits with the BBC’s search for its own standout brands that can hold their own in the increasingly global market for children’s TV.

The announcement coincides with the launch of the BBC’s “parenting promise”, touted as a commitment to “help every child learn through play”.

The original Play School, which first aired in 1964, was designed as a way of recreating the nursery experience at home. The new series will also be live-action.

Producers are being invited to pitch their vision for the show, with the BBC envisaging a traditional blend of songs, stories, movement, music, poetry and imaginative play.

Potential producers have been told the aim is to retain “the values that made it one of the BBC’s most enduring children’s programmes”.

Patricia Hidalgo, the director of BBC Children’s and Education, said: “Parents and carers place enormous trust in CBeebies and that is a responsibility we never take for granted. Behind every programme is a team of experts, programme makers and storytellers committed to creating content that helps children learn, grow and thrive.

“In a changing media landscape, we believe trusted, high-quality children’s content has never been more important.”

She added: “Play School has always embodied so much of what CBeebies stands for: creativity, curiosity, imagination and learning through play. Bringing it back for a new generation is a meaningful opportunity to build on that legacy, while continuing to support parents and carers through CBeebies Parenting and the wider commitment set out in our parenting promise.”

Hidalgo is one of the most senior people in the media world raising concerns about children’s content and the need to retain quality. Earlier this year, she told MPs there had been an alarming decline in shows for younger audiences among British broadcasters.

With broadcasting budgets under huge pressure, she said investment into the sector by the BBC, ITV, Channel 4 and Channel 5 fell by 40%, to below £80m, over the 14 years to 2024.

Over the same period, the amount of original content halved to less than 400 hours. Meanwhile, online, scrollable content aimed at children has proliferated.

Last year, Hidalgo told the Guardian the amount of American content children were consuming on YouTube risked weakening their connection to British culture and language.

Pre-production for the reinvented Play School show is expected to begin in February 2027, with the first episodes airing in the 2027-28 financial year.

I love my life and my cup is full but I’m drowning in shame for things left undone. How can I balance it all?

The Guardian Thu, 24 Sep 2026 15:00:22 GMT

You are not the only one, advice columnist Eleanor Gordon-Smith writes. It will help to ask whether you have a time problem or a bandwidth problem

Read more Leading questions

I love my life in so many ways. I have a rewarding job, I’m making stellar progress towards a graduate degree, I have incredible friends and community, plus I’m even reconnecting with estranged family. My cup is very full but I still feel grief and shame for how much falls to the wayside.

I have missed countless doctors’ appointments. My vehicle’s license plates have been expired for almost a year. I often apologise to angry friends and acquaintances after they confront me for not seeing them in months. My significant other says she doesn’t see me enough. So do my parents. I clock out of work and shudder at the thought of facing my growing avalanche of text messages. I panic whenever I receive an email that demands I arrange yet another appointment or submit to a lengthy phone call. The stack of forms I’m overdue to submit makes me feel so irresponsible, as if I’m the only adult alive who can’t seem to take care of business.

I cannot imagine how anyone stays afloat in this world. When I divulge a little bit about these struggles – such as sneaking away from police cars on my daily commute because I keep running out of time to go to the DMV – people seem to react with utter shock. Am I really the only one drowning in modern bureaucracy and relationships? How can I balance it all? Or, at least, navigate it with some more grace?

Eleanor says: I think there’s an important clue in the fact that requests from people you love go in the same mental bucket as the DMV.

But I want to start by saying: you are not the only one. I’m so sorry you hear incredulity when you divulge this. There should be an amnesty each year when we confess our administrative stuff-ups so we wouldn’t feel so alone; you wouldn’t believe what’s out there.

Some of us are at the more ultraviolet end of the spectrum, admittedly. But there are leagues upon leagues of us who understand this feeling all too painfully well. Ask any tax agent.

You might want to look into the possibility of ADHD.

You don’t have to be totally sold on a hypothesis of what ADHD is to know that management can be life-changing. That doesn’t have to just mean medication. It can also be astonishingly helpful to offload executive function on to your physical (not digital!) environment; making time visually very salient, externalising things you need to remember.

As a more general strategy for “balancing it all”, I think it helps to ask whether you have a time problem, or a bandwidth problem.

If you need more time, you need more time. You need your tasks to chew up less of it – outsource, batch, ban perfectionism, insist on a timer, use this email charter, say no. And you need the people who want more time from you to understand how little you have. If you’re the only one who knows how many plates you’re spinning, you’re the only one who knows how fair or unfair these requests are.

However, it’s also possible that there is time but it isn’t usable, because you just don’t have the bandwidth.

If you end every day exhausted and pulled in dozens of directions, and if each call or request feels so heavy and hard to “do right” that it requires self-steeling and psychic warm-up and you’re completely exhausted afterwards, then having the minutes technically available isn’t useful. You might as well tell me, as I collapse across the triathlon finish, that there’s time to run another 10km. Yeah, sure. But I can’t. I’m in no condition to use that time to that end.

Bandwidth problems show up as mismatches between how we experience things and how other people do. They think: “Why haven’t you ticked off those to-do list items, it would take 20 minutes?” But because each one is so emotionally expensive, they may as well ask why you haven’t yet called an estranged lover to bury the hatchet, or confronted your childhood bully, given it would take 20 minutes. The time is not the issue, the effect on my nervous system is.

I suspect for most of us, overwhelm is at least partly a bandwidth issue. (One way to check: keep a time audit.) To be clear, I am not saying this could be solved by working harder or “making time”. It’s precisely the opposite. If time itself doesn’t help, what you ultimately need are ways for these things to feel less like horrific burdens, so there’s less reason to avoid them and less exhaustion from encountering them.

How you do that depends on why they feel so horrible to start with.

We can make such thickets of shame.

It could be about competence; “I’m not sure I can do this, and I hate how it feels to be bumbling.” It could be about the fear that people will always want more, no matter how much you can or want to give them: so “I’d like to see you!” hits the ear like “I want something from you, and after that I’ll want more” – a request for your time can feel like the threat of being consumed. (Are there any unsatisfiable parents in your past?) It could be perfectionism; I’d rather not do this at all than do it only to the level it can be done quickly. It could be screen overload, if work and admin and a lot of your socialising all happens through the same demand-communicating device.

How to make these things feel less like running another 10km depends on why they exhaust you, particularly – on why exactly your loved ones and the DMV can feel somehow the same. Understanding the specifics of your overwhelm may feel like yet another task but, once you do, the rest may come easier.

The eyes have it: Rory Stewart’s ‘magnificently strange’ Newsnight moment goes viral

The Guardian Thu, 24 Sep 2026 14:39:37 GMT

Clip of the former Tory MP staring intently at fellow panellist is shared widely online

Rory Stewart has been an Afghan NGO leader, a Conservative leadership candidate, a Harvard professor, a popular podcaster, and the deputy governor of an Iraqi province.

This week, he created a moment that drew wider attention than any of them: he fixed a beady gaze on a fellow Newsnight panellist for the longest four seconds in television history.

Stewart, who now co-presents The Rest Is Politics podcast with Alastair Campbell, appeared on the BBC programme on 18 September – but in the last few days, a clip of the moment in question has taken on a life of its own on social media.

Stewart appeared alongside the former Labour leader Neil Kinnock and the New Statesman’s political editor, Ailbhe Rea, to discuss the day’s main news stories, including the race between China and the US to develop artificial intelligence (AI).

After Stewart made his comments, the presenter Matt Chorley asked Rea what Westminster could do about the development of AI. Stewart then swivelled around in his chair and stared directly at the journalist with an expression – and posture – of absolute focus.

Chorley told the Guardian the behaviour had not appeared overly strange in person: “I didn’t notice Rory looking particularly intently at anyone during the course of the programme,” he said.

He only became aware of what had happened when several friends texted him. “You know a moment from Newsnight has cut through when friends and family who don’t normally watch it are suddenly sending me clips,” he said. “But it is just quite a funny moment.”

He added that as it was the first Newsnight episode to move to the programme’s new earlier slot at 7pm, it had been “quite manic” in the runup. He had even joked to the panellists: “Anything that can be used to go viral, maybe a punchup or whatever, a tiff at the table, if you want to do that, that’d be great.”

Chorley observed that Stewart was “used to this”, after another clip of him taking his tie off during a Tory leadership debate had gone viral in 2019.

“It’s not the first time that something he’s done has gone wild online. I think he was genuinely probably just intently listening to what Ailbhe had to say. But there was something about the camera angle and his very direct look,” he said.

Many behaviours that appear normal in person can look strange on screen, Chorley added.

He said he had learned to “remember you’re always on” and to control his naturally emphatic hand movements, which can “look crazy” on screen. He also recalled an early Newsnight episode which had surprised viewers when Tim Stanley, a columnist at the Telegraph, winked at the camera.

“This is just the beauty of live telly,” he said. “It’s a reminder that even when the camera is on the person who’s talking, you might be in shot.”

Rea, who was on the receiving end of the stare, posted the clip on X to joke that she would “please like attention levels like this on my latest interview” after sharing a link to her most recent reporting.

The clip has turned into a meme online, with commenters imagining situations in which the stare could have taken place.

The Larry the Cat social media account posted: “When HR tells you that you need to listen better to female colleagues.”

Total Politics Group’s chief executive, Mark Wallace, compared Stewart’s behaviour to the comedian Kevin Eldon’s surreal style, writing: “There’s a high degree of Kevin Eldon energy to this. Magnificently strange.”

After so long in Trump’s sights, hopeful Greenlanders breathe a collective sigh of relief

The Guardian Thu, 24 Sep 2026 14:27:35 GMT

Locals hope agreement signed this week is step towards independence and end to US threats to annex island

Greenland’s prime minister, Jens-Frederik Nielsen, and Múte B Egede, the foreign minister, received a hero’s welcome when they landed back in Nuuk from New York on Wednesday night – and a nation took a collective sigh of relief.

Colleagues, friends and members of the public turned out to greet them at an airport where, just 20 months ago, the landing of a Trump-branded plane containing Donald Trump Jr had kickstarted a geopolitical crisis that the people of Greenland now hope is over.

To cheers and applause, and waving red and white Erfalasorput flags, the politicians were credited with saving the nation thanks to a new defence agreement between Greenland, Denmark and the US signed this week at the UN in New York. It comes after an unprecedented period of turbulence in which Donald Trump repeatedly threatened to invade the Arctic island and almost tore apart Nato in the process.

“Welcome home,” the speaker of Inatsisartut, the Greenlandic parliament, Kim Kielsen, said. “Welcome to a country that we were about to lose. You have ensured that we have a future here.” Like many Greenlanders, for the last year-and-a-half he said he had been holding his breath.

Nielsen, who became prime minister last year in the middle of the crisis, told the crowd: “We can be calm. Our land will not be taken. Our land will not be bought. The road has been long, and it has been very difficult and dangerous.”

Hundreds then attended a celebratory coffee party at Katuaq, the Greenlandic capital’s cultural centre. Aqqalukkuluk Fontain, 38, who was there with his girlfriend, Stella, and their youngest daughter, Aura, who is three, said the collective release of tension was palpable. “It was a joyous moment. It’s going to linger for a while,” said the IT manager, who earlier this year organised a protest outside the new US embassy in Nuuk.

He cautioned he could not entirely relax – concerned that, after the midterms, Trump could change his mind and relations could “take a turn for the worse” – but hailed the deal with the US as a moment of pride for Greenland and a stroke of “strategy genius” from Greenlandic and Danish negotiators. “Trump is trying to angle it that he made a great deal. But he wanted total control, ownership of Greenland. He didn’t get that,” he said.

Its full text contains some key differences from the 1951 defence agreement it is intended to update – for example, the US gets underwater access to Greenland and specific permission to construct a missile defence system – but is a far cry from Donald Trump’s original threat to annex the Arctic island. And in terms of tangible outcomes, the biggest winner is arguably Greenland, where it is seen as a potential stepping stone to future independence.

When the 1951 agreement was signed, Greenland was still a colony of Denmark. Now, it is a largely autonomous territory that has signed an agreement alongside Denmark with the US that it played a central role in negotiating.

A big question hanging over Greenland independence was what would happen to its status within Nato and relationship with the US.

The new agreement answers that question. It stipulates that if it did become independent, the governments of Greenland and Denmark would “together ensure that the independent Greenlandic state will agree to remain in Nato, including by applying to become a member if necessary”.

The centrality of Nato to the agreement is also seen as a boost for an alliance that was creaking under US claims against one of its fellow members’ territory.

Greenlandic politician Qarsoq Høegh-Dam, who earlier this year became the first member of the pro-independence party Naleraq to be elected to the Danish parliament, said there was still considerable work to do in terms of gaining independence but that “a lot of what ifs” have now gone.

“It’s a point of relief for Greenlanders,” he said. “They can lower their shoulders a bit, so we can talk about domestic issues, the road to independence more freely, instead of the search of what if?”

Much of the agreement already existed in practice, he said, but now “it is written in ink” with Greenland’s explicit involvement. “It’s a continuation of an agreement since the 1950s. The difference is now that Greenland has some say in it. They want to agree for themselves instead of a country overseas agreeing on behalf of them,” he said. “That’s the difference first and foremost and it is significant.”

He said, however, there were still questions about what the words will equate to in practice, for example on investment. “It’s a good foundation, but the details are missing,” he said.

Given that just a few months ago Trump was threatening to invade Greenland, and a few weeks since he posted a map of Greenland covered with the US flag to social media, in many ways the very fact that a diplomatic agreement has been reached is a victory in itself.

Ulrik Pram Gad, a senior researcher at the Danish Institute for International Studies (DIIS), said: “For Danes and Greenlanders, it’s a win to be able to force Trump into doing something diplomatically. And if this actually puts the Greenland crisis to rest, it will be felt as a win for Greenland, Denmark and Europe because then we can concentrate on real problems and trying to find ways to work with the US on that.”

Aviaja Fontain, 41, a student from Nuuk, said the agreement puts to rest months of anxiety. At one point, amid government warnings about preparedness, she thought Nuuk was being attacked by the US during what turned out to be a power cut caused by a storm. “Many of us have been afraid that Trump will use force, but now I can feel relief,” she said. Now she feels she can finally relax. “We don’t have to think about getting attacked and just live our peaceful life again.”

Price hikes, ads and lower quality: has ‘streamflation’ ruined the TV experience?

The Guardian Thu, 24 Sep 2026 14:04:25 GMT

US consumers are starting to opt out of the streaming world as several services raise prices without offering many perks

It may not be quite as politically buzzy as the price of gasoline or eggs, but another household expense is going up for millions of people. Disney has brought the price-gouging experience of its theme park home again by raising the prices of most iterations and bundles of its Disney+ and Hulu streaming services. Whether you pay to watch them with or without ads, separately or bundled together, you’re probably getting a price hike of a couple of bucks per month. The few bundles that will remain the same price feature ad-supported versions of both services (plus ESPN). Don’t worry, though; paying extra to avoid the ad-supported versions of those services won’t mean that you’re missing out on some cross-promotional opportunities. Disney’s terms of service note that they reserve the right to insert ads before and after programming on whatever subscription tier they want, regardless of what you’re paying for. True magic!

This particular magic isn’t reserved for Disney, though. Price hikes among streaming services have become so common that The Verge has a dedicated page aggregating the news of them, which tends to arrive every few months. Apple, apparently high on Emmy fumes, has raised its prices four times in four years, keeping pace with many of its competitors despite a vastly smaller dedicated catalog. Depending on which version of Peacock subscribers use, they’ve seen their bills padded by five or six dollars a month just since the summer of 2025, including another increase last month. Netflix, meanwhile, hasn’t gone up since March 2026. That’s not a reprieve; that’s a sign another hike must be around the corner.

Consumers have noticed. Reportedly an estimated 39% of Americans canceled a streaming service in the past six months due to what’s been dubbed “streamflation”. Another survey indicates that a majority of people subscribe to at least three such services, which is consistent with estimates of streaming households spending about $70 per month. Access to the six big streaming services (Netflix, Disney+/Hulu, HBO Max, Paramount+, Apple TV, Peacock) will boost that number somewhere in the neighborhood of $120, on top of which subscribers need broadband internet for the services to actually work. For the total price, you might as well call the whole thing Cable+, in that it’s like your old cable bill, only there’s more of it. No wonder cancellations are rampant.

To retain subscribers without putting the screws directly to them, it might be viable for streaming companies to stabilize annual prices – typically a discounted lump-sum payment covering a full year of a service – even when raising monthly costs. Some, like Netflix, don’t offer this option. While those that do have kept annual subscriptions cheaper than the a year’s worth of month-to-month, companies don’t seem interested in maintaining bargain levels. The annual price for Disney+ at launch was $70. Now it’s $190, an increase of 170% – presumably to stay competitive with eggs. Amazon Prime, whose streaming service began as a perk for members already paying an annual membership fee for unlimited shipping and other benefits, has also risen while inserting more ads into its programming and downgrading the picture quality. You want higher resolution and fewer ads? That’s another $50 a year.

The reasons for all this shameless gauging are pretty simple: Wall Street doesn’t just demand profits (though those have sometimes been scarce in the streaming world) but endless growth, and some services don’t have all that much more room, realistically, to sign up more users any more. Netflix has 325 million subscribers worldwide. What’s their reach goal? 500 million? Three billion? What happens when everyone on Earth with an internet connection and a credit card already has Netflix?

Not every service is so close to a saturation point (unless you count electricity as a streaming service). But it’s notable that even a supposedly lower-tier streamer like Peacock commands over 40 million monthly subscribers, equivalent to more than 10% of the United States population. (It’s a heavily US-skewing service, so unlike Netflix those users aren’t especially global.) By comparison, the biggest magazine in the US has a subscriber base of around half that (and that’s the AARP magazine, an outlier in that it’s distributed to paying members). The New York Times, considered an especially successful recent example of the subscription model, has 13 million subscribers. The AMC Stubs A-List program that allows moviegoers to see four films a week has about 1 million.

That’s all to say that streaming has unprecedented reach, which means the only realistic way to boost profits is to either raise subscription prices, or make less stuff. The latter might sound ridiculous, especially given that we’ve been living in the post-boom age for streaming shows for a while now. Then again, that’s worked out well for the catalog-based Tubi, whose original works are lower-profile and lower-budget than its competitors. One of several free streaming services, Tubi outstrips some of those paid competitors in market share and turns a profit based only on its ads.

Watching a movie or a show on a free service isn’t exactly an optimal experience; there are those ad breaks, sometimes the transfers aren’t top-notch, and the content churn tends to be a little faster than the subscription streamers. It’s definitely not a place where you can catch much of anything nominated for an Emmy in the past five or six years (though some Oscar movies or second-tier popular hits from that period might turn up). On the other hand, free streamers often manage to under-promise and over-deliver; at a time when paid subscriptions seem eager to offer less than ever, especially in the quite broad field of films made before 1995, Tubi, PlutoTV and their ilk always have at least a couple dozen stone-cold classics on hand that more than make up for not including the latest big-name time-wasters (looking at you, Matthew McConaughey/Woody Harrelson sitcom where they play themselves!). And the price always stays the same.

Still, some free streaming services with surprisingly robust and shifting catalogs aren’t exactly the dream of cord-cutting that was fed to consumers throughout the 2010s. The initial idea was to shed the bloat from all-or-nothing cable services that hold monopolies, or something close to it, in plenty of geographic areas. Competition for subscribers would keep good deals in the offing. Instead, what’s been happening over the past five years or so is a redistribution of that money from one set of giant companies to another. There’s slightly more consumer control over the size of the bills, in the sense that, yes, it’s possible to cancel a couple of services in a way that picking and choosing individual cable channels wasn’t possible outsidea few premium subscriptions. But there’s also far less clarity about how to catch the best shows and movies of any given year. For ages, it was mostly a simple formulation: have cable, add HBO. Now even the prestige of HBO seems a little more niche – a Game of Thrones spin-off; a well-liked Green Lantern show – than in the past.

There’s also a strange sense that this scramble of greed isn’t paying off as well as it should; many streaming services feel like they’re in far more precarious financial positions than most cable companies or channels were at their peak. It’s a dystopian development: corporations still want consumers on the hook for endless subscription payments, but also seem to want them to share in the nervous stock-checking of a shareholder, without any particular upside. Each month, you check your streaming holdings and see if you’re about to be charged even more, and whether you need to pick one to divest (cancel, whether for good or for now). You can toggle some of them on and off timed to the occasional appearance of a major series like Severance or The Pitt, but the onus for keeping track of erratic streaming schedules is on the subscriber. None of these shows are as necessary as basic groceries. But the ability to relax and watch TV after a long day is still in danger of becoming another budget-related stressor – an unholy combination of cable bloat and the endless doomscroll.

It’s funny, you still miss them. I wish I could phone them up and tell them what was happening, what was going on. As a parent, my kids are never off their phones, but you never hear from them unless they want money. I think back to when I left home at 16 and, if I wanted to phone my parents, I’d have to grab a handful of coins and head across the street to the phone box, which I probably did once a month. Recognising how things are now as a parent, I sort of wish I’d got to know my parents better. If you asked me who I could have dinner with, alive or dead, I’d speak to my mum and dad. I’d ask them all this shit I wish I could have asked them before.

You’ve had a really diverse career, despite some people’s attempts to pigeonhole you as a Scottish mummy’s boy. What’s left on the bucket list? AmongstTheWavesWell, when I turned 60, I joked with my kids that I was retiring. What that meant was I felt comfortable with what I’d achieved. Maybe there were sort of gaps, maybe it wasn’t quite as great a career as I would have liked, but I was going to step back from trying to have a career. I think I spent too long seeing jobs as a step to the next job, and didn’t really appreciate the moment. So turning 60 I thought: “Bollocks to this, I’m just going to do stuff that I like, that’s filming somewhere nice, or is especially well paid. If it’s got two out of three of those things, I’ll do it.”

The reality is that I’ve probably never been busier. Stuff like Bad Day at the Office comes out of left field. After decades of complaining about playing cops and being a Scottish mummy’s boy it was nice to do something that was so ridiculous, strange and experimental that, at 64, you could never have imagined it.

Do you and James Nesbitt ever go out for a pint together just to watch the confusion on people’s faces? RobinGoodfellowWe used to play five-a-side back in the 90s. The last time I bumped into him was when his daughter and my son graduated from Manchester uni, last summer. It’s good if people think I’m Jimmy Nesbitt, because I can then swear at them and be rude and he gets the blame.

When did you last use the expression “by Jupiter’s cock”? wellywearer2This morning, funnily enough.

Northampton lead Prem charge but history shows title defence will be no simple task

The Guardian Thu, 24 Sep 2026 14:00:20 GMT

Boosted by retaining Henry Pollock, champions are eager to keep improving but a revitalised Saracens and Exeter should push them all the way

It used to be simple. Win the Prem once and people would assume it was just the beginning. At various times no one could dethrone Bath, Leicester or Saracens, serial winners by fair means or foul. And now? It is so long since any club defended their English domestic title that “doubling up” feels almost as quaint as reading a physical newspaper or chatting up a complete stranger in the pub.

Which explains why Northampton’s Phil Dowson, whose side are chasing a third title in four years, is keen to draw a distinct line under what happened last season. Yes, the Saints were unplayably good on occasions and deservedly claimed the trophy in June. But that was then. The last team to win two in a row were Saracens in 2019, shortly before the salary cap small print intervened.

Three of the past six champions, as highlighted by the keen-eyed stats guru Russ Petty, did so having finished sixth or lower the previous season. Northampton, for example, finished a lowly eighth in 2024-25. Dowson, accordingly, is wary of assuming anything. He says: “We have to be mindful of complacency and saying: ‘We won the league last year doing this, all we need to do is do this again.’ When actually the key is: ‘What do we have to develop?’”

Watching Saints train recently was to sense they will be absolutely fine, early-season injuries permitting. Dowson and his coaching partner, Sam Vesty – rapidly becoming the East Midlands’ answer to Starsky & Hutch – are impressively smart and have been liaising closely with the club’s performance psychologist, Oli Dixon. And, of course, there is Henry Pollock, strutting around the paddock like a thoroughbred racehorse and visibly hungry for more. We’ll forgive him, this time, for all the agent-driven hot air just prior to re-signing for Northampton, the biggest load of Pollocks since Jackson was in his prime.

The truth, either way, is that Saints are nicely placed to go back to back, unless the rest can locate another gear. Bath should be right up there, albeit with one or two caveats. The biggest is the departure of Thomas du Toit, their set-piece colossus. Also gone is Alfie Barbeary, who did not start every game but was unfailingly good for squad morale. Nor is it ideal that, if they do make the playoffs, they will not be able to host a semi-final at the soon-to-be-redeveloped Rec. They will be reliably competitive but maybe not impregnable.

Behind them in the queue are plenty of other rejuvenated contenders, led by Barbeary’s new employers, Saracens. Brendan Venter, back at the helm in place of Mark McCall, knows only one way and it has never been backwards. Add in the power of George Martin and Barbeary, the class of Tomos Williams and some of the most exciting young backs in the land and, even without the departed Tom Willis, Sarries could be rather more than just makeweights.

It is equally hard to imagine Exeter fading quietly away having made last year’s final. On the subject of forceful back-row forwards who love a hard carry, how about Greg Fisilau, Ethan Roots and Kane James, potentially among the league’s fastest-rising talents? Not to mention Tom Hooper, the yet-to-arrive Kiwi centre Dallas McLeod and the irresistible Immanuel Feyi-Waboso. Keep that lot fit and Rob Baxter’s squad will be top-four material again.

Leicester? They remain perhaps the trickiest side in the league to assess, not least because Ollie Chessum, Joe Heyes and the rest of the Tigers’ international contingent will have so much on their plates between now and next year’s World Cup. If they finish fifth – one place lower than last year – it will be further proof of the league’s increasing depth.

A 10-team Prem without relegation also leaves little margin for error, particularly for those who start sluggishly. Which makes this a massive season for Sale Sharks, underachievers last year but bolstered by the arrival of Courtney Lawes, Joe Marchant and Alex Lozowski. They will be desperate to improve on last season’s seventh-place finish but there may be slicker teams out there in a league that quickens in pace by the year.

after newsletter promotion

That trend might suit Gloucester who look better organised and more focused than has mostly been the case in recent seasons. No side with Chris Boyd involved lacks for strategic nous and they are not overly constrained by expectation. Again injuries will be crucial but their pre-season form has been positive and the arrival of Dewi Lake and Jac Morgan should deliver the kind of forward dynamism the Shed can get right behind.

It is even possible they could finish ahead of Bristol Bears for the first time since 2022. At their best the Bears attack as slickly as anyone but memories of their sobering 94-33 loss to Northampton at Franklin’s Gardens last season have not entirely faded. Keeping AJ MacGinty and the lock Pedro Rubiolo fit – they won seven of the eight league games in which the latter started last year – will be pivotal if they are to prosper.

All of which leaves Newcastle Red Bulls and Harlequins eyeing each other nervously. Both have reshuffled coaching staffs and can be relied upon to be better in a year’s time. As things stand, though, they have a lot to prove, all the more so if they stumble on the season’s opening night. Newcastle are at Franklin’s Gardens while a slightly depleted Quins entertain Bath; start sluggishly and it could be another long, hard winter.

The collective big picture, though, is tantalising. It is entirely possible that, by Christmas, the makeup of Steve Borthwick’s 2027 Rugby World Cup squad will also have altered significantly. While Northampton and their chatty man Pollock are in pole position to defend their crown, the modern-day Prem is rarely that straightforward.

Toxic bosses: why do companies protect managers who make working life hell?

The Guardian Thu, 24 Sep 2026 13:53:33 GMT

Bullying, manipulation and intimidation can destroy lives, yet abusive authoritarians continue to rise to the top. How do they get away with it – and can they be brought to heel?

When Andrea finally resigned, her colleagues told her the truth they had always known about her boss. Some apologised. Others admitted they had watched what happened to her and said nothing. One offered the sentence I have been unable to forget: “You’ve been an emotional stab vest for us. You protected us.”

Andrea was a senior legal executive with decades of credibility when she began reporting to a powerful new colleague. Within months, something was wrong. Expectations shifted without warning and feedback contradicted itself. He spoke over her in public and undermined her in private. Slowly she began questioning not just him but herself, her competence, even her grip on reality.

What disturbed Andrea most was the gradual discovery that everybody already knew. Colleagues confessed that when they heard this executive was returning to the organisation, they had cried. When Andrea approached HR, a senior executive told her: “People work longer at McDonald’s than they work for him.” That was acknowledgment, not discovery. And there is something brutally revealing in the stab-vest description. Andrea had become the organisation’s psychological shock absorber. While she took the blows, everybody around her was safer.

Stories like Andrea’s are usually told as stories about monsters: the bullying boss, the narcissistic founder who finally, spectacularly, falls. I have come to think of such framing as the least useful way to tell them. Instead, I’m interested in how such people keep acquiring power and why, once their behaviour is visible to almost everyone, nobody stops them.

I have encountered power through three lenses. For 20 years, I was an executive-level headhunter, spending thousands of hours assessing the people organisations were preparing to entrust with authority. I then held that authority myself, as a global chief marketing officer in New York. Now, as a psychotherapist, I meet power from the opposite side, through people trying to understand what happened to them when somebody wielded it badly. The industries differ; the consequences rarely do. Brilliant people become convinced they are incompetent. Experienced professionals stop trusting their own judgment. Good leadership enlarges people. Bad leadership, at its darkest, persuades a person, slowly, to disappear.

It never begins that way. The leaders who do the most psychological damage rarely arrive as tyrants. They arrive as answers, wrapped in charm and certainty, mirroring your values back to you. That first meeting can feel like the best of your professional life. Clinically, this can create a rapid sense of attachment, in which trust and emotional closeness develop before the relationship has had time to be tested. What follows – withdrawing warmth and then restoring it just often enough – is the logic of the slot machine: intermittent reward keeps people hopeful and vigilant, working ever harder to recover the golden beginning. By the time the storm breaks, the job has been accepted and the mortgage signed – leaving feels unthinkable.

Some of this starts at selection. Consider the language of the senior job specification: bold, decisive, resilient, charismatic, comfortable under pressure, possessed of “executive presence”. There is nothing wrong with any of it. The problem is that a healthy leader and a dangerous one can look almost identical at interview. One candidate is decisive because they have experience and a secure enough ego to make the difficult call; another because doubt itself is intolerable. One is resilient through self-regulation, another through emotional detachment. Both interview beautifully. Corporate language launders the difference: low empathy is repackaged as decisiveness, ruthlessness as “high standards”, emotional detachment as resilience, manipulation as influence.

In 2015, a meta-analysis led by the psychologist Emily Grijalva found that narcissism meaningfully predicts leadership emergence, which is to say getting the job, but has almost no relationship with leadership effectiveness. People high in the so-called dark triad traits – narcissism, machiavellianism and psychopathy – are disproportionately skilled at impression management, and although psychopathic traits appear in roughly 1% of the general population, studies of corporate samples suggest markedly higher concentrations among business leaders.

As a therapist, I am also interested in what forms such leaders. Research published in the Leadership Quarterly found an association between supervisors’ experiences of family undermining during childhood and abusive supervisory behaviour in adulthood, particularly among those with lower self-control. This demands careful interpretation. Trauma in itself does not create toxic leaders and disqualifies nobody from leadership. Many remarkable leaders have transformed painful experience into empathy and wisdom.

The distinction that matters is between trauma and unprocessed trauma. There is a profound difference between a leader who has made sense of their lived experience and one whose unexamined wounds continue to seep into the way they use power. The child who survived chaos by monitoring everything can become the executive who must control everything. Somebody who once felt profoundly powerless may spend an adult lifetime making sure they never feel powerless again.

The survival mechanisms do not necessarily disappear. They can professionalise. Hypervigilance becomes “strategic oversight”. The inability to trust becomes “strong leadership”. Emotional suppression becomes “composure under pressure”. What once protected a person from vulnerability can become, under the authority of office, the very thing that makes everybody around them unsafe.

The psychoanalyst and organisational psychologist Manfred FR Kets de Vries has spent decades examining the psychological forces beneath executive ambition, and in conversations I had with him about narcissism, his warning about what happens when personality meets authority has always stayed with me. “When people get into a situation of power, unfortunately, narcissism is a very heavy drug and many people cannot handle it,” he said in a 2025 interview. The corporate world can compound that risk because it often rewards the very behaviours it produces: intensity, certainty, relentless drive and control.

But explanation is not exoneration, and an explanation of the leader must never become an alibi for the institution. The facts of each case vary, but what is most striking about the public cases is not what the leader did but how many people knew. The CBI’s implosion under misconduct allegations, the Ted Baker staff petition against their founder’s culture of “forced hugging”, Harvey Weinstein as Hollywood’s open secret: in account after account, the recurring detail was that none of it was hidden. The Ethics & Compliance Initiative reports that about three-quarters of employees who witness wrongdoing do report it, either internally or externally. The signals arrive, yet too often they fail to prompt meaningful action, particularly when the person involved is judged too valuable to lose.

Around a destructive leader grows what I think of as an architecture of accommodation: colleagues who privately disapprove, boards that soften the language, investors who admire the numbers, and employees who decide, entirely understandably, that their mortgage matters more than becoming the next target. Nobody has to intend to protect abuse. Each person simply has to make the safest decision available to them.

Inside a hierarchy, these forces compound. We doubt what we are seeing because nobody else appears alarmed, we assume somebody senior must know more than we do, and we watch what happens to the first person who speaks before quietly deciding not to become the second.

The silence is expensive. When MIT Sloan researchers analysed 34m employee profiles, toxic culture proved 10 times more powerful than pay in predicting who quit. Britain’s Health and Safety Executive identifies the way managers manage staff as a major cause of work-related stress, and Stanford’s Jeffrey Pfeffer, studying workplace mortality, concluded that harmful management practices are “literally killing people”. We banned smoking in offices, so why do we still tolerate this?

Curiously, we govern almost everything except behaviour. A serious company has audit committees, risk registers, compliance functions and external auditors, because financial integrity is never entrusted to goodwill. Yet when the issue is the conduct of the most powerful person in the building, we become oddly informal. It’s a “leadership style”, a “personality clash”, a HR matter, something sensitive to be mediated quietly. And HR is structurally the weakest player. Research I conducted across the media industry in 2022 found that HR ranked as the least respected function by senior executives, which means the people charged with guarding behaviour are marginalised precisely where power most needs guarding.

This is the point at which personality becomes organisational. One person’s personality can become policy. One person’s psychology can become culture. One person’s appetite can become the company’s strategy. Personality, when combined with authority, can become a system.

So what would behavioural governance look like in practice? Boards could independently test whether people can safely disagree with senior leaders. They could look for patterns in attrition rather than treating every departure as a separate event, connect complaints, settlements and confidentiality agreements rather than letting organisational memory reset with each exit, and assess a leader at three, six and 12 months in, once the interview performance is over and the experience of working beneath that person has begun.

Above all, such mechanisms must be independent, because asking a function embedded within a hierarchy to investigate the most powerful person in that hierarchy is an obvious conflict. If we insist on independent governance for finance, why do we accept its absence for people?

The law, at least, is beginning to evolve. Since October 2025, new NDAs in England and Wales cannot prevent victims, or those who reasonably believe they are victims, from making specified disclosures about criminal conduct. The Employment Rights Act 2025 will go further: when its NDA provisions take effect, contractual clauses will be void insofar as they prevent workers speaking about harassment or discrimination, or about how an employer handled their complaint.

Zelda Perkins, the former Weinstein assistant whose Can’t Buy My Silence campaign has been at the forefront of this reform, described NDAs to me as sitting “at the foundation of that architecture of silence”, concealing patterns of behaviour and preventing organisations from recognising the risk. It is a striking description because secrecy does more than protect one individual. Left unchallenged, one person’s pathology can become an organisation’s dysfunction.

Workplace bullying itself, though, is not a stand-alone criminal offence, and Britain still has no specific law against it. Legislation is beginning to tackle the secrecy surrounding workplace abuse. But protection against bullying still lags behind.

Toxic leadership survives through repetition. One generation learns to tolerate it and quietly teaches the next how to survive it: keep your head down, toughen up, don’t become difficult, protect your income, guard your reputation, learn to manage the boss. That inheritance can be refused by the board member who asks the harder question, the colleague who declines to join the whispering afterwards, the investor who asks how the numbers were achieved, the organisation that protects the person telling the truth rather than the person holding the power.

The people who have benefited from our silence are counting on us to keep it that way. We should give them reason to think again. Through structured governance, yes, but more than anything by treating our colleagues with something far less onerous – simple humanity.

Andrea is a pseudonym

Sly & Mighty: How to Recognise, Resist and Rise Above Toxic Power by Kathleen Saxton is published by Sheldon Press, £16.99. To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop. com. Delivery charges may apply.

Fury v Joshua fight confirmed for December at Cardiff’s Principality Stadium

The Guardian Thu, 24 Sep 2026 12:49:37 GMT

Fight on 11 December will start in UK Saturday small hours

Non-title all-British bout to be streamed globally on Netflix

The Battle of Britain is officially fixed for Wales. Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua will stage their long-awaited heavyweight blockbuster in Cardiff on 11 December after an 11th-hour standoff over the venue that threatened to derail the encounter.

The agreement ends years of false starts between the former world champions and clears the way for one of the biggest all-British fights in boxing history. The undercard will take place on a Friday night, with the main-event ringwalks at the Principality Stadium expected in the small hours of Saturday morning – widely reported to be around 2am.

That is to accommodate a prime-time American audience for Netflix, which will broadcast it globally after its preferred plan to stage the fight at New York’s Madison Square Garden was scuppered.

The non-title bout will represent the culmination of a rivalry that has played out in fits and starts and largely from afar for nearly a decade, but securing the necessary signatures required one final round of brinksmanship between the parties.

While both fighters had initially agreed to a November date following their respective July tune-up bouts, the original contract stipulated that the fight would take place in the UK.

But Netflix, backed by the Saudi power broker Turki al-Sheikh and Zuffa Boxing executives, pushed for New York after expressing disappointment with the audience for Fury’s July fight in a UK-friendly time slot, according to a source familiar with the negotiations.

That preference became the ultimate impasse in the final negotiations. Eddie Hearn, Joshua’s promoter, resisted the proposed move to New York, seeking a contractual addendum to account for the heavier US tax burden. On Thursday, Hearn said the UK provision had proved decisive.

“If we hadn’t put that in the contract, which was a request from Anthony Joshua that the fight must be in the UK, we wouldn’t have had a leg to stand on,” he said. “This fight would have been in America.”

The dispute also drew in the UFC chief executive, Dana White. Fury welcomed White’s involvement, while Hearn opposed him serving as lead promoter, prompting an expletive-laden broadside from Fury. Thursday’s announcement said Al-Sheikh’s The Ring and White “will collaborate to promote” the fight, while making no mention of Hearn, Frank Warren, Matchroom or Queensberry.

Fury, 38, and Joshua, 36, remained on course for the lucrative meeting after winning against limited opponents on successive nights in July. While Joshua survived a scare in Saudi Arabia, Fury stopped the 46-year-old Mariusz Wach inside seven rounds in Thailand.

Both men are attempting to return to the summit of boxing’s prestige division after suffering two defeats apiece against Oleksandr Usyk, the unbeaten former undisputed heavyweight champion from Ukraine who relinquished his remaining world title belts in June but insists he has not retired. Fury has won twice since returning to the ring, while Joshua has spent the year rebuilding after his devastating knockout by Daniel Dubois in 2024.

after newsletter promotion

Joshua (30-4-0, 27 KOs) held the IBF’s version of the heavyweight title across two stints from 2016 to 2019 and 2019 to 2021, making seven successful defences while also winning the WBA and WBO belts.

Fury (36-2-1, 25 KOs) first became the lineal and unified world champion y dethroning Wladimir Klitschko in 2015, before being stripped of the IBF title and later relinquishing his remaining belts during a 31-month layoff that saw him swell to nearly 28st amid public battles with addiction and bipolar disorder. The Manchester native completed an extraordinary comeback to hold the WBC title from 2020 to 2024, defending it three times successfully after ending Deontay Wilder’s five-year reign.

The rivals came closest to meeting for the undisputed championship in 2021, but the fight collapsed after a US arbitrator ruled Fury was contractually obligated to face Wilder for a third time.

Joshua subsequently lost his titles to Usyk, with several attempts to revive the Fury contest falling apart in the years since.

The bloom is inevitably off the rose. A fight that once promised to determine the world’s best heavyweight will instead bring together two former champions in their late 30s, each twice beaten by Usyk and closer to the end of his career than the peak. Incredibly, boxing’s long-suffering fans didn’t get it before GTA 6, yet the many years of thwarted negotiations and mutual ill will between Fury and Joshua have endowed the matchup with an aura compelling enough to eclipse its diminished stakes.

There was always something incongruous about an all-British affair of this magnitude finally playing out in New York rather than on UK soil, in front of the supporters whose loyalty and spending helped make both men global stars. Only months after hosting Taylor Swift’s wedding and the Knicks’ drought-busting NBA title run, the Garden appeared to have saved its least likely spectacle for last. But after myriad twists and turns, the biggest British fight that can be made today found its way back to where many felt it always belonged.

‘First there’s the gruelling task of trying to charge my laptop’: a day in the life of a university lecturer in Gaza

The Guardian Thu, 24 Sep 2026 11:00:17 GMT

As the war in Gaza approaches its fourth year, the Guardian follows five ordinary Palestinians as they go about their lives. Each tells the story of their day, revealing the terrible toll of the conflict. Overcoming internet cuts and power outages, Mahmoud battles to provide his students an education

It is time for Mahmoud Seydam’s online lecture on museum architecture. He squats in front of the step he calls a table and opens his laptop.

“Is Mohammed the only one here?” He pulls out his phone and types into the students’ chat group that the lecture is about to start. There are two students now. Mahmoud decides to wait a little for the others to join.

“Today, we have a simple presentation: an overview of museum design.” He asks his students to imagine the museum as honey in a glass. “The museum is a beautiful interior space. It becomes an element that attracts people.”

The internet connection drops out and halts the lecture.

Mahmoud, head of engineering sciences and applied arts at the University College of Science and Technology in Khan Younis and a lecturer at al-Aqsa University, does not seem frustrated. He is used to this.

In his usual calm and professional tone, he records a voice message to his students: “Hello everyone … There seems to be an internet problem, so I will record the lecture, upload it to YouTube and send you the link.”

This is what a day in the life of a university lecturer in Gaza looks like.

double quotation markSleep itself is a struggle. Sleeping isn’t easy while living in tents. Anxiety dominates everything … because there’s no sense of stability.

You compare how your life was before the war to your current life and, psychologically, you’re unable to accept this reality. You’re living in a tent, which doesn’t protect you from anything and doesn’t provide any privacy. You can’t even do your work peacefully because of the noise.

Not to mention the anxiety about an emergency occurring. There was a strike on the tents around us before. There’s fear for the children, of harm to any member of the family. There’s anxiety about being displaced again. We were displaced more than 15 times, including from a place that was uncomfortable, unstable and didn’t support human life, to one that was even worse, sometimes abandoning all our belongings just to save our lives. We slept for three or four nights on the street, on the pavement.

You feel anxious at night. I wake up around dawn, pray and open my mobile phone. I make a cup of coffee and sit outside the tent to respond to messages from students and colleagues that came overnight. I preserve some of my phone’s battery specifically for this task. It’s easier for me to send them voice notes than to type. This is how I start my day.

The morning tasks begin with fetching water. Mahmoud grabs a plastic container and walks to where the water truck stops. His children – three sons and a daughter, studying engineering, nursing and computer science – often help out. He brings the water back to the tent and pours it into their tank, then into buckets of different sizes and colours in front of their tent.

double quotation markWe use these buckets to store some of the water for daily use to make it last as long as possible, because the tank only holds 200 litres.

We don’t have any other tanks. They were all destroyed when our house was bombed. And the water doesn’t reach us every day.

In displacement, we face things we didn’t expect in life. The tent constantly needs repairs. Plus, there is the gruelling task of trying to charge my mobile phone and laptop to start my day and do my work.

Sometimes we have breakfast; sometimes we don’t. Currently, there is flour and we knead and bake in the tent, but the bread spoils from the heat and then there is no breakfast. Meals are not regular, but if I get absorbed in work, I forget about food.

Mahmoud starts to set up for the day’s lecture. As soon as he plugs his laptop into the power strip, the system shuts down. He has learned basic solar energy technology to manage these recurring breakdowns. He grabs the broom, steps on to a plastic chair and cleans the dust off the solar panels on top of the tent. He records the museum design lecture and then it is time to set off for the Scholars Without Borders offices, the college’s temporary headquarters.

double quotation markNot everything is online; there are meetings and student issues for which you need to be present. The distance to Scholars Without Borders is about 6km.

I usually go on foot because of how difficult transportation is: the roads are rough and everything is packed with tents and carts. Today, I used a cart pulled by an old car – it’s the kind that is usually pulled by a horse or a donkey – and then a rundown tuk-tuk. It takes me an hour to get there.

Being in these circumstances and still being able to carry on, to give my all – frankly, I find it incredibly difficult. The basic necessities of life must be in place for a person to be able to excel in their work. People don’t even have the bare minimum for life right now.

The application and practical side of learning has become extremely difficult. Most sessions are online. Most of the basic tools and materials needed for the learning process have become difficult to access or simply unavailable.

From the early stages of the war, we noticed that the universities were deliberately targeted. The university has a certain symbolic significance. It brings together all the future talent and potential, whether among students or the teaching staff.

At one point, we were displaced in an area between Rafah and Khan Younis, where my university was visible from a distance. I saw with my own eyes the military strikes against the university buildings and facilities. When the ceasefire was broken, a video emerged showing the demolition of all of the university buildings, a complete levelling of the site.

We continue with a certain degree of patience and perseverance.

double quotation markBefore the war you could take your family out to eat in a restaurant.

As an architect, I was also quite interested in archaeological and heritage sites, and I’d pop into some of the shops selling antiques to have a look around.

All of this is lost now. There is no time for leisure; we can barely secure the bare necessities. Our life runs like a machine. Every day is just like the next.

My parents and two siblings live in tents nearby, a 10-minute walk. My parents – because of the war, illnesses and old age – have been really affected. It’s a responsibility, so almost every day I visit them to see if they need anything.

I sometimes sit outside my tent and talk with others to unwind after the long day. Then I resume my communications with students. This doesn’t stop until I sleep.

From the moment you wake up until you go to sleep, you’re barely able to keep up with anything other than the tasks you have to do.
