Tom Watson’s move to Palantir is the latest sign of how far the rot has spread in UK politics

The Guardian Thu, 24 Sep 2026 11:00:17 GMT

When a former Labour deputy leader joins a firm built on surveillance and military targeting, it deepens public cynicism – and democracy depends on trust

Whatever is said about Tom Watson, the former deputy leader of the Labour party has a knack for landing headlines. In the past he did it at the expense of the rich and powerful – from News International, over phone hacking, to the Home Office, over its mass surveillance of our data. But his latest headline – that he has joined Palantir as a senior vice-president – has been at the expense of public confidence in the political class.

His new appointment is more than just a private career choice. It sends yet another signal to a weary public about just how far the rot in our democracy has spread.

Now, the former scourge of mass surveillance finds a surveillance company “the most interesting … on the planet”. It’s quite a journey, and one not many of us will want to take with him. Palantir does do work of real consequence. That’s rather the point. Watson says some criticism of Palantir is propaganda. Some of it is also true, which is the part he will find harder to square.

Palantir is a company built on surveillance and military targeting. Its co-founder Peter Thiel wrote in 2009 that he no longer believed freedom and democracy were compatible. He sees technology as an alternative to politics, a way to change the world without having to persuade voters, and backs private “startup cities” run by chief executives. This attitude runs through the company’s DNA. Palantir’s co-founder and chief executive, Alex Karp, has boasted that its work is there “to scare enemies and on occasion kill them”. Its software is used to target people for ICE raids in the US, and civilians in Gaza. This isn’t just another global corporation with some unsavoury corners to its business.

I can’t parse Watson’s mind or motivation. Palantir probably doesn’t hire a former deputy leader for his coding skills. But does it hire access? Access to networks across party and government, and to the doors behind which Palantir would fight to keep a £330m NHS England contract and legally challenge Sadiq Khan’s block on a £50m Metropolitan police contract?

Watson won’t be alone. He will join more than 30 former UK officials at a company that Peter Mandelson’s former lobbying firm, Global Counsel, counted as a client. Mandelson accompanied Keir Starmer to Palantir’s Washington office in 2025, while still retaining a stake in Global Counsel. The MoD has since signed a major partnership with Palantir. And none of this will have broken a single law. The rules on jobs for former ministers last only two years and have no legal force. Therein lies the problem.

Whether it’s Tony Blair and his relationship with Oracle, Mandelson and Global Counsel or Nick Clegg and his time at Meta, the section of the political class meant to oppose vested interests and promote public service appears to have switched sides.

According to the Institute for Public Policy Research’s latest findings, the main political parties, including Labour and the Liberal Democrats, have been accepting donations from wealthy individuals at an accelerating pace. The research found 72% of all £1m-plus donations from individuals since records began in 2001 had come since 2019. Sadly, none of this can be described as an aberration. Rather, it’s how the system increasingly works. Now politicians’ proximity to wealth and the “elites” who own it has fostered a growing public mistrust. One need only listen to Danny Dyer at a rally last week, calling for public ownership of water, to get a feel for that sentiment. These examples are all symptoms of the growing proximity between political power and the wealth it is supposed to hold to account.

In the recent Robin Cook memorial lecture I gave, I termed this malaise the “integrity gap”: the widening gulf between what governments and politicians say and what people believe. Every flagrant act deepens public cynicism about politics, and about the democracy that depends on public trust. This is a fact of which those around Trump are well aware. They know every allegation of presidential corruption erodes people’s willingness to defend democracy.

Thiel understands this implicitly. His vision for our society is simply not compatible with a progressive worldview. That is why a former Labour deputy leader lending his name to Palantir matters so much.

The integrity gap will not close with better messaging. It will close only when politicians show whose side they are on. That means revolving-door rules with the force of law, and a regulator with teeth. It means capping political donations and ending second jobs in the House of Commons, while abolishing the House of Lords altogether. And it means public ownership and democratic control of the things firms such as Palantir want to run, from our health data to our water.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Those who sell access to power have made their choice. Those who oppose Thiel’s vision need to make theirs, and act on it. It’s time to pick a side.

Clive Lewis is the Labour MP for Norwich South

I’m an avid fan of chard – but you can have too much of a good thing

The Guardian Thu, 24 Sep 2026 10:00:15 GMT

My veg patch has turned into a chard jungle and now it’s chard for breakfast, lunch and supper

Chard. It’s hard with so much chard. As Jennifer Lopez might put it if she were in my gardening shoes, I used to have a little, now I have a lot. There was too little last year, for whatever reason. I probably did something wrong. This year, I sowed more. Come summer, the crop underwhelmed me again. So I sowed still more, throwing around seeds of as many varieties as I could get hold of. Then I went off to Croatia for most of August, where there is chard aplenty. That’s not why I go there, incidentally, but it suits me because I really like it, which is just as well because on the Adriatic coast it comes with every meal.

If you have not tried chard, I’d describe it as like spinach, but more substantial. In Croatian it’s called blitva, which oddly enough is the sound my belly starts making when I eat too much of it, as I do every summer there. It can get too much. In Split, I met a woman who was so sick of chard she got rather angry at the very mention of it. She was the cousin of the wife of a famous Serbian footballer I know. She wrote pop songs for a living, but she won’t be penning a love song to blitva any time soon, I can tell you that. As she started forking it off her plate on to mine, she spat out the word blitva as if it were a profanity rather than the sound of a stomach-gurgle. And now I, too, am taking its name in vain.

While I was away, my neighbour kindly watered my garden. I almost wish she hadn’t. My chard patch is now a chard jungle, featuring stems of many colours and leaves of all shades of green. Some of the leaves are so big that if I was naked they would cover not just my bits, but my whole lower half. Strip the leaves and I’m left with stems thick enough to do service as lethal weapons.

And it’s chard for breakfast, chard for lunch and chard for dinner. Chard for the freezer, chard for friends and more for enemies. Chard, chard, chard. I do love chard, but too much chard is hard.

Adrian Chiles is a broadcaster, writer and Guardian columnist

From idealists to struggling sceptics: how Labour’s majority depends on five progressive voter types – in charts

The Guardian Thu, 24 Sep 2026 09:15:01 GMT

Analysis reveals groups with sharply contrasting priorities – and who has drifted the most from Labour towards Greens and Reform

Tactical voting at next election could push Reform into fourth place, poll finds

A new MRP poll suggests Labour would remain the largest party if a general election were held now, but would fall well short of an overall majority as Reform surged into second place.

Behind those headline figures, research from Survation and 38 Degrees casts new light on five distinct voter groups who are collectively defined as the “progressive majority”. These people share concerns about living costs and the NHS, but differ over immigration, the environment, political trust and the pace of change needed to address the UK’s policies.

To build a parliamentary majority, Labour must hold on to the groups that have remained relatively loyal, while winning back voters drifting towards the Greens, Reform or political disengagement. In short, they need enough of this “progressive majority” to stay within the fold.

Labour strategists – including Keir Starmer’s former chief of staff Morgan McSweeney – have often been wary of a tactic that seeks only to unite the progressive bloc. But while it would result in Labour losing huge swathes of seats that it won in 2024, it may be enough to lock Nigel Farage out of No 10 if there were significant tactical voting.

It also gives a clue to how Andy Burnham might seek to structure his priorities – and why the cost of living will be at the heart of the prime minister’s policy platform at the Labour conference, one with salience for voters considering either the Greens or Reform.

The charts below, which are based on polling of more than 8,000 voters, show how Labour’s support cuts across age, class and geography – and reveal five distinct voter groups with contrasting priorities.

The researchers identified five groups of people who collectively make up what they call the “progressive majority”.

It is a key group of voters who they argue the Labour government should be targeting if they want to win an overall majority at the next general election.

The five groups are described as:

Rooted traditionalists: Older, economically left-leaning voters who are highly concerned about immigration and less interested in environmental issues. Many moved from the Conservatives to Labour but could shift again, including towards Reform. Cost of living pressures and NHS access provide the strongest common ground with other progressive voters.

Open-hearted idealists: Affluent, highly educated and the most socially liberal, pro-immigration and politically engaged group. They lean strongly towards Labour, the Greens and Lib Dems and are particularly open to tactical voting. Bills, NHS access and progressive taxation matter most, while tougher immigration policies risk alienating them.

Quiet persuadables: The youngest and least politically committed segment, often holding centrist or uncertain views. Their support is spread widely across the parties and they are the most likely to vote tactically. They are potentially winnable, but need a compelling reason to engage with politics.

Trusting optimists: Young, affluent, urban and highly educated, with strong confidence in their finances, the government and the country’s future. Most support Labour and economically progressive policies, but they are also the most socially authoritarian group. Their political loyalty could weaken if their circumstances deteriorate.

Struggling sceptics: The least financially secure, trusting and electorally engaged group, with many believing voting changes little. Although economically left-leaning, their support is divided between Labour, the Greens and Reform. Winning them back could depend on tangible improvements to bills, wages and living standards rather than political messaging alone.

There are clear demographic differences between the groups.

Quiet persuadables are the youngest-leaning group, while very few rooted traditionalists are young; more than a third of them are over 65.

Trusting optimists are twice as likely as voters overall to live in London, while rooted traditionalists are half as likely.

Struggling sceptics are most likely to have no or low-level qualifications. Meanwhile, almost two-thirds of trusting optimists are graduates.

While nearly a third of struggling sceptics are in lower-income households, trusting optimists and open-hearted idealists are the most affluent groups, with most households earning more than £40,000.

Rooted traditionalists are overwhelmingly white, while trusting optimists are by far the most ethnically diverse group.

Rooted traditionalists and struggling sceptics contain the most leave voters, while open-hearted idealists are overwhelmingly remain-aligned.

These five constituent groups collectively account for nine in 10 current Labour voters.

This is up from eight in 10 at the 2024 general election, showing that Labour’s support has become more concentrated among progressive voters in the last two years.

Open-hearted idealists provide the largest share of Labour’s support at 28%, followed by quiet persuadables at 21%. Trusting optimists have recorded the largest increase, rising four percentage points in the last two years.

At the time of polling, Labour led among all five progressive voter groups – although support ranged from 25% among struggling sceptics to 57% among trusting optimists.

Open-hearted idealists lean heavily towards progressive parties, with the Greens being supported by 23% of this group.

Struggling sceptics are the most fragmented group: Labour leads on 25%, but the Greens and Reform both attract substantial support. Thirteen per cent remain undecided – the highest rate of any group.

Reform performed relatively strongly among rooted traditionalists, whereas the Conservatives reached their highest level among quiet persuadables.

The shifts since 2024 are often down to the fact that, while Labour has lost support across the board, some of these groups are more likely to have found another political home – despite the government switching prime minister.

The Greens have gained the most support among open-hearted idealists, while Reform’s rise is most concentrated among struggling sceptics and rooted traditionalists.

The struggling sceptics are the group among which Labour has lost the most support, falling from 39% to 28%. Both the Greens and Reform have gained among these people, rising to 21% and 18% respectively.

The quiet persuadables and trusting optimists are the groups that have stuck with Labour the most, recording only small drops in support since the general election.

While this is probably due to the stronger financial position of the trusting optimists, who are more likely to trust progressive politicians, the quiet persuadables are less committed to politics and generally don’t hold stronger political views.

Looking at the concerns of these five groups reveals conflicting priorities which could be hard for Burnham to bridge.

The cost of living is the dominant concern across every progressive voter group, cited by between 54% and 77%.

Health and the NHS generally ranks second, peaking at 56% among open-hearted idealists, while the economy is a significant but less prominent concern across all groups.

The sharpest divide is over immigration: it is cited by 34% of rooted traditionalists and 28% of struggling sceptics, but just 5% of pen-hearted idealists.

The climate crisis shows a reverse pattern, reaching 29% among open-hearted idealists but only 10% among rooted traditionalists.

Rooted traditionalists are also notably more concerned about pensions, while housing and jobs feature more strongly among trusting optimists and quiet persuadables.

When looking at the salience of different issues among voters as a whole, the research concluded that immigration is the area where Labour is least trusted – but also that this might not be a significant vulnerability.

It is named as a vote-deciding issue by 40% of voters – level with the NHS and second only to the cost of living – but Reform leads Labour on it by 10 points. Thirty-one per cent of the public trust Reform on this issue, compared with 21% trusting Labour.

But the researchers point to the fact that these figures are population-wide, and that immigration is not a driving factor in the votes of most people within the progressive majority. Instead, the cost of living and the economy are bigger drivers of people’s votes.

Across the public as a whole, Labour led Reform on every other major issue, including the NHS, by 12 points, and the cost of living, by six.

Damian Lyons Lowe, the founder and chief executive of Survation, said: “Labour’s potential coalition is best understood as five distinct segments making up a ‘progressive majority’ – those voters that strongly consider voting for one or more of Lib Dems, Labour, the Greens, Plaid and the SNP. They have very different views on social and economic policy – the balancing act is real – but our data suggests it’s more manageable than the conventional wisdom implies.

“The issues that divide these groups, immigration above all, are largely ones where Labour isn’t trusted and where the voters it could win are already spoken for. The issues that unite them – the cost of living, energy, food and housing bills, and cleaning up politics – are exactly where even the most sceptical parts of the coalition trust Labour more than anyone else. The way to build such a winning coalition isn’t to referee their disagreements. It’s to deliver visibly on the concerns every one of them shares.”

We’re in a crisis of loneliness – but is buying friends on an app likely to help solve it?

The Guardian Thu, 24 Sep 2026 09:00:13 GMT

Shortcuts work against the rewards of friendship: authentic relationships can surely only be forged when you’re not expecting a return on your money

What price would you put on friendship? In these hyper-capitalistic times, where nothing is beyond being given a monetary value, perhaps even Mastercard wouldn’t dare to claim that it’s priceless. A YouGov survey found that 15% of Britons say they have no close friends, while nearly one in 10 (8%) have no friends at all. The numbers are similarly dismal in the US. As we face this contemporary crisis of connection, it is little wonder that friendship, or at least the possibility of it, is increasingly being marketed for sale.

There has been a striking increase in online platforms and apps that promise to introduce you – algorithmically, through social mixers or a combination – to your next BFF. There’s Cliq, PLY, standing for “People Like You”, and RealRoots which promises user satisfaction with the tagline: “Make new friends. Guaranteed”. Meanwhile, 222 boldly declares it is “not a friend-making service”, but a means to “explore serendipity” through social experiences with compatible people.

And this new sweep of pay-to-play friendships doesn’t stop at apps and algorithmic matchmaking. It is accompanied by supper clubs, book clubs, running clubs and other opportunities for you to mingle with people in your area – for a fee, of course. CircleUp, for example, holds regular social mixers across the UK for paying members, so that you can “keep seeing the same faces”. Others cultivate a more exclusive crowd. Gathering Tables hosts dinners for a “curated mix of guests”, united by their willingness to pay £145 a head.

These initiatives dangle community, but whether this trumps their commercial reason for being is debatable. The price of these apps and events is sometimes framed as a means of securing commitment, not just covering costs. “When you do things for free, people often don’t turn up,” PLY’s founder told the Guardian. But the effort becomes less civic-minded when you consider the desire for friendship is what makes these services valuable in the first place. These friend-making apps and paid-for gatherings may well offer opportunities for social connection – they are at least a date in the diary. But make no mistake, they exist primarily to encourage investment in a brand and even create opportunities to spend. Of course it is possible to make genuine connections in commercial spaces – many of us have made close bonds at work – but paying for introductions feels antithetical to the spirit of true friendship.

This new commercial interest in facilitating “gathering” speaks to the sense of collective untethering from community. Many of us understand we are lacking community, perhaps even more than friendship. It is unsettlingly common to hear people complaining of their current social network, as though a more suitable or nourishing one already exists, just waiting for you to slot into it. No wonder brands are attempting to package them up.

Cliq claims the first step to “start your community” is to download its app. But real community is built, not bought (and certainly not downloaded). It takes time, shared investment and often some weathering on both sides. It is certainly possible that meaningful, enduring ties can begin at a paid-for meet-up. But while the payment can create the conditions for friendship, it can’t manufacture the friendship itself.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Tellingly, ease is often central to the offering: Cliq claims “finding your people shouldn’t be difficult”. Shouldn’t it? No matter how you meet, it takes time and effort to turn an acquaintance into a friend; that same process, multiplied and sustained, is what creates a community. Seeking shortcuts or higher-quality connections is not only beside the point, it works against the rewards: authentic relationships can only be forged without expectation of a return on investment.

That’s not to say we don’t need more places and opportunities to meet new people; the very existence of these services at least demonstrates that we do. But before entrusting our need for greater intimacy and affection to a third party, we might ask ourselves if we could be doing more to put ourselves out there socially. Could we extend an invitation to friendly strangers, or introduce our mutuals and turn acquaintances into friends?

The best community-building exercise I’ve heard of lately was before a performance of Austentatious – the Jane Austen comedy play – where all solo ticket-holders were invited to come early and mingle before the show. The event was free, organised around a preexisting commitment and people could opt in. There was the opportunity to meet people; the work, and potential reward, of making a new friend was left to you.

Elle Hunt is a freelance journalist

The west is in freefall – and the worst part is that we were warned, but chose not to listen

The Guardian Thu, 24 Sep 2026 07:00:12 GMT

Endless pursuit of wealth and power by western leaders led us here. What strikes me most is how many saw what was coming

The symptoms of decline are everywhere you look. On Sunday, Germany’s far right won another state election, taking nearly 40% of the vote in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. France is preparing a €54bn fiscal squeeze, which could turn the screw still further on a foundering so-called European social model. At the UN general assembly, Donald Trump once again threatened to “annihilate” Iran, even as the fourth failed western war on a Muslim nation this century has added more than $100bn to Americans’ fuel bills.

There is little dispute over the symptoms. The great fight of our age is over the diagnosis, and the right has been winning it for years. Its story is simple and, as the latest German state election underlines, effective: the west is dying because of migrants, Muslims, trans people, “woke” and the “deep state”. So when I told friends I was writing a book called The Fall of the West: How They Really Lost It, they worried I had shape-shifted into Liz Truss, who, after being outlasted in office by a lettuce, produced Ten Years to Save the West.

My diagnosis is rather different. The west is in decline because after the cold war, its elites declared a victory from which they have never recovered. They proclaimed an economic model that channelled wealth upwards as the inevitable future, while treating an apparently invincible military as free to reshape the Muslim world. Both convictions were terribly convenient for those who benefited from them. The result has been catastrophic: an economy that no longer delivers sustained improvements in living standards or public services, and western military interventions humiliated in Kabul, Baghdad, Tripoli and now the strait of Hormuz.

Abroad, the west’s claims of moral superiority have been incinerated, not least by Israel’s genocide of the Palestinian people in Gaza. At home, the disillusionment and despair spawned by these overlapping disasters have fuelled the rise of the far right, threatening democracy itself.

What struck me while researching the book was how often people had seen what was coming – and how little difference their warnings had made.

In the spring of 1994, one of the most senior political officers at the US embassy in Moscow sent Washington a long dissenting cable. Its argument was stark enough to make its author an outcast within the foreign-policy establishment.

Wayne Merry is nobody’s idea of a radical. He grew up in a wheat-country settlement in Oklahoma called – no joke – Kremlin, and admired the then Russian president, Boris Yeltsin. But he had spent two years witnessing “shock therapy” – the overnight conversion of a planned economy into a casino – being imposed on the wreckage of the Soviet economy by Washington, Harvard economists and the IMF. He had taken to stuffing his pockets with cash for old women begging in the streets, “because,” he told me simply, “they were starving”.

Russia was ruled by westernisers, but Merry’s cable warned that “democratic forces in Russia are in serious trouble” and that “there is no reason to believe the Russian economy is capable of rapid market reform”. If the US chose “the role of economic missionary rather than true partner”, he predicted, it would strengthen extremists and revive an “adversarial relationship between Russia and the west”.

As Merry told me: “We’re gutting working-class living standards, and then expecting people to vote for us.” Washington’s answer was to make him persona non grata. The cable remained classified for three decades, quietly released only at the end of 2024. By then, one study estimated there had been 12.2 million excess deaths in Russia during the transition. Meanwhile the strongman who rose from the wreckage was nearly three years into his murderous full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

The men who ignored Merry were not coy about their assumptions. Russia had to move towards “our way of doing things,” said Strobe Talbott, President Bill Clinton’s main Russia adviser. If that sounded like “an obnoxious confirmation of our doctrine of exceptionalism”, his answer was simple: “Well, tough. That’s us; that’s the US. We are exceptional.”

This was the basic structural problem of the post-cold war order. It has never gone away. However strong the evidence behind a warning, when it collided with the interests of western power, the warning gave way.

I spent two years travelling from Baghdad to Pittsburgh, and Nairobi to Ramallah, for the book, and Merry’s experience turned out to be less the exception than the rule. In a 2005 interview, the US envoy Edmund McWilliams said he had warned in 1988 that Washington’s Afghan policy was “going very, very badly”, as US weaponry flowed to Islamist fundamentalists. But the overriding objective was defeating the Soviet Union. McWilliams said he was frozen out, smeared as mentally ill, alcoholic and gay, and reassigned. CIA analysts themselves had warned in 1987 that a victorious Islamist regime might inherit a “mountain of weapons” and use them to arm or train Islamist guerrillas elsewhere. The weapons kept flowing.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

The same triumphalism took hold at home. Western economies were not starved of wealth: they were increasingly organised to extract it rather than invest it. As the economist Mariana Mazzucato told me, 80% of British finance now flows back into finance, insurance and real estate. Western economies became increasingly good at rewarding ownership, but increasingly bad at building the productive foundations on which prosperity depends.

In early 2007, an executive director of the World Bank told his friend, the economist Ha-Joon Chang, that a huge crisis was coming. His evidence was his cleaner, who he suspected was undocumented: she had a $300,000 mortgage. Stagnant wages had been papered over with cheap credit – “let them eat credit,” as one economist summed up the model – and the paper was about to tear. When it did, the crash should have finished off this failed economic model. Instead, ordinary people were forced to pay to save it, through shredded social provision.

Where this chaotic fall could lead is frightening. Israel’s genocide has normalised limitless depravity. Trumpism has repurposed the rhetoric and institutions of the “war on terror”, now used to target domestic dissent. Authoritarianism and barbarism are entirely plausible futures.

There is another possibility: the left makes a different case. That it was the endless, unchecked pursuit of wealth and power by western elites, at home and abroad, that brought us here, and that the task is to rebuild what Margaret Thatcher sought to destroy – society – by investing the wealth we collectively produce. Or, as the man who wrote that buried cable put it to me: stop gutting people’s living standards and then expecting them to vote for you.

Owen Jones is a Guardian columnist. His latest book, The Fall of the West: How They Really Lost It, is published on 1 October. Order your copy at the Guardian bookshop

Abandoned, dismissed and gaslighted: there is no excuse for the way ME sufferers have been betrayed

The Guardian Thu, 24 Sep 2026 05:00:08 GMT

Changes in guidance and science seem to have little impact on millions of devastated lives. It’s a shocking social crisis playing out behind closed doors

I’ve spent my working life covering neglected issues. But few are neglected like the devastating chronic condition ME/CFS (myalgic encephalomyelitis, or chronic fatigue syndrome). In severe cases, the illness shuts down people’s lives almost entirely, causing an extreme loss of energy and a wide range of physical and cognitive symptoms that can prevent patients from working, socialising and, sometimes, even moving or eating. Yet these people have been more or less airbrushed from our minds.

To find out what this neglect looks like in practice, this week I put out a call on Bluesky asking people with ME/CFS about their recent experiences of treatment. I was immediately inundated with horrifying testimonies. “I’ve just been completely abandoned”; “a 10-year waiting list for treatment”; “we’ve given up seeking medical support”; “stuck in limbo”; “I just felt utterly unheard, invalidated”. I’ve been sent hundreds of shocking and heart-rending accounts.

Exact numbers are hard to establish, but in the UK alone, an estimated 400,000 people live with the condition. It affects women far more than men, by a ratio of about 4:1, according to a study in England. The number of people with long Covid, some of whom meet the diagnostic criteria for ME/CFS, was estimated in 2024 at 2 million in England and Scotland.

You might have imagined politicians and the media would be all over it. Instead, this great social crisis is met with silence or worse. Some outlets, despite the overwhelming weight of evidence, have mocked or trivialised these conditions.

There’s a long, dark history here, rooted in centuries of dismissal of predominantly female illnesses as “hysterical”, and amplified in recent decades by government attempts to reduce the benefits bill and insurers’ attempts to reduce payouts. If you can establish that a condition is caused by malingering, poor self-care or a negative attitude, you won’t have to cough up.

Official guidance in many countries was informed by a series of deeply flawed studies that purported to show these illnesses could be treated with cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT), or graded exercise therapy (GET). In 2020, the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (Nice) found that the quality of all the research promoting these therapies as curative treatments for ME/CFS was either “low” or, in most cases, “very low”. In 2021, it stopped recommending these therapies as primary treatments. We now know CBT cannot treat the condition (though it can sometimes help patients to come to terms with it), while GET is not only useless but actively dangerous, as exercise can trigger one of the most devastating ME/CFS symptoms: post-exertional malaise (PEM). PEM robs people of their remaining energy, rendering many patients bedbound, sometimes incapable of almost all movement.

Since then, two other things have happened. At the inquest into the death of a young ME/CFS patient, the coroner ruled that provision in the health service for patients with severe ME “was and is nonexistent”. Something would have to be done. And a number of seeming scientific breakthroughs, some very recent, have begun inching towards identifying possible biological causes of both ME/CFS and long Covid. Now, or so we should hope, it’s undeniable.

So what has changed as a result of these shifts? Alongside the horror and heartbreak in the testimonies of the people who emailed me, I was struck by the sense of sheer relief that someone, anyone, was asking the question.

Many said they are still being treated as if they have a psychological illness, and still being pushed into GET and CBT. One patient told me: “I’ve gone from relatively mild to now mostly house- and bedbound, largely thanks to repeated attempts at graded exercise and ‘pushing through’.” A few days ago, an NHS clinic told another patient to undertake “graded exercise” and “simply to walk, despite the fact I’m a wheelchair user”.

One mother told me “the consultant cardiologist recommended a graded exercise programme” and “a treadmill test” for her bedbound son. When she told him this contradicted Nice guidelines, he replied: “Well, what do you want me to do?” Another made the same challenge to her GP, but the doctor “denied this strongly and reiterated to my daughter that she should do the exercises”. This is very common: many doctors, I’m told, seem unaware of the new guidelines and react defensively when challenged. In many practices, GET has simply been rebranded as “building tolerance” or “pacing up” or “a little more activity each day”.

Patients report being treated with “contempt and derision”. Loads are still being offered CBT. Some have been propelled by NHS doctors towards quack private “cures”, now offered by a growing industry that preys on people’s desperation.

Others tell me they’ve not been pushed into inappropriate treatments, but “that’s only because I receive no treatment for it whatsoever”. Some have had to explain to their doctors what ME/CFS is. And it gets worse. I’ve been contacted by parents who have been accused of fabricating and inducing illness and even referred to social services, because doctors who seem to know nothing about ME/CFS believe they are making up their children’s symptoms.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

It’s as if nothing has been learned. Perhaps that’s not surprising. A freedom of information request to NHS England found that, of the tens of thousands of practitioners who would benefit from it, after a year, only 74 had completed the new learning module on ME/CFS guidance. Meanwhile, as recently as last summer, the Department for Work and Pensions was still teaching its trainees elements of the old, discredited view of the condition. And, as the Liberal Democrat MP Tessa Munt, a hero of this story, tells me: “The piecemeal offerings in the government’s final delivery plan are not going to touch the system-wide failings.”

It’s not only the UK. I’ve been contacted by patients from around the world. In Sweden and Australia, official guidance still recommends GET and CBT. In Switzerland, I’m told, treatment is spiralling backwards, with a new wave of psychologisation. Norway, Finland and the Netherlands, despite their progressive medical reputations, sound like a waking nightmare for ME/CFS patients.

Of course, as there is no effective treatment, it’s a difficult situation for doctors as well as patients. But even worse than no solutions is false solutions, and a dangerous, gaslighting, even punitive approach to a terrible disease.

Across the decades, millions of people have been neglected, dismissed and mistreated, and still it goes on. We need to ask why so many patients have been abandoned, why discredited and dangerous treatments continue to be prescribed and why ignorance and neglect still dominate, in the health system and beyond. In other words, there has seldom been a stronger case for a public inquiry.

George Monbiot is a Guardian columnist

Labour’s last chance? The people shaping Andy Burnham’s grand plans for Britain

The Guardian Thu, 24 Sep 2026 04:00:09 GMT

The new prime minister has declared he wants to end 40 years of neoliberalism. But is he really prepared to be that radical?

In May 2025, when Keir Starmer was still prime minister, Labour politicians, campaigners and journalists gathered at the Ministry of Sound in London to watch a series of panel talks and presentations illuminated by the lucid glow of club lights. The day-long event was organised by a campaign group called Compass, and the subjects included child poverty, the Murdoch-owned media and the rise of the radical right.

“We felt as though the Labour government was failing, and needed to be pulled into the 21st century,” Neal Lawson, the founder of Compass, told me. The Starmer government’s support for the Conservatives’ two-child benefit cap, its equivocating stance on Gaza and its emulation of far-right rhetoric – crystallised in a speech on immigration, during which the prime minister suggested Britain risked becoming an “island of strangers” – were causing Labour supporters to rapidly desert their party. “The Starmer project was so obviously intellectually bankrupt. He was personally so disinterested in ideas and big thinking that I thought, this is never going to fly,” Lawson said.

At 4pm, the mayor of Greater Manchester, Andy Burnham, got up on stage to deliver the closing address. “It’s the latest any Labour people have been in the Ministry of Sound on a Saturday,” he joked, cheerfully sweating under the lights. He spoke for 15 minutes, speeding up with excitement. Unlike Starmer, Burnham seemed to have a clear theory about the “dark and divided times” the country found itself in, identifying the long-term cause of Britain’s “modern malaise” as the privatisation of essential services, such as water and electricity, under Margaret Thatcher. Rather than mimicking the rhetoric of the right, he suggested that Labour should take concrete steps to improve voters’ lives, “things that matter to people every single day”.

The prospect that Burnham might replace Starmer seemed distant. He wasn’t an MP, and any route back to Westminster was unclear. But he was the most high-profile Labour politician to eloquently diagnose the causes of Britain’s widespread sense of political disenchantment and economic injustice, something that Starmer had never managed to do. “It wasn’t just the speech of a mayor of Manchester,” Lawson recalled. “It was the speech of someone who looked and sounded like they wanted to be prime minister.”

A few months later, Compass launched a new membership organisation, Mainstream, with the aim of funnelling leftwing ideas into a new Labour government. It wasn’t intended to be a campaign organisation for Burnham, Lawson told me, but it was “a happy coincidence”. Burnham signed its founding statement. As the political momentum for an alternative to Starmer increased, and as Burnham started to look like the only real contender, a small group of economists in London began working together to persuade him that, were he to become leader, he should make the unaffordability of everyday life his focus.

For years, Labour had prized economic growth as the main route to improve living standards. But economists such as Alfie Stirling, the director of policy at the Joseph Rowntree Foundation (JRF); Hannah Peaker, deputy CEO of the New Economics Foundation (NEF); and Carys Roberts, a former policy adviser to Starmer who had resigned in October 2025, argued that this approach was mistaken. The government didn’t have long enough until the next election to wait for growth to materialise, they believed, so it should try to improve people’s living standards now by intervening in the market to lower the cost of living. On 14 May 2026, the Labour MP for Makerfield, Josh Simons, announced he would be standing down and cleared the way for Burnham to run in a byelection. On the same day, the JRF and the NEF published coordinated research proposing a new system of rent controls. (The Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR), the thinktank where Roberts formerly worked, had published similar research a few days earlier.) “We were anticipating political movement,” Stirling told me. “And we wanted to make sure we were landing the right policies.”

Burnham seemed to take their message on board. In his first weeks as prime minister, he threw out a confetti of new announcements. He slashed energy bills and lowered bus fares. He pledged to end homelessness, to build more council housing, and to fix adult social care. “The mood is feeling so much more positive than most of the last year and a half in parliament,” the Labour MP and economist Yuan Yang said this month during a lecture she gave in London.

And, yet, owing to the way that Burnham became prime minister – with no leadership contest or general election manifesto – it’s difficult to tell how radical his government wants to be. Already, he has watered down the council housing announcement (60% of funding for new homes in England outside London will go to social housing, rather than all of it), backtracked on his intention to cap political donations at £500,000, and has stopped talking about “public ownership”, instead using the vaguer language of “public control”. His chancellor, John Healey, is not known as an economic thinker (during his first major speech, Healey spoke mostly about growth, sounding hardly different from his predecessor, Rachel Reeves). “Burnham is the master of vibes. He’s a figure who pops up with a positive story,” Karel Williams, an emeritus professor at the University of Manchester, whose economic thinking has been influential in Labour circles, told me. “It feels as though he’s become a screen on to which different Labour factions project their hopes, telling us more about what other people want to happen than what he might do.”

Nonetheless, Burnham styles himself as the most radical prime minister since Thatcher and has not backed away from his stated ambition to end 40 years of neoliberalism. His willingness to name her ideology suggests that, unlike Starmer, Burnham understands the importance of ideas in politics: having them, spreading them, making them seem like common sense. Many of the ideas that have guided Britain’s governments in the past half century have been produced by a small group of thinktanks within two miles of Westminster. “When there’s the prospect of a new Labour government, that machine goes into overdrive,” Mark McVitie, the co-founder of the Labour Growth Group, a caucus of MPs formed in 2024 with a self-described mission to “smash the status quo”, told me.

In the past few months, a deluge of ideas – some large, some small – have been suggested by people seeking to influence the government. Burnham could nationalise Thames Water, scrap the triple lock that protects state pensions, or put workers on company boards. He could rewrite the mandate of the Bank of England, ban Palantir from the NHS, or tax social media giants to rejuvenate local high streets. He could build the equivalent of London’s Elizabeth line in all of Britain’s major cities, introduce proportional representation or require all new bicycles to have built-in lights. Whether any of these ideas have a chance of becoming reality will become clear over the next few months, first with the publication of the budget, and then with the government’s 10-year plan for Britain. “Nothing is off the table,” one source close to Downing Street told me in August.

This summer, in the weeks after Burnham became prime minister, I began interviewing the small core of people who are trying to shape this agenda. Some have radical ideas about economic ownership, while others spend their lives thinking of ways to devolve political power away from London to Britain’s neglected cities and regions. But for all their different prescriptions, they agreed on one thing: the government can’t afford to wait if it is to have a chance against the threat of a globally resurgent right, funded by oligarchs who are hostile to democracy. “There’s a ticking clock with this,” McVitie said. “I talk about democratic breakdown. And my big fear is that tweaking the current model is not going to work. If you don’t break from the path you’re on, eventually, some form of that is going to arrive.”

One phrase that Burnham has repeated since becoming prime minister is that Britain’s great mistake has been privatising economic power and centralising political power. More than one person I spoke with attributed the phrasing to Mathew Lawrence, the founder of the thinktank Common Wealth. In June, he and the economist Alex Williams published a paper called The Productive State: A Framework for Manchesterism. It was intended as an alternative to a failed status quo.

“The Blair line was always ‘what matters is what works,’” Lawrence told me. “But is private equity really working to deliver social care? Have leveraged buyouts of the water industry really worked for rivers? Has the privatisation of energy really worked to deliver value for money or energy security?” Faced with the worst decade for living standards on record, the paper argued for a different kind of economy. It would be based upon a foundation of essential services delivered by publicly run corporations, a second tier of privately owned manufacturing and retail businesses, and a third tier of startups in industries such as AI and clean energy that would be regulated and supported by the government.

Lawrence, whose Dr Martens and scruffy beard cut a more casual impression than that of most policy advisers, is always having at least two conversations at once: one in person and another on the phone. I’ve known him for nearly a decade (we briefly shared a flat in 2020), and when we met recently, he took three calls in the space of 20 minutes: one from an MP, another from an MP’s special adviser and a third from a journalist. Although his research has been cited as an influence on Burnham, Lawrence has not been given a role in the new government (neither has Lawson, who helped write the script for Burnham’s byelection campaign video and advised him before he became prime minister). But Common Wealth certainly is influential. As secretary of state for energy security and net zero, Ed Miliband consulted its research when founding the publicly owned company Great British Energy, and Lawrence has since discussed the Productive State paper with the team of Miliband’s successor, Miatta Fahnbulleh.

In Britain, the world of leftwing policy ideas is really a small network of close friends and former colleagues. Fahnbulleh, who previously worked at the IPPR and was then chief executive at the NEF, has hired a number of people from the network into her department. Carys Roberts, formerly director of the IPPR, is her chief of staff. George Dibb, another IPPR alumnus, was seconded to Fahnbulleh’s department to advise on industrial strategy. Another influential thinker in this world is Arthur Downing, a friend of Lawrence who worked as an adviser in the energy department under Miliband. Today, Downing is a strategy director at Octopus Energy and author of a recent book arguing for public ownership of Britain’s energy networks. He recently founded a monthly discussion group called the Haldane Society – named after a hero of his, Thomas Haldane, a Scottish engineer who created one of the world’s first heat pumps – bringing together Westminster insiders and people working in the energy industry to discuss public ownership. “Privatisation is a form of self-loathing,” Downing said at a recent event. “It’s believing that your own government can’t own and operate assets that another state can.”

The thinkers surrounding the Burnham government share certain characteristics. They are mostly men who live in inner London, wear dark blazers over open-collared shirts, and write essays on Substack or for the New Statesman using phrases such as “dynamism” and “productivism”. Some of them have worked for MPs, some have spent most of their careers at thinktanks, and others have come up through what one described as the social media “posting to policy pipeline”. Many of them are under 40, and all of them bear the disappointment of having witnessed Labour finally win an election and then struggle to govern.

It’s possible to discern three distinct camps seeking to influence Burnham. The first, which is closer to Fahnbulleh and Miliband, draws on the more radical ideas of thinkers such as Lawrence and includes organisations such as Common Wealth and the NEF. Its central argument is that the privatisation of life’s essentials, including energy and social care, has created an affordability crisis that is driving up inflation, and that many of these assets should therefore be publicly owned.

The second camp is closer to Burnham’s powerful ally the first secretary of state, Louise Haigh, her adviser Nick Williams, and Josh Simons, the former Makerfield MP. It includes thinktanks such as the newly founded Centre for British Progress and the Good Growth Foundation. For this more centrist camp, the problem with Thatcherism has less to do with privatisation than the erosion of state capacity that resulted from it. “We rely on an army of consultants, lawyers and third-party providers”, because Britain has “forgotten how to build”, wrote David Lawrence, the co-founder of the Centre for British Progress, in a recent essay. The answer to Britain’s economic problems, according to this school of thought, lies in winnowing down the vast apparatus of regulations, particularly planning policies, that protect large and established companies, prevent startups from emerging, and are holding back a potential abundance of new homes and power plants.

Finally, there is a third, older camp of thinkers who might be called the communitarians; they have more power than either of the other two camps, since they hold key positions in No 10. Among them is James Purnell, Burnham’s chief of staff and one of his most trusted friends, and Purnell’s close friend Graeme Cooke, a former director of the IPPR, who is now director of Burnham’s No 10 policy unit. Newcomers to the Burnham government have been reading a 2010 essay that Purnell and Cooke wrote during a period of soul-searching after Gordon Brown lost the general election. They argued that New Labour had failed to develop a philosophy for what a good society looked like, one that rejected the paternalism of the state and put people in charge of their lives.

This month, Burnham hired an adviser named Marc Stears, an influential political theorist in this communitarian tradition. Stears is more concerned with political philosophy than the granular details of economic policy, and believes Labour’s major challenge has less to do with the minutiae of planning regulations or public ownership than with the need to renew people’s faith in politics. “For decades now, the professionalisation of political parties [has] generated a cult of expertise and detachment, a sense that ordinary people do not understand their own lives, that the fundamental aspects of their affairs are better run for them from on high,” he wrote in Out of the Ordinary, a wide-eyed study of English writers such as DH Lawrence and George Orwell that was published in 2021. He argued that what Britain needed most of all was a “thoroughgoing devolution of power”.

One challenge for the small army of thinkers trying to influence Burnham is that, unlike his predecessor, the prime minister is not a blank slate: he has strongly held principles, derived not from policy papers or Westminster advisers, but from his own experience of governing. At the heart of this is an approach that he has famously dubbed “Manchesterism”. In a speech he gave this March, Burnham defined this as a means of softening the harder edges of capitalism by combining economic growth with social progress. For the prime minister, Manchesterism is also, crucially, a vindication of the policy of devolving power away from London. (The Greater Manchester mayoralty, along with five other new “metro mayor” posts, was introduced in the 2010s under the Tories.)

The British media rarely covers cities outside London in great depth, and Burnham’s “ism” has generated its own micro-genre of commentary from journalists and policy experts using the city as a guide to what he might do as prime minister. Yet the idea of combining social and economic progress is hardly a radical philosophy. In that speech, Burnham likened Manchesterism to Benjamin Disraeli’s one nation Toryism. So what does it actually tell us about what the prime minister wants?

Burnham’s most high-profile achievement as mayor of Greater Manchester was the creation of the Bee bus network, the result of a deal that Richard Leese, the former leader of Manchester city council, agreed with George Osborne in 2014. Under Thatcher, England’s buses were effectively privatised in 1986, allowing companies to choose which routes to cover and how much to charge. This meant that from 1986 to 2019, the number of bus journeys in Greater Manchester dropped by nearly half. After Theresa May’s government passed the Bus Services Act in 2017, allowing England’s metro mayors to bring buses back into public control, Burnham was the first to use these new powers.

While the buses wouldn’t be fully run and owned by the state, the newly formed Transport for Greater Manchester now decides all the routes, timetables and fares, and operators bid for these contracts. Stagecoach and Rotala, two of Britain’s largest bus operators, took the mayor’s office to court, arguing that the decision was unlawful (the high court dismissed their challenge). “Getting this done was really, really hard work – for Andy in particular,” Leese told me. “He had to be very precise at all times in exactly what he said. One wrong step and Stagecoach and the others would have had us back in court. They were watching the commas.”

The sunflower yellow Bee network was launched in 2023 and burnished Burnham’s credentials as a savvy political salesman. His emphasis as mayor on regenerating communities outside the city centre and making Manchester more affordable, by pledging to build council housing and pressing employers to pay the living wage, has drawn retrospective comparisons to New York City’s mayor, Zohran Mamdani, who introduced rent freezes, city-run grocery stores and free childcare to reduce the cost of living. But a number of people I spoke with worried that there would be limits to how much the Manchesterist approach could be applied at a national level.

This year, Haigh wrote a piece for Renewal – an influential centre-left journal published by Compass – setting out her arguments for economic change. It recommended a series of fiscal policy tweaks, but made no mention of public ownership, nor how to tangibly improve living standards in the here and now. Since then, Burnham has put Haigh in charge of a cabinet taskforce that will examine how to bring housing, energy, water and transport under “public control” rather than full-on state ownership. Lawrence, McVitie and other members in that first, more left-leaning camp around the prime minister are sceptical that the system of public control that worked for Manchester’s buses could ever work for England’s water system. England already has five separate regulators to police these companies, yet not one of them has managed to control the industry’s excesses. “We risk giving local leaders more responsibility for a system they don’t have the power to fundamentally change,” McVitie recently told the Guardian.

At her lecture in London this month, Yang, a former Financial Times journalist who has a government role in the Treasury, sketched out a vision for what Burnhamism might look like. “Many words have already been written about which isms might replace neoliberalism: Manchesterism, productivism, localism,” Yang said. “What interests me is not just the switch from one ideology to another, but the end of a neoliberal consensus, the idea that there’s one economic theory to rule them all.”

Yang falls somewhere between the first and second camp: she is a member of the Tribune group of moderate Labour MPs led by Haigh, but is also regarded as someone who has distinctively progressive ideas about the economy. In her lecture, she explained that Manchesterism is about places being able to make choices for themselves. But if power is further devolved to individual regions, she admitted, “there are some regions with Reform mayors [who] will pursue quite different economic structures”, perhaps by pursuing “light-touch regulation and financial services”. If this is the case, a Manchesterist approach to running the UK government wouldn’t represent the end of neoliberalism so much as the beginning of an experiment in letting hundreds of municipal flowers bloom. From Labour’s perspective, some of those flowers would probably turn out to look more like weeds. Yang struck a hopeful, but uncertain note: “I think we have to be really quite brave about admitting that there’s a significant amount of uncertainty about how different regions will pursue their different methods.”

The world of policy debate and thinktank research can sometimes feel very insular. These organisations have such similar names – Compass, Mainstream, Tribune, Renewal, Progress, Common Wealth, the Productivity Institute, the Future Governance Forum, the New Economics Foundation – that only an insider could be expected to keep them straight. Since he became prime minister, Burnham’s big idea has been to challenge the notion that politics is something that only happens among a small clique in a couple of square miles in central London. In late June, he announced the creation of No 10 North. It is currently located in a sleekly refurbished 1980s office block opposite Manchester’s Victorian town hall. The vibe is more casual than Downing Street: inside, there are break-out rooms and open-plan offices. Some ministers hot desk. When I passed the building on a sunny Friday evening in August, two police officers were guarding its entrance. A passerby asked what was inside, and one of them replied: “No 10 North,” with a shrug and a smirk, as if to say: me neither.

No 10 North could be remembered in a few years as just a gimmick, but it could also turn into one of Burnham’s most consequential policies. It is partly a means of wresting power back from the Treasury in London, which is often accused of blocking investment in the north. Civil servants responsible for local growth are being relocated into a new government department called the Office of the Prime Minister and Cabinet, which will be led by Haigh. The idea for such a department originated in a paper produced by the Future Governance Forum, which argued for a new centre of executive power within No 10. “You need a centre that is strong enough that it can give different government departments a direction on devolution they can’t ignore,” Jack Shaw, who runs a small thinktank called Groundwork, told me. “Paradoxically, in order to get the most out of devolution, Burnham needs a more powerful centre.”

Many of the thinkers most excited by Burnham’s devolution plans are people like Shaw, a 33-year-old from Dagenham who has spent many years working on these ideas at smaller thinktanks, including IPPR North. Shaw belongs to a WhatsApp group of 120 devolution experts, which pinged with excited messages when the government recently published an ambitious statement called Rewiring the State. The statement laid out the cabinet’s plans to give local leaders greater control over income taxes, skills, transport and public services. Its policies reflected ideas that have circulated for decades, but its timeframe – many of these policies will come into effect over the next two years – suggested a new sense of urgency. “It was like Christmas for devo wonks,” Shaw told me. “It’s the most radical document in devolution policy that we’ve seen. And I don’t use ‘radical’ lightly.”

Burnham sees devolution not just as a technical policy challenge, but as a moral imperative. The received wisdom among politicians and civil servants has long been that people care far more about the NHS and other national services than they do about their councils. But the erosion of the public realm has exposed the flaws in this thinking. It is, after all, local government that is responsible for litter, high streets and many of the services that people interact with in their everyday lives. The all-too-visible decline in these areas has fostered a widespread disillusionment. “We now have a hollowed-out local state combined with soulless, top-down public services,” Burnham said in a 2025 speech. “That is becoming, in my view, a toxic combination. Citizens no longer trust these systems to improve their lives.”

One initiative that Burnham launched as Manchester mayor shows what an antidote to this might look like. In 2023, the city created three new community health hubs that offer people healthcare and employment advice in their neighbourhoods. Instead of funnelling people through the NHS or DWP, these “Live Well” hubs connect them with local charities and community organisations. They’re an attempt to instil what Burnham, quoting Pope Francis, has called a “culture of encounter”, where the local state works alongside organisations that people already trust, and listens to their needs. “Live Well captures the sense that being a part of our community, being tied to people around you, having relationships of mutual obligation and reciprocity, is the stuff of life,” said Rich Bell, the director of We’re Right Here, a team that has been meeting with No 10 advisers about devolution. “I think Burnham, in his gut, feels the need to directly empower people and communities,” Bell told me. “But I have concerns that these ways of working are quite alien to the state, and to the Labour party in general.”

If the central idea of Manchesterism or indeed Burnhamism is devolving power away from Westminster, the prime minister will have to confront a deep-rooted anxiety in the UK. Writing about the fragility of the British state in the 1970s, the historian Tom Nairn noted Westminster’s resistance to constitutional change: rising Scottish and Welsh nationalism were always seen in London as “destructive forces” that needed to be managed. Labour, too, is inclined towards hoarding power. “The party was born in an age of industrialised, mechanical, top-down, Fordist empire,” Neal Lawson told me. “That’s its culture. And old-school Labourism is monopolistic, controlling, ‘we know best’.”

For Patrick Diamond, a professor at Queen Mary University of London, who worked in Downing Street under Tony Blair and Gordon Brown, the Labour party’s controlling tendencies mean it is inclined to worry about the political consequences of devolution. “There’s a fear that if decision makers outside the centre do things that are unpopular or incompetent, that will boomerang back to the centre.” One episode has already illustrated the political headaches that might come for Burnham and his new devolutionary settlement when Ben Houchen, the Conservative mayor of the Tees Valley, said he would use any new share of income tax he was given by Burnham’s reforms to fund tax rebates, rather than spend it on programmes a Labour government might prefer.

In the past two centuries, every politician armed with grand ideas that managed to change Britain did so through the central state. Reforming Labour governments, such as Clement Attlee’s and Harold Wilson’s, relied on Whitehall’s powerful bureaucracies. Thatcher recognised that her free-market reforms depended on the existence of a strong state that could police opposition, including restive trade unions and Labour-led councils. Tony Blair once said: “If you want to drive through systemic change, you’ve got to drive it through from the centre.” Burnham has said he wants economic change, but it’s unclear how this will be achieved by giving power away to people who may not share this desire. “Just because you devolve something, doesn’t mean you’ll get what you want,” Andrew O’Brien, who leads the Reindustrialisation Research Group, a caucus of Labour MPs that is pushing the government to revitalise manufacturing, told me.

Burnham hopes that devolving power will improve Britain’s economy and drive “growth in every postcode”. “There are really strong rationales for this,” Diane Coyle, a professor of public policy at Cambridge who co-authored a report whose policies were credited with spurring Manchester’s 21st-century revival, told me. “But I think every ‘postcode’ is overambitious. It’s not going to happen at that granularity, because some places will mess it up.” In Greater Manchester, the economic benefits of devolution have been uneven. The average rent in central Manchester is now at least 200% higher than housing benefits. Outer boroughs such as Oldham and Rochdale are as far removed from central Manchester as Dagenham is from Belgravia.

Not long before Burnham became mayor, Howard Bernstein, the former chief executive of Manchester city council, told him that the real test of devolution “will be judged by what it can do for Oldham and Rochdale”. In late August, the leader of economic development at Rochdale council took me on a drive around Atom Valley, where the council is attempting to attract a cluster of high-value manufacturing businesses that produce things such as batteries for electric vehicles and fibre-based alternatives to plastic. The government has funded a research and development centre for manufacturing techniques, an attractive glass and steel building in the creases of the Lancashire hills.

Atom Valley could be an example of what the grand talk of ending neoliberalism and new economic models looks like in practice: government-backed manufacturing, focused on the industries of the future. The council officer told me excitedly about the 20,000 jobs that the businesses one day housed at Atom Valley would create. I wanted to believe him. But as it has become more advanced and automated, the number of people employed in manufacturing has shrunk, while postindustrial towns have been transformed into hubs of logistics warehouses and low-waged care work. “The political classes, for statecraft reasons, want to restore growth, because it would make it so much easier to manage everything,” Karel Williams told me. “But they can’t restore growth because the good jobs that were partly responsible for growth aren’t coming back.” Williams told me about Ambition North Wales, a regional initiative that is supposed to create 4,200 new jobs by 2036, including roles in advanced manufacturing. After five years, it has produced just 63 full-time roles.

Next week, Burnham will give his first speech at Labour’s annual party conference since becoming prime minister. Not long after that, the budget will be announced. People will be watching anxiously to see whether the rhetoric of Burnham meets reality. Undoing decades of economic privatisation and political centralisation can hardly be accomplished in what remains of Labour’s parliamentary term. But the job of building a more visible and democratic state, one that is rooted in place, is something that Burnham understands needs to start now. It may sound wildly idealistic. It may not work. But if anything is to really change, perhaps Britain will need to relearn how to govern itself.

Haiti Turns to Roger Stone to Lobby Trump Administration

The New York Times September 24, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

The Haitian government hired Mr. Stone, a confidant of President Trump, weeks after hundreds of thousands of Haitians lost deportation protection. The contract is worth nearly $800,000, a document shows.

By David C. Adams

Reporting from Florida

Few people have better access to the White House than Roger J. Stone Jr., a close friend and associate of President Trump. Even so Mr. Stone’s latest lobbying deal, worth nearly $800,000 with the government of Haiti, is raising eyebrows.

The Republican political operative was hired by Haiti’s Foreign Ministry to conduct unspecified “issue advocacy” on U. S. government policy relevant to Haiti, according to a document filed last week with the Department of Justice.

Haiti’s prime minister, Alix Didier Fils-Aimé, declined to discuss details of the contract, though he highlighted migration as a priority.

“Certain matters of importance to the Haitian people are being addressed at the highest levels of the U. S. administration, notably at the White House,” he wrote in a text message. “The issue of migration is among the topics of concern to us.’’

Mr. Stone, 74, confirmed the contract but declined to discuss the nature of his work for Haiti’s government.

“I have a policy of not talking about the work I do for my clients beyond that which is legally required which is in my filing,” he said in a brief phone call.

He declined to say if he had ever visited Haiti.

Mr. Stone, a self-described “dirty trickster,” is a close confidant of Mr. Trump, though he is not well known for work related to Latin America. In May, he weighed in on Haiti in a brief social media post about a political debate over the timetable for long overdue elections in the country.

“There cannot be elections until there is security and stability,” he wrote. “The Trump administration is moving in the right direction, but we are not there yet.”

Haiti has not held elections for president, or its Parliament, in 10 years, having delayed them since its last president was assassinated five years ago. Violence fueled by gangs that control much of the capital has set off a humanitarian crisis.

The country is entering a key phase in international efforts to restore security and push gangs out of their stronghold. Elections have been scheduled for December, though there are serious doubts that the vote will actually happen.

Haiti already pays $35,000 a month for lobbying services to Continental Strategy, a firm run by Carlos Trujillo, Mr. Trump’s former ambassador to the Organization of American States and a Cuban American from Miami who is close to Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

Mr. Stone could work with Haiti’s government on the Trump administration’s recent decision not to extend protected status for Haitians, which shielded an estimated 300,000 Haitians lacking legal status in the United States and are facing deportation.

The end of the protection has led to a spike in detentions and an increase in deportations to Haiti, a major challenge for a poor country lacking basic services.

Migrants are also an important financial lifeline for Haiti. Money sent back home by Haitians living abroad totaled $4 billion in 2025, about 17 percent of the value of all goods and services produced within the country, according to official government data.

Beyond the scant details about Mr. Stone’s work, it is unclear why Haiti hired him.

Mr. Stone has built a reputation, in part, for using his connections to Mr. Trump to win pardons for people convicted of wrongdoing. Last year he was a key intermediary in Mr. Trump’s pardon of a former Honduran president, Juan Orlando Hernández, who was convicted of trafficking more than 400 tons of cocaine into the United States.

“His value is that he could talk directly to the president,” said Damian Merlo, a former lobbyist for Haiti who is now registered to work for the government of El Salvador.

Mr. Stone was convicted in 2019 for lying to Congress during its investigation into Mr. Trump’s connections to Russia, but Mr. Trump commuted his prison sentence.

André Michel, a lawyer in Haiti and opposition political leader, criticized Mr. Stone’s hiring, saying his contract was “a scandalous amount for a country like Haiti. It’s a waste of public funds.”

Mamdani Accuses Netanyahu of Spreading ‘Baseless Lies’ After U. N. Speech

The New York Times September 24, 2026

U. N. General Assembly

Advertisement

Supported by

The Israeli prime minister accused Mayor Zohran Mamdani, an outspoken critic of Israel, of antisemitism. The mayor has become a political foil for the prime minister.

By Liam Stack

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel again attacked Mayor Zohran Mamdani during a speech to the U. N. General Assembly on Thursday, accusing the mayor of antisemitism and saying his criticism of Israel had endangered New York’s Jewish population.

Mr. Netanyahu said that since Mr. Mamdani took office, “many Jews no longer feel safe in New York.”

Mr. Mamdani, New York’s first Muslim mayor, has long been an outspoken critic of Israel’s treatment of Palestinians and has denounced Mr. Netanyahu as a war criminal. Mr. Netanyahu has repeatedly assailed the mayor over his views, and many of the claims the prime minister made during his speech echoed his past attacks on Mr. Mamdani.

Mr. Mamdani’s stance on Israel has made him a potent political foil for the prime minister, who is in the midst of a critical re-election campaign. The tension between the two men grew in the days before Mr. Netanyahu’s U. N. appearance, with the mayor again referring to the prime minister as a war criminal in an interview and calling for his arrest, and Mr. Netanyahu releasing a video attacking the mayor.

Over several minutes in a roughly 37-minute speech on Thursday, Mr. Netanyahu took particular aim at Mr. Mamdani’s assertion that Israel’s conduct of the war in Gaza amounted to genocide.

A United Nations commission, as well as international and Israeli human rights groups, have concluded that Israel committed genocide in Gaza during the war there, which was sparked by the deadly Hamas-led terrorist attacks on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023.

Mr. Netanyahu has vigorously rejected those claims, and in his speech on Thursday said that “accusing Israel of genocide is the greatest lie of the century.”

He also mentioned Mr. Mamdani’s wife, Rama Duwaji, who has been criticized for liking social media posts supporting the Palestinian cause immediately after the Oct. 7 attacks.

In response to Mr. Netanyahu, Mr. Mamdani accused the prime minister of using his U. N. speech “to repeat baseless lies meant to sanitize his genocide of Palestinians.”

“Yet no lie can change the fact that he remains the subject of an International Criminal Court arrest warrant alleging war crimes and crimes against humanity,” the mayor said in a statement.

Mr. Mamdani did not attend Mr. Netanyahu’s speech. While it was taking place, he was scheduled to join the prime minister of the Netherlands for “a discussion with L. G. B. T. Q.+ youth.”

Shortly before the speech began, Mr. Mamdani posted a wordless, one-minute video on social media that showed him planting an olive tree at Gracie Mansion, his official residence, and eating dinner with Palestinian families from Gaza.

“May peace be our future,” the mayor wrote in a caption.

Though he is campaigning far from New York, Mr. Netanyahu has repeatedly invoked Mr. Mamdani. His Likud party has put Mr. Mamdani’s face on billboards and campaign posters in Israel, alongside images of the leaders of Iran, Turkey and Hezbollah.

Earlier this month, the prime minister posted an A. I.-generated campaign video that portrayed the mayor celebrating at the prospect of Mr. Netanyahu’s electoral defeat alongside President Recep Tayyip Erdogan of Turkey, Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei of Iran and President Mahmoud Abbas of the Palestinian Authority.

Earlier this week, Mr. Netanyahu released a video broadside against the mayor, falsely accusing him of supporting Hamas and inciting anti-Jewish riots in New York.

Mr. Mamdani vowed during last year’s mayoral campaign to execute an international warrant for Mr. Netanyahu’s arrest the next time the prime minister visited New York. Mr. Netanyahu was accused of war crimes in 2024 by the International Criminal Court; he has denied the charges.

Mr. Mamdani backed off on his pledge in July, acknowledging in a video that the city does not have legal authority to make the arrest, but he urged the federal government to do so. In a Fox News appearance after the video was posted, Mr. Netanyahu accused the mayor of “fomenting hate.”

The mayor has condemned Hamas as a terrorist organization and described the Oct. 7 attacks as “a horrific war crime.” And while there has been an increase in antisemitic hate crimes in New York in recent years, as well as anti-Israel protests that have sometimes turned chaotic, there have been no riots targeting Jews during Mr. Mamdani’s time in public office.

In the first week of Mr. Mamdani’s term, the government of Israel accused him of antisemitism after he revoked two executive orders signed by his predecessor, Eric Adams, which barred city agencies from boycotting Israel and defined some criticism of Israel as antisemitic. Mr. Mamdani said at the time that “protecting Jewish New Yorkers is going to be a focus of my administration.”

Mr. Mamdani’s continued criticism of Israel has nevertheless alienated or unsettled many Jewish New Yorkers and has drawn warnings from Jewish leaders who believe his commentary inflames antisemitism. But progressive Jewish groups that support the mayor have praised his positions.

Brad Lander, one of Mr. Mamdani’s key allies and the Democratic House nominee in a Brooklyn and Manhattan district, called Mr. Netanyahu’s attacks on the mayor “appalling.”

“Antisemitism is genuinely on the rise, and a real strategy is needed to do something about it,” said Mr. Lander, who is Jewish. “It makes Israelis and American Jews less safe for Netanyahu to weaponize charges of antisemitism so cynically instead of facing accountability for his own crimes.”

When Mr. Mamdani admitted that the city could not arrest Mr. Netanyahu, he all but encouraged protests against the prime minister, prompting questions about whether he might make an appearance at any of the demonstrations planned to coincide with Mr. Netanyahu’s speech on Thursday afternoon. The mayor opted not to attend any protests ahead of the speech.

Liam Stack is a Times reporter who covers the culture and politics of the New York City region.
