In a New Anthropic Lab, A. I. Turns to Biology

The New York Times September 24, 2026

Artificial Intelligence

Advertisement

Supported by

Scientists at the company announced their first finding: a group of enzymes whose function is unknown.

By Carl Zimmer

Biologists at Anthropic announced on Wednesday that they had used artificial intelligence to identify genes in viruses that produce enzymes that work in a new way, the first discovery emanating from a research lab the company opened this spring.

“We have chosen biology and medicine as the primary way that we believe the benefits from A. I. can come about,” said Eric Kauderer-Abrams, the head of life sciences at Anthropic.

Dr. Kauderer-Abrams and his colleagues described their work in a technical report posted on the company’s website. The results have not yet been submitted to a scientific journal for publication.

Dario Amodei, the chief executive of Anthropic, saw great potential in the finding. “Today we announced the Claude-led discovery of a molecular machine that we suspect could represent a new gene editing mechanism,” he wrote on X on Wednesday.

Outside experts said that such claims jumped far ahead of the evidence the team has gathered so far.

“It’s not yet a breakthrough,” said Philip Kranzusch, a microbiologist at Harvard Medical School. “It’s a wrinkle on what we know in the field.”

Anthropic’s foray into biology comes amid intense controversy about the safety of A. I. Earlier this month, Anthropic reported potentially dangerous uses of its models, including queries that could potentially assist people in building biological weapons.

Two days after that announcement, Dr. Amodei called for slowing development so that humanity can enjoy the benefits of A. I. without risking catastrophe.

Dr. Amodei, who has a Ph. D. in biophysics, has long argued that one of those benefits will be new treatments for diseases. “The first step is showing that AI can first help with, and then drive, biological discoveries,” he wrote on X.

In hopes of safely demonstrating that, Anthropic opened up a biology lab earlier this year, as first reported last week by Reuters.

“Our team is still relatively small, but we are growing very rapidly,” said Dr. Kauderer-Abrams. “This is one of the most significant investment areas for the company.”

Anthropic is far from the first organization to use artificial intelligence to probe biology. A number of academic labs and start-ups are training A. I. models to discover hidden molecular machines, design new proteins or even predict how entire cells will respond to drugs.

Dr. Kauderer-Adams and his colleagues are using Anthropic’s own products, such as the large language model Mythos and Claude Code, which writes computer programs on demand.

In the new report, Anthropic’s biologists describe their search for enzymes, called reverse transcriptases. These enzymes can read the sequence in an RNA molecule and produce a matching piece of DNA.

Viruses and bacteria make reverse transcriptases for many purposes, and scientists have found them to be powerful tools. One type of Covid test, for example, uses reverse transcriptases to detect the coronavirus. Scientists have also harnessed the enzymes to develop new ways to edit genes.

As promising as these enzymes are, however, scientists have barely begun to document their diversity in the natural world. Dr. Kauderer-Adams and his colleagues created A. I. agents to search through databases of viral and bacterial genes in search of new reverse transcriptases.

The agents wrote their own programs to examine genes that serve as blueprints for 1.9 billion kinds of proteins. They searched for molecular patterns that were similar to known reverse transcriptases, along with the proteins and RNA molecules that help the enzymes do their job.

The search yielded a list of 17 possible reverse transcriptases, but 14 turned out to be errors. In some cases, they were not new. In other cases, they were not reverse transcriptases at all. But the remaining three held up to scrutiny.

The researchers claim that one of the new kinds works very differently from previously discovered ones.

The enzymes, which the scientists call array-associated reverse transcriptases, are carried by viruses. They are produced along with a set of RNA molecules that appear to work with them in some way.

But the experiment described in the technical report mostly involved analyzing DNA sequences and estimating the shapes of enzymes and RNA. There was relatively little wet-lab work with real molecules.

Dr. Kranzusch said that the Anthropic scientists have yet to do a series of basic experiments to figure out if array-associated reverse transcriptases actually work the way the researchers suggest.

They could, for example, delete the gene for the enzyme from viruses and see if they can still infect bacteria.

“This would be the first stage in dissertation research,” Dr. Kranzusch said. “They’ve published a really exciting beginning, but it’s the beginning of a story, not a complete unit that we typically see in the field.”

Nicholas Perry, an Anthropic biologist, said that he and his colleagues are now going “to try to figure out what exactly these systems are doing in the natural world.”

For Dr. Kauderer-Abrams, one of the most revealing insights was not about enzymes, but about the capacity that A. I. has to perform science. “There’s been a lot of debate about whether A. I. can have creativity, or is it only good at just executing on instructions,” he said.

Dr. Kauderer-Abrams saw evidence of scientific creativity in the transcripts that the agents generated as they carried out their assignments.

When an agent inspected array-associated reverse transcriptases, it initially determined that they were not something worth examining. But then it flagged the RNA molecules that accompanied the proteins, which were peculiar enough to warrant a second look.

“You can see the agent say, ‘Huh, that’s interesting,’” Dr. Kauderer-Abrams said.

Carl Zimmer covers news about science for The Times and writes the Origins column.

In Alaska, Rowdy Members of Congress Are a Tradition

The New York Times September 24, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Revelations about the conduct of former Representative Mary Peltola may not faze voters who have long elected abrasive and sometimes violent figures to represent them.

By Carl Hulse and Adam Sella

Reporting from Washington

One threatened a fellow congressman at knife point in a dispute over pet spending projects.

Another routinely wore an Incredible Hulk tie to the Capitol in a proud acknowledgment of his foul temper when he wasn’t getting his way.

Revelations about the conduct of former Representative Mary Peltola, a Democrat, toward her staff — including angry outbursts and the use of slurs — drew criticism on Thursday from Republicans who suggested they showed her unfitness for the Senate seat she is seeking.

But it was not clear whether Alaskans, who for decades have elected abrasive, bellicose and occasionally violent individuals to represent them in Congress, would find it disqualifying.

Alaska’s representatives on Capitol Hill have long brought a special brand of coarseness to Washington, part of a frontier mentality and a rough-and-tumble political tradition that comes with a bare-knuckled approach to securing federal resources for their remote state. They often seem to operate with a chip on their shoulder, arguing that their state’s distance leads to its getting short shrift.

“In Alaska, abrasiveness can sometimes read as political charisma, or sometimes even as authenticity, given that Alaska has a political culture that rewards independence,” said Alexander Hirsch, a political science professor at the University of Alaska Fairbanks. “What sometimes reads like irreverence in Washington, D. C., can simultaneously signal to Alaskan voters something that’s really politically attractive.”

Here is a look at a few of the state’s more aggressive characters.

Serving in the Senate for 40 years, Senator Ted Stevens was known as a fierce and often hot-tempered advocate for Alaska. As a member and then chairman of the powerful Appropriations Committee, he funneled billions to his state, including to create the Trans-Alaska Pipeline, which made the state rich. Republicans made Mr. Stevens their second-highest ranking official in the Senate in 1977, a position he held for eight years.

An Army pilot during World War II, Mr. Stevens moved to Alaska in 1953 to practice law and soon afterward became the federal prosecutor there. He used to recount how he accompanied police on raids, gun strapped to his hip. In 1956, he went to Washington to work in the Interior Department on Alaska statehood, helping to bring Alaska into the union and then becoming a ferocious champion of it. He was named Alaskan of the Century in 2000 and a statue of him greets visitors at the Anchorage airport he showered with federal money and which is now named for him.

He was briefly convicted of concealing more than $250,000 in gifts by a federal jury in the District of Columbia in 2008, about a week before he lost a Senate re-election bid. About six months later, a judge threw out the conviction. He died in a plane crash in 2010, at 86, after surviving a serious crash in the 1970s.

When he faced a tough Senate debate, Mr. Stevens wore a tie featuring the image of the Incredible Hulk, the comic book superhero.

“I’m a mean, miserable S. O. B.,” he proclaimed in 1977 as he took over as chairman of the appropriations panel.

Decades later, Mr. Stevens once grabbed a reporter by the lapels in a Capitol hallway and urged him to help vanquish environmental activists who were thwarting his efforts to open a nature preserve to energy development. (The reporter did not.)

Angry that his daughters were not allowed to play Little League Baseball, Mr. Stevens became a fiery proponent of Title IX, guaranteeing gender equity in sports.

His temper was voted the “hottest” on Capitol Hill in a 2006 poll of congressional staff members by Washingtonian magazine.

Mr. Stevens did not argue with the characterization, instead boasting of how he used his hotheadedness to help his state.

“I didn’t lose my temper,” he once said. “I know right where it is.”

Gruff and irascible, Representative Don Young, who survived occasional allegations of shady ethics in his 49 years in the House, was a staunch opponent of environmental causes and a tough defender of Alaska’s oil, mineral and logging industries. He used his powerful leadership positions on two committees to fund highways, bridges, pipelines and many other projects. He passed away in 2022, at 88, while traveling home to Alaska.

Mr. Young moved to Alaska soon after it became a state and tried his hand at fishing, trapping and panning for gold. He was inspired, he said, by “The Call of the Wild,” the 1903 novel by Jack London about a sled dog in Alaska.

In Congress, he cultivated the image of a rugged frontiersman, and at times was crude in public. In a 1994 House debate on the right of Native Alaskans to sell sex organs of endangered animals as aphrodisiacs, he waved an 18-inch walrus penile bone at the face of the fish and wildlife commissioner.

In a radio interview in 2013, he referred to Latino migrant workers with an ethnic slur. In 2014, he forcefully grabbed a congressional staffer’s arm. In 2019, he shoved and cursed at a reporter. And in 2017, the former House speaker John Boehner of Ohio told Politico that Mr. Young had once pinned him against a wall in the Capitol and held a 10-inch knife to his throat, a story the Alaskan conceded at the time was “mostly true.”

His lapses rarely hurt him at the polls. He was elected to 25 consecutive terms, usually facing moderate to light opposition and winning more than 70 percent of the vote five times.

The former senator and governor was much less combative than the other two Alaskans and was overshadowed by Mr. Stevens in some ways. But he was known to be gruff and impatient in his pursuit of federal aid for the state. He left the Senate in 2002 when he was elected governor and he appointed his daughter, Lisa, a state lawmaker, to his seat in what many criticized as a blatant act of nepotism.

Ms. Murkowski went on to become a popular figure who used her positions on key committees to funnel federal money to Alaska and push for more oil drilling. She also had a thick skin, winning re-election in a write-in campaign in 2010 after losing the Republican primary to a Tea Party-affiliated candidate.

Ms. Murkowski, who remains in the Senate, is now known for cultivating an independent streak and breaking with her party on big issues, drawing the wrath of President Trump, whom she voted to convict at his 2021 impeachment trial.

In an Oval Office showdown in 2017, she told Mr. Trump her loyalty was to her state, not her political affiliation.

“With all due respect, Mr. President, I didn’t come here to represent the Republican Party,” she told him then, according to some of those present. “I am representing my constituents and the state of Alaska.”

Carl Hulse is the chief Washington correspondent for The Times, primarily writing about Congress and national political races and issues. He has nearly four decades of experience reporting in the nation’s capital.

Adam Sella covers breaking news for The Times in Washington.

Massachusetts Is Investigating Gambling Companies’ Use of A. I.

The New York Times September 24, 2026

Artificial Intelligence

Advertisement

Supported by

In response to a New York Times report on DraftKings, the state’s gaming commission said it would evaluate how each company deployed the technology.

By Jenny VrentasAlex Klavens and Walt Bogdanich

Massachusetts’s gambling regulator said on Thursday that it would examine how DraftKings and other betting companies that operated in the state used artificial intelligence. The inquiry follows a New York Times investigation that showed how DraftKings has deployed the technology to target losing gamblers with promotions that encouraged more betting.

Jordan Maynard, the chair of the Massachusetts Gaming Commission, which licenses and sets rules for gambling operators in the state, said during a public meeting that he had instructed the commission to “engage with” DraftKings about what The Times reported, and to learn more about how all licensed betting companies in Massachusetts were using A. I.

“These A. I. technologies are evolving rapidly across our society, and we share the concern over their application,” Mr. Maynard said during the meeting. Another commissioner, Paul Brodeur, described The Times’s findings as “troubling” and said the commission needed to “find out what the facts are on the ground.”

The Times reported that DraftKings had used machine learning, a form of artificial intelligence, to analyze customer betting records and identify those most likely to continue gambling — and losing — when sent promotional offers. Six former employees who built those systems told The Times that they worried the technology would harm people struggling with addiction. The company has also sidelined efforts to use similar technology to predict which gamblers may need an intervention based on their betting activity, The Times found.

DraftKings said in a statement that it “works diligently to comply with all Massachusetts sports betting regulations and vehemently denies the suggestion that we do anything to make our offerings addictive.”

“DraftKings does not use A. I. to target anyone based on losses and does not market to customers based on indicators of potential problem gaming,” the statement added.

Massachusetts prohibits using customer data to offer promotions based on any automated system, including those using artificial intelligence, that is “known or reasonably expected” to make a gambling site more addictive. The state also requires licensed operators to report to the gaming commission at least twice a year how they analyze customer behavior to promote responsible gambling and mitigate potential addictive behavior.

DraftKings has submitted those reports, said a spokesperson for the commission, who declined to provide them.

Operators can face discipline for not complying with regulations, including fines or a suspension or repeal of their license. Mr. Maynard said the commission would use the results of the inquiry to determine when or if any further action or policy-making was needed. The spokesperson said the commission had not previously taken any enforcement actions related to the use of A. I.

FanDuel, which also operates in Massachusetts and is DraftKings’ largest competitor, said in a statement that it used machine learning and other technology to look for signs of harmful play by customers so it can better protect them. It did not address whether or how it used A. I. for other business purposes.

A handful of other states either have or are considering rules governing how gambling companies use A. I. This week, Maryland’s governor, Wes Moore, called for a law that would stop gambling companies “from using algorithmic and other means to identify and target users showing problem-gambling patterns.”

Federal lawmakers have proposed a bill that would set nationwide standards for the industry. It includes a ban on the use of A. I. to monitor betting activity and target customers with individualized promotions.

A co-sponsor of the bill, Senator Richard Blumenthal, Democrat of Connecticut, said at a news conference on Wednesday that gambling companies “are relentlessly and tirelessly taking advantage of vulnerabilities, simply to make more money.” He added that The Times’s investigation “provides graphic and powerful proof of what their business model is.”

Jenny Vrentas is a Times reporter covering money, power and influence in sports.

Alex Klavens is a data journalist at The Times, building computational tools that power data-driven reporting.

Walt Bogdanich joined The Times in 2001 as investigative editor for the Business desk. Since 2003, he has worked as an investigative reporter. He has won three Pulitzer Prizes.

Reporters Return to the White House, but TV Standoff Persists

The New York Times September 24, 2026

Trump’s Media Ban

Advertisement

Supported by

A judge ordered President Trump to reverse his ban on three media outlets, but it took several hours for them to get back in. The White House TV pool remains suspended.

By Michael M. Grynbaum

The reporters are back, but the television coverage isn’t.

Journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico were allowed back into the White House around noon on Thursday. Their return came after a chaotic morning in which the Trump administration had blocked them from entering, despite an overnight order from a federal judge that required the immediate restoration of their access.

It was another twist in a nearly weeklong standoff between President Trump and his press corps that has not yet been fully resolved.

Mr. Trump abruptly barred the outlets from the White House last week, citing coverage he deemed “fake.” In response, the major TV networks suspended the White House television pool, which provides video footage for daily presidential events.

As of Thursday afternoon, the TV pool remained suspended. The networks had indicated that they would not resume coverage of the president until the White House had formally agreed to allow CNN to participate once again in the pool.

The result, on Thursday, was a bizarre spectacle: a president hosting China’s top leader, Xi Jinping, for a pomp-filled summit at the White House, with no American network airing any live footage.

“Normally we’d be watching an elegant affair on the South Lawn,” the Fox News anchor Bill Hemmer told viewers, “and we don’t get access to that now.”

The Chinese government has cracked down on independent news media and evicted foreign journalists whose coverage it dislikes. Chinese state television was on hand for the proceedings in Washington on Thursday.

Around 1 a. m. Eastern time on Friday, Judge Timothy J. Kelly of the U. S. District Court in Washington ordered the White House to “immediately return, reinstate, and restore” the press credentials held by journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico.

Hours later, when journalists from those outlets arrived at the White House, they were still not permitted to enter. Lawyers for the three news organizations requested an immediate hearing on the matter, and Judge Kelly ordered the Trump administration to respond by 12:30 p. m.

Betsy Klein, a CNN correspondent, said that she tried three times on Thursday morning to enter the White House and was repeatedly turned away. One CNN producer was allowed in. “It’s an open question right now whether this is a matter of bureaucracy, a clerical error or if the White House, the Trump administration, is in open defiance of a court order,” Ms. Klein said during an on-air interview.

Around noon, Ms. Klein was allowed back in. “Very happy to be getting back to work here,” she said when she returned to the air.

Lawyers for the Trump administration said in a filing with the federal judge that the White House operations team had been instructed to restore reporters’ access at 7:10 a. m. on Thursday, and that confiscated press passes were made available for reporters to pick up at 9:55 a. m.

It was not clear why the reporters continued to have trouble passing through the security checkpoint after that.

With the television pool out of action, Mr. Trump’s summit with Mr. Xi was covered by still photographers and print and radio journalists. The Associated Press, which is not part of the network TV pool, provided video coverage of the leaders at a military review in the Rose Garden, and planned to film an event later on Thursday at the North Portico.

A New York Times spokesman, Charlie Stadtlander, said that the publication would resume publishing and distributing photographs of Mr. Trump’s events now that a judge had heard the case brought by the banned outlets. For the past few days, The Times had stopped publishing the images in support of the outlets.

When Mr. Trump met with Mr. Xi in the Oval Office, the White House allowed a limited number of photojournalists, but no print reporters, to attend. During the event, Mr. Trump made a remark about how the Chinese had the friendliest press corps, according to photographers who were present.

Erik Wemple and Katie Robertson contributed reporting.

Michael M. Grynbaum writes about the intersection of media, politics and culture. He has been a media correspondent at The Times since 2016.

Senate Defeats Bid to Direct Trump to End Iran War or Seek Approval

The New York Times September 24, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The vote came as a growing number of Republicans have broken from President Trump on the conflict, reflecting voters’ concerns ahead of midterm elections.

By Robert Jimison

Reporting from Washington

The Senate on Thursday narrowly rejected an effort to direct President Trump to end the war in Iran unless he wins authorization for it, defeating a measure aimed at rebuking his handling of a conflict he has continued to wage despite repeated votes by Congress to halt it.

The resolution, which passed the House over the summer, failed 50 to 49, with four Republicans — Senators Susan Collins of Maine, Rand Paul of Kentucky, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and Thom Tillis of North Carolina — joining Democrats in support. Senator John Fetterman of Pennsylvania was the lone Democrat to oppose the measure.

Mr. Tillis was the newest Republican to break with his party over the war, joining a small bloc that has challenged Mr. Trump’s authority to continue directing the conflict without congressional approval.

But Senator Bill Cassidy, the Louisiana Republican who had previously voted with G. O. P. defectors to curtail Mr. Trump’s war powers, switched his position and sided with the majority of his party on Thursday, leaving the resolution short of the support to pass.

It was the 20th vote on such a resolution since the war began on Feb. 28.

Since the conflict began on Feb. 28, Congress has collectively held 20 Iran war powers votes, six in the House and 14 in the Senate.

Ashley Wu/The New York Times

The vote, which came as lawmakers continue to grapple with growing voter backlash to the war weeks ahead of the midterm elections, effectively disposed of one possible vehicle for challenging Mr. Trump over the war: the resolution the House passed in July. But another remains.

The House passed a separate war powers resolution last week directing Mr. Trump to remove American forces from hostilities against Iran, with seven Republicans joining Democrats in their largest bipartisan margin since the war began. That measure could still come before the Senate, giving lawmakers opposed to the war another opportunity to send an identical resolution through both chambers of Congress.

Such a measure would not have the force of law, but would amount to a political rebuke. A growing number of Republicans in both chambers have broken with the president on the conflict as they battle to maintain control of Congress in November and win over constituents feeling the impacts of the war.

Again and again, Democrats have forced votes seeking to restrict Mr. Trump’s ability to carry out the war and to compel him to seek authorization from Congress. And again and again, the president has brushed aside those objections, continuing military operations while Congress debates resolutions that have done nothing to alter their course.

The last time both chambers passed a resolution directing him to end the war, in June, he arrived on Capitol Hill and berated Republicans who supported it, demanding that they reverse their votes. Still, G. O. P. lawmakers have slowly grown more outspoken about the impacts of the war and more willing to vote to challenge the president’s handling of it.

The rebukes have grown more bipartisan and, at times, more emphatic even as their practical consequences have remained negligible.

But the war powers votes have also demonstrated the limits of their strategy. The administration has maintained that the president has sufficient constitutional authority to conduct military operations, and even measures that have cleared Congress have failed to meaningfully constrain him.

Robert Jimison covers Congress for The Times, with a focus on defense issues and foreign policy.

The New York Times September 24, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The rise came a day after a sharp sell-off in government debt.

Note: Data delayed at least 15 minutes.

Source: FactSet.

The New York Times

By Joe Rennison and Veronica Majerol

Global government bond markets swung erratically on Thursday, a day after markets were jolted by a sharp rise in yields tied to rising economic growth expectations and persistent inflation worries.

European and U. S. markets were subdued in early trading on Thursday, but fresh data provided another indicator of hotter-than-expected economic activity and prompted a renewed sell off before the afternoon.

Reports of a potential path to reopening the Strait of Hormuz led to another sharp reversal, lowering yields, before yields drifted higher again in afternoon trading.

The 10-year U. S. Treasury yield, which underpins corporate and consumer borrowing costs across the globe, inched higher, cementing itself at its highest level in more than two decades, having traded around that level over the past week. The yield on the 10-year U. S. Treasury note recorded on Wednesday its biggest one-day jump since last year.

Also on Thursday, the 30-year Treasury yield extended its rise from Wednesday, with the yield moving to over 5.4 percent, its highest level since 2004. Yields across Asia also rose sharply. The five-year Treasury yield rose above 5 percent, to its highest since 2007.

Thursday’s moves came after data showed that new home sales increased more than 6 percent in August from the month prior, far exceeding expectations of around 1 percent growth and reversing a sharp contraction in July.

A measure of manufacturing activity from the Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City also showed surprising strength, adding to data on Wednesday that had also showed manufacturing activity exceeding expectations.

Oil prices also rose on Thursday, further fueling inflation concerns. The price of Brent crude, the global benchmark for oil, rose as much as 5 percent, before easing to a rise of around 2.5 percent, or $105 a barrel. The Brent price had fallen below $100 earlier in the week.

Stocks also swung higher and lower, with the S&P 500 index moving between small gains and a loss of roughly 0.5 percent.

The war in Iran, which has interrupted crucial shipments from the Persian Gulf, has pushed energy prices higher and stoked inflation concerns. Ship operators in the Persian Gulf remain wary of sending vessels through the Strait of Hormuz, the vital waterway between Iran and Oman. Advances by the Iranian-backed Houthi militia in Yemen have threatened oil shipments through the Red Sea, an alternative route to the Persian Gulf used by Saudi Arabia to get oil out to global markets. Saudi authorities had to temporarily shut the critical East-West pipeline that shuttles oil from the Persian Gulf to the Red Sea, blaming a drone attack by an Iranian-backed Iraqi militia.

Central banks around the world have responded by raising benchmark short-term interest rates to slow growth and contain rising prices.

Last week, the Federal Reserve raised rates a quarter of a percentage point, to a range of 3.75 to 4 percent, citing the need to counter inflation. It was the first increase in rates in more than three years. Central banks in Japan and Europe also raised rates this month.

While higher yields can signal economic strength, they also make it more expensive for businesses and consumers to borrow money. The rates of mortgages are particularly sensitive to the increase in certain bond yields. The average 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage rate, the most common home loan in the United States, breached 7 percent on Thursday, a level not seen in nearly two years.

Joe Rennison writes about financial markets, a beat that ranges from chronicling the vagaries of the stock market to explaining the often-inscrutable trading decisions of Wall Street insiders.

Federal Council Terminates Review of Arch’s Effects on Historic Sites

The New York Times September 24, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

Trump’s allies end a legally required step, one of the final hurdles for the project to advance.

By Emily Badger

Reporting from Washington

An advisory council composed largely of allies of President Trump has terminated a legally required review of how his proposed triumphal arch in Washington could detract from historic properties around it, removing one of the final hurdles for the project to advance.

The move brushes aside the National Park Service’s acknowledgment that the 250-foot-tall monument would obstruct symbolic views between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery and “adversely affect” more than 40 historic sites.

The Park Service said it could not come to an agreement with local preservation officials and outside organizations about how to address those effects, under a process required by a federal preservation law. It then notified the Advisory Council on Historic Preservation (A. C. H. P.). The panel, an independent federal agency created by the 1966 law, sent a letter to the Park Service on Thursday formally terminating the process, a step it has rarely taken.

“It is clear that the proposed undertaking and its potential effects on historic properties have raised significant public interest,” wrote Travis Voyles, the vice chair of the council. But he noted that the Park Service believed additional consultation wouldn’t lead to an agreement, and that it had said changes to the arch would alter the goals of the project. “In recognition of the public’s significant concerns regarding the adverse effects the undertaking would pose to historic properties, we are hereby terminating consultation.”

The council will share with the Interior Department its own comments on the project by Oct. 7, it said, inviting the same preservation groups whose feedback has been dismissed so far to comment again. But the effective result is that the president’s allies — who now control the review panels approving his designs, the advisory council overseeing preservation disputes, and the Interior Department managing the project — are swiftly pushing the arch toward construction.

The administration is planning for the arch to come before the National Capital Planning Commission for a final vote on Nov. 5, two days after the midterm election. But it has not yet publicly explained how the arch could function as a military facility, as Mr. Trump announced earlier this week, while officials still intend for it to remain open to the public as a tourist site.

Preservationists dismissed the idea that the Park Service was unable to resolve the harms it identified, arguing that officials had made no effort to do so. The Park Service declined to consider relocating the arch, making it smaller, or altering the design to avoid or minimize effects on surrounding monuments and historic landscapes.

Outside organizations also said they couldn’t respond to a draft agreement when they did not even understand what the administration was now proposing to build. On Sunday, Mr. Trump upended the review with his announcement that the arch would be a “military complex” — a shift in purpose that would normally require redrawing plans for the project and restarting environmental and historic reviews of it.

“Do you turn right for the gift shop, and left for the arsenal?” said Charles Birnbaum, the president and chief executive of the Cultural Landscape Foundation, one of the outside groups participating in the review. “None of us know how to make heads or tails out of this.”

He said the administration’s behavior with the arch was a preview of how it would conduct historic preservation reviews more broadly under new proposed rules that sideline public participation and empower federal agencies to operate as they see fit.

It’s rare for the advisory council to terminate reviews, said Sara Bronin, a George Washington University law professor who was the chair of the council during the Biden administration. That step normally takes place only after extensive efforts at resolving disputes. Ms. Bronin terminated a review only once during her tenure, she said, with a wind energy project that went through years of consultation before reaching an impasse.

By moving so quickly to terminate the process for the arch, she said in an email, the council is “making a farce” of the historic review process.

“True consultation has never occurred for the triumphal arch,” she added, “and it looks like the Park Service and A. C. H. P. will bend over backwards to avoid it.”

The preservation law doesn’t require federal agencies to reach particular outcomes, nor does it give preservationists a veto over projects. But the review process was designed to force agencies to identify historic properties that would be harmed by federal actions, and to consider ways to address those harms. By failing to meaningfully consider any alternatives to the current arch proposal, preservationists warned, the administration was inviting new legal challenges on top of the lawsuit the arch already faces from a group of veterans.

“This isn’t the way to make good public policy — it’s the bare minimum and they are just going through the motions,” said Brent Leggs, the president and chief executive of the National Trust for Historic Preservation, in a statement. The trust is a voting member of the advisory council but was alarmed to learn of the announcement Thursday, he said (the action the council took Thursday did not require a vote).

An advisory council spokesperson pointed to an earlier case, when the panel terminated the review for a copper mining project in Arizona in 2021, as precedent for its action with the arch. But the council declined to comment further.

The National Park Service did not respond to questions for this article.

The historic review was one of the final steps the Park Service had to legally complete before the project could receive final approval from the planning commission. It already received approval earlier this year from another review body, the Commission of Fine Arts.

Opponents of the arch suggested that the timing of the announcement Thursday, and the Sept. 29 deadline for any public comment, were designed to bring the review to a close in time for the Park Service to submit materials ahead of the November planning commission meeting.

The administration is now running out of time to begin construction before House Democrats, favored in the midterms, could take power in January. They have vowed to stymie the arch and the president’s other construction projects that have tried to skirt congressional approval.

The Park Service has also begun work this week at the proposed arch site, which the administration has described in court as archaeological excavation. That excavation work was intended to be part of the historic review. And so it was unclear on Thursday why it was proceeding if the review had been terminated.

A Democratic congressman, Don Beyer, who represents part of Northern Virginia where the arch would be located, said he had visited the site Thursday morning to see the equipment operating there.

“The logical conclusion,” Mr. Beyer said in a statement, “is that the presence of this heavy equipment and additional surveyors is a clear indication that the Trump administration is preparing to move forward with construction.”

Mr. Trump’s announcement that the arch now has a national security purpose appeared intended to help speed it along, following a similar legal strategy that the administration deployed with the White House ballroom. But it could ultimately complicate the administration’s legal defense of its design, environmental and historic reviews. Up to this point, just weeks from when the administration says it expects a final approval, none of those reviews have taken into consideration an arch that is also a repository for ammunition and a platform for snipers and drones.

Emily Badger writes about cities and urban policy for The Times from Washington. She’s particularly interested in housing, transportation and inequality — and how they’re all connected.

American Bar Association Fights to Keep Power to Vet Law Schools

The New York Times September 24, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

Losing its accreditation ability would be a blow to the nation’s largest association of lawyers and another example of how the Trump administration is reshaping higher education.

By Michael C. Bender

Reporting from Washington

The American Bar Association is on the precipice of losing its power to accredit law schools after a federal advisory panel declined to take a position on whether to strip the group of that influential role.

The decision on the association’s accrediting power now rests with Nicholas Kent, the No. 2 official at the Education Department, who has been a key enforcer of the Trump administration’s bid to reshape academia. Mr. Kent has 90 days to decide whether to oust the group from its perch as the country’s gatekeeper of legal education, a role it has held since the 1950s.

Stripping the nation’s largest association of lawyers of its accrediting ability would be a significant blow to a group that has battled the Trump administration over its punishment of law firms, and open a new front in the administration’s pressure campaign on higher education.

A law school must be accredited under federal law for students to have access to billions of dollars in federal aid, including work-study programs and student loans available to law students. Most states require students to graduate from an accredited law school to practice law.

The bar association oversees about 200 juris doctorate programs in the country. It has been fighting with the federal government since last year, when it sued to stop the Trump administration from punishing law firms it did not like.

Earlier this month, Education Department employees urged the advisory panel to recommend stripping the role from the accreditation arm of the bar group. The agency argued that the accreditation arm had failed to demonstrate that it was operating on a “separate and independent” basis from the larger association, as required under federal law.

The bar association and its accreditation arm have both said they follow federal rules on independence.

The advisory panel, known as the National Advisory Committee on Institutional Quality and Integrity, regularly reviews all school accreditations. It remained deadlocked on the American Bar Association after two days of hearings, ultimately agreeing on Thursday to send no recommendation to Mr. Kent. Instead, the panel asked Mr. Kent, the under secretary of education, to review the transcript of the hearing.

The panel’s longtime representatives and staff members said they could not recall a time when they had failed to reach a majority decision on a recommendation. The panel’s 18 members are appointed by the education secretary, the Senate president and the House speaker, with several appointees recommended by minority party lawmakers.

Later on Thursday, the advisory panel voted to recommended that Mr. Kent suspend accreditation power for one year from the American Psychological Association, which accredits hundreds of graduate and postgraduate training programs. The panel cited concerns about what it said was a failure from the A. P. A. to “address the pervasive culture of antisemitism within the programs that it accredits.”

The association did not immediately respond to a request for comment Thursday.

Melissa Hart, the chairwoman of the bar association’s accreditation agency, said the group would continue to work with the Education Department.

“We take our accreditation and our recognition as an accreditor very seriously,” she said.

On the 2024 campaign trail, President Trump referred to accreditation as his “secret weapon” to take on academia, and vowed to “fire the radical left accreditors.”

Democratic lawmakers and law professors have said the focus on the bar association was political retribution after the group sued the Trump administration last year over its pressure campaign on law firms.

“These attacks are driven by the administration’s desire to exert increased government control over universities, and to punish lawyers for challenging the administration and representing clients opposed to Trump,” said Jenny S. Breen, an associate law professor at Syracuse University. “The theme here is the goal of increased government control over traditionally independent spheres of life in the United States.”

A White House spokeswoman did not immediately respond to a request for comment. An Education Department spokeswoman declined to comment.

At the hearing on Thursday, Zakiya Smith Ellis, a former New Jersey education secretary and a member of the advisory panel, said that a recent change to the Education Department’s recommendation process gave more influence to political appointees.

“There has been a concern across the Trump administration about political pressure,” Ms. Smith Ellis said, adding that she had “no way of knowing” how much input political appointees had on the department’s recommendation to strip the bar association’s accrediting power.

Universities seek accreditation from independent groups, which perform a deep, internal evaluation of a school’s programs, student services and academic outcomes, measured against the accreditor’s standards. Accreditation agencies, such as the bar association, face regular review by the Education Department.

If the bar association loses its vetting powers, law schools would have to cobble together different forms of accreditation.

Law schools attached to universities could rely on their school’s institutional accrediting body. Education Department officials said about a half-dozen stand-alone, independent law schools do not have accreditation from regional bodies. But they said that they expected those schools to find other accreditation.

The bigger blow appeared to be aimed at the bar association, which was founded in Chicago nearly 150 years ago.

The association, which has battled the Education Department and the advisory panel multiple times in the past 20 years, tried to curry favor with the Trump administration earlier this month by repealing its diversity requirement for law schools.

But whether that concession would be enough to save its accreditation powers remained unclear. Bar association officials on Wednesday maintained that they were in compliance with federal regulations.

“We think we have the right focus,” said Daniel Thies, who until recently was the chair of the bar association’s accreditation agency.

Half of the panel was in favor of extending time to the bar association on compliance issues.

But other members of the advisory panel said they were uncomfortable with what they viewed as too cozy of a relationship between the association’s accreditation body and the association itself.

Arthur Keiser, an advisory panel member who manages the operations of about two dozen Keiser University campuses in Florida and abroad, said the association’s accreditation body had a history of noncompliance with federal standards. He supported stripping the group’s power.

“They have been out of compliance for a long time,” Mr. Keiser said. “I don’t feel sorry for them.”

Michael C. Bender is a Times correspondent in Washington.

The New York Times September 24, 2026

U. N. General Assembly

Advertisement

Supported by

The Palestinian leader renewed his call for a two-state solution on Thursday, as he accused Israel of prosecuting “a genocidal war” against Palestinians.

By Farnaz Fassihi and Zane Irwin

Farnaz Fassihi reporting from the United Nations, and Zane Irwin from New York.

The Palestinian leader Mahmoud Abbas renewed his call for a two-state solution in a videotaped address to the General Assembly on Thursday, as he accused Israel of prosecuting “a genocidal war” against Palestinians “that has created an unprecedented humanitarian catastrophe.”

For the second year in a row, Mr. Abbas, 90, did not appear in person at the annual gathering because the Trump administration denied him a visa to travel to New York. The General Assembly requires all world leaders who give speeches to the body to show up at United Nations headquarters in New York for the event. But it can make an exception under extreme circumstances, and the U. N.’s 193 members voted last week, as they did last year, to allow Mr. Abbas to send a videotaped speech.

Mr. Abbas, the president of the Palestinian Authority, forcefully renewed calls for the creation of an independent Palestinian state, one that he said would exist peacefully alongside the state of Israel.

“We seek a democratic Palestinian state that respects the rule of law and human rights, a non-militarized state that lives in security and peace alongside the state of Israel,” Mr. Abbas said. “It is possible.”

Palestinian statehood has widespread support at the U. N., with 157 out of 193 member states recognizing Palestine as an independent state. In 2025, some major Western countries, including France, Britain, Canada, Australia and Portugal, formally recognized a Palestinian state at a conference on the sidelines of the General Assembly.

Mr. Abbas condemned the persistent Israeli violence toward Palestinian civilians in Gaza and the occupied West Bank. Israel’s annexations of land in the West Bank for Jewish settlements have been heavily criticized as an impediment to the creation of a Palestinian state.

He characterized the continued Israeli attacks in Gaza and settler violence in the West Bank as “a malicious colonial scheme aimed at making the lives of Palestinians more difficult in their homeland and forcing them to leave it.”

Israel has rejected those accusations, justifying its conduct in Gaza as an attempt to root out terrorism by Hamas that it says threatens its national security. The Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, 76, is expected to address the General Assembly on Thursday afternoon.

The conflict in Gaza is in its fourth year. Israeli attacks have continued despite a cease-fire brokered by the United States, and Hamas, the militant group that once controlled the enclave, has not been disarmed. Much of the enclave lies in ruins, and reconstruction efforts are suspended.

In the West Bank, extremist Israeli settlers are still attacking Palestinians and have in some instances taken over their land by force. The Israeli government also has expanded the building of new settlements even though they have been deemed illegal under international law.

Mr. Abbas welcomed President Trump’s Board of Peace plan for Gaza, which U. N. Security Council adopted in a resolution, as a blueprint for ending the war, disarming Hamas and rebuilding the enclave its shattered infrastructure. That plan has since stalled.

“Regretfully, we have not seen any of this materialize on the ground,” Mr. Abbas said.

The Palestinian leader rejected the notion that Palestinians would ever voluntarily leave their land. Israel has been accused of pursuing policies in Gaza that make life for Palestinians impossible by destroying their homes, schools, universities, hospitals and infrastructure.

“We will not leave our homeland,” Mr. Abbas said. “We will not accept resettlement. We will not allow anyone to decide for us.”

Farnaz Fassihi is the United Nations bureau chief for The Times, leading coverage of the organization. She also covers Iran and has written about conflict in the Middle East for 15 years.

Zane Irwin is an international reporter and a member of the 2026-27 Times Fellowship, a program for journalists early in their careers.

Who Is the Trump-Appointed Judge Who Blocked the White House Media Ban?

The New York Times September 24, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

Judge Timothy J. Kelly had worked as counsel for Senator Charles E. Grassley, who called him a “very talented attorney” in 2017.

By Mattathias Schwartz

Mattathias Schwartz reports on the federal judiciary.

On Thursday, Judge Timothy J. Kelly ordered the Trump administration to restore White House access to journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico.

In his ruling, he found that barring the news outlets without due process likely amounted to “constitutional harm” that had an impact on the public, as well, “given the importance of the free press.”

Thursday’s ruling made Judge Kelly the latest jurist appointed to the federal bench by President Trump during his first term who has issued a high-profile ruling blocking one of Mr. Trump’s second-term policies.

It was not the first time that Judge Kelly had signaled his independence from Mr. Trump’s preferences. In a similar case from 2018, when Judge Kelly had been on the bench for a little more than a year, he ordered the administration to restore press credentials to Jim Acosta, then CNN’s chief White House correspondent.

Earlier this year, he also called the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol “a perilous event” that jeopardized “the peaceful transfer of power from one president to the next.” He reluctantly dismissed a criminal case against five far-right extremists who had all been convicted of charges stemming from the attack, only to have their sentences pardoned or commuted by Mr. Trump. In that ruling, Judge Kelly questioned whether Mr. Trump’s views about prosecuting Jan. 6 rioters were “based on fact or fiction.”

In 2017, when Judge Kelly was appointed by Mr. Trump to the Federal District Court for the District of Columbia, he already had a record of public service. He had served for a decade in the Justice Department under both Democratic and Republican presidents. As a federal prosecutor, he helped assemble a criminal case against Jeffrey A. Sterling, a former C. I. A. officer convicted in 2015 of espionage on charges that he told a reporter for The New York Times about a secret effort to disrupt Iran’s nuclear program.

He also had strong conservative credentials. He clerked in the Eastern District of Pennsylvania for a judge appointed by President George H. W. Bush. He joined the Federalist Society, a conservative legal group, in 2009 and, according to written testimony he submitted to the Senate, has attended at least four of its annual conventions.

Beginning in 2013, Judge Kelly worked as counsel to Senator Charles E. Grassley, Republican of Iowa, who went on to become chairman of the Senate Judiciary Committee, including when Judge Kelly was confirmed by a 94-to-2 vote. At Judge Kelly’s confirmation hearing, Mr. Grassley called him a “very talented attorney,” praising his “vast legal experience” and “thoughtful approach.”

When asked by a Democratic senator whether he agreed with Mr. Trump’s false claim that millions of people voted illegally in the 2016 presidential election, Judge Kelly declined to answer, citing rules that restrict judges from engaging in “political activity.”

A longtime resident of Washington, Judge Kelly graduated from Georgetown University Law Center before working for Arnold and Porter, a storied Beltway law firm. According to his official court biography, he spent several months of his time there on loan to Legal Aid Society, where he represented low-income Washington residents in matters like landlord-tenant and family disputes.

In 2003, he wrote a letter to the editor of Newsweek reminding readers that $100 million in cash reported to have been found with two sons of Saddam Hussein, the deposed Iraqi dictator, was “the property of the Iraqi people, from whom it was stolen.”

Mr. Trump has repeatedly expressed anger when his picks for federal judgeships and Supreme Court seats at times rule against him. Other trial-court judges chosen by Mr. Trump have blocked his efforts to send the National Guard into Portland, Ore., constrain legal assistance for detained immigrants and summarily deport Venezuelans using an obscure wartime law.

But in at least one instance, in 2017, Judge Kelly issued a major decision supporting Mr. Trump’s policies, when he ruled that Mr. Trump’s pick to lead the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau as acting director could remain in place. The bureau’s deputy director, a career civil servant, had sued, claiming that she had the legal right to lead the agency.

The order restoring White House access to CNN, MS NOW and Politico is temporary and expires after 14 days. Judge Kelly could choose to issue a more lasting ruling, which the government could then appeal.

With the major networks suspending the White House TV pool this week, two small conservative outlets decided to form one of their own to cover daily presidential events.

On Thursday, Mr. Sigg noted on the network that “not a single mainstream media network” had requested access to the feed in the past four days.

Since Monday, the networks that typically operate the White House TV pool — ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox News and NBC — have declined to film Mr. Trump’s public events as an act of solidarity with CNN, which, along with MS NOW and Politico, were barred by the Trump administration. Early Thursday, a federal judge issued a temporary restraining order and ordered the administration to restore access to the three news outlets, and their reporters were allowed back into the White House Thursday afternoon.

The fledgling pool’s first days have not gone entirely smoothly. On Tuesday, Real America’s Voice broadcast footage from Mr. Trump’s motorcade after leaving the United Nations General Assembly, which the former White House Correspondent’s Association president Weijia Jiang pointed out was a potential risk to the president’s safety.

As of Thursday afternoon, the TV pool had not resumed. The networks had previously indicated that they would not film daily presidential events until the White House provided clear reassurance that CNN would be allowed to once again participate in the pool.

This week, hosts on America’s Real Voice and LindellTV, as well as the outlets’ executives, have criticized the mainstream networks for sitting out the press pool.

Mr. Sigg complained on “Steve Bannon’s War Room,” which also airs on America’s Real Voice, that reporters from the outlets had been present at the arrival of President Xi Jinping of China at Joint Base Andrews but did not film it. “There were spaces on that media riser marked off for the mainstream media where they actually came, stood there and observed with no cameras, no equipment, no gear whatsoever,” he said. “They literally took up the space but refused to do anything else.”

South Asians Face Surging Racism in America

The New York Times September 24, 2026

U. S. Immigration Crackdown

Advertisement

Supported by

Social media posts, including from the Department of Homeland Security and a Texas Republican candidate, have helped stir fear among people of South Asian heritage.

By Amy Qin

Amy Qin writes about Asian American communities.

For months, many Indian Americans said that they had noticed what seemed to be a marked uptick in racist comments against South Asians in some corners of social media.

But two recent incidents have left some in the community wondering whether the anti-South Asian hate that they thought was a fringe sentiment was perhaps not so fringe after all.

As part of the rollout of a new tip line to report truckers suspected of fraud, the Department of Homeland Security posted an image on Sept. 9 of a “Transformers” character facing off with a Sikh man, along with the words: “America for Americans. Get off our roads. You don’t know how to drive Mr. Singh.” Singh is a common surname for followers of the Sikh faith.

A few days later, Bo French, a Republican candidate for statewide office in Texas, posted an image from a University of Texas football game showing cheering students who appeared to be of South Asian heritage. He wrote: “I heard UT graduation this year looked like this. I didn’t believe it. The problem is now obviously far worse than anyone imagined.”

For many, the posts confirmed an uneasy sense that the immigration debate has led to rising animus against people of South Asian descent and that it has crept into mainstream American politics, particularly on the right.

“What we’re seeing now is full blown and out in public view,” said Manjusha Kulkarni, co-director of Stop AAPI Hate, a nonprofit that tracks discrimination against Asian Americans and Pacific Islanders. “When agency officials and candidates use this language, it gets weaponized and utilized by those who are perpetrating hate.”

There was backlash to the posts and some backtracking. Mr. French later said that his post was “not about race, it’s about policy,” specifically what he believed to be an admissions policy that favored international students over Americans. (By state law, 90 percent of first-year students at the University of Texas at Austin must be in-state residents.) Mr. French did not respond to a request for comment.

The Department of Homeland Security said that its post was a depiction of Harjinder Singh, an Indian citizen accused of causing a high-profile fatal crash in Florida last year. It later removed the image without explanation.

A few days later, on Sept. 13, a Sikh trucker named Gurvinder Singh was stabbed 17 times at a Wyoming rest stop. Many Sikh Americans couldn’t help but draw a connection to the heightened rhetoric.

“Before, nobody cared about your race, nobody cared about your color, but now it’s a problem,” said Harinder Singh Dhanoa, 71, a Sikh American trucker based in Sacramento who has been driving trucks for more than 40 years. “They look at you different.”

In a statement, the Homeland Security Department said that any attempt to blame the agency for the Wyoming attack was “RECKLESS” and “FALSE.” It called criticism of its deleted post “nonsensical drivel.”

While the stabbing may have been a rare episode, it fueled fear, leaving many South Asians wondering about their place in the United States.

They are not alone. The Trump administration’s aggressive immigration enforcement has hit the Latino community especially hard. Rhetorical attacks on Muslims by some Texas officials have recently surged.

For some people who trace their heritage to South Asia — which includes India, Pakistan and Bangladesh — the rhetoric has been surprising, in part because many had embraced the stereotype, however problematic, of their community as a “model minority.”

Indian Americans are among the wealthiest demographic groups in America, the most highly educated and the most civically engaged, according to AAPI Data, which collects statistics about Asian Americans. While they make up only 1.5 percent of the country’s population, they are one of the fastest-growing ethnic groups and have become increasingly visible in pop culture, business and politics. Prominent Trump administration figures of Indian descent include Kash Patel, Harmeet Dhillon and Usha Vance.

But lately, some South Asians have found themselves wondering whether that success is now a double-edged sword, especially when economic anxieties are high.

Vivek Ramaswamy, the Trump-endorsed tech entrepreneur running to become Ohio’s first governor of Indian descent, addressed the concerns in an opinion article last year. Criticizing the rising vision of American identity based on heritage, he said, “My social media feeds are littered with hundreds of slurs, most from accounts that I don’t recognize.”

For many South Asians, the concerns have intensified as the Trump administration has sought to restrict legal and illegal immigration, and federal and some Republican state officials have repeatedly accused immigrants of taking jobs from Americans.

A dominant theme in the recent surge in online hate speech has been the xenophobic narrative of an Indian “invasion” or “great replacement,” according to a recent report from Stop AAPI Hate.

“It feels like everybody is looking at Asian Indians now with a little bit of skepticism,” said Shiva Peram, 52, a naturalized American citizen who immigrated in 1997 from India.

Mr. Peram moved to Frisco, Texas, about a decade ago, drawn by the warm weather and the top schools for his two sons. He felt safe in the Dallas suburb and voted for President Trump twice because of concerns about illegal immigration, part of a recent rightward shift among Indian Americans, who mostly vote Democratic.

That began to change late last year when Frisco, with a fast-growing South Asian population, became the epicenter of a right-wing furor over H-1B visas, a skilled worker program. In 2023, around three-quarters of the 400,000 or so approved H-1B applications were for workers from India, according to Pew Research Center.

Since then, Mr. Peram said he often found himself overthinking everything. Were people at Costco smiling less at him? When the Caucasian teenagers harassed him and his friends at the volleyball court, were they acting out of racism or were they just acting like kids?

“It’s always in my subconscious,” Mr. Peram said.

Beyond Frisco, some people of South Asian descent said they had heard about growing racism but had not felt an impact in their daily lives.

“I have not seen it become more prevalent,” said Satinder Bharaj, 61, a Sikh American and longtime resident of Ohio.

To some, the animus felt worse after the Sept. 11 attacks, when many South Asians — particularly Sikhs, whose turbans are a visible marker of their faith — were the target of widespread racial profiling and hate attacks.

But Pawan Dhingra, an American studies professor at Amherst College, said that in some ways, events today were more troubling. After Sept. 11, Mr. Dhingra said, the primary concern was about terrorist threats and loyalty to the country. Many Arab Americans and South Asian Americans could respond by flying the American flag and denouncing terrorism.

But Mr. French’s University of Texas post, he noted, attacked students who were celebrating their team’s victory while wearing school colors and cowboy hats. What could be more American — and Texan — than that?

Some people, he said, are worried about a threat to their overall culture and their way of life.

“That is a much deeper fear,” he said. “You can’t wear or say anything that’s going to mitigate that fear.”

Rahul Kodali, a senior majoring in computer science, was one of those students wearing a cowboy hat whom Mr. French later referred to as “foreigners.” Mr. Kodali was born in Syracuse, N. Y., and grew up in Flower Mound, a suburb of Dallas.

In an interview, Mr. Kodali said international students were not a “problem,” emphasizing that most people he knew had come legally and worked hard.

Mr. Kodali said he had not experienced any racial discrimination before this incident and seemed equally at ease talking about his love of the Dallas Cowboys and his favorite childhood Indian meals.

But after Mr. French’s post, he said that he had to reassure his mother that she should not regret her decision to raise her children in the United States.

“I told her, ‘I never feel that way, so don’t ever worry about that,’” he recalled.

For many Sikh truckers, the recent events have felt personal.

Some Sikh truckers said that while they supported boosting safety measures in the industry, the Trump administration was embracing policies that disproportionately affected immigrant truckers, like a rule that limits certain immigrants from obtaining truck driver’s licenses. They worry that the Homeland Security Department’s new fraud tip line could encourage racial profiling.

And, they say, the administration seems to be seizing on fatal accidents involving immigrant drivers as pretext to further crack down.

Now there are also fears about physical safety. After Mr. Singh, the Sikh truck driver, was stabbed at a rest area near Rock Springs, Wyo., the police arrested a man but they have not disclosed a motive. The county sheriff’s office declined to discuss the case, citing its ongoing investigation.

In a phone interview last week, from the hospital where he was recovering, the driver said that he did not know why he was attacked. But he wonders whether the Homeland Security Department’s recent post — “You can’t drive Mr. Singh” — may have played a role.

“What is being built up in people’s hearts,” Mr. Singh asked, “that they would want to do something so terrible to another human being?”

Amy Qin is a national correspondent for The Times, writing primarily about Asian American communities.

Trump’s Failure to Lead Is Costing America and the World

The New York Times September 24, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The Editorial Board

By The Editorial Board

The editorial board is a group of opinion journalists whose views are informed by expertise, research, debate and certain longstanding values. It is separate from the newsroom.

The world is facing at least three crises today that cannot be resolved by any one country. Two are longer-term and arguably existential: the threat of uncontrolled artificial intelligence and the growing impact of climate change. One is shorter-term and damaging the global economy: the disruption of shipping lanes in the Middle East. All three require the kind of high-level international cooperation that helped manage other challenges, like the threat of nuclear warfare during the Cold War and the damage to the ozone layer.

Yet almost nobody expects meaningful progress during this week’s meetings in Washington between the leaders of the two most powerful countries, President Xi Jinping of China and President Donald Trump. Beneath the pomp of Mr. Xi’s visit, the agenda appears notably unambitious. At most, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent signaled that America can hope for commercial deals and modest A. I. safety progress.

The low expectations for the visit underline the damage that Mr. Trump is doing to American influence and global well-being. He is an undisciplined politician who puts his personal interests above the nation’s, running an administration that has no coherent strategy for solving major problems. He is instead often exacerbating the world’s biggest problems.

No matter who was president, negotiations with China would be difficult. Mr. Xi is an autocrat who has centralized authority, oppressed his country’s citizens and built partnerships with the world’s most repressive regimes. Yet Mr. Xi does tend to be a ruthless tactician, and China and the United States do have overlapping interests on several major issues, including A. I., climate change and Middle East shipping lanes.

The notion that Mr. Trump could effectively represent America’s interests on these issues seems ludicrous at this point. Even on his own terms, his signature second-term actions, like the tariffs and war in Iran, are failing. No wonder that China’s leaders reportedly see his presidency as a gift to their ambitions for greater global influence. Americans are left to imagine the progress that could have been attempted this week with another president.

The first area of potential cooperation is A. I. safety. The rapid advancement of A. I. capabilities requires government regulation to limit the possibility that such tools could become uncontrollable and destructive. No one country can assure its own safety from these dangers. International cooperation is needed to mitigate the threat.

American A. I. models pose great risks because they are the most powerful. But China’s models are not far behind and pose their own risks because they tend to be open-weight, with their internal rules available for other users to alter. Fortunately, China has reasons to want safeguards. China’s spy chief recently warned that A. I. threatens one-party control there. China, like every country, also fears biological weapons.

Mr. Trump evinces little concern about A. I.’s risks and little interest in regulating it. He has said that the United States must beat China in the A. I. race, without regard for safety. That race does matter, but there are ways for the United States both to compete with China and to work together on the risks. The right policy is a mix of competition and cooperation, as this country pursued with the Soviet Union during the Cold War. Today, the United States should make the scientific investments to remain ahead of China while negotiating over shared threats like bioweapons and A. I. systems that escape human control.

A second issue on which America urgently needs China’s help is in the Middle East. In response to Mr. Trump’s reckless war, Iran has restricted traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, while the Houthis, a terrorist group allied with Iran, have expanded their disruption of traffic through the Red Sea. The price of oil has risen worldwide as a result.

Persuading Mr. Xi to pressure Iran to reopen the strait would not be easy. Mr. Trump is damaging America’s international status so badly that the Chinese leader can follow the dictum attributed to Napoleon: “Never interrupt your enemy when he is making a mistake.” Still, China has an interest in the free flow of oil and lower energy prices. China’s economic growth has weakened in recent years, and higher oil prices do not help. The government’s stated position in talks with Iran is that it should reopen the strait. China certainly has the leverage to push Iran for a deal: It has been Iran’s largest customer for oil, buying 90 percent of its exports in recent years.

If anything, the third issue — climate change — is the one on which U. S.-China talks could offer the most promise if Mr. Trump were not president. China once was an obstacle to climate progress, complicating the attempts of the Obama administration to negotiate a global framework. Over the past decade, though, China has increasingly been willing to address climate change. Its world-leading renewable energy industry would benefit from international agreements that increase reliance on batteries and electric cars.

These three issues obviously do not represent a complete agenda for an ideal U. S.-China summit. Several others would be even trickier, including China’s support for Iran’s and Russia’s militaries and China’s increasing aggression toward Taiwan and several Asian countries. Realistically, any one meeting would probably not make much progress on the thorniest issues. But the United States and China are not merely rivals for international power; they also have shared interests in global stability.

American presidents going back more than 100 years have believed the country had an interest in taking a leading role in the world. America is far from perfect. But when it led, the world often benefited through expanded prosperity, security and democracy. The progress enhanced this country’s global prestige and influence along the way.

Mr. Trump shows little care for these benefits. He uses international relations to seek personal enrichment, praise from sycophants and equal standing with authoritarians. His flailing presidency leaves Americans with the thinnest of hopes for this week’s summit: that he does not further damage the national interest.

A great editorial. Let’s not forget that the shipping lanes were fine until Trump started an endless war. The economy was fine until he ruined it. And he has spent the rest of his presidency destroying previous attempts to stem global warming. A complete disaster of a president. The fact that some people still support him is SHOCKING.

I had no idea that to make America great our country had to attack our allies, cozy up to dictators, alienate our neighbors, and become a pariah in the world. Trump is leading America into an isolationist era. This will not end well.

This week Prime Minister Carney laid out a new vision for the UN, where nations come together to tackle common global problems. That is what is needed now. Regardless of Trump's America First project, our problems are global and it will take cooperation to fix them.

Powerful Fall Storm Is Strengthening as It Moves Up the East Coast

The New York Times September 24, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Rain, flooding and gusty winds are all in the forecast for the Northeast this weekend, but just how much is still a little uncertain.

Notes: Forecast from Sept. 24 at 8 p. m. Eastern to Sept. 29 at 8 p. m. Updated as of Sept. 24 at 5:22 p. m. Eastern. Values are shown only for the contiguous United States and are in inches of water or the equivalent amount of melted snow and ice. Source: National Weather Service The New York Times

By Judson Jones and Nazaneen Ghaffar

Weather team

A potent storm that has threatened to upend weekend plans all along the East Coast was rapidly strengthening off the Carolina coast on Thursday. The storm is expected to deliver strong winds, coastal flooding and heavy rain as it moves through the Northeast this weekend.

Precipitation intensity

Note: Times are Eastern. Source: National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration via Iowa State University William B. Davis, Joel Eastwood and Bea Malsky/The New York Times

Meteorologists have been watching this storm and weighing its potential effects for days, but its precise track was still in question on Thursday.

“It’s just the track and the exact position of how west or east it is,” said Richard Bann, a meteorologist at the Weather Prediction Center. “That is the uncertainty still.”

The storm’s path and position will be crucial to determining where the greatest effects are felt. Mr. Bann explained that a track farther east would keep the heaviest rain and strongest winds farther offshore, while a storm moving closer to the coast could bring more substantial effects to more populated towns and cities farther inland. At least one major airline, United, has begun telling customers to keep a close eye on the shifting forecast.

“Right now, the closest that it looks to get is somewhere in the vicinity of Cape Cod,” he said early Thursday. “With a lot of rain across southern New England, starting late Thursday into Friday and Saturday.”

A forecast track with this degree of uncertainty is not unusual — think of a snowstorm that is forecast to bring anywhere from two to 10 inches across a single county — but it poses a grueling challenge for local officials attempting to prepare. A few outlying computer models still show the storm coming ashore in New Jersey as early as Saturday, while other projections keep the system well out to sea through the weekend.

As the storm bore down on Thursday morning, however, meteorologists had reached a consensus on the most probable trajectory tracking slowly along the coast.
