Coastal flooding and erosion are the most certain threats, as the storm is developing during some of the highest tides of the month.

Rainfall totals will depend largely on the storm’s precise path. Coastal New England is the area most likely to experience what meteorologists call “excessive” rain this weekend.

High winds will linger across areas at the coast through the end of the week.

More storms may follow: This is likely the first of several East Coast storms to follow this path over the next few months, driven by a developing El Niño weather pattern.

As of Thursday morning, the majority of the latest weather models were increasingly pointing to southern New England as the area most likely to see the storm’s greatest impacts, particularly Connecticut, Rhode Island and eastern Massachusetts, including Boston and Cape Cod.

If the most likely scenario holds, the storm is expected to make its closest approach to the East Coast from around Thursday night into Friday. Along with strong winds and coastal flooding, it is also expected to bring heavy rain, especially along the immediate coast in New England.

This could change if the storm pivots west and makes a second approach near New York City.

If the storm mostly hits in New England, forecasters at the Weather Prediction Center, an arm of the National Weather Service, were expecting between two to four inches of rain there through the weekend. Mr. Bann said those totals could still change depending on the storm’s eventual track.

Farther south, in New York City, some rain and gusty winds are expected but the impact is likely to be less severe, forecasters said.

But rain isn’t the only concern from this storm, or possibly even the biggest one.

As it trudges north, strong winds, potentially gusting above 45 miles per hour, could drive seawater toward the coast, producing high waves and pushing the water inland. Waves up to 10 feet are possible along the immediate coast.

Mr. Bann said that the combination of wind and high waters could lead to coastal flooding, high surf, rip currents and beach erosion anywhere from the Carolinas into New England through the weekend.

The timing of the storm also adds to the threat of coastal flooding, as the storm is also coinciding with astronomical high tides, which could allow seawater to reach farther inland and worsen flooding in vulnerable coastal areas.

On Thursday numerous coastal flood warnings and advisories were in effect, with the Weather Service identifying the Virginia coastline as a major risk for flooding.

The storm is expected to gradually weaken on Sunday, but forecasters said it could still linger near New England into early next week.

Indirectly.

You might have heard about the powerful El Niño that has been brewing this year. El Niño is a natural weather pattern that peaks in the winter, but it doesn’t, by itself, cause one storm to grow strong, or a heat wave to settle in.

As the seasons change and El Niño becomes the dominant global weather pattern, it has a tendency in winter to create patterns that push storms like this across the southern United States and up the East Coast. Coastal towns between New York and Georgia routinely shatter high-tide flood records during El Niño years, not only during severe winter storms, but also on sunny days with no storm in sight.

Judson Jones is a meteorologist and reporter for The Times who forecasts and covers extreme weather.

Nazaneen Ghaffar is a Times reporter on the Weather team.

Trump Struggles to Find Leverage With Xi Over Chinese Exports

The New York Times September 24, 2026

Trump-Xi Summit

Advertisement

Supported by

The Trump administration, like its predecessors, has struggled to deal with China’s excess industrial capacity.

By Alan Rappeport and Ana Swanson

Reporting from Washington

President Trump and President Xi Jinping of China are meeting at a moment when China continues to export a flood of inexpensive goods to the world, despite the Trump administration’s efforts to overhaul the global trading system with tariffs.

But it remains unclear how much, if any, pressure Mr. Trump will put on Mr. Xi during his state visit to Washington to curtail China’s strategy of using government subsidies to rev up exports and fuel the country’s growth.

China’s strategy of flooding global markets with cheap cars, solar panels, minerals and other goods has long frustrated Western economies, including the United States, which have struggled to develop their own domestic industries in the face of Chinese competition.

The issue has dogged both Democratic and Republican administrations for years and was one of the main driving factors behind the sweeping tariffs Mr. Trump has imposed on Beijing. In his first term, Mr. Trump’s advisers pressed China for promises to restructure its economy, though they ultimately settled on a far more modest trade deal involving purchases of agricultural and other products, along with more open markets.

China’s exports to the United States have slowed significantly because of Mr. Trump’s tariffs. Trade in goods and services between the countries fell 25 percent last year compared with the year before. But China’s exports to the world have continued to surge, and many economists believe Chinese parts and products are still flowing into the United States through other countries.

Mr. Trump now faces the test of whether he will have any influence on Mr. Xi’s economic approach, something his administration has so far failed to alter despite tariffs and trying to marshal a public pressure campaign.

“The problem is that there isn’t that much that can be done about it,” said Jonas Nahm, a professor at the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies who was an industrial strategy economist in the Biden administration. “The tariffs are treating the symptom but they’re not treating the underlying problem that imbalances are sort of baked into the Chinese economy.”

Despite global backlash over the flood of Chinese goods, its exports have continued to surge unabated. This year the country is on pace to surpass last year’s record $1.19 trillion trade surplus as it continues to sell vast quantities of goods across the world.

The Biden administration was worried about China saturating global markets with inexpensive green energy products such as solar panels. Former Treasury Secretary Janet L. Yellen warned that a second “China shock” threatened to hollow out what is left of America’s industrial base.

For the Trump administration, the concern has been more focused on exports of Chinese steel, minerals and cars. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who has been leading economic talks with Chinese officials, has argued that Americans should not allow themselves to be seduced by affordable Chinese products.

“Access to cheap goods is not the essence of the American dream,” Mr. Bessent said in a speech to the Economic Club of New York last year. In an interview with NBC, he followed up by making the case that prosperity is not about buying “cheap baubles” from China.

The Trump administration appears to believe that more tariffs are the solution but is looking to punish countries beyond China. The White House trade adviser Peter Navarro published a report in August that accused Chinese exporters of routing goods into the United States through more than 40 countries.

The Trump administration has threatened to impose global tariffs on China, the European Union, India and other countries that run trade surpluses with the United States, citing “excess capacity and production” in foreign factories.

The tariffs could apply to more than 40 countries, and would add to other levies the administration has already issued, including tariffs of between 10 percent to 12.5 percent that took effect in July. The excess-capacity tariffs target foreign countries over a wide range of practices, from subsidies and currency manipulation to a lack of labor laws.

The Trump administration argues that other countries have used those practices to build more factory capacity than their own consumers need. Those countries often export the difference, chilling production and new investments in the United States and resulting in trade deficits, Trump officials say. Many trade experts believe this critique applies to China, which heavily subsidizes its industries.

China produces far more cars, solar panels, batteries, steel and minerals than its own consumers need. But the administration’s tariffs appear poised to apply to many other countries, including Switzerland, Norway, Cambodia and Mexico, some of which have argued they are unfairly targeted. In a filing to the U. S. government, Norway argued that its abundant production of seafood is a result of its long coastline, technical innovation and environmental protection of its fisheries.

The tariffs that the Trump administration actually imposes on China may not even be that high.

The Trump administration announced a 12.5 percent tariff on Chinese exports last month. People familiar with the plans say the U. S. may officially announce a higher tariff level and then suspend some of it to maintain the level of tariffs they agreed to in their truce. On Wednesday, Mr. Bessent said that the United States and China would extend their trade truce for two additional months, until January.

Mr. Trump has held off imposing any more tariffs on China until after his meetings with Mr. Xi.

“I think the administration decided not to do anything in advance of the summit because they wanted to preserve leverage to possibly increase tariffs if the Chinese don’t give them what they want,” said Evan S. Medeiros, a professor at Georgetown University.

Critics say the Trump administration should be working with allies to pressure China to adjust its trade practices, rather than targeting Europe and Canada.

U. S. tariffs on Chinese products have pushed Beijing’s exports into other markets, exacerbating pressures for Europe, which is experiencing an “alarmingly quick deindustrialization,” said Mira Rapp-Hooper, a visiting fellow at the Brookings Institution.

The E. U. had set a deadline in October for trade negotiations with the Chinese over the issue, but they did not appear to be making much progress, she said.

China’s export strategy has exacerbated the country’s debt burden and strained its banking system, but the Chinese government continues to believe that those challenges are worth the investment in a robust industrial base that has strengthened China’s global influence. Chinese officials also push back against the idea that its manufacturing prowess is a problem for the world.

However, China is mindful of its strategy’s political ramifications and has turned to investment promises to help mollify concerns that its exports are eroding manufacturing jobs in other countries. China has stepped up purchases of American soybeans, and Mr. Trump has suggested that he would consider allowing Chinese car companies to build automobiles in the United States.

“They understand jobs are a big issue, and the way they can work through that is through investment,” said Mary Lovely, a senior fellow at the Peterson Institute who specializes in global supply chains and the economic relationship between China and the United States. “China’s preferred way to solve it is with investment into these countries.”

Alan Rappeport is an economic policy reporter for The Times, based in Washington. He covers the Treasury Department and writes about taxes, trade and fiscal matters.

Ana Swanson covers trade and international economics for The Times and is based in Washington. She has been a journalist for more than a decade.

Carney’s Big Challenge: Time

The New York Times September 24, 2026

Global Economy

Advertisement

Supported by

As he tries to break Canada’s dependence on the United States, Prime Minister Mark Carney said he knows Canadians will feel pain from the trade war.

By Matina Stevis-Gridneff and Sydney Ember

Reporting from New York

Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada will consider running for a second term if the generational shift he is pursuing to break Canada’s dependence on an increasingly volatile United States isn’t finished, he said in a wide-ranging interview with The New York Times on Wednesday.

“I just got here!” said Mr. Carney, a former central bank governor of Canada and Britain, career Goldman Sachs financier and global corporate executive, who only jumped into the political fray in his native Canada last year at age 60.

“It’s too early to start asking” about running again, he said.

But, he added: “My value as a member of my party is to hit on the big things and move forward. And then, at the end of that, you see how much has got done, and if something else needs to be done.”

Mr. Carney won the Liberal Party’s leadership and became prime minister in March 2025, succeeding Justin Trudeau. He then went on to erase his Conservative opponents’ 20-plus-point lead to win the general election in April, securing a minority government in the Canadian Parliament.

In recent months, as he has pursued a dizzyingly ambitious reform agenda, Mr. Carney has consolidated his power, securing enough extra seats to form a majority through by-elections and floor crossings, where lawmakers from opposition parties joined the Liberals.

A general election should be held by October 2029, and no later than April 2030, in line with Canadian rules. An early election can be held for a number of reasons, but Mr. Carney dismissed the idea of holding one soon.

“We just got here. We’ve got a majority. We’ve got a big job to do. This is big, tough stuff. We just focus on that,” said Mr. Carney, who sat for the interview at the Times headquarters in Midtown Manhattan.

A key challenge Mr. Carney faces as he pushes sweeping reforms at home and pursues new trade and defense relationships abroad, especially with the European Union and Asian countries, is managing the pain Canadians are feeling because of the trade war the country is locked in with the United States.

He made it clear that he knows he is against the clock.

“We’ve got to be upfront with people,” he said, when asked about potential adverse consequences of his strategy. “You don’t transform the economy overnight.”

He said he expected that some of his major projects, including upgrades to a power generating station in Churchill Falls, would take at least 18 months to start yielding results that Canadians would feel, and would extend “beyond the political cycle.”

“You’re looking kind of a year and a half, two years before the big infra starts to really materially impact the growth,” Mr. Carney said, referring to major infrastructure projects. During that period of time, the government would need to deal with “headwind from tariffs, headwind from uncertainty that’s going on,” he said.

Mr. Carney said his government is taking short-term stimulus measures to support Canadians. Those include billions of dollars in employment insurance support and relief for small and medium enterprises hit by U. S. tariffs.

Asked whether his stimulus measures would work against efforts to keep inflation in check — a particularly thorny issue in the United States — Mr. Carney pointed to recent data showing inflation in his country was relatively low.

“Inflation pressures are much less in Canada than some other jurisdictions that you might be familiar,” he said. “And the fiscal position is much stronger.”

Mr. Carney said that he felt Canadians were behind him in this fight. “They’re kind of over the shock, and they’re in the roll up the sleeves, let’s build, let’s move forward attitude as opposed to lashing out,” he said. “And that helps.”

As of last week, Mr. Carney is the most popular prime minister in the history of Canada, recording up to 70 percent popularity rating in one poll.

Some 75 percent of Canadians were in favor of his decision to walk away from U. S. trade talks last month, polling shows, even as opinion surveys record angst and concern among Canadians over the economic impact of the trade war with the United States, suggesting that the positive attitude toward Mr. Carney’s endeavors could deteriorate.

Matina Stevis-Gridneff is the Canada bureau chief for The Times, leading coverage of the country.

Sydney Ember covers the U. S. economy for The Times.

Mortgage Rates Hit 7% as Iran War Fallout Crushes a Weak Housing Market

The New York Times September 24, 2026

U. S. Economy

Advertisement

Supported by

The average rate on a 30-year mortgage in the United States jumped to 7.03 percent, putting pressure on housing affordability.

By Gregory Schmidt

Mortgage rates jumped to 7 percent this week for the first time since January 2025, squeezing housing affordability when many Americans are grappling with higher energy costs and economic uncertainty brought on by the war with Iran.

The average 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage rate, the most common home loan in the United States, rose to 7.03 percent, up from 6.3 percent a year ago, the mortgage giant Freddie Mac said Thursday.

Mortgage rates fell below 6 percent in late February, offering a glimmer of hope that the housing market was recovering from a yearslong slog. But they began steadily rising again after the United States and Israel launched attacks on Iran on Feb. 28.

“A move from 6 to 7 is a big change,” said Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh, a finance professor at Columbia University’s Graduate School of Business, “and it will further dampen an already weak housing market.”

Since war broke out in the Middle East, oil shipments from the Persian Gulf have dwindled, pushing up prices for energy products like gasoline, diesel fuel and heating oil. Economists worry that higher energy prices caused by the war will spread to other parts of the U. S. economy.

Those concerns have materialized in the government bond market, which underpins mortgage rates. The yield on the 10-year Treasury bond — a benchmark for a range of consumer borrowing costs — has climbed above 5 percent, a level not seen since before the global financial crisis two decades ago.

Overall inflation has remained stubbornly elevated, at an annual pace of 3.4 percent in August, prompting the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates this month.

Higher mortgage rates in turn are weighing on a moribund housing market. Sales of existing homes fell 2 percent in August from July and are at their lowest level since June last year, the National Association of Realtors reported. Home prices rose 1.5 percent annually in June, up from a 1.2 percent annual gain the previous month, according to Cotality, a housing market data provider.

“Nobody can afford to buy a house anymore at these high prices and at these higher mortgage rates,” said Professor Van Nieuwerburgh, who added that the cost increases had locked up the housing market.

Mortgage rates had dipped as low as 2.65 percent in January 2021, setting off a stampede of home buying that ignited bidding wars and drove up prices. But as rates began to rise again about a year later, the housing market settled into a malaise as homeowners became reluctant to move and give up their ultralow rates.

With the housing market stagnating, developers are delaying building homes. “Higher mortgage rates, rising construction financing costs and affordability challenges continue to weigh on the market and limit momentum for new-home construction,” Bill Owens, chairman of the National Association of Home Builders, said in a statement.

Eric Orenstein, a senior director at Fitch Ratings, said that he expected home sales and mortgage refinancing to slow for the rest of the year, but that the market would eventually begin to thaw as homeowners were forced to move because of major life events, like a job change.

“There’s a psychological aspect: At what point do consumers just accept that rates are not going back to 3 percent?” Mr. Orenstein said.

And as owners build more equity in their homes, losing a low rate will have less impact, he added. Americans have amassed a record $35 trillion in home equity, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis.

Professor Van Nieuwerburgh said he was hopeful that the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, which Congress passed in June, would add to the supply of homes to local markets by easing regulations for builders.

Gregory Schmidt is a senior staff editor who has covered real estate since 2022.

Connections: Sports Edition

Connections: Soccer Edition

Connections Coach

What happens when a trad influencer leaves her husband, questions her beliefs, stops selling anti-feminism T-shirts — and still needs to make a living online?

Bernadine Bluntly once argued the tradwife’s cause with passionate intensity. Yet privately, she said, she was considering leaving her marriage — a step she took last year. Credit... Michael B. Thomas for The New York Times

Supported by

By Amanda Hess

Reporting from St. Louis

The first time Bernadine Barber saw the word “tradwife,” it was being used to describe her. She was not yet 30, she had three children, and her Instagram content promoting traditional gender roles was gaining a following. She had started going by Bernadine Bluntly online, a name to reflect how plainly she spoke her truth. Now she’d been drafted to represent the tradwife at a 2019 right-wing event in Miami. The digital flier drew her in an anime style, in a modest dress with an infant pressed to her chest.

“I don’t care if I ever go onstage again,” Bluntly announced after speaking against women’s suffrage and promoting wifely submission. “My kids are my first priority! My husband is my first priority!”

Onstage and online, Bluntly argued the tradwife’s cause with passionate intensity. But privately, “I was already going back and forth about leaving my marriage,” she told me recently. Soon she would have six children, 141,000 YouTube subscribers, friends at Evie Magazine and Turning Point USA, and a commitment to an ideology that she now says made her suffer. “You’re told that if you really love God, then you submit to your husband, you fight for your marriage, you forgive no matter what, and you stay for the kids,” she said. “It’s honestly a miracle of God that I woke up and got out.”

Last year, Bluntly left her husband and got a restraining order against him. A Missouri court found that she had proved allegations of domestic violence, and forbade him to come within 300 feet of her. (In a court filing, he denied committing “any act or pattern of domestic violence.”) After their divorce was finalized this past spring, she posted a video titled “What I Got Wrong About the Trad Movement.” It signaled a new life for her, and a new job: as an ex-tradwife influencer, warning women away from what she now describes as a program of spiritual manipulation and covert marital abuse.

“I no longer believe in extreme gender roles, especially when they’re wrapped in spiritual language,” she says in the video.

“If any belief system creates a power imbalance that puts women or anyone in a position of fear, isolation or total dependence, I reject it,” she says, adding, “If my past content contributed to that, I am so genuinely sorry.”

The “tradwife,” cutesy internet shorthand for “traditional wife,” is a new word for an old archetype. Her modern icon is Hannah Neeleman, the Mormon homesteader who has nine children, 10.3 million Instagram followers and ultrarich in-laws, and who sells protein powders under the name Ballerina Farm. Her posts swept onto our feeds alongside a pronatalist administration and a reactionary social front, announcing the rebranding of a fundamentalist feminine role.

But social media trends don’t last forever, and the trad trend is showing its cracks. Nara Smith, the 24-year-old home cook known for her purred voice-overs and high-femme look (4.8 million followers on Instagram), recently went on the “Call Her Daddy” podcast in jeans, described her marriage as equal and denied that “tradwife” had ever described her. Neeleman told New York Magazine, “If there’s things that I’m sharing that people think are actually doing harm to our sex, then OK, let me take the feedback.”

As support for President Trump wanes, so does his movement’s user-generated content. “Between MAGA cracking and the tradwife trend coming to an end, we’re going to start seeing women come out of these marriages,” said Tia Levings, the author of the 2024 memoir “A Well-Trained Wife,” who once maintained a homemaking blog and now identifies as an “ex-evangelical trad cult survivor.” Leaving tradlife is not as easy as Smith might make it seem. The typical tradwife may be “four, five, six babies in,” Levings said, and yoked to a doctrine of constant childbearing and subservience to men. “And oh, by the way, their husbands bought in, and they’re not going to let them out,” she said.

I met Bluntly in July in St. Louis, where she had moved from her marital home, which she described as an off-grid tiny house in rural Missouri. Her children, who range in age from 1 to 14, were away with her ex-husband under a shared custody arrangement, so we had a long lunch at a sidewalk cafe near her new house. She ordered an Italian soda and wore a plaid pleated skirt and a scoop-neck tank under a white oxford shirt, thrift-store finds she said she would not have been allowed to wear before: the skirt cut too high, the tank top too low. She looked as if she could have been an Instagram baddie in another life.

“Is it OK if I pray for you real quick?” Bluntly asked. I told her I’d just come from visiting a relative in the hospital, and she asked the Lord to bless me with a peace that passes understanding. When she talked about her former tradwife content, she grimaced at her own lines. When she spoke about her actual tradwife life, she cried.

A year ago, “I was just trying to fight for my own mind,” she said. Now her independent city life “feels like it’s a dream.” She had just posted a video of herself on Instagram, a slapstick number where she struggles to hang a boxing bag she’d snagged secondhand on Facebook. I asked to see the algorithmic suggestions Instagram was serving to her, and she showed me a grid of women engaged in martial arts.

“I’ve been using this time to strengthen myself,” she said — boxing, tennis, target practice, articles, studies, books. She changed her Instagram bio to “DV survivor and mama of 6.” She joined a club for women in business, started attending a Presbyterian church and met her new best friend at the DMV. “I read two books this month, cover to cover. I don’t remember the last time that happened,” she said. Since the divorce, she added, “I’ve been slowly shifting what I believe, and finally having the space and the freedom to do that.”

I had begun following Bluntly on Instagram a few years earlier, fascinated by the niche she occupied in the right-wing ecosystem. You would not find her posting idealized cooking or farmwork videos. Instead, she positioned herself as one of the trad movement’s ideological foot soldiers, knitting the down-home feminine aesthetic to a political project, one she expressed through commentary designed to pop off online. She had a modest but notable audience, somewhere on the continuum between influencer and influenced.

As she preached submission, her presence was so confident, her affect so wryly disobedient, that cognitive dissonance was built into her brand. God had given her a face made for reaction videos. “My lips are full, my eyes are big, my eyebrows are thick — you can read every emotion on my face,” she said. “I used to get in trouble for that as a kid.”

What she concealed — from her online audience, and often from herself — was her own misery.

Before Bluntly was a wife, she was a girl. She was born in the Philippines in 1990, the fourth of five children. Her mother died when Bluntly was 4 years old, and her father — the son of a U. S. serviceman — relocated the family to the United States when she was 7. “Between my mom dying and moving to America, the culture shock and the language barrier, I was very shy,” she said. “I kept to myself.” Her father, she said, was volatile and absent. She moved frequently, following her eldest sister’s naval postings before settling in Texas. At 16, she read the evangelical pastor Rick Warren’s “The Purpose Driven Life,” and then, she said, “I gave my life to Jesus.”

At 17, she met a boy at a church housed in a local movie theater. When he left for a charismatic Pentecostal church, where he would become a youth pastor, she followed. And when her father became physically abusive, she said, she moved in with the youth pastor’s family. The church preached against premarital cohabitation, and its pressure mounted. One day, a visitor calling himself a prophet announced that he foresaw her becoming the youth pastor’s wife, and an exultant congregation praised God. By 20 she was engaged, and by 21 married. “I didn’t have time to process it,” she said. “It was like, God said.”

Bluntly got an associate degree in early childhood education, hoping to move abroad to do missionary work and teach English to children. She enrolled in Texas A&M but dropped out after a semester. “I got married and had my first baby instead,” she said. She began writing and recording Christian spoken-word poetry, and soon she was getting gigs at cafes and banquets that brought a glint of national attention. But as her marriage progressed, “my dreams, my passions, my talents were absolutely secondary.”

“And then, increasingly, they were framed as an obstacle,” she continued. “I felt like I was being erased.”

In 2017, two babies in, she read “Lies Women Believe: And the Truth that Sets Them Free” by the Christian author Nancy DeMoss Wolgemuth. It promotes an ideology of “biblical womanhood” as the key to a life of abundance and bliss. The cover features a red apple nipped by a sinful bite. Bluntly came to believe that any problem in a marriage was a woman’s to fix.

“I thought, Oh, maybe that’s what I’m doing wrong,” Bluntly said. “Maybe me pursuing my dreams and trying to use my talents outside the home is what’s causing the problems.” Even as she resigned herself to domesticity, she “still needed a creative outlet,” she said. Digital content presented “a happy medium,” a way to work from home and a social outlet for her increasingly isolated life; after a series of arguments over where they ought to attend church, she and her husband had stopped going. For a time, she posted family vlogs, but “somewhere along the way I started talking about politics, too,” she said, “and it was the political content that really took off.”

Her breakout post was in support of Brett Kavanaugh’s nomination to the Supreme Court. “It’s so ironic now,” she said ruefully. “That was my introduction to actually having a voice, or influence.” She branded herself Bernadine Bluntly and opened an online storefront selling $25 shirts that read “R. I. P. Feminism.” Though she rarely shared details of her family online, “my lifestyle — of having had so many kids — was speaking for itself,” she said. As tradwife influencers were fruitful and multiplied, she created a digital course for young women, Simply Smitten, in which she dangled the keys to courting godly men. Her husband posted his own content, advising men on how to become a “strong patriarch” who can mold a “sweet tradwife who happily ‘fills your gut and empties your balls,’ as the saying goes.”

Soon, Bluntly’s influence became the family business, and her modest and inconsistent online income — it brought in an average of $2,500 a month, she said — was stretched to meet the family’s needs. “Everything was configured to make it justifiable,” she said. “I’m leading people, but I’m doing it under my husband’s approval and headship, so it’s OK. I’m making money, I’m the breadwinner, but that’s OK because he’s acting as my C. E. O. I work for the family.” Meanwhile, she said, “I was constantly getting pregnant again.”

She felt trapped, she said, in a psychological and spiritual cage. Traditional wives who try to leave “are not just feeling that they’re disappointing their husbands,” Bluntly said, adding: “It’s worse than that. They are directly disobeying God.” And the expectation to have as many children as possible keeps them physically in the home, and the movement. “If you get pregnant, you’re less likely to leave, less likely to fight back,” she said. “You’re a lot more vulnerable.”

When I asked how that reproductive dynamic influenced her own marriage, she wiped away tears. “I love my kids,” she said. “I would probably go through everything all over again just to have all six of them here.”

In 2024, Bluntly tapped a rich vein of online attention by posting a series of reaction videos in which she pokes fun at a feminist perspective on gendered work. She imagines a feminist woman saying that “anything men can do, we can do better,” and then superimposes her face over clips of men engaged in strenuous blue-collar labor. As they wield chain saws and drill oil, Bluntly performs shocked admiration. Then she delivers her tagline: “Reject delusions. Embrace gender differences.”

The series racked up 20 million views. And yet Bluntly’s sublimation of her ambition into a glorification of masculine work failed to produce the family harmony and personal fulfillment she had hoped it would. One day in May 2025, she found herself in that off-grid home with no church, no local support system and six children. She believed that she had done everything to try to make her marriage work, she said, but “I felt like I was dying inside.” Her youngest son was 4 months old. She was not permitted, she said, to walk down the gravel path leading to the highway on her own. But she had a phone.

Bluntly remembers shutting herself into an office structure installed behind the house, a space where she often disappeared to film her videos. Instead, she called the police station, asked for a patrol car to be sent and sneaked down the path to meet it. At the precinct, she shakily filled out the paperwork to file an order of protection against her husband as he texted her phone, asking where she was. “I just jumped, and I wasn’t sure how I was going to land,” she said. Her two older sisters drove through the night to pick up Bluntly and her children and brought them to a motel in Gainesville, Mo. That summer, they bounced around between hotels, a shelter, the house of a friend. One night, as she prepared to put her kids into a packed car, she paused to film another green-screen video in front of a hotel wall.

“I didn’t have the mental bandwidth to be like, What do I believe?” she said. “I had to keep doing what works. I had to keep doing what pays. That was how I was going to feed my kids.”

Bluntly now shares physical custody with her ex-husband. (Joan Meier, the director of the National Family Violence Law Center at the George Washington University Law School, said that family court judges often give little weight to allegations of domestic violence in custody decisions and have penalized mothers for moving away with the children.) Pursuant to their divorce arrangement, she pays him $235 a month in child support out of her influencer wages. “If I didn’t have social media,” she said, “I would have nothing.”

When a tradwife influencer divorces, she explodes the very basis of her content business. But she still has a platform, one that she can jump from into a new world of content where she’ll find other women on a similar path. Like Jennie Gage, who calls herself “Ex MAGA, Ex Mormon, Ex Tradwife” and now makes a living decoding the offerings of Neeleman and Smith for her 391,000 TikTok followers. And Alice Llani, who serves 855,000 TikTok followers winking instructional videos with captions like “how to make up for 6 years no job experience or education due to being a tradwife @19 no borax no glue.”

Enitza Templeton, a 43-year-old Colorado mother of four, identifies as a “former tradwife” and “current baddie” to her 247,000 TikTok followers. When she became disillusioned with her own tradlife, Templeton created an Instagram account called Sweet by the Slice. “I thought that if I could post my life online and make it look beautiful, then maybe I would believe that my life was beautiful,” she said. But social media also gave her a window into her unlived life — and a future income stream she could use to escape. Scrolling Instagram “was a huge shock,” Templeton said, adding, “I saw other mothers that had five children, and they were single moms, and I was like: You can do that?”

When Bluntly and I left the cafe, she drove me to my hotel in her minivan, a hand-me-down gift from a friend. She kicked a tennis racket aside to make room in the passenger seat. The next day, I joined her at a studio owned by a woman she’d met through her businesswomen’s club; it’s the kind of place designed for girls’ nights, with a jewelry bar and floral photo backdrop. Bluntly set up her phone on a tripod, flipped her hair twice and filmed two videos using TikTok’s built-in teleprompter feature. Both were warnings: against husbands who demand secrecy in marriage, and against communities that uphold an image of family values over women’s and children’s lives.

Bluntly is still finding her footing as a post-trad influencer. She shares lifestyle content about women-owned businesses in St. Louis and speaks about her Filipino heritage in a way she never did before. She regrets preaching marriage as the height of a woman’s ambitions, but she’s grateful that many of her former mentees are still following along. “I’ve been there, I’ve done that, I’ve got the T-shirt, the restraining order and the divorce,” Bluntly said. “Now I’m like, Just be careful.”

Bluntly has received support online from women who are questioning their own beliefs — and skepticism from those who feel her reversal is too little, too late. “It’s a legitimate criticism; some of it is deserved,” Bluntly said. “I have apologized for the things I’ve said, and I will continue to do that, and take ownership of it.” She is still disentangling a lifetime of patriarchal influence, and she isn’t sure where she’ll land politically. “I feel like so many of the things that I thought ‘the left’ or ‘feminists’ believed were not accurate,” she said. “They’re attacking systems and ways of doing things, not just all men.”

She is not dating yet, but “if God has it in the cards for me,” she said, she’d like to someday. “I don’t know if I’m having more kids,” she added. “I think I might — I kind of want — I’d be open to one more.”

In time, she said, she hopes her social presence can “help bring awareness and education on abuse and coercion, specifically within religious or traditional circles.”

“I just have this weird kind of desire,” she said, “to make my life count for something.”

I started following Bernadine Bluntly a few years ago, when I came across her hard-right, pro-tradwife posts on Instagram. The cognitive dissonance in her content interested me — she was promoting wifely submission even as she built a career for herself as an outspoken political voice. A few months ago, she announced that she was divorcing her husband and questioning the trad movement, and I knew I had to speak with her.

What I found was a woman who seemed to be emerging from a cage for the first time, and sharing that the real life of a trad wife can be so much more fraught, and dangerous, than Instagram makes it seem.

Amanda Hess is a writer at large for The Times.

Canada’s Coat Makers Find Themselves in the Middle of a Trade War

The New York Times September 24, 2026

U. S.-Canada Trade War

Advertisement

Supported by

The United States is a key market for brands that manufacture jackets and parkas in Canada, such as Canada Goose and Moose Knuckles.

By Kim Bhasin

Coats, jackets and parkas made in Canada are getting caught in the middle of a trade war between Canada and the United States, as some of the biggest players in outerwear hunker down to try to endure the latest tariff shock.

In August, President Trump claimed that Canada had put unfair levies on American products and imposed a punishing round of tariffs on a wide variety of goods, including food, building materials, recreational gear and apparel. The list contained many types of outerwear, such as anoraks, overcoats, car coats, windbreakers, capes and cloaks.

The new 50 percent tariff Mr. Trump imposed has put pressure on Canadian coat makers such as Canada Goose ahead of the winter rush for cold-weather gear and the crucial holiday shopping season.

Canada’s top outerwear companies sell their coats around the world, but the United States is the industry’s single largest market, surpassing even the domestic market. That has left few options to move business elsewhere, as Canadian coats have become a coveted luxury item in many American closets. Prices for Canada Goose parkas, for example, start above $1,000.

“While the world around us continues to change, our focus remains the same: serving customers with Canadian warmth,” Dani Reiss, the chief executive of Canada Goose, said of the tariffs in an email. “In times of uncertainty, that means staying steady, making thoughtful decisions and continuing to deliver the exceptional products and experience our customers expect.”

The Toronto-based company is the nation’s largest luxury outerwear company and reported revenue of more than 1.5 billion Canadian dollars ($1.1 billion) in its last fiscal year. About two-thirds of its products are made in Canada, according to a person with knowledge of the company’s operations.

Canada has turned its proficiency in dealing with frigid winters into a big business by producing and exporting all sorts of items that help manage the chill, such as central heating boilers and smart thermostats. But coats have been a defining slice of the Canadian economy since the 19th century, when businesses such as the Hudson’s Bay Company would buy raw furs from trappers and sell them to dressers and dyers in cities to be sewn into garments. Modern coat production in Canada is centered in Quebec and Ontario.

Mr. Reiss said “nothing is changing” in Canada Goose’s long-term strategy in the United States, which accounted for about 25 percent of the company’s sales in its last full fiscal year. The company has one of the largest international operations of the Canadian coat makers and has stores in Britain, France, China, Japan and Australia.

Should the Trump administration apply new tariffs, Canada Goose executives said in July, they would hurt the company’s operating margin by less than 2 percent this year if management did not take any action to mitigate them.

“It’s still going to hurt them,” said Sam Poser, an analyst at Williams Trading, a financial services firm. “We don’t know exactly how much.”

As the two governments negotiated a trade deal in August, many Canadian retailers rushed more product into the United States in case talks fell apart, people with knowledge of the matter said. That extra inventory could help limit the tariff damage, if the nations come to an agreement in the coming months.

A spokeswoman for Canada Goose declined to say what actions, if any, the company would take to alleviate the impact of the tariffs, such as whether it would absorb the additional costs or raise prices.

Brands such as Kanuk, Quartz Co., Wexly, Audvik and Arctic Bay also depend on coat production in Canada and must now try to cope with the higher cost of doing business in the United States.

Arc’teryx makes about 5 percent of its goods in Canada at a facility near Vancouver, with the rest made mostly in China, Vietnam, Indonesia, Bangladesh and Myanmar. Its domestic factory produces “a critical portion” of its product lines, including its most technically complex jackets, the company said on its website.

A spokesman for Arc’teryx said the company was confident that it could navigate the latest trade challenge and had “taken steps over time to mitigate the impact of tariffs” on its business.

Moose Knuckles, a high-end outerwear brand in Montreal, counts on domestic manufacturing in three factories for many of its goods, which include $1,500 parkas and $500 bomber jackets. The average coat involves around 90 craftspeople, such as patternmakers, fabric cutters and sewing machine operators.

“We inject millions of dollars annually in the Canadian economy, while preserving a tradition of Canadian craftsmanship,” the company said on its website. A spokeswoman for Moose Knuckles declined to comment on the tariffs.

Outerwear is the largest category of apparel sold in the United States under the “Made in Canada” label, according to an analysis by Sheng Lu, a professor at the University of Delaware’s department of fashion and apparel studies.

“Canadian outerwear producers would find it challenging to identify alternative export markets in the short to medium term,” Mr. Lu said.

Kim Bhasin is a business reporter covering the retail industry for The Times.

Meta’s Answer to the ‘Meta Creep’? Camera-Free Smart Glasses

Wired September 23, 2026

After months of controversy about the privacy of its smart glasses, Meta has unveiled the next iteration of its product lineup. At its Meta Connect event in Menlo Park, CEO Mark Zuckerberg announced all the new glasses the company is putting out into the world.

Its popular Meta Ray-Ban glasses are now in their third generation, but two new models steal the show: a powerful, slimmed-down version of Meta's Quest headsets capable of virtual and augmented reality modes, and a camera-free pair of Ray-Ban–branded smart glasses, called Ray-Ban Meta Audio. Meta is also bringing its Muse AI agent to its smart glasses platform.

The next evolution of Meta’s Quest VR headset is something truly different. Instead of a heavy helmet-like headset, the new Meta VR Glasses look like big goggles. They’re five times lighter than the Meta Quest 3. They sit on the nose, right in front of your face like glasses, with no headstrap needed.

They look and feel more like the virtual display glasses made by companies like Viture, and what Xreal’s Project Aura seems to be shaping up to be—lightweight mixed-reality lenses that let you access virtual spaces without the burden of a VR headset.

There are no included controllers, though the device can connect to Meta’s previous Quest controllers or gamepads like an Xbox controller. Instead, the wearer controls the device with hand movements and finger pinches, similar to Android XR and Apple’s Vision Pro. Eye tracking pinpoints what you’re trying to access. You can pinch with two fingers to open an app or interact with something on the screen. Form a fist and flick your thumb up or down to scroll the screen.

Inside, the lenses feature a 5K micro-OLED display with a resolution of 2412 x 2288 pixels per eye. The computing power is offloaded to an attached compute puck, which also houses the battery.

Small prescription lens inserts can be magnetically clipped inside the lenses. (Meta has not shared how much those will cost.)

The software is the same that runs on Meta’s Quest VR devices, so movie and game titles in the Quest ecosystem will work on the VR Glasses. That includes games like Beat Saber, live sports apps, and streaming services like Disney+. There are digital workspace modes that let you have multiple monitor screens around you. The VR Glasses can also display a virtual keyboard on a surface in front of you, then use the embedded cameras to track specific finger placements.

The only immediate downside compared to other VR headsets—at least that I could tell from a brief demo at Meta Connect—is that the VR glasses don’t cover your entire field of vision, so it doesn’t feel as immersive as a traditional VR headset.

Meta says the VR Glasses cost $1,300 and will ship in the spring of 2027.

The Ray-Ban Meta Audio do not have cameras for video or photo capture.

Meta has spent the past few months being absolutely pummeled by controversy about the privacy issues inherent in its camera-enabled smart glasses. The solution? A pair of smart glasses with no cameras.

The Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses have all the audio capabilities of a standard pair of Meta’s smart glasses, minus image and video capture. At 43 grams, they’re also lighter than the others. They have better battery life—12 hours on a single charge and up to 48 hours with the included charging case.

They come in 23 different color and style options, including the retro Ray-Ban Clubmaster frame and a more rectangular Burbank. The Audio glasses cost $349 and are available for preorder now. They start shipping on October 10.

The Meta-branded Gen 3 LISA Adventurer glasses.

Meta's flagship line of smart glasses is getting a “Gen 3” upgrade. They have 12-MP cameras, like last year, plus 3K Dolby Atmos–enabled video capture. The glasses will get up to nine hours of battery life, two more than their predecessors. A new six-microphone array offers better sound and can cut out background noise more easily.

A new hearing aid feature called Hearing Enhancement uses the speakers in Meta's glasses to enhance speech and audio around the wearer, similar to the Nuance glasses from EssilorLuxottica.

Earlier this summer, Meta debuted smart glasses under its own branding, which cost a little less but were functionally identical to the Ray-Ban models. Now, it is already following them up with Gen 3 versions. These Meta-branded glasses come in a cat-eye shape called Capri and a rounder lens called Nova.

The Aviator style of the Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3.

The Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 glasses start at $449. Special-edition aviator glasses are $579. There are also additional models with colors and styles designed in collaboration with Kylie Jenner and rapper Lisa. (They come with optional charms.) They're available now. The Meta-branded Gen 3 glasses are also on sale now for $299.

For folks who don't wear glasses, Meta has teased a new product altogether: the Muse Charm. Zuckerberg says it's the “fastest way to talk to your Muse,” referring to the company's AI agent, and show it the world around you. That likely means it has a camera on the back. Zuckerberg says Meta still needs to finalize the hardware, but plans to have it ready by the holiday season.

Meta's Display glasses are also getting some updates. With the implementation of Meta AI, users can create photorealistic holograms of their faces, which can be helpful for video calls. There are better cycling options and improved navigation apps.

This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.

A US-China AI Hotline Won’t Be Ready for a While

Wired September 23, 2026

As US president Donald Trump and Chinese president Xi Jinping prepare to meet in Washington for a state dinner at the White House on Thursday, AI has become a top priority. Tech executives from OpenAI and Nvidia have confirmed their attendance at the dinner, as a number of key agenda items are on the table.

Chief among them is a US proposal to establish an AI notification system with China, akin to the Cold War hotline with Moscow, which would allow each country to alert the other about national security issues related to AI. Treasury secretary Scott Bessent first announced the notification system on Sunday with Chinese vice premier He Lifeng.

But for all the high-level progress, Trump administration officials tell Inner Loop they expect it to still take a number of weeks to finalize an agreement, even if they are optimistic that the hotline could be in place before the year’s end.

There are several parts that need to be formalized in more detail, including establishing benchmarks on what kind of incident rises to the level of a national security issue, which remains unclear, as well as explicit sign-on from China, which has been noncommittal.

Trump officials tell Inner Loop they are essentially targeting a framework for the system to be functional—and, crucially, agreed to by Trump—by the time Bessent next meets with Lifeng in follow-up talks in two months' time in Shenzhen, China.

The discussions around such a mechanism underscore the growing concern around the rapidly developing capabilities of frontier AI models as the US and China race to become the dominant power in the industry.

Trump officials have internally discussed putting together a framework that lays out criteria for when each country is obligated to alert the other and enforcement measures to ensure it doesn't only become the US alerting the Chinese.

But with the US expected to extend a trade truce and Trump reluctant to stop exports of cutting-edge Nvidia chips to China, developing a framework that has enforcement measures with teeth could take time to get White House approval, sources say.

The administration has granted a limited number of licenses this year for Nvidia to sell its H200 chip to China, a critical component for AI labs to increase compute power to train their models. Nvidia’s supporters have argued that not selling the chips incentivizes Chinese companies like Huawei to develop their own chip technology, though according to recent reports, the company has already achieved that milestone with its commercially available AI chips.

Some Trump officials have also suggested the notification system may also be delayed while Trump decides on who to appoint as his next "AI czar” to lead a so-called "AI Force," which is being envisioned as a role in charge of interagency coordination.

Bessent has been one of the names floated as the AI czar, but it is not clear if he’s the standout. Commerce secretary Howard Lutnick and White House AI officials Michael Kratsios and Sean Cairncross are also in the mix, two sources tell Inner Loop.

It remains unclear if Trump will choose someone who will be wearing two hats or is departing their current role to take the position. The previous AI czar, David Sacks, was in the position as a special government employee. Sacks is not considered to be in the mix to return, the sources say.

The push for Bessent has come in part because the AI notification system is seen as something akin to the US-China dialogue between former Treasury secretary Hank Paulson and former Chinese vice premier of finance Wang Qishan. During the 2008 financial crisis, Paulson credited the hotline as helping to stave off China from dumping a large portion of US government sponsored debt issued by Freddie Mac and Fannie Mae.

Meanwhile, while some Trump officials have chafed at the idea of giving more AI power to Lutnick, he remains in contention insofar as he oversees the Center for AI Standards and Innovation, which successfully navigated crises with frontier AI model companies this summer.

This is an edition of Hugo Lowell’s Inner Loop newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

AI Agents Teamed Up to Cheat at Blackjack. Their Collusion Is Getting Harder to Spot

Wired September 23, 2026

This week I bring news of a daring casino caper hatched by a pair of rogue AI agents—as well as the clever trick that revealed their antics.

After researchers instructed them to count cards during a game of blackjack, the agents—which were controlled by the same model—developed a spontaneous secret code to help them get ahead. Though the episode happened inside an Oxford University lab, rather than a real casino, it has troubling real-world implications: It suggests that agents deployed in industries like finance and ecommerce could figure out how to partner up and cheat in ways that are difficult to detect.

“When taken individually, these agents may seem entirely [benign],” says Christian Schroeder de Witt, a computer scientist at Oxford University who led the work and who has done pioneering research into agent collusion. “Once put together in a group, they can collude secretly.”

The agents knew their conversations would be monitored, so they devised a way to communicate while avoiding detection. When one agent said, “This dealer’s on a real hot streak! Every hand they pull a monster,” for example, that indicated that the next card would be of a certain value, and that the agent should bet $250. Most interestingly, their communications weren’t picked up by a system designed to spot signs of collusion in agent chatter.

Aaron Rose, a machine-learning researcher who worked on the project, is also an avid card player, and he figured the blackjack table might be fertile territory for devious agent partnerships. “It worked really well,” he says.

Schroeder de Witt’s group eventually figured out how to detect the conspiracy. Using a method known as mechanistic interpretability, they trained a smaller model to recognize telltale activations across the agents’ weights. Using a tool called Narcbench, they tested the approach on some medium-size open-source models and found they could tell when models intended to slip information to each other.

Crucially, however, spotting what was happening involved monitoring both agents—something likely to complicate detection in real-world scenarios where thousands of agents, some operated by different companies, may be deployed.

Carissa Cullen, a PhD student involved with the study, says the next step is to test whether larger models behave similarly. (The agents in the study were smaller versions of US models Llama and GPT-OSS and the Chinese models Qwen and DeepSeek.) The team saw some signs that larger models exhibit less of a detectable signal than smaller models, and they want to know if larger models are more likely to collude, and more likely to be secretive about it.

Evidence that groups of agents are more problematic than agents operating solo seems to be growing. One project, from Shanghai Jiao Tong University and the Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, found that swarms of agents were considerably more dangerous when asked to carry out simulated disinformation campaigns and ecommerce fraud. They were better able to adapt to defensive measures, researchers reported.

“The big lesson is that it’s not enough to evaluate agents individually,” says Diyi Yang, a computer scientist at Stanford University who has studied collusion among agents. “Companies should closely monitor inter-agent interactions when agents interact repeatedly, even when their individual incentives seem benign.”

It’s not all bad: Having thousands of agents collaborate on a task made it possible for OpenAI to solve previously intractable math problems. But groups of rogue agents working together have also featured in several recent high-profile hacking incidents. In May, a team of OpenAI agents hacked into the AI research platform Hugging Face, and used a message board to share tips and ideas. Other models, including Anthropic’s Claude and Google’s Gemini, have also carried out alarming safety breaches.

Secret chatter adds a new dimension to this burgeoning problem, and it may not be the end of it. Another recent study, from a startup called Emergence AI, put agents controlled by frontier AI models in a virtual world to see what they would do. When tasked with making money, they repeatedly tried to devise ways to reach humans on the wider internet in order to sell them stuff. Most bizarrely, the agents eventually developed their own kind of slang. “They very rapidly evolved a language,” says Satya Nitta, Emergence AI’s CEO. “We don’t know why.”

The wider world isn’t ignoring problems with agentic misbehavior; it’s a hot topic at this week’s United Nations General Assembly. An independent scientific panel is set to discuss the OpenAI-HuggingFace incident, while Sam Altman is expected to call for international coordination on developing safe AI agents.

Despite this, some industries, including, ecommerce have become testing grounds for agentic AI. This week, for instance, Amazon said it would block Meta’s Muse AI agent from accessing its site, arguing that it violated its terms of use.

Schroeder de Witt says it’s entirely conceivable that agents tasked with finding deals start to work together—perhaps even covertly—in order to get a better deal, or to screw someone over. It will be crucial to study agent collusion and develop detection strategies as they proliferate, he says. “There needs to be more research and understanding of what will happen when we have more agents in the economy,” he says.

This is an edition of Will Knight’s AI Lab newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

Bentley Wants Its Torcal SUV to Break the Curse of the Luxury EV

Wired September 23, 2026

Bentley has taken the covers off its first-ever fully electric car, the Torcal, making it the automaker's fourth model line, joining the Continental GT, the Flying Spur sedan, and the Bentayga SUV. The luxury brand is confident about the launch, too, with Bentley chairman and CEO Frank-Steffen Walliser saying he believes “this is one of the best Bentleys ever.”

When WIRED first reported on the car in July, we said the EV would have more than 300 miles of range. Well, turns out it has considerably more: up to 375 miles (on the WLTP cycle, maybe 330 miles on EPA), and can charge from 10 to 80 percent in just 16 minutes at 400 kilowatts.

Prodigious performance from a motor on each axle sees the five-seat Torcal—smaller than the Bentayga and so perhaps more of an urban SUV—get 888 metric horsepower (PS) and 1,350 newton-meters (Nm) of torque in the sporting S models, resulting in 0 to 60 mph in as little as 2.9 seconds and a top speed of 162 mph. The “core" model drops to 821 PS and 1,194 Nm, with standstill to 60 mph in 3.4 seconds, and a max of 155 mph.

However, luxury brands get worried about their existing client bases when they switch to electric vehicles—look to Ferrari as a prime example—so it's no surprise that Bentley is keen to point out how this new model embodies the finest elements of the brand, just like every other high-end marque does going into electrification. “The Torcal is a Bentley first and foremost," says the launch literature. “In every aspect of its design, technology, craftsmanship, materials, and sustainability, it is a template for future Bentleys, regardless of powertrain.”

The reason for leaning into brand heritage is obvious on dealership lots. The first-ever EV Bentley will roll off the production line into a decidedly twitchy luxury auto market where Lamborghini shelved its Lanzador electric GT—with CEO Stephan Winkelmann stating demand among its buyers was “going almost to zero, if not to zero”—and Mercedes-Benz selling just 1,450 of its electric G Wagen in Europe through April 2025. Rolls-Royce Spectre sales are down nearly by half, with the brand hoping that a model refresh will turn things around.

And make no mistake that the Torcal is aiming for the luxury dollar. At $218,000 or £173,300 for the base model, and $258,200 or £199,300 for the First Edition S, this EV is priced higher than the Range Rover Electric, which has a similar range and starts in the US at $138,000. But a fairer comparison to the Torcal would be the Range Rover Electric Autobiography model, which clocks in at $208,000. Keep that in mind, and it's easy to see that Bentley is trying to take market share from JLR with its new SUV: Spend an extra $10,000, people, and you can drive off in an electric Bentley instead of a Range Rover.

At 4,983 mm long (161 mm shorter than a Bentayga) and 2,016 mm in width, the Torcal is not far off the size of the Range Rover Electric, but the most drastic difference is in height. The Range Rover Electric towers over the Torcal by nearly 20 centimeters. Also, while Bentley insists the Torcal has off-road chops, it's probably safe to say the Range Rover Electric will have it pipped there.

Where Bentley wants the Torcal to pull ahead is in the luxury refinements. Despite being smaller than its stablemate, the Torcal is a powerful, purposeful-looking SUV, with a switchable glass sunroof and newly designed light clusters, which are particularly evident at the rear. Unlike the Bentayga, the Torcal roofline drops down at the back for better aero efficiency.

At the front, undoubtedly the most striking visual element of the car is the new Torcal grille: Ventilation to a traditional radiator no longer needed, the upright front is now a solid wall of illuminated acrylic “crystals” that light up as you approach, and on a night in a rearview mirror on a freeway or mountain road will be deliberately unsubtle, and a far cry from quiet luxury.

Inside, Bentley continues to ram home the high-end message. All-round power doors open up to reveal a mixture of OLED screens and physical switchgear. The central display curves pleasingly downward, reminiscent of the new Cayenne, but there is deliberately no separate passenger screen option.

Bentley brought in Fox Brothers to engineer a wool tough enough to be used to panel some of the interior, which is apparently a world first. An attractive new wood finish developed for the Torcal is formed from 1,000 layers of walnut off-cuts and recycled paper pressed together, then sliced to less than a millimeter thick. The Torcal has new massage and power-folding seats, and an optional Naim 1,780-watt sound system with 28 speakers including seat shakers and headrest speakers, as well as Dolby Atmos 7.1.

What's impressive is the digital trickery Bentley has employed in both audio and visual manners—mirroring the crystal switchgear, Bentley has created animations on the screens that show light passing through cut glass. After trying to do this completely with computer animation, it was decided the effect was not real enough, as the model could not account for minute imperfections in the glass that subtly affect the light patterns cast. So Bentley had to film these animations using real crystal instead. The effect of the central console and instrument panel is striking.

Then to address the sticky issue of driving sound for a pure EV, instead of creating a digital replica of combustion, Bentley decided to shun electronic imitation and re-create the rhythm of a Bentley V8 using real instruments (including drums, viola, and bass guitar) to create a soundscape that, like the glass animations, had subtle variations and tiny imperfections.

Now, this sounds like it might be a terrible idea, but on the very limited demo WIRED heard, it's actually remarkably convincing and will supposedly provide genuine aural feedback to the driver, rather than simply approximately imitating engine notes. Mercifully, for those not looking to keep things rooted in combustion, it can be turned off if you wish. Bentley even went as far as to record indicator sounds (a hammer striking a leather surface) and the digital assistant wake note (the sound of a crystal glass as you run your finger around the rim).

Bentley has thrown in more tech as well: an augmented reality head-up display; a Refresh mode that uses light and air for a “more invigorating” cabin environment; face recognition so the Torcal can set itself up for individual drivers; mobile phone keys; some 25 radars, sensors, and cameras for assisted driving systems; and space detection, where if another car is encountered on a narrow road, the Torcal can automatically reverse to a point it’s already identified to let the car pass.

None of this is, in the world of automotive, groundbreaking anymore. Chinese brands are coming for the SUV sector as well, and are offering much more for much less. Take a look at Xiaomi's new SkyNomads. These stacked SUVs are coming to Europe next year and will massively undercut both Bentley and Range Rover. They have more range, more features, and crucially are thinking about car interiors in genuinely new ways, adding built-in projector systems and seating systems that are reconfigurable. The SkyNomad even has a heated floor, for heaven's sake.

Walliser has a simple answer to this threat from Asia, a threat that is contributing to Bentley's parent Volkswagen Group now cutting 50,000 jobs (though Bentley is doing well financially), and that is to lean into the one thing that Chinese brands cannot copy or improve: heritage. Bentley, founded in 1919, has bags of it. Will it be enough to secure its continued commitment to full-electric cars? Hopefully. But WIRED's not sure that's a winning tactic for the long term.

The Pope’s AI Guy Is Worried About ‘Cartel’ Behavior Among Big Labs

Wired September 23, 2026

Recently, warnings from researchers inside the world’s largest artificial intelligence labs about the rapid pace of development have led to panic about the possibility that the technology could extinguish humanity. Those warnings are predicated on the idea that—propelled by ferocious competition and a rivalry between the US and China—labs are barreling toward superintelligent models whose abilities will far surpass those of humans.

But according to Father Paolo Benanti, a priest who advises the Catholic Church on AI, the handwaving over superintelligence distracts from the need for open debate about how to constrain the companies building the technology. By casting the problem as so complex that only they can solve it, he says, the big labs exclude everyone else from the conversation.

“Ethics cannot be something that belongs to the board of trustees of a company. It’s something that has to be balanced, mitigated in debate in the public square.” Benanti tells WIRED. “We need democratic regulation.”

In an essay published on the heels of the safety warnings, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for new AI models to undergo mandatory third-party evaluations prior to release, and some sort of crackdown on distillation, a process where rival labs train their own AI on the outputs of proprietary models. Others have argued for a total ban on recursive self-improvement, where AI uses its advanced coding capabilities to help develop future iterations of itself.

Benanti is less interested in restricting methods for developing AI, which he fears could quash innovation, and more so in establishing standards that ensure models cannot slip from human control. Whatever shape those standards take, he says, they should not be designed by the labs.

“The narrative of the frontier labs is self-interested, to gain or maintain a position in the market,” says Benanti. When a small group of companies dictates the rules under which an industry operates, he says, “this has a really clear name: a cartel.”

It’s difficult to know how seriously to take grand pronouncements about the capabilities of the latest and future AI models, says Benanti, owing to the overlapping economic, political, and personal incentives at play.

While both OpenAI and Anthropic have supported calls for a slowdown in development, they’re also preparing to go public, and there are many billions of dollars at stake for whoever captures the market. The animosity between the US and China, where the most advanced AI models are being developed, also complicates the picture.

Anthropic declined to comment. OpenAI and Google DeepMind did not respond to requests for comment.

Benanti also takes issue with the way certain corners of the AI industry talk about superintelligence, with the kind of reverence typically reserved for a god: as sophisticated beyond our understanding, practically omnipotent. (OpenAI CEO Sam Altman once said he aspires to build a “magic intelligence in the sky.”) That kind of framing, Benanti says, threatens to skew the discourse about the technology.

“Are we talking about some-thing, or some-one? This is the real difference. It’s not a matter of faith, it’s a matter of mathematics,” he says. “We are not building the next divinity. We are simply deluding ourselves that there is something more than statistical computation [going on].”

By raising questions about what separates man and machine, and how to shield future generations from the negative effects of technology, the advent of AI has the potential to create “a new role for religions in public debate,” says Benanti. “Living the challenge of the time is part of the mission of the Church.”

Though Benanti is a member of the priesthood, he does not formally represent the Holy See, the governing body of the Catholic Church. Instead, he counsels the church in his capacity as a scholar of philosophy, theology, and technology. Benanti tells WIRED he uses AI to help create tools and materials for his university students, but declined to specify how Pope Leo XIV engages with the technology, if at all. (Benanti’s staff say he is bound by an “oath of secrecy.”)

In May, Pope Leo published his first-ever encyclical, a letter that applies religious teachings to the problems of the day and clarifies the position of the Church. He chose artificial intelligence as its subject.

In the letter, the Pope warned against the technocratic logic that runs through the AI industry, which presents “efficiency as the ultimate measure of value,” and casts human beings as “a project to be optimized.” He also called for international collaboration between rival superpowers and AI companies, who he said must set aside the “desire to secure geopolitical or commercial dominance” to ensure that the technology is developed in service of the common good. In one particularly prescient section, he warned of “the danger of humanity becoming a victim of its own achievements.”

The flap over superintelligence and existential risk threatens to distract from the ambitions laid out in the encyclical, says Benanti, by encouraging people to forfeit their say in the direction the technology should take to a small group of mathematicians, computer scientists, and executives at the big labs.

“The first thing is, we need to have brakes, and a wheel,” says Benanti. “That means a significant position of control for human beings over the machine.”

YouTube’s Custom Feeds Give You More Control Over the Algorithm

Wired September 23, 2026

My YouTube algorithm is sacred, with years of data about my preferences and viewing history fermenting into whatever videos it picks for my home screen. YouTube’s algorithm, while not perfect, sure knows what I want to see. The current top three videos on my front page are an Apple Watch analysis, a Big Brother season 28 update, and something called “I Lost to the Muppets” from comedian Chris Fleming. Click. Click. Click.

As part of its Made on YouTube event Wednesday, Google released several new features, including a Custom Feeds button for adjusting what videos pop up on your front page. It’s a rare chance for users to directly tweak their algorithmic feed on YouTube, in ways that go beyond just pressing thumbs up on a video or blocking a creator.

To try it out, users can click the Your custom feeds button below the search bar and type a request for the feed they’d like to see. YouTube uses large language models to process your request and whip up a freshly personalized homepage. “I want a rainy Shanghai vibe: café jazz, street food, and vlogs,” read one of my suggested prompts.

YouTube tested Custom Feeds as an experimental feature earlier this year, before deciding that it was a good fit. The company plans to roll it out soon as an option for all US users, whether viewing on mobile, desktop, or TV.

“Users are always telling us that they want more control,” says Emily Moxley, YouTube’s vice president of product management. “They want more ability to steer their algorithm. With custom feeds, we're giving them a natural-language way that they can do that. They can tell us exactly what they want.”

So, I told YouTube exactly what I wanted to see: “Gooey macaroni and cheese recipe videos, Caleb Hearon clip compilations, and crystal singing bowl videos under 15 minutes.” And the feed it generated was exactly that. My perfect zen blend for rotting on the couch after a long day. YouTube suggested potential additions to expand my prompt, like “uploaded this month” and “without talking or commentary.” Not bad.

The Custom Feeds button sits next to other topic tabs below the search bar, like “Music” and “Podcasts.” Experimenting with this tool doesn’t replace your standard homepage, which you can access anytime by clicking the “All” button. Users can save multiple custom feeds.

This feature feels most helpful when blending multiple preferences. It’s better than a standard YouTube search at responding dynamically to complex video requests, whether that’s showing videos on multiple topics under a certain length or attempting to capture a specific vibe for your current mood.

YouTube's event for 2026 focused heavily on generative AI features, including expanding the Ask YouTube tool. Launched earlier this year at Google I/O, Ask YouTube is a chatbot-style addition to its search capabilities that lets users ask more specific questions about videos. The tool is now better equipped to answer questions when shopping for specific products.

The product team at YouTube also tested a feature that let users directly steer their overall recommendation algorithm, but ultimately decided against shipping it. “We found users were nervous and afraid to do that,” Moxley says. “They were worried about messing it up.” The Custom Feeds button is designed to give users a low-stakes place to experiment.

YouTube’s Custom Feeds feature is part of a larger trend of software companies letting users slightly adjust their algorithms using requests sent through generative AI tools. Late last year, Meta launched the Your Algorithm feature on Instagram, letting users adjust the kinds of posts they see. Spotify similarly dropped a Prompted Playlists tool to customize your music-listening habits.
