She’s 28, Loves God and Her Family, and Might Be the Reason You Can’t Have Kids

Wired September 23, 2026

By 5 am every morning, Emma Waters is on the sofa with a blanket, plotting America’s baby-making future. For two hours, she stays off her phone, inspired by Deep Work, the self-help bestseller. At 7:30, she does emails. Waters, 28 years old, is a monk of productivity who makes motherhood look like all-­natural Adderall.

At 8 am, it’s time for breakfast and the Bible. Waters tries to live her life according to the mantra “Love God, get married, have babies.” She asks that I not use the real names of her two daughters for their safety, even though they’ve been printed elsewhere. I’ll call them Gertie and Ophelia, which are close enough.

All morning, they play. Ophelia, the baby, runs around in white tights, shirtless, clutching a pink purse; Gertie’s doll won’t stop crying. Jack, Waters’ husband, flits in and out. There isn’t much to say about Jack, other than that he’s hot, is studying to be a preacher, and has a big desk at home, much bigger than Waters’, featuring a bust of Nietzsche. In the same room, Waters has a pull-out secretary where she takes meetings, not far from a portrait of a glowering President Trump.

The only thing Waters doesn’t really do is exercise; she hasn’t found the time.

Not many people outside of DC have heard of Waters, who mostly works from home in a dreary Pennsylvania suburb named after a long-offshored manufacturer. Yet Waters is a factory for policy papers and op-eds extolling the harms of unregulated reproductive technology, probing the moral issues that liberals don’t want to touch with a 10-foot turkey baster. At least once a month, reporting on fertility, I ask for an academic source and am instead directed to Waters, author of a biblical women’s leadership book that basically says the best thing about the Barbie movie was the patriarchy.

Emma Waters, her husband Jackson, and their two daughters.

The craziest thing is that, in certain ways, she’s a voice of reason. America’s $10 billion fertility industry is suffering a massive PR crisis that makes the embryo mix-ups and baby-selling schemes of yore seem quaint. A few recent headlines: “The Chinese Billionaires Having Dozens of US-Born Babies Via Surrogate,” “The Family Law Loophole That Lets Sex Offenders Parent Kids,” “California Couple Busted for Running Suspected Baby Mill,” “Surrogate Mother Who Refused to Abort Baby Gives Birth Amid Ongoing Legal Dispute.” Polygenic testing companies promise today’s parents that they can pick the tallest, smartest, least-bald offspring, mainstreaming debates about the “Black-white IQ gap.” OpenAI CEO Sam Altman—a father via surrogacy—and Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong are invested in an embryo-editing startup. If you believe what they told The Wall Street Journal, their first gene-hacked baby has probably already been born.

Many right-wing techies are jazzed about these developments, which might bump up birth rates or create “better” spawn. Many liberals don’t know how to talk about the ethical pitfalls. Emma Waters fills in the gaps. As a kind of backroom wheeler-dealer and political strategist, she is the mastermind behind Florida’s recent ban on international surrogacy, the Texas GOP’s souring on IVF, and the squashing of Trump’s “fertilization president” initiatives. This God-loving, JD Vance–stanning Gen Z-er might be standing between you and your ability to have a family, or she might be, somehow, the force that makes it possible. Waters has so much to teach us about optics and politics and why, in so many arenas, Democrats are losing so dramatically. Waters wants to dismantle fertility as we know it. And she wants to do it politely, during nap time, with her husband’s permission.

Waters wasn’t always political. She and her three younger siblings were homeschooled by their mother in a poor, rural part of southern Georgia, while their father worked 60-hour weeks as a facilities manager and HVAC repairman. (Waters describes her local high school as the kind of place where one-third of students got chlamydia.) Growing up, Waters never felt aligned with either party: Republicans praised free trade and cheap widgets; Democrats pushed equal pay and shoved kids into day care.

Then, in her junior year at a Christian college in Tennessee, Waters heard a podcast interview with JD Vance. “Everything he says, I relate to,” she remembers thinking. When she graduated a year later, in 2021—as valedictorian—she applied for an internship at American Moment, a training ground of sorts for rising conservatives. They gave her a full-time job.

Around this time, she met Jackson Waters at a mock-government event. Emma recounts their “whirlwind romance” in her book, Lead Like Jael. After “a summer of tense conversations,” she broke up with him “on a whim.” She wanted a career in politics; the thought of being a wife and mother felt like “a major letdown.” With the help of a pastor, she realized she only had these notions because of girlboss feminism. She begged Jack to take her back and got married at 24. She was an anomaly even among Republicans. Waters had heard older colleagues refer to women who got married at that age as “child brides.”

“Take up your ladle like a sword,” Waters writes in her book. “Stand behind your stove like a sentinel.”

Waters loved life in DC: walking 24,000 steps a day, getting coffee with everyone and their mom, hosting dinners in her basement. When she got pregnant with Gertie, she and Jack wanted to prove that life didn’t end with a baby. But she needed a job with more flexibility that would eventually allow Jack to attend in-person seminary. In 2022, Waters approached the Heritage Foundation, the most influential conservative think tank. Heritage had recently shed its intellectual bona fides to become a MAGA mouthpiece; the next year, it would release Project 2025, the playbook for Trump 2.0.

Waters pitched Heritage that she would cover emerging fertility tech as an analyst: crafting policy briefs, penning op-eds, whispering into politicians’ ears. Waters found traditional pro-life policy banal—everything was about abortion. Debates around IVF started and ended with “Are embryos people?” She wanted to apply her dual major in political science and biblical studies to cutting-edge science. At the time, it seemed like “the least popular policy issue,” she says, but she promised the bosses it would soon be a big deal. They were sold.

Waters found her conservative colleagues ignorant about the state of assisted baby-making. One Hill staffer emailed Waters about a test that counts embryos’ chromosomes, asking, “Will this be around in 10 years?” It had been around for decades. At that point, a Chinese scientist had already embryo-­Crispr’d babies, gone to jail for it, and gotten out. Sex selection had become a standard part of American IVF; the first sex-selected people were in their thirties. It was easier to open a surrogacy agency than an ice cream cart or a tanning salon.

Then there was China. In 2023, more than two years before mainstream media outlets reported on Sino-US infant import-exports, Waters was on Fox News, accompanied by an article headlined “Chinese ‘Rent-a-Womb’ Industry Using American Surrogates Is a National Security Threat.” She called it “the new face of birth tourism.” Intended parents didn’t even have to leave the country. Our nation’s lax laws meant that you could ship sperm over and get an American citizen shipped back.

Nobody wants to talk about women in tech anymore—not even women in tech. Is that progress?

Waters hates it when people harp on what she’s anti. Instead, she wants people to focus on what she’s pro: pro-“human flourishing”; pro-“the human person,” including embryos; pro-man-woman marriage; pro-life (duh); pro-Natural Procreative Technology, by which infertile heteros of breeding age clean up their diets, reduce their plastics, and ultimately get knocked up according to God’s will. Pronatalist? She prefers “pro-family,” which implies more straight marriages where straight penises and vaginas produce tons of babies. (Critics would add that the goal is really white Christian babies.)

Waters never says she’s against IVF per se. She doesn’t talk about “murdering” embryos; she makes it sound more like negligent manslaughter. She mostly argues that IVF doesn’t work. It encourages young women to postpone their true calling by falsely reassuring them that there’s still time.

To Waters, IVF is the conduit for many horrors. Ranking and selecting embryos tricks parents into thinking they can choose and control what kind of children they have, cheapening God’s handmade gift into an off-brand dustmop plucked off an Amazon wish list. It allows you to outsource reproduction to surrogates, objectifying women and commoditizing babies. Decoupling sex, marriage, and procreation distorts the natural order. Infertility explodes. Civilizations collapse. In her work, Waters fastidiously avoids mentioning gays, singles, or women over 40. When I ask her about this omission, she gets defensive: “It’s not about the desires of adults. It’s about the rights and well-being of children.”

Waters is a Republican, but that doesn’t mean all Republicans agree with her. The vast majority of Republicans support IVF as is. The pronatalist movement has two factions, the tech right and the trads. The tech right sees artificial wombs, surrogacy, and genetic optimization as tools to boost birth rates. Trads, like Waters, think these things will make the problem worse.

Besides China, nothing rankles Waters like embryo screening tools that promise to let parents “have your best baby.” Nobody really expects these so-called polygenic tests to move into the mainstream or ever become very accurate, but they set the tone for a future where parents can edit their children’s genes. On X, Noor Siddiqui, CEO of the startup Orchid and one of Waters’ least favorite founders, wastes no time in shaming breeders who fail to optimize. Getting knocked up the old-fashioned way is irresponsible: “What if your baby never walks?” Siddiqui has posted. “What if they’re never able to live independently? What if you could have stopped it … but chose not to?” (Stopping it, in this case, means making sure your disabled child isn’t born.) “Just be honest: You’re OK with your kid potentially suffering for life so you can feel morally superior, or because you can’t be inconvenienced.” In a decade, Siddiqui warns, all babies will be born using IVF and her test—Waters’ definition of dystopia.

Like many at Heritage, Waters was disappointed when Trump included free IVF in his 2024 platform, later declaring himself the “father of IVF” and “the fertilization president.” But Waters still found fertile ground (sorry) filled with low-hanging fruit. There were zero federal regulations governing surrogacy—she would shepherd the first one. “We have model legislation to SHUT DOWN foreign nations who rent the wombs of American women,” she wrote on X. She would rail against the creepy, unpopular polygenic tests that are opposed by every professional society. With the nation’s most influential conservative organization backing her, she’d push to mainstream so-called restorative reproductive medicine that co-opted the language of social justice while addressing the root causes of women’s broken, barren bodies.

Last November, waters sat onstage at the Heritage Foundation wearing a faux leather dress, slouchy boots, and a periwinkle double-breasted blazer while dozens of protesters in red Handmaid’s Tale cloaks screamed on the sidewalk outside.

I’d come to DC to meet Waters in person. It was a tough week for the organization. Its president had taken heat, and nearly had to resign, for defending Tucker Carlson’s choice to platform Nick Fuentes, a white supremacist. (Fuentes: “Hitler was awesome. Hitler was right. And the Holocaust didn’t happen.”) I wondered if there were always a dozen cops outside of the building. Sometimes the roar and the sirens were so deafening it was hard to hear Waters, but the disturbance seemed to make her smile.

First, Waters warmed up the room by having a “chat” with a mom who gets told by libs that she should’ve aborted her disabled son. Then Waters turned to the main event. “Welcome, gentlemen,” she said. She had assembled four white experts for “Editing Destiny,” a panel on the subject of polygenic tests and gene editing. Two seemed like MAGA partisans. Two were legitimate academics.

Waters had the energy of a high school newspaper reporter with a blowout and makeup that perfectly concealed her prominent chin. Everyone agreed that somatic gene editing on “born people” was good. Waters pointed out how it served the MAHA goal to eliminate disease at the source. But germline gene editing, the panel also agreed, was risky and unnecessary. No one said “fetus” or “God”; instead they evoked “the human person” and “flourishing.” Ben Hurlbut, one of the academics, made a moving, secular argument against polygenic selection. This was the “first relational act” you make with your future children, he told me, and it invites a serious rift.

Around the room, young female staffers in tight dresses held microphones for Q&A. The panel took a few questions. One attendee noted the harms of Tylenol.

After the event, Waters introduced me to Austin Rogers, then general counsel to Florida senator Rick Scott. Rogers wore a green Rolex with his hair gelled up in the front—he wouldn’t have looked out of place at a nightclub. Rogers told me they were using Waters’ model legislation to try to ban surrogacy from “foreign adversaries.” He was looking for a Democratic partner. He mentioned the latest story, covered by every major outlet, of a Chinese couple in California who had commissioned at least 25 surrogates to carry their children—a perfectly legal scheme—only to allegedly abuse most of those children in a mansion. He said, “I read it and my hair was on fire.”

That night, I walked Hurlbut, the academic, back to the train station and asked him why he agreed to speak at the Heritage Foundation. It wasn’t about party politics, he said. These issues couldn’t be split cleanly into left and right. “Anyone taking this seriously is creating a service to the public discourse,” he said. I asked who the big players were on the liberal side. “Big players? There are no big players. Just a few voices crying in the wilderness.”

Two months later, I visit Waters at home, in the type of town where hotels keep their lobby doors locked at all times. “I’ll have lunch to share with you,” Waters emails. When I arrive, she is wearing heeled boots and trendy jeans, making a butternut squash soup with bacon and brie. Ophelia watches from her high chair, wearing white tights underneath a fancy outfit. Over the next 27 hours, Waters will serve her husband and me a parade of elaborate orange foods: frittata with broken spaghetti, clementines, clam chowder (yes, also orange). (The girls will also eat Cheez-Its, Goldfish, and chicken nuggets.)

I recognize her hospitality tactics from Lead Like Jael, specifically the chapter titled “Motherhood as Warfare.” Waters advises women to embrace distinctly feminine means of influence. “No woman in the Bible picked up a sword to fight,” she tells me. Waters named her book after a biblical matriarch who offered an enemy commander a place to stay and then pierced his head with a tent peg, thus winning the battle.

I fear I am the enemy commander in this story.

In the book, Waters urges: “Take up your ladle like a sword. Stand behind your stove like a sentinel.”

Waters’ book was published in March.

Her house is modest yet beautiful, full of damask furniture. Christmas cards ring the kitchen doorway. In one photo, Simone and Malcolm Collins, the prominent pronatalist couple who embrace the term “hipster eugenicists,” smile from behind thick black glasses. On the credenza next to the dining room table, there’s a gilded Bible, a Venetian clock, and a ring light that never turns off.

Jack, home for lunch, says grace. Even 13-month-old Ophelia clasps her hands, closes her eyes, and bows her head.

Waters gets things done by being very, very nice. Simone Collins tells me, “I don’t know a single person in the pronatalist movement who doesn’t like Emma. She’s golden.” Even though the Collinses promote polygenic testing, IVF, and surrogacy, Waters considers them friends and makes a point not to publicly criticize them. In any given hour, Waters laser-focuses on a single issue. Another conservative tells me, “She could do an event with someone on Tuesday and be on the opposite side of a protest on Friday.” When she gets into a flame war with someone on X, she invites them to collaborate.

That’s how she secured the special guest for today’s Zoom working group: the founder of a polygenic testing company. One Tuesday a month, during nap time, Waters hosts private discussions with a group of bioethicists, activists, and policy wonks. Many potential collaborators do not want to be associated with Heritage, so Waters does much of her work in secret. She paraphrases a sign that Ronald Reagan kept on his desk in the Oval Office: “There is no limit to what a man can do or where he can go if he doesn’t mind who gets the credit.”

In the glow of the ring light, Waters and I huddle around her dining room table. I’m allowed to join if I don’t name names: I recognize a few prominent pro-lifers, and one or two liberals. “There is no dispute about how the technology works,” the polygenic testing founder says. He hammers home that two papers a day are being written about the associations between genes. His vibe oscillates between nerd and evil professor. He repeats at least a dozen times that his technology works. “There are ideologues masquerading as experts. You can easily fool a WIRED reporter into writing into her story that it doesn’t work.”

Waters asks a question about “children who have been born already.” Then someone asks about a recent paper showing that the sibling with the tallest-seeming genes is actually only the tallest about 25 percent of the time. This implies that, three out of four times, “picking the tallest baby,” well, wouldn’t work. The founder is irritated. One person might be predicted to be taller by 1 centimeter, but the error bars are 2 centimeters. “Falling within the error bars of the model means it’s successful,” the founder says.

Waters chimes in: “If the solution from a polygenic risk score for breast cancer was euthanasia, people would have a problem with it.” Then, she adds with a smirk, “That’s probably already happening in Canada.” To Waters, embryos are “human people”—but she won’t belabor the point or argue about metaphysical priors. The founder reminds us, “If you want to call it eugenics, you can, but don’t say it doesn’t work.”

Many of Waters’ critics dismiss her as a fool because of her retrograde gender views, which underpin all her other ideas.

I read Lead Like Jael in one sitting; my eyes got dry from popping so far out of my head. “There’s a hierarchy in marriage,” Waters writes. She advises her readers to become “good at being a woman” by “cultivating distinctly feminine strengths,” such as good posture. In an analysis of Greta Gerwig’s Barbie movie, patriarchy was “the first real innovation,” she writes. “Strong and godly men propel society forward.” Waters analyzes how, in the official portraits of First Lady Melania Trump, even her nails and eyebrows focus on the greater mission. She urges readers to redefine success as a joint pursuit, beginning with a husband’s career. Parents should start talking about marriage and motherhood at the same age as they ask kids what they want to be when they grow up. Women’s work should be flexible and easy to pause: “To neglect the home to pursue work is to invert God’s design.” Women are there to “support and strengthen” but not replace men. “Rightful authority” begins with husbands in the home. Women can lead, but only about 8 percent of the time.

Sitting in a trendy café, radiant in a puffy-sleeved red sweater and an Oura ring, Waters explains to me that the difference between men and women goes back to Genesis. Adam’s names mean “ground” and “man.” Eve’s names mean “fire,” “woman,” “mother.” So men are supposed to dig holes while women launch rockets? No: “A man is pulled toward the ground,” Waters says. “The wife is pulled to her husband and her children.”

Waters tries to live her life according to the mantra “Love God, get married, have babies.”

She goes on: “We don’t want to go back to the 1950s. God put us in our time for a reason.” Still, there’s a lot to learn from the halcyon days when all 50 states allowed marital rape. Waters explains that the problem with the 1950s was that technology, like the dishwasher, stripped women of meaningful labor. “What would have been amazing is if women had radically rethought what they could do with the time they’d been given”—instead of just turning to wage labor. Despite providing most of the childcare, working full-time, and supporting her husband through school, Waters claims that balancing work and motherhood hasn’t been that hard. (Waters isn’t even so hot on federal paid family leave, since it encourages moms to go back to work.)

Here’s where I admit that Waters and I have more in common than I could have imagined. I got married at 25. I love being married and raising my child. We both go to church every Sunday (though mine has a gay pastor). I find it sad how young people see pregnancy as a funeral dirge for their hopes and dreams. I, too, expect low birth rates to cause big problems, and I suspect many “childfree” people will experience regret in 20 years. I’m inspired by Waters, how she cranked out more than 150 policy papers, interviews, and op-eds while I wrote this measly profile. I’m jealous of the time she spends with her daughters and how well behaved they are and how she managed to travel alone with a 4-month-old to Hungary to speak at a conference. But when Waters tells me that once you become a wife you have to subjugate yourself to your husband, it’s hard to keep a straight face.

If she wants to boost marriage rates, I ask, wouldn’t egalitarian partnership be an easier sell? She doesn’t have an answer. “It never crossed my mind.”

There’s a glaring gap between what Waters professes—that a woman’s highest calling is the home—and what she does, which is support her family financially while being way more influential and successful than her husband. She reconciles this by, literally, doing it all, while swearing she will slow down her career at a moment’s notice. By that same token, it’s also hard to distinguish between what Waters really thinks, what she is supposed to say, what’s rage-bait, and if there’s any meaningful difference between those categories. Her X background used to be a photo of “What’s Wrong With ‘Equal Rights’ for Women?” by Phyllis Schlafly, an activist who started speeches by thanking her husband for allowing her to be there. When I ask her about it, Waters says, “If your enemies think you’re oppressed, play up the trope.”

On the right, optics are everything. “How you project yourself is a political message,” Waters says. Before coming to DC, she had eight piercings, including belly button and eyebrow rings, but she didn’t want to be perceived like that. “Your appearance shows what you value,” she says. “I really value dressing well and pleasing my husband.”

If Waters had her way, there might be some IVF, but it wouldn’t involve ranking, destroying, or indefinitely freezing embryos. The only lawful surrogacy would be altruistic for heterosexual married couples with a documented history of infertility. (The gays, singles, and AOCs of the world would, in other words, put children’s well-being first and just not have them.)

In an international context, some of Waters’ views are perfectly normal. Almost every wealthy country besides the US bans elective sex selection. Every other wealthy country bans commercial surrogacy, which the UN called a form of violence against women and “the sale of children.” UN committees see anonymous gamete donation as incompatible with children’s rights. Most Western countries require tests to undergo some kind of approval process before going to market, so polygenic tests are out. In Germany, parents need government approval to genetically test embryos. Through a global lens, American Big Fertility is bizarro.

But for Democrats, it’s often seen as too politically toxic to criticize the largely unregulated industry. Challenging almost anything about it—even just that private-equity-backed clinics conduct most IVF cycles—opens the door for critics like Waters. Businesses have framed picking the sex of your baby, or even picking your Aryan-est baby, as a matter of “reproductive autonomy” on par with abortion. Lefties who disagree mostly keep their mouths shut. It’s almost too easy for Waters. Google will send anyone disturbed by the status quo straight to her op-eds.

While Waters invites journalists to her home and cooks them elaborate meals, some fertility professionals blame the reporters who dissect the scandals. After I wrote about a surrogacy gone wrong last year, Ron Poole-Dayan, the executive director of Men Having Babies, told me, “You are the problem. Journalists like you are a big part of the reason gay men can’t have families.”

People working in assisted reproduction see so many happy stories of family formation, they don’t even seem to understand what the problem is. At a recent conference for a surrogacy and egg donation ethics group, one attendee remarked, “An airplane takes off and lands a thousand times, and no one writes a story. A plane crashes once—everyone writes about it.” Someone else chimed in, “And flying is safer than driving!”

At the conference, surrounded by attorneys and professionals who seemed earnestly invested in doing the right thing, I thought of the left’s purity test problem: wanting so badly to be 100 percent correct that you forget how you look; ceding the hard topics to your opponents, who can wrap a kernel of truth in a bundle of nonsense; getting defensive when you could’ve invited the enemy in for a bowl of orange soup.

The biggest criticism lobbed at Waters is, obviously, that she wants to turn America into The Handmaid’s Tale. The second biggest criticism is that she’s a hypocrite. Waters’ kids aren’t in day care, but that doesn’t mean she doesn’t have help. At Waters’ house, I was surprised to meet a relative who consoled sobbing dolls and occupied the children while Waters entertained me and Jack studied the Bible or whatever. Waters’ mom is also a “full-time grandma” to Gertie and Ophelia.

The third biggest criticism is, let’s say, her credentials. “She’s not an academic. She’s not someone who actually has experience in these things,” says Lauren Hall, a political science professor at Rochester Institute of Technology. The feminist writer Jessica Valenti has essentially called Waters a failed influencer.

It’s not easy being an influential conservative mom who tells other moms of young kids to stay home. Criticisms of the Heritage Foundation, meanwhile, come from both the left and right. It’s “the worst-case scenario for a woman,” says Hall. She says Heritage puts “token” women forward, who have to hew to “a very particular party line.” In early 2025, an anonymous staff member sent letters to Heritage trustees alleging discrimination against childless women.

Waters disagrees, of course—she’s a fierce defender of Heritage. “America first,” she tells me. “MASS DEPORTATIONS NOW!” she tweets. She admits that Nick Fuentes says some “disgusting” things and describes him as “a young white man” who was “disenfranchised by the Republican Party because he dared to question our relationship with Israel.” When I ask her about the GOP’s unofficial strategy of “no enemies to the right,” a big-tent welcome for neo-Nazis and white nationalists, she snaps back, “Don’t you think the left is the same? Normalizing pedophilia. Abortion until birth. Rampant antisemitism … Why do you think Josh Shapiro wasn’t the vice presidential nominee?”

Waters’ master plan to undermine the fertility industry seems to be working. In November 2025, Senator Rick Scott proposed the SAFE KIDS Act, banning citizens of “hostile foreign regimes” from participating in surrogacy. In Florida, a similar law passed at the state level in May. At the start of 2026, Florida attorney general James Uthmeier stepped in to try to get two French dads un-recognized as their son’s legal parents, calling surrogacy “unconstitutional” and “modern-day slavery.” In July, Uthmeier intervened in another case, arguing that Florida should ignore an intended parent’s California parentage order, seemingly in opposition to the Full Faith and Credit clause of the Constitution. A proposed bill in Kentucky would ban all commercial surrogacy.

When Trump called himself “the father of IVF” in 2024, it looked like Waters had lost the battle against petri dish kids. But in June, Texas’ GOP denounced the procedure, and Trump has thus far reneged on his promises to make it free. In a recent grant application, the Department of Health and Human Services called frozen embryos “children.”

Many observers tell me they think Waters’ work is “the driving force” in pushing fertility regulation out of the fringes and into the mainstream. They also tell me the new laws are insincere and bad, fraught with unintended consequences. For example, the Florida attorney general’s anti-surrogacy argument would seem to prohibit Evangelicals’ sacred cow, adoption. Courts may challenge some of these laws in the coming months and years, but there’s no denying that American baby-­making is going trad. On August 6, Trump issued executive orders banning birth tourism and denying passports to surrogate babies with foreign parents—measures proposed by Waters.

Her star continues to rise. Waters got a second book deal earlier this year (working title: Rethinking Fertility) and is contributing to a documentary about cryopreservation called Frozen Orphans. She recently presented at a Harvard summit on embryo law and ethics; four of the 20 other speakers have referenced Waters in their work. She is not opposed to running for office, although of course it will have to wait until her kids are older. In early September, she gave birth to her third child: another girl.

The Best Space Heaters of 2026

Wired September 23, 2026

Amazon

Amazon

Amazon

Amazon

The Best space heaters are winter’s rear guard, the last line of defense against goose bumps and cold feet. Though not a great way to heat a whole home, space heaters can be indispensable for a late-evening movie night, a workbench in a chilly garage, or the home’s odd corners that refuse to heat. And if you live in an apartment building where you don’t control the heat, it may be your only way to feel OK in January.

But safety and reliability are prime concerns, and so is a lot of dodgy and opaque marketing about “Hyperamics,” “Velocity Tuned Heat,” and whatever-wave technology. Whatever the marketing, large space heaters usually aren’t more powerful or more effective than small ones. So I turned down my thermostat and tested dozens of space heaters to find the ones that’ll warm you up as quickly and quietly and safely as possible.

Alongside WIRED’s blessedly balanced and quiet top pick, the Dreo Whole Room Heater 714 ($100), I also sorted out which heaters might best suit specific needs, from the best bathroom heater to a space heater that doubles as an air purifier. For those on a tight budget, the bare-bones Honeywell 360 Surround ($47) often goes on sale.

Looking for more ways to tailor your air? Check out our guide to all things that improve your indoor air quality, as well as our specialized guides to the Best Air Purifiers, Best Humidifiers, Best Fans, and Best Dehumidifiers.

Update September 2026: I tested and added Honeywell’s 2026-model Surround 360 as my new top budget pick, replacing Honeywell’s Uberheat 5. I also tested and added the Heatbit Maxi Pro bitcoin miner and heater; re-added this year’s De’Longhi Dragon as WIRED’s top radiator pick; and removed discontinued products and updated prices, descriptions, and products throughout.

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.

Dreo

Amazon

This Dreo is the best answer to what I’ve been looking for in a space heater ever since I started testing them. I want simple things. I want a heater to be safe, with reliable tip-over and overheat protections. I want it to be quiet. And I want it to use the full capacity of an American outlet, 1,500 watts, to heat quickly and evenly around the room. I like a remote control, but I don’t want to be crippled if I lose it. And I like precise digital temperature control, with a thermostat that actually works. And I don’t want to hate how the thing looks: It’ll be here with me all winter.

The Dreo Whole-Room Heater 714 checks these boxes better than any other heater among the three dozen I’ve tested in the past two years—with thoughtful design touches that make it possible to actually kind of like the thing. It’s a nice modern update on the classic fan design, able to oscillate not just side-to-side but also up and down. The counter-spiral grill, familiar from competitor Vornado’s models, leads to good heat distribution around the room. And while it’s not as quiet as our near-silent previous top-pick Vornado MVH, it’s still quieter than my refrigerator on high fan speeds.

But especially, the thermostat works—largely, I suspect, because the bipartite design of this compact heater allows the temperature sensor to be isolated from the heating elements. Huzzah! This is a rare quality among space heaters. Other nice touches include buttons whose beeps can be muted and digital screens that dim themselves. The housing is cool to the touch. The heater remembers its settings from previous use, so you don’t have to reprogram it each time you turn it back on. Oscillation is silent, with no squeaks, and the brushless fan is whistle-free.

It’s not perfect, of course. I’d like the ability to set a shutoff timer, and the on-device controls are a bit hard to see and close to the floor. There’s also one hot spot on the exhaust grill: the exact center where the Dreo logo sits. Vanity is a vice! Still, this is a great little heater.

Vornado

Amazon

Walmart

The Home Depot

Kansas-based fan and heater company Vornado offers a dizzying array of heaters with much the same shape: an oblong plastic box with a circular whorl on its face. This can make shopping a bit difficult, but there are good reasons that Vornado is wedded to this design. It’s wonderfully effective and quiet, with some of the most even heat distribution I’ve seen among any devices on the market. Indeed, the quietest and best fans on the market at any given time are often also named Vornado.

I’d previously favored Vornado’s all-analog, no-frills MVH heater, which is a little less quiet than it used to be. These days, the Goldilocks Vornado is digital. The Vornado TAVH10 has a remote, two heat settings, a fan-only setting, and a timer so you can set your heater to shut off after you sleep or turn on when you wake up.

But especially on low heat, this thing is beautifully silent—less than 40 decibels. This is much quieter than any previous digital devices I’d tested from Vornado. It is also gentle in its heating, pushing out air almost imperceptibly to the opposite corner of the room. This is the result of Vornado’s whole-room “vortex” technology, essentially a spiral grate that’s counter-rotated to the movement of the fan. This creates a column of spiraling air that pushes to the far corner, then scatters around the room. The downside is that how you place the heater is very important. Face it so it has an unbroken line to the opposite wall or corner. But anyway, if you don’t want to notice your heater at all but still feel warm, this is the heater you want.

De'Longhi

Amazon

Oil-filled radiators like this Dragon from De’Longhi are a different beast from the resistive heaters that make up the rest of this list. The Dragon contains a reservoir of temperature-stable, diathermic oil that circulates within the radiator. The oil takes a little while to heat up, meaning it may be an hour before the temperature stabilizes in a room. But when it does, the large thermal mass means that the heat radiated by the Dragon is stable and even. But in trade, the Dragon is also a large device, 2 feet tall and more than a foot deep, and its entire surface gets quite hot to the touch.

So why would you prefer it? It is utterly silent, for one. Anecdotally, oil-filled radiators seem to dry out the air less than a fan-blowing ceramic. And the Dragon’s radiant heat remains stable and even for long periods, which makes it great for bedtime. The hot oil inside the radiator keeps emitting heat even after you’ve turned it off, which means you can turn it on an hour before bed to warm up the room, then shut it off before you sleep and still remain toasty. (The Dragon also has a timed shutoff function.) The antifreeze feature also makes this a great tool for greenhouses and basements: The Dragon can be set to turn itself on whenever the ambient temperature reaches 41 degrees Fahrenheit or lower.

Honeywell

Amazon

Walmart

North Carolina-based Honeywell offers the best value among affordable heaters, without sacrificing safety features that make other low-cost heaters kinda scary sometimes. Among a few different low-cost options, this bare-bones Surround 360 is Honeywell’s most popular model for a few reasons.

The heat is fast and even, emitting in a full 360-degre circle from all sides—making this an effective whole-room heater. (If anything, it actually heats a little more at the rear than at the front.) The vents remain safe to the touch, and a handle makes it easy to move around. An immediate mechanical tip-over switch and overheat shutoff both keep it fire-safe.

It’s not quiet by any stretch. There are just two settings, 900 watts and 1,500 watts. The thermostat is a truly analog mechanical switch, which can offer fine-tuning and a lot of flexibility across a broad temperature range, but hardly offers the precision of digital. But for this, it’s a reliable heater that’s priced reliably under $50, and often on sale for significantly less.

Best budget garage heater: Note that while the Surround 360 is the Honeywell I’d recommend for indoor heating, it’s not as good for open or airy spaces. If you’re looking for a budget heater for your garage that’ll offer directed heat while you work, you’re better off with the no-nonsense Uberheat 5 ($55). It’s about the same price, but it blasts heat directly in front of it instead of spreading heat evenly around the room.

Dreo

Amazon

Dreo

A cold bathroom in the morning feels cruel and unnecessary. But a space heater on the floor can feel reckless in a room with a bathtub. A fixed wall unit, mounted away from the shower, is a more credible solution to early-morning shivers. This slim-profiled Dreo offers IP24 certification against splashes, plus the same ALCI plug you’ll find on your hairdryer to prevent shocks. The heater’s app-enabled smart function means you can turn the heater on from the warmth of your bed, and bask in the glow of a warm bathroom by the time you arrive. (Only fixed space heaters are allowed app-controlled temp control, so it’s a real boon.)

It’s also great for your home’s other cool spots that lack convenient floor space. The wall-mounted Dreo heats a mid-sized room within 15 minutes, though even heat distribution depends strongly on central wall placement. Other helpful phone-app features include usage tracking over time, Alexa voice compatibility, and button-push calibration of the thermostat. You’ll need that calibration: The thermostat on this unit fares better than earlier-generation devices from Dreo, but can still be confused by light breezes or the device’s own heat source.

Installation is pretty straightforward, provided you’ve hung a framed picture before. But make sure to mount the Dreo high enough to be out of reach for curious youngsters. While the housing stays cool, the heat exhaust vent can get hot to the touch.

Dyson

Dyson

Dyson heaters are tall. And Dysons look cool, or a bit discomfiting—like a droid without a face. But especially, they do lots of things. The Hot + Cool HP1 is an app-enabled air quality sensor, a HEPA and carbon air filter, a hygrometer, a mostly accurate thermometer (see below), a cooling fan … and, yes, a classic resistance heater.

It’s nifty. Though priced accordingly, the HP1—like the prior HP07— is the most sophisticated home atmospheric management tool I know. It heats the room evenly and quickly, has no exposed elements or blades, cleans easily, looks kinda fun, has an accurate thermostat, continually filters small particles from the air, and remains cool to the touch. Plus, Dyson actually lowered its prices from the previous-generation device without lowering functionality.

So far, so good! Just note that, as with all Dysons, there are quirks. If you turn the fan setting up to 10, it sounds like something got turned up to 10—though it’s quiet at more reasonable wind speeds. There are no paper instructions included. And while temp readings are mostly accurate, the thermostat reads at the device—and so tends to read a few degrees high unless the room temperature equalizes. The most troubling quirk is that there are no temperature control buttons on the device or the app (at least if you live in the United States.) Which means if you lose your remote, you will not be able to adjust the temperature until you get another remote or connect your device to a smart-home system like Alexa. Luckily, the remote is magnetic and can stay affixed to the device, but woe betide ADHD folks like me who’ll wander off with the dang thing anyway. Buttons, please!

Anyway, this Dyson is on sale a lot. Buy it when it’s on sale.

Vornado

Amazon

Ceramic heaters like this new one from Vornado aren’t my usual pick for whole-room heaters. But when it comes to personal heaters, I tend to prefer ceramic elements for their wildly fast heat-up times, which can bring me from bone-chilled to toasty within minutes or even seconds of turning them on. A ceramic heater is basically a small, heated ceramic plate with a fan behind it. These heat up quite fast, and can focus heat intensely and rapidly on the short path right in front of the vent. This is great for fast foot-warming but less great for distributing heat evenly and efficiently around a room.

That’s what makes this Vornado VC-01 such a welcome surprise: It’s a personal ceramic heater that can also be useful (but not as good as our top pick) for heating a full room. Set the little VC-01 on “personal” mode, and it’s a quiet heater that delivers heat near-immediately at close range, whether for foot-warming or on your desktop. Minutes after turning it on, the landscape directly in front of the heater is warmer by as much as 10 degrees, even on the low setting. Vornado’s excellent safety features, including near-instant tip-over shutoff, mean that if you knock it off a desk or couch-side table, it’ll already be turned off by the time it hits the floor.

This was also true of my previous pick as the best space heater for foot-warming, the Lasko Ellipse ($70). What’s different with the Vornado is that this device’s “whole room” setting is able to disperse heat rapidly around the room as well, largely through the operation of a powerful fan. It’s hardly quiet heater when the fan’s blasting on high, but this feature adds some nice versatility if you mostly need a personal heater but sometimes have company on the couch.

But note that, like all ceramic heaters, this one gets painfully hot at its vent, so I’d never recommend it (or any ceramic I’ve tested) around kids or dogs unless you’re nearby and paying attention. Also note it’s a quite effective close-range heater even at the lower, 750-watt “personal” setting. Keep it 3 feet away or you may swelter.

Dreo

Amazon

Dreo

Tower heaters don’t warm up a room faster or better than compact ones, but they do have their merits: A larger surface area makes for cooler surfaces, and the controls tend to be more accessible. This low-key conical Dreo Solaris 718 has won me over, despite its nonzero resemblance to a Dalek from Doctor Who. It’s among the most wondrously silent heaters I tested, nearly inaudible at its lowest setting and still restrained at full steam.

The Solaris heats quickly and distributes its warmth nonchalantly about the room. Its housing stays approachably cool. It rotates without groans or squeaks, a surprisingly rare quality among towers. And it’s now in its third cold season without incident. Alas, the built-in thermostat is just as wonky as most other space heaters on the market, so you’re better off using the remote to choose among the Solaris’ five steady heat settings.

Why Large Space Heaters Aren’t More Powerful Than Small Heaters

Nope! It may seem counterintuitive, but large space heaters don’t necessarily heat any better than small ones.

Whatever their physical size, most space heaters in the US and Canada deliver about the same amount of heat. Space heaters top out at 1,500 watts, which is the highest safe operating load for a 15-amp household circuit. And aside from some low-power personal heaters here and there, most space heaters you’ll find on the market are 1,500-watt heaters.

What’s more, electric space heaters are all pretty much 100 percent efficient in converting that electricity to heat. Whether directly or indirectly, nearly all of that energy will eventually become heat.

So if space heaters are the same power and the same efficiency, why are some 1,500-watt heaters advertised for small rooms and some for large rooms? This likely has as much to do with marketing as science. Pretty much every ceramic, electric-coil, or PTC heater has about the same amount of juice and thus the same ability to heat a room … at least eventually.

What differs among heaters is how and where the heat gets distributed and how fast. All other things being equal, the efficacy of a heater is mostly about whether it puts the heat where you want it to go.

What Are the Different Types of Space Heaters?

Basically all electric space heaters do the same thing: They take electricity off the grid, usually 1,500 watts of it if you're in the United States, and turn that power into heat.

The vast majority of space heaters, including ceramic heaters and PTC heaters, are electric resistance heaters. This means they run an electrical current through something that creates resistance: maybe an electric coil or maybe a specially designed ceramic. This quickly turns electricity into heat.

Most space heaters use a fan to disperse this heat out into the world, where we all live. These forced-air convection heaters tend to be the fastest at quickly raising the temperature of the surrounding air. The air then heats you. And so while this variety heats quickly, it can take quite a bit of electricity to heat up a whole room.

Oil-filled radiators, in contrast, heat up oil that circulates inside the device, which then emits heat to the surrounding room. These tend to heat up slower but offer even and lasting heat and are very quiet. These radiators operate on the same principle as steam radiators in buildings with a boiler room. And just like steam radiators, they can get really, really hot to the touch.

Radiant heaters, such as infrared heaters, operate much like the sun or a campfire: Rather than heat the air, they heat objects or people directly by radiating energy toward them. Infrared devices heat the air only indirectly, via the objects it heats—much the same way the sun's heat radiates off baking city streets. The glow is immediately palpable as warmth, but you’ll need to be in the path of the radiation to feel it, and the thermometer might not immediately register the warmth you perceive. Infrared heaters tend to be best at making an individual in front of the heater feel a little warmer without using a lot of energy, making them a more common decision in large and lofty spaces or outside on a patio.

Though they deliver heat differently, both infrared and oil-filled heaters are subject to the same wattage limitations, and have about the same efficiency, as electrical resistance heaters.

The same cannot be said for heat pumps, a newer technology that’s expected to provide the next generation of household heat. Heat pumps don’t use energy to create heat. Instead, they move heat energy from one place to another. Accordingly, they require far less energy than other forms of heater. But household systems cost thousands to install. And while more affordable window and portable heat pumps are ramping up, they’re not yet broadly available.

Are Space Heaters Safe?

Yes, but also definitely no.

Space heaters are much safer than they used to be. Modern space heaters are heavily regulated, especially regarding exposed heating elements and automatic shutoff switches to prevent overheating. But all heating devices require caution, and so do all devices that pull a lot of energy over long periods.

The vast majority of residential heating fires start with actual fire—specifically in fireplaces and fuel burners. But space heaters accounted for more than a thousand fires in the US each year from 2017 to 2019, according to the US Fire Administration. Though this accounted for just 3 percent of heating fires overall, these led to more than 40 percent of fatalities, in part because portable heaters tend to be placed precisely where people are and because the resulting fires are far more likely to be unconfined.

So treat your space heater with the caution and wild skepticism that it deserves. See WIRED's Guide to Space Heater Safety for a full rundown about how not to start fires or cause othr hazards. Our guide follows recommendations from federal experts at the the USFA and the Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC), as well as the Association of Home Appliance Manufacturers (AHAM).

But for the short version:

Don’t leave a space heater unattended. "Unattended” includes sleeping, y’all! Might we suggest a wonderful down comforter instead? When possible, safety experts also recommend you don't leave a portable heater running unattended in a room with a baby, nor a person with mobility issues. The risk isn’t just fire but hyperthermia.

Plug your heater directly into the outlet. Don't use extension cords or power strips with space heaters, lest you build up too much electrical load and risk a fire.

Don’t plug another appliance into the same outlet or circuit as the space heater.

Place a space heater only on the floor, on a level surface. Heat rises. You don't need to prop up a heater on an unstable chair or table.

Keep your heater at least 3 feet from flammable objects. This includes bedding, drapes, furniture, clothes, papers, books. All of that.

Keep space heaters away from water and dampness, whether in bathrooms or in moist basements prone to dripping or flooding.

Read the manual. Manufacturers have good advice.

How We Tested and What We Tested

When it comes to testing space heaters, there are a few main questions: How safe is it? How loud is it? How quickly and evenly can it heat a room?

During intensive testing of dozens of space heaters, I lived for weeks in a home with the thermostat set to a chilly 65 degrees Fahrenheit.

I tested how well and quickly each device heated a medium-size room (14 by 14 feet), and also how well it heated a small seating area in a larger, open-format space. To test each heater’s thermostat and also measure the evenness of heating, I placed thermometers at three or more locations in each room, including behind the heater.

I tested the loudness of each device with a decibel meter at 3 feet away and verified power usage with a wattmeter. To see whether the heater’s exhaust put out painful levels of heat, I used an infrared thermometer to gauge precise surface temperatures. When in doubt, I put my own fingers on the line.

Finally, I tested safety features and basic durability. I looked at independent safety certifications, of course. But I also rudely knocked over each device to verify how the device’s tip-over protections functioned, if at all, and verified that the device started working again when set back on its feet.

To test overheat protection, I smothered each device with an old sheet to see whether the device shut itself off or whether it adjusted its power output to keep internal temperature low. After the device shut itself off, I then checked how soon it could turn back on, if it ever did. (Some heaters gave up, in permanent complaint!)

If any device fails the tip-over or overheat tests, we don’t recommend it. If it’s significantly louder than 50 decibels at 3 feet, we don’t recommend it. If the heater breaks during routine operation, we don’t recommend it. Maddening rattles and squeaks are also disqualifying.

We keep on testing our favorites through the cold season and beyond, to see how they hold up over time. And, of course, we continually subject more heaters to our testing regimen to see if other devices can oust our current faves.

Vornado AVH10: Vornado has an unholy variety of models that look quite similar but have different levels of loudness and different feature sets. Some are built in America, some in China. In general, the models I’ve liked best are the ones that advertise “vortex action,” a fancy name for spinning a fan into a spiral grate oriented opposite to the action of the fan. This leads to a mostly quiet and nigh-undetectable column of warm air, directed out to the back of the room, where it scatters. The TAVH10, which is basically this model but with a timer and remote, is my current favorite, though if you need neither, you can save $30 and get this.

Vornado MVH+ and Vornado VH240+: These two devices are very nearly the same device. And the previous year’s non-digital MVH was my favorite model before getting displaced by a couple newer models of Dreo and Vornado. It remains among the most silent, the most even in its heat, and among the most reasonably priced. However, the TAVH10 got a little quieter and the MVH got a little louder, and the addition of a remote and a timer makes it more attractive. This said, there are reasons to favor an analog device. Because they’re analog, the MVH and VH240 can also be regulated by a temperature-controlled power outlet in order to get the most accurate version of a thermostat.

Lasko Ellipse Ceramic Tabletop Heater: This little ceramic number from Lasko was the space heater I kept reaching for while testing dozens of other space heaters last year. It’s not the most obvious choice: It doesn’t heat a room evenly, its grill surface gets wackily hot, and the thermostat is an inside joke. I’m not sure I’d run it near babies or small dogs. And yet I still kept voting for it with my cold, cold feet. Why? Because this little thing can radically change my whole experience of life within about 15 seconds of being turned on. It brings the heat, as they say, though mostly within an 8-foot radius. Within that manifold, it’s like living inside a hair dryer, which is more pleasant than it sounds. You’re warm and lovely from your heart-cockles to your cankles. This is our previous pick for best foot warmer, and it’s still a good pick. It’s just not as versatile as our new top pick personal heater from Vornado.

Shark TurboBlade Cool + Heat: WIRED reviewer Kat Merck enjoyed the customizable airflow of Shark’s original TurboBlade cooling fan (7/10, WIRED Recommends), which can be angled every which way for optimized airflow and is the perfect height for blasting air onto a bed. On cooling fan settings, these virtues remain true of the new Cool + Heat version. True to its name, the Cool + Heat model also adds a 1,400-watt heater to the equation, with emphasis on “little.” The TurboBlade does not push air through its blade-like “wings” for heating, the way it does for cooling. Rather, it blows hot air only out of the small vent at the center of the device, whose aperture is only somewhat larger than some hair dryers. The versatility of heating and cooling is nice. So is the ability to direct air upward or downward. And especially, I love that this Shark device’s thermostat is actually accurate to within a single degree, and that the Shark automatically modulates its energy output to maintain temperature in a room. This avoids the wild on-off swings of some less sophisticated heaters. But for such a small heater, the TurboBlade is quite big and loud. Even on low settings, the high-pitched jet engine whir never stops. Standing in front of it on high settings, my phone registers 70 decibels. So I’d recommend this for someone who predominantly wants to use the device as a fan. The heater is more of a secondary function.

De’Longhi Slim-Style Portable Panel Heater: This electric panel heater is an interesting hybrid, with dual heat exhausts on each side but also a broad radiant heat panel. This makes for a middle ground between radiators and resistive fan heaters—heating a room much faster than a classic radiator would but still maintaining warm radiant heat over time. This said, it shares a radiator’s main fault, which is that it’s painfully hot to the touch across a large surface—but still issues the same amount of fan noise as a fan heater. Still: It may be your choice if you need to heat up a space quickly and evenly and maintain that heat over time.

Dreo MC706 Fan and Heater: Dreo’s innovative 2-in-1 fan/heater won top marks in our fan guide for its auto-shift positive temperature coefficient (PTC) technology, which moves the heater’s ceramic element aside to allow full fan airflow. Its 1,700 ft/m wind speed is a rarity among tower fans, let alone tower fan/heater combos. It’s not the strongest space heater, but it is sufficient, with five settings, 120-degree oscillation, and tip-over protection. Note that though there is a remote, there are no smart features, and it does not work with Dreo’s app.

Dreo Bathroom Heater: Like Dreo’s smart wall-mounted model I far prefer, this ceramic heater comes with an ALCI plug for safe use near water. I prefer to keep bathroom heaters away from the floor, but not all bathrooms have mountable wall space. This remains a possible, though not ideal alternative, with a somewhat janky thermostat.

Vornado VC-02 Ceramic Heater: Vornado put out two new ceramic heaters at the tail end of 2025. The less expensive, smaller, horizontally oriented VC-01 is WIRED’s top personal heater pick. The VC-02 is a bit like the 01 turned on its end and made into a tower heater. The VC-02 is in most ways a premium model, with more options in terms of power and fan settings. It’s even quieter than its sister model—in fact, it’s one of the quietest heaters I’ve tested, period. It has a thermostat that’s reasonably accurate. It’s also got a remote and the ability to swivel from side to side for full room coverage. (It does not pivot up and down, the way the VC-01 does.) But while I like all these features, its tower-heater shape makes it less optimized than the VC-01 for up-close heating, which is what ceramic heaters do best. At the beginning of the season, this had not yet come back in stock, but I’ll continue monitoring.

Heatbit Maxi Pro: The Heatbit Maxi Pro (5/10, WIRED Review) is a cool-looking, luxury-styled air purifier and heater with a twist: It offsets its energy use by mining Bitcoin. At the high energy rates and lagging Bitcoin price of 2026, the Bitcoin mining certainly wasn’t profitable. But it did offset the cost of heating with the device by about a third, and made onboarding quite easy for Bitcoin novices. The app and safety features are admirable enough. But the Heatbit is neither a quiet heater nor a great air purifier, and its Bitcoin mining might take most of a decade to make up the $1,500 to $2,000 price tag of the device. In the end, the Heatbit is a conversation item, something to show off to houseguests. But I couldn’t find a way to make it practical.

Boldr Kelvin (Gen 2): The Kelvin is a much different heater than the others on this list: It is a silent white or black panel that slowly heats up over the course of an hour, emitting what the company attests is far-infrared radiation, similar to those mail-order saunas you can find on Wayfair. The standard model tops out at just 450 watts, so the sell isn’t really that it emits a lot of heat: rather, far-infrared feels warmer if you stand in front of it. It operates on the same principle as heat from the sun, warming surfaces (including people) directly rather than heating up the air. In the ideal case, this means you can feel more warmth while using less energy than a traditional heater. Its makers recommend it for those stubborn cold spots in a house. But I struggled with this heater. A wall-anchored heater offers less flexibility, and in the shorter term, a radiant heater provides warmth only directly in the path of the panel, meaning it must be positioned with quite a bit of care to be useful. The Kelvin also uses up quite a bit of wall space, and must be located near an outlet. By design, its front gets quite hot to the touch—near boiling, in fact—and the device projects quite a bit of heat backward into the wall even after a second-generation upgrade to its insulation. It’s an interesting concept, with a smart app to track energy use, but the caveats add up. At $400, it’s hard to make it pencil.

Pelonis 16-Inch Space Heater and Pelonis 23-Inch Space Heater: Both of these towers heated up quite quickly. Both were also enormously hot at the surface of their vents, with relatively little shielding from the visible heating elements. The 23-inch was significantly quieter than the 16-inch, however.

Vornado Velocity Cube 5S: This cube’s outer housing stayed quite cool, and the fan functionality is welcome. But its surface vent got a little hot, and the fan was a bit on the noisy side compared to other Vornados.

Vornado Velocity 5R Whole Room Heater and Vornado VHEAT: The MVH and TAVH line from Vornado are among the quietest space heaters I’ve tested. These were two of the loudest. The 5R topped 70 decibels. The vintage-looking VHEAT is quite lovely, but it’s also a bit of a noisemaker.

Lasko MyHeat Mini: This little thing looked cute, and I thought it would be a nice desktop or under-table personal heater. But even with its low output at 400 watts, the vent got way too hot to want it anywhere near your laptop or papers.

Lasko 22-inch Oscillating Tower With Remote: This one failed our tip-over test when we knocked it over, blasting heat endlessly into the rug until it overheated and sent a burnt-plastic smell into the air. It did restart hours later, meaning this shutoff was a safety feature. But this tower’s a bit too tall and tippable to risk repeating these events often. It’s out of stock on most sites as of February 2026.

Honeywell 2-Position Heater: This compact, simple, analog heater was a nice enough idea, able to rest vertically or on its side. Lord, it’s loud when its fan is in operation, though. As of February 2026, this device is out of stock, but we’ll monitor restocks.

Honeywell Compact Ceramic Tower: This Honeywell performed well in terms of fast heat and safe surface temperature. Its fan wasn’t too loud either. But the one we received had a maddening squeak each time the tower oscillated fully counterclockwise.

Vornado Sensa Cribside Heater: I loved the idea behind this Vornado Sensa Cribside Heater when I tested it: A space heater with an external temperature sensor, with therefore accurate temperature management (hard to find among space heaters!) But it’s disappeared from Vornado’s website, and has dwindled on retail sites. It’s no longer available on Amazon, but if you see it on sale at another site, I still like it.

Also tested but discontinued: Vornado VMHi600, Morento 26-cm Heater, Morento 40-cm Heater, Dyson HP07, many other models of Vornado before the brand’s late-2025 refresh.

Review: Kiwibit Bird Feeder 2 Pro

Wired September 23, 2026

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, when you buy something through our retail links, we may earn an affiliate commission.

7/10

Every bird enthusiast has probably heard of Birdfy and Birdbuddy smart bird feeders, but a handful of competitors have quietly been refining their models over multiple generations—to the point where they’re starting to outpace the OGs in engineering, features, and design. Kiwibit is one of them.

I tested Kiwibit’s first feeder, the Beako, in mid-2025 and was impressed by its robust plastic body, removable dual-sided seed reservoir, and three-minute video captures—there was nothing quite like it at the time, and almost all of its features were available sans subscription. However, the optional rooftop solar panel stopped working after six weeks, which kept it from being a pick in my guide to the Best Smart Bird Feeders.

The Beako’s subsequent update, the Feeder 2, made the solar panel standard on all units, upped the panel’s output from 4.4 to 5 watts, and fixed the longevity issue—it’s currently my top pick for Best Design. The Feeder 2 Pro, meanwhile, has totally redone the camera to offer phase detection autofocus (PDAF) in 4K HDR—one of the most impressive smart feeder hardware offerings on the market. The companion app upgrade, however, still has some kinks to work out.

I tested the Feeder 2 Pro for a total of four weeks: one week at the non-subscription tier, and three weeks with Kiwibit Plus (also alternately referred to as “Family Premium” or “Premium Family), which at $90 a year offers AI ID, 60-day cloud recording (the feeder also supports microSD storage up to 512 GB), and new gallery views and roundup reports.

Without a subscription, camera quality is the same (some other feeder brands, like Birdbuddy, will paywall higher resolution), but here you’re limited to a bare-bones feed of video captures, and there’s no AI ID to sort or identify them—you’ll have to look at every image to make sure you didn’t miss anything interesting. This can be especially laborious if the same bird visits 15 times or more per day, especially since the camera placement means the thumbnails often show only the top of the bird’s head, if they show anything. This is atypical for a feeder with an MSRP of $290—most models at this price point include a lifetime subscription.

Thankfully, it is still easy to download and share 8-MP images and videos, and the camera records as long as the bird is there—up to three minutes—to ensure no movements are missed. The PDAF works to minimize blur and ensure all features are sharp. At various points during my test, I did notice the motion of the lens zooming in and out being clocked by multiple birds, who either immediately stopped eating to watch the camera warily or flew away. It didn’t happen often enough for me to wish the feature didn’t exist, but it is something to consider if your local birds are easily spooked.

The subscription gives you the same feed of video captures, but with labels of the bird species so you can skip past the ones that aren’t worth opening. There’s also a tile view under “Visits” that shows which birds have visited over the feeder’s lifetime and when they were last seen.

However, this is only so useful given that the AI ID is wrong a hefty percentage of the time—fish crows, Cape May warblers, mangrove warblers, red fox sparrows, and grackles are not found in western Washington state, where I live, but according to the Kiwibit app they are frequent visitors to my backyard. (I even had a “pileated woodpecker” visit the feeder, which would have been exceptionally rare, except the misidentified bird was a crow.) Also note that, unlike Birdfy feeders, the camera is not able to ID multiple birds on the feeder at a time.

One area where Birdfy and Birdbuddy still beat their competitors is their intuitive, user-friendly apps. While Kiwibit’s non-subscription view has a simple interface, the subscription experience is a bit chaotic, as Kiwibit tries to cram a lot of information into too many places. There’s the tile view under “Birds,” the list of captures under “Feeds,” and a live view under “Live,” which you can click into to see a calendar of captures by day. Then, under “Me,” there’s a different calendar view with the number of bird visits per day, and a weekly Report tab that gives stats on that week’s visits. Even after four weeks of testing, I’m still not sure where I should first look when I simply want to see the birds that visited that day.

Kiwibit Bird Feeder 2 Pro

Rating: 7/10

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

The main reason for buying the Feeder 2 Pro is, of course, its dual-lens camera. If you have the subscription, clicking birds in the tile view will give you the option to download Ultra HD stills in different aspect ratios and with or without a watermark identifying the species, which is unique. Despite recording 4K footage at only 15 frames per second (fps), the camera’s bottom lens captured surprisingly crisp images of birds taking off, landing, and fighting. The camera’s top 1080p lens, meanwhile, offers 120 fps but only if you’re recording to an SD card.

If you’re looking for a smart feeder that can produce quality stills and footage rivaling a budget action camera, the Feeder 2 Pro is what you want. The sensors don’t capture every bird visit, but unlike Birdbuddy, they only missed a handful here and there—not large swaths of the day. If needed, you can also record and save footage live through the app.

The two solar panels built into the roof stayed fully charged throughout my testing, even on cloudy days. If something were to go wrong, there’s a removable 5,200-mAh battery in the bottom of the feeder that can be brought in to charge via USB-C. The Feeder 2's wonderfully designed, dual-compartment 1.7-liter seed hopper is on the Pro as well, with little stoppers that slide in and out to hold or release seed as needed. You can bring it into the house for filling without needing to take the whole feeder down. Upon unboxing, once the battery is charged, it takes just a few minutes to snap this IP65 (water-resistant against heavy rain) feeder together and pair it with the app. It runs on either 2.4- or 5.0-GHz Wi-Fi bands.

Kiwibit Bird Feeder 2 Pro

Rating: 7/10

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

Because so many features require an additional subscription, I’m not sure I would buy the Feeder 2 Pro as a gift, but I would consider buying it for myself. I don’t love that the full experience costs almost $100 extra per year, but it’s been fun to collect and share truly camera-quality images. Casual bird-watchers can find a more polished experience for less than half the price (see my recommendations here), but photography fans may find the image quality worth the app foibles and the recurring fee. If you’re not sure, Kiwibit offers 60-day returns.

Top Google Workspace Promo Codes for September 2026

Wired September 23, 2026

Google Workspace is that ubiquitous modern business tool that almost feels invisible. We use it every day here at WIRED, whether that's for writing first drafts of articles in Docs, analyzing data in Sheets, or sharing files in Drive. And recently, I've been using the Gemini AI implementation that's built right into these tools, which is handy in all sorts of ways.

Google Workspace grants access to all kinds of productivity features that can help streamline processes and increase communication within a team or organization. It's not free, but here's the good news: If you're looking at a Workspace account for yourself (or for your team), Google is offering discounts until the end of 2026 using one of the Google Workspace coupon codes below. You can save up to 14 percent on plans for the first three months, whether you're signing up as an individual or as a business. Either way, the Google Workspace promo code down below is what you want to use.

There are some notable differences between each Workspace plan – I’ll dig into them in the next section – but all three plans come with access to the full slate of Workspace apps. You get Gmail, Drive, Calendar, and Meet, of course, but even the cheapest Starter plan includes basic access to Google’s other apps, such as NotebookLM and Gemini inside the Workspace suite. If you want to save, make sure to click one of the promo codes at the top of this page to secure your discount.

Google offers four different Workspace plans, though only three are relevant for most people. There’s Starter, Standard, and Plus, as well as Enterprise, which is only available if you contact Google’s sales team. There isn’t a minimum number of users on any of the plans, but the bottom three options (Starter, Standard, and Plus) support up to 300 users. If you need more than that, you’ll need an Enterprise plan.

Although you have access to all the apps regardless of the plan you choose, there are some important differences, particularly between the Starter and Standard plans. Both include secure storage through Google Drive, but Starter comes with 30GB per user while Standard comes with a massive 2TB per user. Plus bumps that up to 5TB per user. Across all plans, storage is in a shared pool, so each additional user adds to the total pool of storage your organization can use.

Gemini is also a big difference between Starter and Standard. Although both have access to the Gemini app, Starter only has Gemini in Gmail and Vids. Standard (and Plus) includes Gemini across the full suite, including in Docs, Sheets, Slides, Drive, Meet, and Chat.

Starter is a great option for anyone just getting started, regardless of whether you’re a freelancer or a small business with a handful of employees. In addition to 30GB per user and limited access to Gemini, Starter comes with a few other limitations. It doesn’t support e-signatures in Docs, nor advanced features of Meet, such as noise cancellation. The bread and butter of Workspace is all here, though. You get a custom domain in Gmail, up to 100 participants in Meet, and the full Google suite of productivity apps.

Standard, as the name suggests, is Workspace proper, and it’s built for teams that need room to grow. That shows up most clearly in storage space, jumping from 30GB to 2TB per user. Standard basically cuts all the red tape on Starter. There aren’t any limitations on Gemini (it’s available across the full suite), Meet features like noise cancellation are available, and you can host up to 150 participants in a Meet call. Standard even comes with expanded access to NotebookLM, Google’s AI-driven note and research tool, with different chat modes and up to 20 generative audio overviews per day.

At the top of the range is Plus, which is focused on larger businesses. You don’t get any extra apps with this plan, but you do get 5TB of storage per user, along with up to 500 participants in Meet calls. The real reason to upgrade to Plus is security and admin controls, however. It includes Vault for data retention, along with LDAP access—basically a server for centralized account management, if you aren’t familiar.

Most people should use the Standard plan, not only for the large amount of storage space over Starter, but also due to the extra Gemini functionality. If you need to upgrade to Plus down the line, you can. And, more than likely, you’ll have a member of your IT team begging you to do so.

Google has updated Workspace a lot over the past several months, building in new functionalities via Gemini throughout the suite. But earlier this year, Google announced that it’s bringing all of those functionalities together through Workspace Flows. It’s a no-code automation tool that lets you build automatic workflows; i. e., update a Sheet when there’s a new email in Gmail from a particular address. The interesting thing about Flows, however, is that Gemini is built into it.

You can set up basic automations, which is great given how interconnected Google’s Workspace apps already are, but Flows become powerful when you throw Gems into the mix. Gems are AI agents built with Gemini, and you can create them with specific parameters.

Let me give you an example. Say you need a marketing plan, and an employee sends you a draft. You can have a workflow set up with a Gem that’s been trained on the budget, requirements, and tone of the campaign to quickly know if it can be approved or not. Or, you can create a Gem to scan your email, trained on your organization chart and role responsibilities, to notify you whenever you receive an email that has action items for you.

Flows give you a way to add a bit of context and reasoning to the often rigid constraints of simple automation systems, and they can save you a lot of time in the process. You may be able to gather customer feedback and put it into Sheets easily, for example, but Gemini can automatically sort, summarize, and categorize that feedback so you know what you should tackle first. Flows are centralized in Workspace, as well; you don’t need to install add-ons or configure anything outside of setting up your Workspace account.

Google Workspace Flows is a new tool integrated with Google Workspace. It is powered by Google’s Gemini AI and helps you get tasks done with Gmail, Docs, Sheets, Calendar and Chat. It can fix up emails, make plans, correct sheets, or write a follow-up message. No apps or links are needed.

Even with a discount, Google offers a free trial for all new Workspace subscribers. Your first 14 days are free, regardless of which plan you choose, and even with the promotional pricing, you can sign up using our links at the top of this article. Just make sure to cancel if you don’t want to continue. After 14 days, you’ll be billed, and that will be the start of your new billing cycle.
